# Decisions

- nanocode-sync's own persistent `OrdMap`, `OrdSet` and `Vector` carry the workspace's ordered copy-on-write state, and imbl leaves with imbl-sized-chunks, archery, rand_xoshiro, wide 0.7.33 and safe_arch 0.7.4 (2026-11-12, Georgios: "make this ~0 deps"). crates/core/sync/src/tree.rs is a persistent B-tree: each node sits behind an `Arc`, holds 8 to 17 items inline (`NODE_ITEMS_MIN` 8, measured against 16 below) and keeps each child's item count beside it, so a clone is one `Arc` clone and an update copies only the nodes on its path with `Arc::make_mut`. The counts let one tree serve keys and positions: ordered.rs puts `OrdMap` over `(K, V)` entries and `OrdSet` over items, with lookups by `Borrow` like std, and vector.rs indexes by position. Pushes at the right edge split unevenly so that appends fill their nodes, both ends pop without searching, and a removal that leaves a node short takes half of a sibling's surplus rather than one item, so a queue's `pop_front` stops copying the sibling on every pop. Iteration runs two cursor stacks, one per end, bounded by the tree's height; `range` turns its bounds into ranks; owned iteration moves items out of nodes nobody else holds. Only the calls the workspace makes are provided: `new`, `len`, `is_empty`, `get`, `get_key_value`, `get_mut`, `contains_key`/`contains`, `insert`, `remove`, `remove_with_key`, `entry(..).or_default/or_insert/or_insert_with`, `range`, `iter`, `keys`, `values`, `get_min`, `get_max`, `split`, `remove_min`/`remove_max`; and for `Vector`: `push_back`, `pop_front`, `pop_back`, `front`, `back`, `last`, `get`, `get_mut`, `retain`, `skip`, `take`, `clear`, `Index` and `IndexMut`. All three also have `Extend`, `FromIterator`, `IntoIterator` by value and by reference, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`, `Debug`, `Clone`, `Default`, `Serialize` and `Deserialize`. Semantics follow imbl 7.0.2: `insert` replaces the key and the value and returns the old value (`OrdSet::insert` returns the replaced item); an inverted range is empty; `split` leaves out the key; `skip` past the end is empty and `take` past the end panics; hashing and `Debug` walk the entries in order. On the wire `OrdMap` is a serde map, and `OrdSet` and `Vector` are sequences in iteration order. Deserializing inserts in order, so a later duplicate wins, and keeps imbl's `expecting` text ("a sequence") so that error messages match too. Call sites change only `imbl::` to `nanocode_sync::` (`crate::` inside sync), plus `const` on five small accessors (state.rs `seals_steers`, replay.rs `new`, history.rs `is_empty` and `len`, durable.rs `sealed_messages`), which clippy's missing_const_for_fn asks for now that `new`, `len` and `is_empty` are const. Public API: nanocode-durability-core's `OperationState::steer_receipts` and `steers` change type from `imbl::OrdMap` and `imbl::Vector` to `nanocode_sync::OrdMap` and `nanocode_sync::Vector`, with the same serialized bytes. GitHub code search of tempoxyz/pyramid-core and tempoxyz/pyramid (default branches) finds no use of these fields or of nanocode's imbl types; pyramid-core depends on imbl itself for its own `HashMap`, `HashSet` and `Vector`, which this change does not touch. Not equal, on purpose: imbl 7.0.2's `Vector::retain` breaks once a vector outgrows one 64-item chunk. output/imbl-equal/src/retain.rs gets a wrong result from 684 of 1,800 retains over vectors of 0 to 300 items; the first comes at 65 items, where keeping the odd numbers of 0..65 returned [42, 11, 23, 3, ...]. On `String` items the harness died with glibc's "double free or corruption". Ours keeps exactly what `VecDeque::retain` keeps, in order, calling the predicate once per item in order as imbl does. nanocode calls `retain` on the slow-wait holders (waits.rs, `Vector<Weak<Holder>>`), so before this change more than 64 registered holders could have corrupted memory. Mutation needs `Clone` items, as imbl's did. Equality: output/imbl-equal (imbl =7.0.2 with serde beside crates/core/sync, the repository's Cargo.lock and arc-swap patch) runs seeded operation sequences on both implementations side by side. It covers `OrdMap<u64, u64>`, `OrdMap<String, u64>`, `OrdSet<u64>`, `OrdSet<String>`, `Vector<u64>` and `Vector<String>` over key spaces of 16, 1,000 and 1,000,000, with bulk rebuilds up to 50,000 entries and 100,000 items. Up to 8 clones are taken mid-sequence and mutated independently. Every result is compared: return values, `get`, `get_mut`, `Index`, ranges with every bound kind walked from both ends interleaved, `split`, `partition`, `entry`, `skip`, `take`, `retain` (call count, and the result against `VecDeque`), equality between clones, owned iteration both ways, and every clone fully compared every 16,384 steps (len, iteration both ways, min and max, `Debug`, `Hash`, serde_json bytes, and decoding each side's bytes into the other). Malformed JSON gives the same error strings. imbl's `retain` result was replaced by `VecDeque`'s before comparing on, and was not called at all on `String` items. 2,160,000 operations (2 seeds, 60,000 per configuration) gave 9,099,024 checks with 0 differences, after earlier runs of 1,507,862 and 377,763 checks with 0 differences; imbl's `retain` disagreed with `VecDeque` in 4,773 of 21,361 calls. Benchmarks (output/imbl-equal/src/bench.rs, release, 5 rounds alternating which side runs first, median ns per operation, imbl -> ours, on the shared 5-core Hand under load from other agents, where single readings vary up to 3x). The `Atom` path, which clones and then mutates, is `OrdMap<u64, _>` clone+insert at 294 -> 237 (16 entries), 1,193 -> 1,064 (1,000) and 3,310 -> 2,353 (100,000), and `OrdMap<String, _>` clone+insert at 1,332 -> 1,302, 3,494 -> 2,796 and 8,895 -> 9,954. Clone+remove of a still-shared map is slower: u64 110 -> 195, 762 -> 1,316 and 3,246 -> 3,919; String 544 -> 903, 2,307 -> 3,240 and 11,660 -> 17,369. For `Vector<Arc<str>>`, clone+push_back is 1,110 -> 678 (16 items), 1,496 -> 2,166 (1,000) and 2,096 -> 3,017 (100,000), and clone+pop_front+push_back is 1,426 -> 1,429, 2,779 -> 3,388 and 2,760 -> 8,584. On 1,000 entries, u64 `get` is 58.5 -> 38.6 and String `get` 274 -> 319. The regressions grow with size: at 100,000 entries String `get` is 1,759 -> 3,340, `range` of 16 is u64 1,084 -> 2,285 and String 1,730 -> 4,345, and u64 iteration is 8.1 -> 30.1. Unshared `Vector` `push_back`, `pop_front` and `index` at 100,000 items are 39.6 -> 163, 33 -> 270 and 43 -> 444. These come from a node being an `Arc` plus one or two `Vec` buffers where imbl's is one allocation with inline 64-slot chunks, and from a deeper tree than imbl's 64-wide nodes and RRB head and tail buffers; inline fixed arrays would close them but were not done here. `NODE_ITEMS_MIN` 16 against 8: String clone+insert at 100,000 was 2.30x imbl's at 16 and 0.84 to 1.12x at 8, u64 stayed within 0.7 to 1.2x at both, and 16 was faster only on lookups. An earlier layout with an `Arc` per item made large `Vector` and lookup paths 4 to 16x slower and was dropped. `cargo metadata --locked` 425 to 418 packages on origin/master efe7f3f12 plus this branch (imbl, imbl-sized-chunks, archery, rand_xoshiro, wide, safe_arch, and rand_core 0.9.5 now that the obs scope removed rand). nanocode-turnlog, added on master meanwhile, keeps its in-memory rows and snapshots in the new `Vector` and `OrdMap` too (its `truncate` calls `retain`, which imbl got wrong past 64 rows), and nanocode-telemetry no longer used imbl after the obs scope rewrote it. version_check (generic-array), equivalent (hashbrown, indexmap) and bytemuck (image) stay for their other users; bitmaps was no longer in the lockfile. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked` for nanocode-sync, nanocode-durability-core, nanocode-durability, nanocode-subagents, nanocode-code-mode, nanocode-backend-claude and nanocode-telemetry; `cargo check --locked --lib` for each, native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`; `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- rustls-native-certs and openssl-probe leave the workspace, and on macOS security-framework and security-framework-sys: nanocode's own trust-store reader, `nanocode_platform::trust::load_native_certificates()`, loads the native roots for nanocode-tls (outside macOS), nanocode-sandbox's egress proxy (outside Linux), the CLI's paying proxy bundle (bin/nanocode/src/tempo/proxy.rs) and the patched rustls-platform-verifier's Linux `system_roots()` (2026-11-12). It lives in nanocode-platform (crates/core/platform/src/trust.rs) because every user reaches it without a cycle and crates that use nanocode-tls from outside this workspace get it from git, where the patched verifier's own API is not there. It is rustls-native-certs 0.8.4 and openssl-probe 0.2.1 reproduced: `SSL_CERT_FILE` set (even empty) or `SSL_CERT_DIR` with a non-empty colon-separated entry loads only those paths; otherwise on unix outside macOS the probe takes `SSL_CERT_FILE`/`SSL_CERT_DIR` when they exist, else the first existing file of openssl-probe's per-OS candidate list, plus every existing candidate directory in its order (the 18 file and 9 directory paths per cfg are copied verbatim; output/probe-lists.py compares them with openssl-probe's source: equal); files are parsed with rustls-pki-types' PEM iterator (non-certificate sections skipped, errors per section, fused on I/O errors), a directory's entries are followed through symlinks, dangling ones skipped, non-files ignored, not recursed, and the result is sorted by DER bytes and deduplicated; errors keep rustls-native-certs' contexts ("failed to read PEM from file", "opening directory", "reading directory entries", "failed to open file", "failed to load user/admin/system trust settings", "certificate not trusted", "failed to open current user certificate store"), its Display (`context: inner at 'path'`) and its Debug shape (`Error { context, kind: Io { inner, path } | Os(..) | Pem(..) }`), so nanocode-tls logs the same counts and messages and the proxy's `{:?}` error is unchanged. The struct is `NativeCertificates { certificates, errors }` (was `CertificateResult { certs, errors }`); no public nanocode type exposed rustls-native-certs, so pyramid-core and pyramid are unaffected. On macOS nanocode-sys gains trust_settings.rs: `certificates(Domain)` returns each certificate of a trust-settings domain as DER with its TLS trust result, mirroring security-framework 3.7.0 (SecTrustSettingsCopyCertificates, errSecNoTrustSettings as empty; SecTrustSettingsCopyTrustSettings per certificate, settings whose kSecTrustSettingsPolicyName is not CFEqual to "sslServer" skipped, a missing or unconvertible kSecTrustSettingsResult meaning TrustRoot, Unspecified and unknown results skipped; errors as OSStatus with SecCopyErrorMessageString's text, Display and Debug as security-framework's `Error { code, message }`), and the platform loader walks user, admin, system, keeps the first domain's result per DER and keeps TrustRoot and TrustAsRoot (no settings meaning TrustRoot), as rustls-native-certs does. Security and CoreFoundation are reached by dlopen and dlsym at first use, not linked, so nanocode-sys (under nanocode-sync in every binary) does not add `-framework Security` to every macOS link; with security-framework gone `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli --target aarch64-apple-darwin` has neither security-framework nor core-foundation-sys, so the CLI again links neither framework (as the macOS launch entry intended; proxy.rs had brought them back). On Windows nanocode-sys gains certificate_store.rs (windows-sys 0.61.2, already in Cargo.lock): the current user's ROOT system store, each certificate's DER, enhanced key usages (all, or OIDs; the server-authentication OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.1 makes it usable) and time validity, as schannel 0.1.29 and rustls-native-certs read them. Unsafe blocks added, all in nanocode-sys behind safe functions, each sound because: trust_settings.rs `dlerror` (no preconditions) and `CStr::from_ptr` on its non-null result (a NUL-terminated string valid until the next dl call on this thread; copied at once); `dlopen` (static NUL-terminated framework path); `dlsym` (a handle from dlopen that is never closed, static NUL-terminated names); one block transmuting the 18 non-null dlsym addresses to function pointer types that match Apple's Security and CoreFoundation header declarations; SecCopyErrorMessageString (reserved argument null), SecTrustSettingsCopyCertificates and SecTrustSettingsCopyTrustSettings (out pointers to locals; the certificate a reference borrowed from a live array), CFArrayGetCount and CFArrayGetValueAtIndex (live array, 0 <= index < count, count asserted non-negative), SecCertificateCopyData, CFDataGetLength, CFDataGetBytePtr and `slice::from_raw_parts` (non-null pointer and length of a CFData owned until after the copy), CFStringCreateWithBytes (null allocator, a static str's pointer and length), CFStringGetLength and both CFStringGetBytes calls (size query with a null buffer, then a buffer of exactly the queried length; written and used lengths asserted), CFDictionaryGetValueIfPresent, CFEqual, CFGetTypeID and the two GetTypeID functions (live references; the borrowed handle types carry the owner's lifetime), CFNumberGetValue (kCFNumberSInt64Type into an i64 local, after asserting the value is a CFNumber), and CFRelease in `Owned`'s drop (each Copy or Create result owned exactly once); certificate_store.rs CertOpenStore (system provider, NUL-terminated UTF-16 "ROOT"), CertCloseStore in drop (a store opened once), CertEnumCertificatesInStore (the previous context it frees, or null), `as_ref` on its non-null context (valid until the next enumeration call, used before it), `slice::from_raw_parts` on the context's encoded bytes, CertVerifyTimeValidity (null meaning now, the context's info), both CertGetEnhancedKeyUsage calls (size, then a u64-aligned buffer of at least that size), the reference to the filled CTL_USAGE, `slice::from_raw_parts` over its identifiers only when the count is non-zero, and `CStr::from_ptr` on each NUL-terminated identifier inside that buffer. Not equal: on macOS rustls-native-certs returns the certificates in HashMap order (random per process) and ours in DER order (the same set, now deterministic); a Security or CoreFoundation symbol that cannot be loaded is an error under each domain's context, where the linked crate could not start without it; a trust setting that is not a CFDictionary or a result that is not a CFNumber is an assert, where security-framework passed it to CoreFoundation, which aborts; on Windows a certificate whose usages cannot be read is the error "failed to read certificate usages" and is skipped, where rustls-native-certs panicked on `unwrap`; openssl-probe checked each candidate directory for existence twice and we check once. Equality: output/certs-equal links rustls-native-certs 0.8.4 and openssl-probe 0.2.1 beside nanocode-platform and compares the certificate list (DER, order) and every error's context, Display, Debug and source over the default environment and seeded random environments: per round a tree of 2 to 6 directories with single and multi-certificate PEM files re-encoded from this Hand's 121 roots at line widths 40, 64, 76 and unwrapped, LF and CRLF, non-certificate sections (private keys, CRLs, requests, unknown labels), garbage, empty files, truncated sections, bad base64, malformed BEGIN lines, random bytes in CERTIFICATE sections, files with non-UTF-8 names, mode-000 files, symlinks to files and directories, dangling and looping symlinks, nested directories, directories at modes 000, 444 and 111, a directory named ":"; SSL_CERT_FILE unset, empty, missing, a directory, relative, the system bundle or a fixture; SSL_CERT_DIR unset, empty, ":", "::", ":::" or lists of 1 to 4 entries with empty, missing, file, relative and system entries; working directory the fixture root or not. Linux (x86_64, glibc, this Hand): seeds 11, 12 and 13, 12,003 environments, 408,599 certificates and 29,977 errors compared, 0 differences. macOS (the thread's Mac, Apple Silicon, macOS 26, rustc 1.100.0): output/certs-equal-mac builds the same two source files (byte-identical, by sha256, before rustfmt) beside security-framework 3.7.0 and rustls-native-certs 0.8.4: per domain, every certificate's DER and trust result in array order equal over 3 runs (user 0, admin 0, system 157 certificates) and again with 8 admin trust settings added by `security add-trusted-cert -d` (trustRoot for all policies, trustRoot for ssl, deny, unspecified, trustRoot for smime only, trustAsRoot on a leaf, deny for smime and ssl, and deny on ISRG Root X1, which the system domain also holds), 0 differences; `load_native_certs` against ours equal as sets with equal errors (161 certificates with the admin settings); the random environments (seeds 21 and 22, 6,002 environments, 65,611 certificates and 15,176 errors, sorting the old list only for the 310 that read the keychain) 0 differences. Not exercised: "reading directory entries" (a directory failing mid-listing), "certificate not trusted" and the user domain on macOS (adding user trust settings needs interactive authorization), and Windows at run time (nanocode-sys and nanocode-platform check and pass clippy for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu). Speed, interleaved: Linux default environment (121 roots) 10 rounds of 20 loads, median 1.46 ms per load before and 1.24 ms after; macOS full load, 7 runs, 80.6 to 91.6 ms before and 80.9 to 91.6 ms after. `cargo metadata` 427 to 425 packages on origin/master efe7f3f12 (489 to 487 and 490 to 488 on the earlier bases it was written against; rustls-native-certs, openssl-probe; security-framework and security-framework-sys leave aarch64-apple-darwin but stay in Cargo.lock for the patched verifier's iOS path; core-foundation and core-foundation-sys stay for nanocode-computer; schannel stays for rustpython-host_env on Windows, whose unused optional native-certs feature still names rustls-native-certs). Commands: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`; `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-platform -p nanocode-tls -p nanocode-sandbox -p rustls-platform-verifier`; `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-cli`; `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-platform --target aarch64-apple-darwin` and `--target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`; `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-platform -p nanocode-tls --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`; nanocode-tls, nanocode-sandbox and the verifier do not check for aarch64-apple-darwin or Windows on this Hand (ring's C build script needs those toolchains), and were not built on the Mac.
- nanocode-platform forbids unsafe code: its `unix` module's libc calls and the iOS CoreFoundation time-zone lookup move unchanged into nanocode-sys, so nanocode-sys is the one crate with unsafe code that nanocode-cli builds besides the vendored patches and nanocode-computer's macOS accessibility calls (2026-11-12). crates/core/platform/src/unix.rs is now crates/core/sys/src/unix/host.rs (a 100% rename in `git diff -M`; re-exported from `nanocode_sys::unix`) and the `apple` module of zone.rs is crates/core/sys/src/apple.rs (compiled for Apple targets other than macOS, as before); `nanocode_platform::unix` re-exports exactly the items it had (`UserEntry`, `SystemRelease`, `user_id`, `process_group`, `user_entry`, `system_release`, `host_name`, `signal_process`, `probe_process`, `signal_group`, `sync_file`, `barrier_sync_file` on Apple, `available_bytes`, `redirect_output`, `thread_cpu_time`, `forbid_core_dumps` on Linux) and `time_zone_name` calls `nanocode_sys::apple::time_zone_name`, so callers are untouched; nanocode-platform drops its `unsafe_code = "deny"` lint block for the workspace's lints and its direct libc dependency. The unsafe blocks that moved, with the invariants recorded when they were written (the nix entry): `getuid`, `getpgrp`; `getpwuid_r` into a `MaybeUninit<passwd>` and a buffer of its stated capacity, read only when it reports success, with `CStr::from_ptr` on the entry's non-null name, directory and shell; `sysconf`; `uname` into a `MaybeUninit<utsname>` read after success; `gethostname` into a 256-byte buffer forced to end in zero; `kill`/`killpg`; `fsync`; `fcntl(F_BARRIERFSYNC)`; `statvfs` on a `CString` path into a `MaybeUninit` read after success; `dup2` onto stdout and stderr; `clock_gettime(CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID)`; `prctl(PR_SET_DUMPABLE, 0)`; and on iOS the CoreFoundation calls (`CFTimeZoneResetSystem`, `CFTimeZoneCopySystem` released with `CFRelease`, `CFTimeZoneGetName`, `CFStringGetLength`, `CFStringGetBytes` into a buffer of three bytes per UTF-16 unit). No behaviour changes: the code is byte for byte the same. `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-platform` for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin and wasm32-unknown-unknown, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`; the iOS module was not built (no iOS target on the Hand). `cargo metadata --locked` stays at 489 packages.
- futures-channel leaves the workspace's crates: nanocode-mcp's `Outgoing` is a `nanocode_sync::unbounded::Receiver<Message>` and its replies travel on tokio's oneshot (2026-11-12). crates/core/sync/src/unbounded.rs is an unbounded channel over tokio's unbounded mpsc (already in nanocode-sync's tree on native and WASM): `channel()`, a cloneable `Sender` with `send` (the message back as the error when the channel is closed or the receiver is gone, as `unbounded_send`'s `into_inner`), `close` (sender-side, as `close_channel`: later sends fail, the receiver yields what was sent before and then `None`, other senders included) and `is_closed`, and a `Receiver` that implements futures' `Stream` (so `next`, `poll_next_unpin` and `tokio::select!` in nanocode-mcp-http and nanocode-mcp-tools work unchanged). A close is a flag plus an end marker queued behind the messages already sent. `Session`'s request replies use `tokio::sync::oneshot` (nanocode-mcp gains tokio with only `sync`, the feature nanocode-sync already enables). Public API change: `nanocode_mcp::Outgoing` was `futures_channel::mpsc::UnboundedReceiver<Message>`; code that only polls it as a `Stream` is unaffected (tempoxyz/pyramid-core and tempoxyz/pyramid: no hits for `Outgoing` from nanocode_mcp in code search). Not equal: a `send` that races a `close` on another thread can return `Ok` and land behind the end marker, where it is dropped unread; futures-channel decides that race inside one state word and reports the send as failed. nanocode-mcp's callers do not observe it: `Session` checks `is_closed` before sending, and a request that loses the race is answered `Error::Closed` by the close that drains `pending`. Proven with output/sync-unbounded, linking futures-channel 0.3.32 beside nanocode-sync: 2,000 seeds of 2,000 random operations (sends from up to six cloned senders, polls with a no-op waker, closes from any sender, sender drops, receiver drop, `is_closed`) comparing every result: 805,964 checks, 0 differences; 8 threads sending 200,000 messages each, all received in per-sender order. Benchmark (release, interleaved, 5 rounds, send and receive in batches of 64): futures-channel 119 to 237 ns per message against 113 to 172 ns. `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sync -p nanocode-mcp -p nanocode-mcp-http -p nanocode-mcp-tools` natively and the first three for wasm32-unknown-unknown, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-mcp -p nanocode-mcp-http --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata --locked` stays at 489 packages: futures-channel stays in the lock through hyper, hyper-util, reqwest and opentelemetry_sdk, and futures-executor through opentelemetry_sdk (the obs scope's).
- RustPython's atomic cells are rustpython-common's own, and crossbeam-utils leaves rustpython-vm and rustpython-stdlib (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-common/src/atomic/cell.rs is `rustpython_common::atomic::AtomicCell<T>` for builds without the threading feature (nanocode's: its RustPython is single-threaded and `PyRc` is `Rc`): a `Cell<T>` with crossbeam-utils 0.8.22's `AtomicCell` API (`new`, `into_inner`, `store`, `swap`, `as_ptr`, `take`, `load`, `compare_exchange`, `fetch_update`, `fetch_add`/`fetch_sub`/`fetch_and`/`fetch_nand`/`fetch_or`/`fetch_xor`/`fetch_max`/`fetch_min` on the twelve integer types with wrapping arithmetic, `fetch_and`/`fetch_nand`/`fetch_or`/`fetch_xor` on bool, `Default`, `From`, and `Debug` as `AtomicCell { value: .. }`); with threading, atomic.rs re-exports `crossbeam_utils::atomic::AtomicCell`, and crossbeam-utils is an optional dependency of rustpython-common that only its threading feature enables (rustpython-vm's and rustpython-stdlib's threading features reach it through `rustpython-common/threading`). The 29 `use crossbeam_utils::atomic::AtomicCell` lines in rustpython-vm (23) and rustpython-stdlib (6) import `rustpython_common::atomic::AtomicCell`, and no call site changes except socket.rs's `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT`: a static must be Sync, which a `Cell` is not, so it is rustpython-common's `AtomicF64` with Acquire loads and Release stores, the orderings crossbeam's lock-free `AtomicCell<f64>` used (socket.rs compiles only with host_env, which nanocode does not enable and which already fails to build at the base in rustpython-host_env's ctypes.rs). `compare_exchange` compares with `Eq`, as crossbeam does (its byte comparison is a fast path that retries when the bytes differ but the values are equal), and returns the stored value in `Ok` and `Err`; `fetch_update` is crossbeam's loop, so a closure that changes the cell runs again. What nanocode's build calls (found by marking every method deprecated and checking nanocode-python): 1,140 calls in 107 files, `store` 504, `load` 474, `new` 128, `fetch_add` 22 and `fetch_sub` 6 on usize, `swap` 3 (bool, `Option<IterFunc>`), `compare_exchange` 2 (bool), `fetch_update` 1 (usize), and derived `Default` and `Debug`, on bool, usize, isize, i32, u32, u64, i64/`PyHash`, f64, `Option<u64>`, `Option<u128>`, `Option<bool>`, the `Option<fn ..>` number, sequence, mapping and type slots, and the `AwaitableState`, `FutureState`, `Newlines`, `SeenNewline` and `FileMode` enums and flags. Not equal: without threading the type is neither Sync nor `RefUnwindSafe` (nothing in that build needs either; the one static is the `AtomicF64` above), `into_inner` is not `const` (a `const fn` cannot drop a `Cell` field's container), and `is_lock_free` and the deprecated `compare_and_swap` are left out (unused). Equality: output/atomics-equal (run on gak-9) links crossbeam-utils 0.8.22 beside cell.rs and drives both with the same seeded xorshift sequences (300 sequences of 2,000 steps per type) of `new`/`from`, `load`, `store`, `swap`, reads through `as_ptr`, `compare_exchange` that hits and misses, `fetch_update` with random and re-entrant closures, every integer and bool `fetch_` operation, `take`, `Default`, `into_inner`, and `Debug` after every step, on the twelve integer types, bool, f64 (NaN, both zeros, infinities), `Option<fn>`, `Option<u64>`, `Option<u128>`, `Option<bool>`, copies of the enums above, and `Option<Rc<u32>>` with its strong counts compared after every step: 25,486,211 checks, 0 differences. The e2e corpus (1,065 programs) run on gak-9 by binaries built from the base and from this change: 25,472 output lines, 17 differ, all printing object addresses or `hash(nan)` (identity-based), which differ between any two runs (the same 17 lines differ between the base and e86dae0d8 builds). Speed on gak-9: corpus 331.2 s before and 334.5 s after (run side by side); eight microbenchmarks, best of 5 over three alternating rounds: with the release profile a generator loop is 3.6% and an itertools loop 2.5% slower and the other six are within 1.3%, but built with codegen-units=1 the generator loop is 164.5 ms before and 164.7 ms after and all eight are within 2.6% (the 2.6% is a StringIO loop that touches no cell), 1,606 ms to 1,619 ms in total, so the difference follows how the release build splits rustpython-vm into codegen units rather than the cell itself. nanocode-sync no longer uses crossbeam-utils (ad685d75c), so it leaves nanocode-cli with this change: `cargo metadata` stays at 427 packages (crossbeam-utils remains in Cargo.lock as the optional dependency of rustpython-common's threading feature) and `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` goes from 233 to 232 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 237 to 236 (aarch64-apple-darwin). Building rustpython-vm with threading fails before and after with the same 12 errors (`dyn Limiter` is not Send or Sync, `BlockingMutex` where `Mutex` is expected, no `rustpython_host_env::thread`). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-common -p rustpython-vm -p rustpython-stdlib` on Linux and `cargo check -p nanocode-cli` on aarch64-apple-darwin pass.
- The ruff parser's parser-thread constants (`STACK_BYTES_PER_RECURSION_MAX`, `PARSER_STACK_BYTES`) and its `TextLen` import are compiled only for non-wasm targets, where the parser thread exists (2026-11-12): the nesting-bound commit left them unused on wasm32-unknown-unknown, three new warnings there. No code changes otherwise; `RECURSION_DEPTH_MAX` applies on both. `cargo check --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` (gak-9) shows only the two rustpython-vm warnings present at e86dae0d8; `cargo check -p nanocode-python` passes natively.
- The vendored RustPython crates write their error impls by hand, and thiserror and thiserror-impl leave rustpython-codegen, rustpython-compiler, rustpython-ruff_python_ast and rustpython-vm (2026-11-12). Each `#[derive(thiserror::Error)]` becomes the impls it expanded to: `CodegenError` and the compiler's `ParseError` keep their hand-written `Display` and get `Error::source` returning their `error` field (their `#[source]`); the compiler's `CompileErrorType` and `CompileError` and the vm's `CompileErrorType`/`CompileError` for builds without the compiler (`#[error(transparent)]` variants) get `From` for each variant and `Display` and `source` that forward to the wrapped error; `PythonVersionDeserializationError` and the jit `ArgsError` get `Display` with the same format strings (`Invalid python version `{0}`: expected `major.minor``, `Invalid major version `{0}`: {1}`, the seven jit messages) and `source` returning the `ParseIntError` where it was `#[source]`; rustpython-codegen's `std` feature no longer enables `thiserror/std` (the impls use `core::error::Error`). Equality: the impls are what thiserror 2.0.18 generates for these attributes (format strings copied verbatim, forwarding for transparent variants, `source` only for `#[source]` fields), and SyntaxError/RecursionError messages, which go through these `Display` impls, are covered by the end-to-end corpus. thiserror stays in Cargo.lock and in nanocode-cli's tree through opentelemetry and opentelemetry_sdk, so the package counts do not change (`cargo metadata` 461, `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 265 on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, 268 on aarch64-apple-darwin); these were its only other users in nanocode-cli. `cargo check -p nanocode-python` on aarch64-apple-darwin and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` on Linux pass.
- The ruff parser bounds its nesting instead of growing its stack, and parses on a long-lived parser thread with a stack sized for that bound; stacker, psm, ar_archive_writer and object leave (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-ruff_python_parser/src/parser/mod.rs: `with_recursion` (the parser's recursion points for expressions, patterns, statement blocks and format specs) counts depth against `RECURSION_DEPTH_MAX` = 20,000; the first time it is exceeded the parser records the current token's range and the number of errors so far and ends the token stream (the lexer jumps to the end of the source with no open brackets, f-strings or pending indentation, so every recursion returns at the end-of-file token), and `finish` drops the errors that recovery produced after that point and reports `ParseErrorType::NestingTooDeep`, which rustpython-compiler (`CompileError::from_nesting_too_deep`, also used by `_ast.parse`) turns into the same `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded during compilation` its AST depth check raised for deep trees. On native targets the parse runs on a per-calling-thread worker (`thread_local!`, started on first use, jobs and replies over std mpsc channels, panics carried back and resumed) whose stack is `RECURSION_DEPTH_MAX * STACK_BYTES_PER_RECURSION_MAX` (12 KiB, from the measured maximum of 9,351 bytes per level: nested f-strings in a debug build on aarch64-apple-darwin; release needs at most 4,173), 240 MiB of reserved, lazily committed address space; a worker that cannot be started is a typed `ParserThreadUnavailable` parse error. On wasm32 the parse runs in place with the same bound, as it did under stacker, which never grows the stack there. rustpython-vm's native stack check reads the stack position from the address of a local instead of `psm::stack_pointer`. Measured on gak-9 with the bound lifted and an 8 MiB parser stack (output/stackmeasure), the deepest parse that fits per construct (debug/release): unary minus 2,786/6,319, `not` 2,785/6,319, conditional expressions 4,365/10,927, lambdas 5,238/7,493, `**` 4,224/11,160, lists 1,489/2,747, calls 916/2,776, nested `if` blocks 1,919/6,100, f-strings 896/2,009; each costs one parser level per source level. Equality: output/e2e's deep corpus (532 programs: 14 constructs at depths 50 to 100,000 in eval and exec mode plus `ast.parse`, and with recursion limits 3,000 and 20,000 at depths 2,000 to 15,000; each program in its own process), old e86dae0d8 against this change on gak-9: 529 byte-identical (including the old crash at depth 15,000 with the limit raised, which still overflows codegen's stack, and every depth-100,000 case), 1 a 166 s run that timed out under the harness's 60 s alarm on one side only (both give the same RecursionError when run alone), and 2 differ: `await` chained 100,000 deep, where old parsed it and reported `SyntaxError: await expression cannot be used here` and the parser now stops at depth 20,000 with the RecursionError. Not equal: a source nested deeper than 20,000 parser levels now raises RecursionError even when it also has a syntax error that old reported (old parsed the whole tree first), and even when `sys.setrecursionlimit` was raised above 20,000 with a thread stack big enough for codegen to walk such a tree (old accepted those); a source nested 1,000 to 20,000 deep behaves as before. Cost: compile() of a 3-line source goes from 19.4 to 33-35 us on gak-9 (two thread handoffs per parse; release, 20,000 compiles, 3 interleaved rounds), and each thread that compiles keeps one parked parser thread; spawning a thread per parse cost 73-88 us and was not kept. TigerStyle departure, bounded to the vendored parser: the worker uses std channels. `cargo metadata` 465 to 461 packages; `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 269 to 265 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 272 to 268 (aarch64-apple-darwin); `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` on Linux and `cargo check -p nanocode-python` on aarch64-apple-darwin pass.
- pyexpat parses with rustpython-stdlib's own XML pull reader, and xml 1.3.0 (xml-rs) leaves nanocode-cli and Cargo.lock (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-stdlib/src/pyexpat/reader.rs is an `EventReader` over any `Read` specialised to the one configuration pyexpat's removed `create_config` built (comments and CDATA as their own events, whitespace reported as characters, character data not coalesced, root-level whitespace dropped, several root elements allowed). It decodes one byte at a time from the source exactly as xml-rs's `CharReader` did (byte order mark sniffing for UTF-8 and UTF-16 LE/BE, the `encoding` declaration matched by common prefix against utf-8/utf8, iso-8859-1/latin1, utf-16/utf16 and ascii/us-ascii with the same conflict rules, UTF-8 errors detected only after four bytes or at the end), so the parser thread pulls the same bytes at the same moments and the `NeedMore` handoff across `Parse()` chunks, `LineTracker`'s byte indices and the synchronous backend's replay are unchanged. A lexer (markup tokens, unread characters, `]]>` and `--` handling, the DOCTYPE lexing context) feeds a state machine that splits character data at markup, expands predefined and numeric references, keeps internal DTD general and parameter entities (first definition wins, external ones empty) and re-lexes them in content and in the internal subset (depth 10, 1,000,000 pending characters), resolves namespaces (first binding per element wins, the default namespace, the xml and xmlns rules, unbound prefixes), rejects duplicate attributes, applies the XML 1.0 or 1.1 character classes and the limits xml-rs had by default (names over 256 KiB, more than 65,536 attributes, 1 GiB of text, DOCTYPE or attribute value), and keeps the 16-slot event position queue that decides `CurrentLineNumber` and `CurrentColumnNumber`. pyexpat.rs builds the reader instead of `xml::ParserConfig` (the config parameter and field are gone) and reads `TextPosition` and `QualifiedName` from it. Not equal, and not observable: pyexpat never surfaced xml-rs's errors (both backends stop dispatching at the first one), so `ReaderError` is a fieldless kind without xml-rs's message text or error position, and events no longer carry what pyexpat ignored (prefixes, the namespace map, `StartDocument` and `Doctype` fields); the point where an error stops the stream (the events before it and the bytes consumed) is equal. Equality: output/xml-equal links xml 1.3.0 beside reader.rs and compares per document every event (names with namespace, attributes in order, text), the position after it, the bytes pulled from the source when it is returned, and the error point, once over a counting slice reader and, for documents up to 200 KB, once through a 64-byte `BufReader` over a source returning random 1 to 97 byte reads. Seeds 11 to 15, 150,000 generated documents each (half leaning well-formed, half noisy: declarations with odd versions, encodings and standalone values, DOCTYPEs with general, parameter and external entities, entity chains up to 14 deep, billion laughs, namespaces, CDATA, comments, PIs, byte order marks, UTF-16 LE/BE and Latin-1, names past 256 KiB, 65,535 to 65,537 attributes), each also mutated (truncations, byte flips, inserted markup and bad UTF-8, deletions) plus every prefix of every tenth short one: 9,249,874 documents, 47,852,738 checks, 0 differences. 60,003 real XML, plist, SVG, XSD, sdef and other files from macOS (/System/Library, /Library, /usr/share, /Applications, /opt/homebrew, /private/etc), each as is, with 4 mutations and a random prefix, twice (seeds 21, 22): 720,036 documents, 87,440,363 checks, 0 differences. On the Linux Hand the same harness passes seed 41 (240,324 documents, 1,245,790 checks) and 3,139 files from /usr/share, /usr/lib/python3 and /etc (18,834 documents, 2,045,059 checks) with 0 differences. End to end: 146 Python programs over 3,643 documents (2,810 generated and mutated, 800 real macOS files, 33 edge cases), each through xml.parsers.expat whole and in 1, 5, 7 and 64 byte `Parse()` chunks with and without a namespace separator and `ordered_attributes`, recording every handler with `CurrentLineNumber`, `CurrentColumnNumber` and `CurrentByteIndex`, then xml.dom.minidom, ElementTree `fromstring`/`tostring` and `XMLPullParser` fed 13-byte chunks, and xml.sax: the old (xml 1.3.0) and new e2e binaries print byte-identical 38,776,186-byte outputs (an old binary first resolved xml 1.4.0, which normalises line ends, and differed; pinned to the workspace's 1.3.0 it matches). Benchmarks on gak-9, interleaved: the reader alone over four macOS documents of 1.6 to 2.8 MB, 7 rounds, twice: xml 1.3.0 33.5 and 34.1 MB/s, new 49.3 and 50.0 MB/s; through Python, best of 5, three interleaved rounds: `ElementTree.fromstring` of 2 MB 153 to 161 ms before, 138 to 144 ms after; expat with handlers 360 to 388 ms before, 359 to 375 ms after; minidom 505 to 518 ms before, 507 to 516 ms after (the VM dominates). `cargo metadata` 466 to 465 packages; `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 270 to 269 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 273 to 272 (aarch64-apple-darwin). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-stdlib` pass.

Medians of five runs in the third of three interleaved rounds on gak-9 (M1 Max, release): `trim` over 200,000 mixed strings 6.80 to 7.96 ms and over 200,000 ASCII strings 5.29 to 1.69 ms, `trim_with` 5.69 to 6.78 ms (mixed) and 1.76 to 1.62 ms (ASCII), `split_str` over 2 MB 0.46 to 0.47 ms, `replace` over 2 MB with a runtime needle 0.66 to 0.66 ms (with a literal needle bstr's inlined copy reached 0.48 ms against 0.61), `find_byteset` 2.27 to 2.17 ms. `cargo metadata` 471 to 470 packages; `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 278 to 277 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 280 to 279 (aarch64-apple-darwin). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p rustpython-wtf8` (native and wasm32-unknown-unknown), `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-wtf8 -p rustpython-ruff_python_parser -p rustpython-vm` pass.
- jiff leaves RustPython: the time module's code for targets that are neither Unix nor Windows (wasm32) uses its own calendar and a jiff-compatible strftime, and the build script dates the commit with nanocode-platform's zone reader; jiff, jiff-core, jiff-static, jiff-tzdb, jiff-tzdb-platform, portable-atomic-util and defmt (with defmt-macros and defmt-parser) leave the lock (2026-11-12). On Linux and macOS time.localtime, gmtime, mktime, strftime, asctime, ctime, timezone, altzone, daylight and tzname never reached jiff: they go through libc in rustpython-host_env and are unchanged; jiff was compiled into nanocode-cli only because rustpython-vm depended on it unconditionally and its build script used it. crates/patches/rustpython-vm/src/stdlib/time/civil.rs (non-Unix, non-Windows only) is a civil DateTime over nanocode-platform's civil_from_days and days_from_civil (now public, and days_from_civil no longer Unix-only), with jiff 0.2.39's limits (years -9999..=9999, Unix seconds -377705023201..=253402207200, the same OverflowErrors), weekday, day of year and ISO week date, and a strftime that reproduces jiff's lenient Display: flags _ 0 - ^ #, widths up to 255 (integer padding capped at 20, the space-padded negative case uncapped), colons, %C %y %g of negative years, %c %x %X %r as jiff's locale-free "%Y M%m %-d, %a %H:%M:%S" family, %f %N %.Nf, and a directive it cannot format (%Z %z %:z %Q %s on a zone-less time, unknown letters, a dangling flag, width or colon, a width past 255) written back literally from its percent sign. The system zone on those targets is what jiff's TimeZone::system() returned on wasm32-unknown-unknown without its js feature, Etc/Unknown, which behaves as UTC with abbreviation "UTC": tm_zone "UTC", tm_gmtoff 0, mktime as UTC. The current time comes from std's SystemTime (it panics on wasm32-unknown-unknown, as jiff's Timestamp::now did with its own message; nanocode's boot.py routes time.time, localtime(), gmtime(), ctime() and strftime without a tuple through the host clock, so only asctime() without arguments reaches it) or, with the wasmbind feature, from JavaScript's Date.now as jiff's js feature did. build.rs takes nanocode-platform as a build dependency: git's commit time (or the clock) is shifted by utc_offset_seconds in the build host's zone (TZ, then /etc/localtime) and printed as "%b %e %Y" and "%H:%M:%S" by hand. nanocode-platform now parses a POSIX rule in TZ with the extended (TZif v3) syntax, rule times from -167 to 167 hours, as jiff and glibc do; before, such a TZ was refused and /etc/localtime used. What is not equal: (1) on wasm32-wasi, which nanocode does not build, jiff read a zone from TZ in the WASI environment; this code uses UTC there as on wasm32-unknown-unknown; (2) with the wasmbind feature, which nothing in nanocode enables, jiff took the browser's zone from Intl and its bundled tzdb; this code uses UTC; (3) for a TZ of the permanent-DST form DST from Jan 1 0:00 to Dec 31 25:00 (EST5EDT,0/0,J365/25), jiff 0.2.39 shows standard time in the five hours after each new year and nanocode-platform (like glibc) stays in DST, which can change the build host's date string within those hours; (4) an invalid TZ falls back to /etc/localtime's zone in nanocode-platform where jiff used UTC (the same on hosts whose /etc/localtime is UTC); (5) a now() reading outside jiff's range is an OverflowError instead of a panic. Equality: output/time-equal links jiff 0.2.39 beside civil.rs (included by path) and compares DateTime::new over random and out-of-range fields, Unix seconds to civil time over the whole range and past both ends with random nanoseconds, to_unix against jiff's to_zoned(Etc/Unknown) (and Etc/Unknown against UTC), the struct_time fields, strftime of every directive under every flag, 18 widths and 0 to 4 colons on boundary and random times, the dot forms, edge strings and random format strings mixing directives, flags, digits, colons and non-ASCII: seeds 1, 2, 3 at 20,000 cases give 724,131, 724,703 and 723,493 checks, seeds 11, 12, 13 at 200,000 cases 5,996,811, 5,996,356 and 6,000,562, 0 differences; build_date runs the old build.rs (jiff) and the new one side by side with git's timestamp stubbed, once per TZ: all 454 files of /usr/share/zoneinfo, 21 TZ values (POSIX rules with southern-hemisphere, half-hour, 45-minute, negative-DST, +13/+14, extended negative and 25-hour rule times; ":name", an absolute path, empty, invalid, "localtime") and TZ unset, each at every transition jiff lists (first 4,000) +-1 s and 900 random times: 2,124,379 checks, differences only in the two permanent-DST strings (6,002 each, case 3). End to end, output/time-e2e builds nanocode-python for wasm32-unknown-unknown from e86dae0d8 and from this tree into a cdylib run by Node with a fixed host clock: four programs (78,126 lines: gmtime, localtime and ctime of 738 timestamps including infinities, NaN and out-of-range values; mktime, asctime and strftime of 1,772 tuples including invalid fields and DST-gap and fold times; 8,817 format strings, every directive under every flag, width and colon count plus random ones, on 8 tuples including years -9999, -50, 1 and 9999; the module constants, struct_time, strptime and error cases) run as 42 slices: 78,258 lines of output, byte-identical. The same corpus was not run natively old against new: on Linux and macOS this change compiles none of the time module's code it edits (only build.rs, whose equality build_date shows), and the scope asked for no more release builds of RustPython on the shared Hand. Speed (release, interleaved, 7 rounds, best): strftime "%a %b %e %H:%M:%S %Y" 150 ns jiff against 203 ns, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S" 98 against 156, every directive 1,089 against 2,008; seconds to civil fields 7.0 against 27.5 ns; mktime 5.5 against 9.2 ns: slower, and only wasm32 builds run this code. cargo metadata 480 -> 471 packages; nanocode-cli on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu 280 -> 278 and on aarch64-apple-darwin 282 -> 280 packages (cargo tree -e normal,build), nanocode-python on wasm32-unknown-unknown 115 -> 113 (jiff, jiff-core, jiff-tzdb and jiff-tzdb-platform leave; the build script's nanocode-platform brings tokio and getrandom for the host). Commands: cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli, cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown, cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-vm (native and wasm32), cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-platform (native and wasm32), civil 1|2|3 20000, civil 11|12|13 200000, civil bench, zones.sh, e2e.sh.
- RustPython's derive macros carry the part of syn-ext they use, and syn-ext leaves (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-derive-impl/src/syn_ext/ is syn-ext 0.5.0's attribute.rs, generics.rs, ident.rs, item.rs, meta.rs, path.rs and punctuated.rs with its `ext` and `types` modules (`AttributeExt`, `AttributeIteratorExt`, `GetIdent`, `GetPath`, `ItemAttrExt`, `ItemLike`, `ItemModExt`, `MetaAttributeExt`, `MetaExt`, the `NestedMeta*IteratorExt` traits, `PunctuatedExt`, and the syn-1-style `Meta`/`MetaList`/`NestedMeta`/`PunctuatedNestedMeta`), with syn-ext's tests, comments and feature gates (all the gates rustpython-derive-impl enabled are on) removed, `ref`/`ref mut` bindings under default binding modes dropped for edition 2024, and `ParseStream<'_>` spelled out; the derive-impl sources import `crate::syn_ext::` instead of `syn_ext::`, and the module is public because `pyclass`, `pyexception` and `pystruct_sequence*` take `PunctuatedNestedMeta`, which rustpython-derive parses with `Punctuated::parse_terminated`. Equality: output/synext-equal (run on gak-9) links the old rustpython-derive-impl (with syn-ext 0.5.0) beside a renamed copy of the new one, collects every `#[pyclass]`, `#[pyexception]`, `#[pymodule]`, `#[pystruct_sequence]`, `#[pystruct_sequence_data]` item (958) and every derive input (1,083: `derive_from_args`, `pypayload`, `pytraverse`) from rustpython-vm, rustpython-stdlib and nanocode-python, and compares the generated token streams: 4,207 checks, 4,142 identical; the other 65 (all `#[pyclass]` on impl blocks) contain the same tokens in a different order, because derive-impl iterates a HashMap when it emits items: the old crate itself produces a different order on a second call for 60 of them. `cargo metadata` 481 to 480 packages; `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 281 to 280 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 283 to 282 (aarch64-apple-darwin). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` on Linux and `cargo check -p nanocode-python` on aarch64-apple-darwin pass.
- widestring is a dependency of rustpython-host_env and rustpython-vm only on Windows, and leaves nanocode-cli (2026-11-12). Every use of `widestring::WideCString`/`WideCStr` and its error types in host_env (crt_fd::wopen, fileutils' Windows stat, io::open_path, nt, overlapped, winapi, winreg, winsound, wmi, the Windows time-zone names) and vm (exceptions.rs' three `ToPyException` impls, fspath/ospath `to_wide_cstring`, nt, winreg, winsound, _winapi, os.rs' Windows environment) is already behind `cfg(windows)` (or the ctypes feature nanocode does not enable), so the dependency moves to `[target."cfg(windows)".dependencies]` in both Cargo.toml files, as rustpython-stdlib already had it; no source changes. Equality: no code compiled for Linux, macOS or wasm32 changes. `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 282 to 281 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 284 to 283 (aarch64-apple-darwin); `cargo metadata` unchanged (widestring stays in Cargo.lock for Windows). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` on Linux and `cargo check -p nanocode-python` on aarch64-apple-darwin pass.
- RustPython's lock types are built on rustpython-common's own port of the lock_api layer, and parking_lot, parking_lot_core and lock_api leave nanocode-cli (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-common/src/lock/api.rs carries what RustPython used of lock_api 0.4.14: the raw-lock traits (`RawMutex`, `RawRwLock` with its `is_locked_exclusive` default, `RawRwLockDowngrade`, `RawRwLockRecursive`, `RawRwLockUpgrade`, `RawRwLockUpgradeDowngrade`, `GetThreadId`), the `GuardSend`/`GuardNoSend` markers, and `Mutex`/`RwLock` with their guards, mapped guards (`map`, `try_map`), `upgradable_read`/`upgrade`, `downgrade`, `read_recursive`/`try_read_recursive`, `get_mut`, `into_inner`, `raw`, `data_ptr` and the same `Send`/`Sync` bounds and `Debug` output (`Mutex { data: .. }`, `<locked>`). Without the `threading` feature (nanocode's build) every PyMutex/PyRwLock is still the Cell-based raw lock of lock/cell_lock.rs, so locking behaves exactly as before; with `threading`, lock/parking.rs adapts parking_lot's raw locks to the new traits and parking_lot becomes an optional dependency of rustpython-vm and rustpython-stdlib that only their `threading` feature enables (it is on rustpython-host_env only for Windows). The places that took a parking_lot lock outside `threading` now use std: the csv dialect registry and field limit, the interpreter-admission gate (vm/runtime.rs, gc_state.rs) and the `_interpqueues`/`_interpchannels` registries take a `rustpython_common::lock::BlockingMutex` (a `std::sync::Mutex` whose `lock` ignores poisoning, as parking_lot has none), `_interpchannels`' blocked `send()` waits on a `std::sync::Condvar` (`wait`, and `wait_timeout` to the deadline in place of `wait_until`), host_env's `AppendLog` uses `std::sync::Mutex` the same way, hashlib's per-object state is a `PyMutex`, and `_functools`' lru_cache reentrant lock is, without `threading`, a depth counter (parking_lot's reentrant mutex on one thread only ever counted). TigerStyle departure, bounded to the vendored interpreter: these are blocking std locks and a condition variable rather than nanocode-sync primitives, because RustPython's object model hands out guards from shared references everywhere and porting it to an owner-and-mailbox design is a rewrite of the interpreter; the new lock layer uses the same unsafe as lock_api (cells handed out under a held raw lock), which the vendored crates already rely on. The `threading` feature did not build before this change either (`dyn Limiter` is not `Send + Sync` in vm/runtime.rs, _thread.rs and thread.rs, checked at e86dae0d8 on gak-9) and still does not. Equality: in nanocode's configuration the raw locks, guard order and unlock points are unchanged and nothing runs on a second thread, so lock behavior is identical; the end-to-end corpus (output/e2e) exercises every object access through these locks. `cargo metadata` 481 packages before and after (the optional dependency keeps parking_lot in Cargo.lock); `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 285 to 282 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 287 to 284 (aarch64-apple-darwin). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-common -p rustpython-host_env -p rustpython-vm -p rustpython-stdlib` on Linux and `cargo check -p nanocode-python` on aarch64-apple-darwin pass.
- rustpython-host_env loses the modules nanocode's Python never compiles a user of, and its remaining system calls go through the libc calls the crate already makes; nix, memmap2, memoffset and cfg_aliases leave (2026-11-12). nanocode builds rustpython-vm and rustpython-stdlib without their `host_env` feature, so the stdlib and vm modules that called host_env's faulthandler, grp, mmap, multiprocessing, pwd, select, shm, syslog, socket (Unix), resource, posix, posix_unix_like, fcntl and thread modules (os, posix, socket, select, mmap, fcntl, grp, pwd, resource, syslog, faulthandler, _multiprocessing, posixshmem, _thread with threading) are compiled out, as the earlier termios deletion was; those 14 host_env files are deleted, and the five `ToPyException` impls in vm/src/exceptions.rs for their error types now also require `feature = "host_env"`. `builtins.input`'s session-leader test (`getsid(0) == getpid()`) moves from host_env::posix to host_env::os unchanged. What nanocode does compile is ported: time.rs's `clock_gettime`/`clock_getres` on Unix use the libc bodies the file already had for WASI, `clock_settime` and `nanosleep` build a `libc::timespec` (seconds that do not fit `time_t` are an InvalidInput error where nix's `as` cast wrapped), fileutils' `StatStruct`/`fstat` are `libc::stat`/`libc::fstat`, io.rs's directory test is `st_mode & S_IFMT == S_IFDIR` with EISDIR, `page_size` is `sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE)`, `set_errno` writes `__errno_location()` (Linux) or `__error()` (Apple), and `copy_file_range` (only the compiled-out os module used it) is gone. These are the same system calls nix and rustix made, through the same libc the crate already calls with unsafe elsewhere (the vendored interpreter is outside the workspace's forbid(unsafe_code)). rustix leaves rustpython-host_env, its last user in nanocode-cli, so rustix, errno and (on Linux) linux-raw-sys leave the tree too. Not equal: the `host_env` features of the vendored vm and stdlib no longer build (nanocode never enables them); `time.sleep`'s error for a failed nanosleep other than EINTR reads `nanosleep: Invalid argument` (strerror) where nix printed `nanosleep: EINVAL: Invalid argument`, a path a valid `timespec` cannot reach. Equality: nothing that was compiled into nanocode's interpreter changed behavior besides the ports above, which call the same functions; the end-to-end corpus (output/e2e, old e86dae0d8 against the branch head) covers time.monotonic, perf_counter, process_time and clock_gettime. `cargo metadata` 484 to 481 packages; `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 291 to 285 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 292 to 287 (aarch64-apple-darwin). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` pass on Linux, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python` on aarch64-apple-darwin (gak-9).
- nanocode-http decodes gzip and deflate responses and sets `Accept-Encoding: gzip,deflate` itself, so reqwest's `gzip` and `deflate` features are off (2026-11-12): with them on (enabled by the Claude client and unified across the binary), reqwest 0.13.4 wrapped every client in tower-http 0.6.11's Decompression layer, which inserts `accept-encoding: gzip,deflate` into a request that has none (after the client's default headers, so a default or request header wins) and, when the first `Content-Encoding` value is exactly the bytes `gzip` or `deflate` (no trimming or case folding; status, method and Content-Length are not looked at), removes every Content-Encoding value and Content-Length and decodes the body with async-compression's GzipDecoder (one member: bytes after the first member in the same frame are dropped, a later non-empty frame is the error `there are extra bytes after body has been decompressed`; the FHCRC flag is ignored and its two bytes are read as deflate data, as compression-codecs 0.4.38 does) or ZlibDecoder, with an empty body (no frames) decoding to an empty body. crates/core/http/src/flate.rs reproduces that from scratch on nanocode-compression's raw and zlib `inflate`: a gzip header, CRC-32 and size check with compression-codecs' messages (`Invalid gzip header`, `CRC computed does not match`, `amount of bytes read does not match`, `unexpected end of file`, `deflate decompression error`, `unexpected BufError` for a zlib stream that ends early), output in 4096-byte chunks as tower-http's buffer. New API in nanocode-http: `accept_encoding(HeaderMap)` (adds the header only where absent, last, as tower-http did), `client()` (Client::new with it), `decode_flate_response` (gzip and deflate only), `decode_response` (gzip and deflate first, then the existing zstd and br), `FlateCoding` and `decode_body` (a whole body, for the blocking client). Every reqwest client reachable from nanocode-cli gets the header (claude client, federation and home login, codex ChatGPT auth, chat and platform clients, codex built-in tools, mcp-http OAuth clients, mcp-tools, the OTLP blocking exporter, the cli's tempo and custom endpoint clients; the tempo proxy keeps none, as before) and every response path decodes where reqwest did: the seven sites that called decode_response keep it, the rest (ReqwestSender, execute, bounded_text, codex responses and chat, auth, tempo session, rpc, payer and flow, mcp probe) call decode_flate_response, so none starts decoding zstd or br; the OTLP exporter checks a gzip or deflate body with decode_body as it was checked before being dropped. async-compression, compression-codecs and compression-core leave, and with them flate2, crc32fast, miniz_oxide, adler2 and simd-adler32, which only async-compression still pulled in once the image stack left (413 to 405 packages); tower-http stays for follow-redirect. Not equal: a decode error's chain gains a `request or response body error` layer (reqwest wraps a rebuilt body's errors; the outer error is still is_decode with the same message, as for zstd and br already), and a transport error inside a decoded body two layers; the bytes delivered before an error can differ (old dropped up to 4 KiB decoded in the poll that met the error); the inflater is the zlib-style one, not miniz_oxide's, so a corrupt stream can fail with a different message (old `CRC computed does not match` or `unexpected end of file` where ours says `deflate decompression error`); the blocking exporter sees the body as one frame, so trailing bytes after a complete member are ignored rather than an error when they arrived in a later frame; a read timeout now restarts on each compressed frame rather than each decoded one; through an HTTP proxy with credentials for an http:// URL, Accept-Encoding now precedes Proxy-Authorization. output/flate-equal: old = reqwest =0.13.4 with gzip+deflate plus the previous nanocode-http, new = reqwest without them plus this nanocode-http; 20,000 seeded frame sequences (text, SSE, JSON, random, runs and repository files up to 1.5 MB; flate2 levels 0 to 9, hand-built headers with every flag, multi-member, zlib with other windows and FDICT, raw deflate under deflate, swapped codings, truncation, bit flips, insertions, deletions, trailing garbage, empty frames, 1 to 30 frames, injected source failures): success or failure equal on all 20,000, decoded bytes equal on all 11,131 successes, error message equal on 8,568 of 8,869 errors once the extra layer is set aside, the 301 others being the inflater difference above (276 CRC vs deflate error, 8 BufError vs deflate error, 6 end of file vs deflate error, 11 injected failure vs deflate error); decode_body equals the streaming decoder on all 18,985 sequences without failures. A local tokio HTTP server served 1,500 seeded responses (gzip, deflate, GZIP, Gzip, padded, x-gzip, identity, br, zstd, unknown, lists, two headers, empty; 200, 204, 304, 404, 500; HEAD; chunked, Content-Length, Content-Length 0, close-delimited; three client shapes, explicit request encodings) to both decode_response and decode_flate_response sites: request headers seen by the server (Accept-Encoding and order), status, headers and content_length equal on all 3,000 requests, success or failure and success bodies equal on all; 2,610 of the 3,000 equal in every field, 376 differ only by the layer (40 of them also in the bytes before the error) and 14 by the inflater message. Gzip decoding through the response, 16 KiB frames, on-CPU getrusage, 5 interleaved rounds, medians: text 7.3 MB 326 to 239 MB/s, SSE 12.1 MB 316 to 247 MB/s, zlib text 292 to 242 MB/s (crc32fast's SIMD CRC and miniz_oxide against our portable CRC and inflater). Commands: cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli, cargo check --locked --lib (native and wasm32-unknown-unknown) and cargo clippy --locked for nanocode-http, nanocode-backend-claude-client, nanocode-backend-codex-client, nanocode-backend-codex, nanocode-mcp-http, nanocode-mcp-tools, nanocode-observability; cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu (285 to 282) and aarch64-apple-darwin (286 to 283). Packages 413 → 405.
- nanocode-image decodes, resizes and encodes with Tempo's own codecs, and image 0.25.6 leaves with png, gif, zune-jpeg, zune-core, image-webp, weezl, fdeflate, color_quant, quick-error and byteorder-lite (2026-11-12). crates/core/image gains decode.rs (`guess_format` with image's 23 magic signatures and masks, `Format::mime_type` as `ImageFormat::to_mime_type`, and `Decoder`, which is `ImageReader::with_format(..).into_decoder()`: PNG through nanocode-png with the allocation limit as png's byte budget, JPEG through nanocode-jpeg, GIF through nanocode-gif with the limit for its frame buffer, WebP through nanocode-webp, BMP and PNM through new bmp.rs and pnm.rs, the other recognized formats `Unsupported` as image built without them; `reserve` is `ImageReader::decode`'s `Limits::reserve(total_bytes)` before the GIF frame buffer takes the rest; `dimensions` is `with_guessed_format().into_dimensions()`), bmp.rs (image 0.25.6's BMP decoder ported: core and info to V5 headers, 1/2/4/8-bit palettes, RLE4 and RLE8 with deltas, 16/24/32-bit, bitfields with its 3-to-7-bit expansion tables, top-down rows, its checks and errors), pnm.rs (its PNM decoder: P1 to P7 headers with its comment and token rules, PAM tuple types, ASCII and binary rasters, maxval scaling with its f32 rounding), pixels.rs (`Image` and `Pixels` in place of `DynamicImage`, with image's 16-to-8-bit conversion `(v + 128) / 257` in `to_rgba8`/`to_rgb8`), thumbnail.rs (`imageops::thumbnail` with its four sampling cases, f32 mixes and wrapping u32 sums as built in release) and a `lanczos3` that now resamples 16-bit images itself with the same f32 passes as `imageops::resize` instead of falling back to it. PNG output goes through nanocode-png (`encode_png` for the Claude media tool's `write_to(Png)`), JPEG through nanocode-jpeg at quality 85 with gray widened to RGB as `encode_image(&DynamicImage)` did, WebP through nanocode-webp; the PNG eXIf CRC uses nanocode-compression's crc32. Callers: the Claude backend's host tools and prompt sizing, the Claude media tool, the Codex image generation tool, the Codex client's compaction estimate and computer use's X11 screenshots call nanocode-image or nanocode-jpeg; their error texts keep image's `The image format could not be determined`. Public API: `nanocode_image::lanczos3` takes and returns `nanocode_image::Image` instead of image's `DynamicImage`, and nanocode-image exports `Image`, `Pixels`, `Format`, `Decoder`, `Limits`, `DecodeError`, `guess_format`, `dimensions`, `thumbnail` and `encode_png`; tempoxyz/pyramid-core and tempoxyz/pyramid use neither nanocode_image nor lanczos3 (GitHub code search, 2026-11-12). Not equal: decode and encode error texts are ours (they reach logs, the Claude media tool's `invalid or oversized image: ...` and placeholders, not pixels); where image's decoders panicked on hostile input (PNG palettes past 768 bytes, zune-jpeg layouts, a PNM raster shorter than its header claims after u32 wrapping) the image now gets an error and its placeholder instead of a panic that took the whole tool output's images down; everything nanocode-png, -gif, -jpeg and -webp list as not equal. API: `header(bytes) -> Result<Header { width, height, alpha }, WebpError>` (what `WebPDecoder::new` + `dimensions`/`has_alpha` give, same errors); `Decoder::new(bytes)`, `header()`, `icc_profile()` and `exif()` (`Result<Option<&[u8]>, WebpError>`, the ICCP/EXIF chunk bytes as `icc_profile()`/`exif_metadata()` return them, errors kept so the caller's `.ok().flatten()` stays explicit) and `decode(pixel_bytes_max) -> Result<Vec<u8>, WebpError>` (RGB8, or RGBA8 when `alpha`); `encode(pixels, width, height, alpha, icc_profile, exif) -> Result<Vec<u8>, WebpError>`. Ported exactly: RIFF/VP8X chunk walk with image-webp's first-chunk-wins table, ANMF size checks, its reading of the first frame's two subchunk headers (the second one read from inside the first subchunk) and the ANIM/EXIF/XMP/ambiguity checks; VP8 (boolean decoder including the one trailing zero byte before end of data, segments, partitions, intra prediction, IDCT/WHT, simple and normal loop filters, fancy upsampling with image-webp's YUV->RGB rounding, including its row arithmetic when an ALPH frame's VP8 size differs from the ANMF rectangle); VP8L (bit reader with its refill rule, so streams that run short in a distance code fail the same way, Huffman tables with u16 wrapping in the completeness check, color cache, backward references, uniform-block shortcut, color cache not updated on distance-1 copies, all four transforms, predictors 14 and 15 as no-ops); ALPH (raw and lossless, filters, preprocessing flag only validated); `read_image` of an animated file composites only the first frame onto a transparent black canvas (image never sets a background color); the encoder builds codes with the same `BinaryHeap` and `sort_unstable_by_key` calls, so its bytes are identical. Limits: image's `Limits::max_alloc` is never applied to WebP (its `WebPDecoder` keeps the default `set_limits`, which only checks max width/height, unset here) and image-webp's own memory limit stays `usize::MAX`, so the only bound is nanocode-image's `total_bytes()` check; `decode` checks `width * height * bytes_per_pixel` against `pixel_bytes_max` (`PixelBytes`) before allocating. Not equal, and why: where image-webp panics (an ALPH animation frame whose VP8 frame is larger than its rectangle, or rows that do not fit; a Huffman table entry whose slot holds a short code; an empty table entry) we return `FramePixels` or `HuffmanCode`; we do not allocate chunk or partition buffers before checking the data is there, and an ICCP/EXIF chunk past the end of the file is `Truncated` without a 4 GiB allocation; a VP8 frame whose size differs from the expected one is first parsed without pixel buffers to find the same error image-webp reports; a VP8X canvas over 2^32 bytes of RGBA would wrap image-webp's u32 canvas size and is computed in u64 here (unreachable under the 512 MiB / 40 MiB bound); io errors map to `Truncated` (UnexpectedEof) and `SeekBeforeStart`. Encoder: 3,646 + 5,926 + 4,380 checks (random RGB/RGBA 1-2000 px incl. skewed residuals that hit the length limit, flat, palette, real decoded images, ICC/EXIF absent, empty or present, invalid sizes), 0 byte differences. Package count 424 -> 425 (image-webp and quick-error leave once nanocode-image switches). Benchmarks, interleaved on-CPU time (schedstat) over all 1,457 files: lossy decode 0.93x, animated 0.74-0.89x, lossy+alpha 0.90-1.04x, encode 1.03-1.06x, lossless decode 1.11-1.14x; user-space perf counters: lossless decode +4% instructions but +11% cycles with 1.9x branch misses, which ablation puts in the predictor transform (a per-pixel rewrite and branchless saturation did not change it; still open), encode -7% instructions and equal cycles.
- nanocode-compression's inflate runs about twice as fast on PNG image data with the same behavior (2026-11-12): nanocode-png spends most of its decode time inflating IDAT streams, where literals are 60% of the output (159 M literals and 12 M matches over the 40 largest corpus PNGs, the matches mostly 64 or more bytes back and 8 bytes long), and the inflate fast loop cost about 19 cycles a symbol. In crates/core/compression/src/inflate the fast loop now works on local copies of the bit reader and the output (they were reached through references and kept in memory, and refill, peek, copy_match and the other small helpers were out-of-line calls at codegen-units 16; they are `#[inline(always)]`); every dynamic block also builds a 4096-entry literal table (table.rs `build_literals`, from the code lengths already sorted for the Huffman table, by doubling as fdeflate 0.3.7 builds its table, and a static one for fixed blocks) whose entries hold one or two root-table literals with their total bits, so a run of literals costs one lookup per two literals and no branch between one and two; matches copy 16-byte chunks from 16 bytes back, 8-byte chunks from 8 and fill at distance 1; the window hands out slices instead of taking the output. The loop keeps zlib-rs's iteration boundaries (two literals, then one symbol, then the input and output exit test), because an error the fast loop finds reads "repeated call with bad state" while the byte-at-a-time path names it: batches of up to three literal entries and one symbol run only while no exit test could fire inside them (output room of 260 + 264 bytes, input of 15 + 11 bytes), then the original loop finishes from the same phase (root-table literals since the last other symbol, mod 3), so every call stops on the same input byte with the same status, counts, bytes, window and message. The decoder state grows by the 16 KiB literal table. Not equal: nothing observable; bytes past what a call produced may still be written, as before (2-byte literal stores, 16-byte match chunks). CRC-32 is unchanged: slicing-by-16 runs at 2.9 GB/s on an M1 Max, a variant with 64-bit loads was slower (2.7 GB/s) and slicing-by-8 slower still (1.6 GB/s), and crc32fast's lead comes from the CRC and carry-less multiply instructions safe portable code cannot use. Proven with output/inflate-equal, which drives zlib-rs 0.6.8 through z_stream, the previous inflate as a path crate and the new one with the same random sequence of calls and compares status, error, message, bytes consumed and produced, totals and bytes after every call (debug assertions and overflow checks on): 10,000 cases over every level, strategy, memory level and window size, raw, zlib, gzip and auto headers, dictionaries, 398,813 mid-stream clones, every flush mode and input and output pieces from 0 bytes to whole streams, 60% of them corrupted, truncated, padded or concatenated, 13,316,303 calls, 13,530 stream ends, 12,039 data errors and 211,547 dictionary requests, 0 differences; and the IDAT streams of the 40 largest corpus PNGs as zlib, raw and auto streams, intact and bit-flipped, fed in 8 to 72 KiB, 0 to 300 byte and whole pieces into outputs of 1 byte to 1 MiB (PNG's 256 KiB among them) with sync flushes, 5,961,281 calls and 3.2 GB inflated, 0 differences. `cargo metadata --locked` 424 to 424 packages. Benchmarks in output/inflate-perf (interleaved rounds, on-CPU time from getrusage, medians; an M1 Max at load 9 to 105 over 7 rounds, the x86 hosted Hand at load 12 over 5): the 40 IDAT streams (134 MB inflating to 253 MB) went from 1075 to 547 ms on the M1 (fdeflate 440, zlib-rs 792, miniz_oxide 853) and from 700 to 518 ms on x86 (fdeflate 501, zlib-rs 659); Python sources at level 6 from 487 to 849 MB/s on the M1 and 560 to 727 MB/s on x86 (fdeflate 825 and 647); binaries at level 6 from 410 to 627 MB/s on the M1 (fdeflate 679) and 425 to 432 MB/s on x86 (fdeflate 523); nanocode-png `Png::new` and `decode` of the 40 files from 1445 to 921 ms on the M1 and 1152 to 937 ms on x86. Checks: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-compression` and `-p nanocode-png` (native and wasm32), `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-compression` (native and wasm32).

- nanocode-compression decodes Brotli (RFC 7932) itself: crates/core/compression/src/brotli/ (bits.rs, prefix.rs, header.rs, blocks.rs, commands.rs, window.rs, dictionary.rs, tables.rs) is a streaming decoder written anew, `Decoder::decompress(input, output) -> Result<Progress, DecodeError>` reporting bytes consumed and written and `Status::{NeedsInput, NeedsOutput, Done}`, resumable after any input byte and any output byte, leaving bytes after the last meta-block unconsumed (2026-11-12). Its acceptance follows brotli-decompressor 5.0.3, quirks included: checks run in the same order (simple-code symbols, code length code space, prefix code space, context map runs, nibbles, padding); a meta-block whose commands overrun MLEN fails only where that decoder writes its ring buffer (input exhausted, ring full at the window, stream end), so a non-last one that overruns between those points is accepted as there; a single literal block type runs out after 2^24 literals; distances beyond the window or before any output become dictionary references, with the same invalid-length and invalid-transform failures. The ring buffer is the stream's window (1 << WBITS, 1 KiB to 16 MiB): allocated at the first data meta-block at its length rounded up to a power of two and doubled up to the window as output grows; prefix tables, context maps and tree groups live in vectors reused across meta-blocks, so nothing allocates per symbol. The static dictionary is dictionary.bin (122,784 bytes, taken from brotli-decompressor-5.0.3/src/dictionary/mod.rs and byte-identical to the hex listing of RFC 7932 Appendix A; the RFC states its CRC-32, 0x5136cb04, which matches, and no SHA-256: it is 20e42eb1b511c21806d4d227d07e5dd06877d8ce7b3a817f378f313653f35c70); the 121 transforms of Appendix B and the Lut0/Lut1/Lut2 context tables are data generated from the RFC text. Binary assets are already committed (crates/core/schema/src/*.bin) and no .gitattributes applies; the wasm32 build passes. Not equal: large-window streams (WBITS 0010001) are rejected with `InvalidWindowBits` as RFC 7932 requires, while brotli-decompressor's `BrotliState::new` turns large window on and accepts them; when brotli-decompressor resumes a read from its 8-byte carry buffer it also writes its ring buffer each time that buffer runs dry, so an invalid stream whose non-last meta-block overruns MLEN can fail there in one chunking and succeed in others; bytes written during the call that fails are not reported (`decompress` returns only the error). Equal: output/brotli-equal compares the two decoders driven alike. 4,871 files (repository sources and text, ~/.cargo/registry, /usr/bin binaries, ~/media-corpus images; 0 B to 19.2 MB) and 10 edge inputs (empty, 1 and 2 bytes, 1 MiB zeros, repeated pairs and words, random, text mixed with random) compressed by the brotli crate 8 at all 180 quality 0..=11 and lgwin 10..=24 pairs: 18,959 streams (336.4 MB of output), 94,137 decodes in up to five chunkings (whole input with 1 MiB and 1-byte output, 4096/4096, random 1..64-byte input with random 1..300-byte output, 1-byte input and output up to 64 KiB): 0 differences in bytes, end status or bytes consumed at the end. 15 br responses saved raw from www.google.com, www.cloudflare.com, www.youtube.com, www.facebook.com, www.bing.com, developer.mozilla.org, discord.com, www.shopify.com, www.npmjs.com, cdnjs.cloudflare.com and cdn.jsdelivr.net (github.com and wikipedia.org answered gzip) in four chunkings: 60 checks, 0 differences. 300,000 seeded mutations of 400 valid streams (bit flips, byte replacements, insertions, deletions, truncations) and random byte strings, each whole and in random 1..16-byte chunks: 600,000 checks, of which 363,310 fail, 171,995 end needing input with all input consumed and 64,203 finish in both; 492 large-window ones rejected; 2 differences, both the carry-buffer case above (confirmed with an instrumented copy of brotli-decompressor); output before a failure equal in all but those 2. Benchmark (CPU time per decode, interleaved, 9 rounds, medians, host load 11 to 15 on 5 cores; brotli-decompressor vs ours): source text 33.6 MB q1 w24 303 vs 274 MB/s, 8.4 MB q5 w22 272 vs 280, q9 w16 274 vs 259, q11 w22 328 vs 272, random words 8 MB q5 w22 242 vs 184, binaries 25.2 MB q5 w22 172 vs 195, 4 MB q9 w18 130 vs 161; the copy-heavy text gap (0.76 to 0.94) is the dispatch per command through the resumable step state. Commands: cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli, cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-compression (also --target wasm32-unknown-unknown), cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-http, cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-compression -p nanocode-http.
