- nanocode-jpeg (crates/core/jpeg: no_std + alloc, forbid(unsafe_code), no dependencies) decodes and encodes JPEG as image 0.25.6 did with zune-jpeg 0.4.21 and its own JpegEncoder, ready for the image stack to switch to (no caller changes yet) (2026-11-12). API: header(bytes) -> Header { width, height, color: Luma | Rgb } parses the markers up to the first SOS as image's JpegDecoder::new did; decode(bytes, pixel_bytes_max) -> Decoded { width, height, color, pixels, icc_profile, exif } refuses more than pixel_bytes_max decoded bytes before allocating; encode(pixels, width, height, color, quality, icc_profile). Decoder: a port of zune-jpeg 0.4.21 as image drives it (strict mode off, no size limits, Luma output for a one-component frame and RGB otherwise, CMYK, YCCK and Adobe transforms converted to RGB, the ICC profile only from a complete set of APP2 chunks, the last Exif APP1 segment, orientation not applied): baseline and progressive Huffman, restart intervals, every sampling layout zune accepts, its integer IDCT, upsamplers and YCbCr conversion, its lenient handling of truncated and corrupt data (the 37-byte overread limit, markers inside scans, unknown markers swallowed, the u16 wrap of (dimension + 7) / 8, wrapping arithmetic as zune's release build computes it) and its error messages. zune's x86_64 AVX2 IDCT and color conversion compute the same integers as its scalar code (the AVX2 DC-only mask test cannot misfire and its saturating packs equal the clamps for in-range samples; the aarch64 NEON paths use the same algorithm), so the scalar port matches what image produced on x86_64 and on aarch64. Encoder: image's baseline encoder (libjpeg quality scaling, the standard tables, jfdctint forward DCT, f32 quantization rounded half away from zero, 4:4:4, JFIF APP0, ICC in 65519-byte APP2 chunks) for Luma and RGB. Not equal: where zune panicked because a layout does not fit its buffers (unusual sampling ratios, a scan for a component without a buffer, a mid-stream SOS naming a missing table) or image's encoder asserted on a wrong buffer length, nanocode-jpeg returns a typed error; where zune looped forever (a progressive image ending in a restart marker after its last scan) it returns RestartAtEnd; quality outside 1..=100 is an error instead of being clamped. Equal: output/jpeg-equal links image 0.25.6 (jpeg) and zune-jpeg 0.4.21. Decode: 3,819 real and generated JPEGs (the image-rs, libjpeg-turbo, zune-image, jpeg-decoder and Pillow test images, large photos, and 3,267 made with Pillow and libjpeg-turbo's cjpeg: qualities 1 to 100, 4:4:4, 4:2:2, 4:2:0 and 4:1:1, factors such as 2x2,1x2,1x1, 4x4 and 3x1, progressive, restart intervals, grayscale, CMYK, RGB, arithmetic, ICC up to 150 KB, Exif) plus 22,914 seeded mutants (truncation, bit flips, byte overwrites, inserted markers, cut and duplicated runs): 26,733 checks of header, dimensions, color, ICC, Exif, pixels and error against success, 0 differences; 240 inputs where image panicked and 1 where it hung get an error; all 15,470 error messages equal zune's. 40 progressive images ending in a restart marker: 28 hang in image, all return an error here. Encode: 58,677 checks (20,000 seeded random images of 1 to 160 px with no, small, multi-chunk or empty ICC at qualities 1 to 100, edge sizes from 0x0 to 65535x1 and 65536x1, 3,040 decoded real images at 85 and a random quality and every tenth at all 100 qualities, their gray planes), 0 differences; 900 checks that image's encode_image of an L8, La8 or Rgba8 DynamicImage equals encoding its RGB (gray replicated, alpha dropped) as 3 components. Commands: cargo build --release in output/jpeg-equal, then decode 6 21 ~/media-corpus/jpeg, encode 20000 11 ~/media-corpus/jpeg, bench 9 <photos>. cargo metadata: 426 -> 427 packages. Benchmarks (on-CPU time from /proc/thread-self/schedstat, median of 9 interleaved rounds on the loaded 5-core Hand): encode at quality 85 is 14 to 24% faster (12 MP 4:2:0 292.8 -> 231.2 ms, 15.5 MP 366.0 -> 281.8 ms); decode is slower where zune used AVX2: 12 MP baseline 4:2:0 45.6 -> 85.6 ms, 4:4:4 56.7 -> 112.0 ms, grayscale 19.5 -> 29.1 ms, progressive 138.1 -> 155.4 ms, 15.5 MP 77.1 -> 134.5 ms. The scalar IDCT is faster than zune's own scalar IDCT (23.6 against 31.6 ms per 200,000 blocks); the gap is zune's AVX2 IDCT and color conversion, which safe code on the SSE2 baseline cannot reach (a lane-wise IDCT and per-column zero shortcuts were built and measured slower, since SSE2 has no 32-bit vector multiply).
- nanocode-gif (crates/core/gif, new) decodes a GIF's first frame exactly as image 0.25.6's GifDecoder drove gif 0.13.3 and weezl 0.1.12 (2026-11-12); nothing calls it yet. `Gif::new` is `DecodeOptions::read_info` with RGBA output (magic, screen descriptor, global palette, extensions up to the first non-extension block, the 50 MB extension-data memory limit, the unknown-block and control-extension-length errors), and `first_frame` is `GifDecoder::read_image`: `next_frame_info` with its palette check, then either the rows of a full-width frame decoded straight into the zeroed canvas or a separate frame buffer, refused above the caller's allocation limit as image's `Limits::reserve_usize` did, composited with wrapping offsets and transparent black outside it. The streaming decoder is ported state for state (gif's quirks included: an empty first sub-block length swallows the next byte, a trailer needs one more byte to be read, interlaced row order from its iterator), and the LZW decoder is weezl's `DecodeState` with LSB codes and no yield on a full buffer, burst decoding and all (six codes per refill, the deferred-clear and implicit-reset rules, the `KwKwK` case, `InvalidCode` for a code beyond the table), because whether a stray code after the last needed pixel is read, and so errors, depends on how many bits sit in its 64-bit buffer; gif's 8 KiB BufReader windows over image's Cursor decide how sub-block data reaches it, so the decoder feeds it the same slices. Palette indices without a color leave the pixel untouched, as gif's converter does. Decoding the 36 real files (12.6 MB): 109 ms old against 108 ms new on-CPU, min of 7 interleaved runs. `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-gif`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-gif --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata` packages 425 -> 426.
- nanocode-png (crates/core/png, new) decodes and encodes PNG exactly as image 0.25.6 drove png 0.17.16 (2026-11-12); nothing calls it yet, the image stack's switch-over follows. `Png::new(bytes, memory_bytes_max)` is `PngDecoder::with_limits` (read_header_info, read_info, read_until_image_data): signature, IHDR checks, the chunk sequence with png's per-chunk rules (ancillary chunks parsed before their CRC is checked and kept on a CRC mismatch, critical ones refused; zero-length chunks never parsed; pHYs, gAMA, cHRM, sRGB, acTL, fcTL, PLTE, tRNS, sBIT, iCCP checks and errors, text chunks ignored), the byte budget png 0.17's `Limits` spends on its chunk buffer's growth, palettes, tRNS, sBIT and the ICC profile, and fdAT-first APNGs; `decode` is `next_frame` with `Transformations::EXPAND` into image's buffer layout (8-bit, or 16-bit as native `u16`), including Adam7, sub-frames from an fcTL before the first IDAT, palette expansion with png's quirks, low-depth gray scaling and tRNS keys. Image data inflates through nanocode-compression's raw inflate after fdeflate's own zlib header test; the stream must end with four trailer bytes (fdeflate's Done) before the next chunk, Adler-32 is not checked (png's default), and every chunk of the IDAT run is read and CRC-checked. The iCCP profile inflates with the Adler-32 check and errors swallowed, as png did. `encode` is png's Writer with Compression::Fast, FilterType::Sub and AdaptiveFilterType::Adaptive (what nanocode-image's `encode_png` and image's `write_to(Png)` use): IHDR, iCCP compressed by nanocode-compression's miniz at level 6 under the name `_`, eXIf, IDAT from fdeflate's fixed-Huffman compressor written anew (its 286 code lengths, header block and run coding, one call per row) or its stored-only fallback when that is smaller, IEND. Not equal: where png 0.17.16 panics (an indexed image whose PLTE is longer than 768 bytes or not a multiple of 3 bytes indexes past its palette table) nanocode-png returns `FormatError::PaletteTooLong`; a deflate block whose literal/length code is a single length-one code is refused by fdeflate and accepted by zlib-rs's inflate (no encoder writes one and the fuzzing below never produced one); error texts are nanocode-png's own. Equal: output/png-equal links image =0.25.6 and png =0.17.16 beside the crate. Decoding 692 real PNGs (PngSuite, image-rs/image and image-png test images, Wikimedia Commons files) and 4,000 seeded synthetic ones (every color type and depth, interlaced or not, palettes, tRNS, ICC, all compression levels and filters) with 40 and 5 seeded mutations each (truncation, bit flips, chunk bytes rewritten with a fixed CRC, chunks dropped, duplicated, resized): 53,274 checks of header success, dimensions, color type, ICC bytes, pixel success and pixels, 0 differences (14,547 decoded, 38,625 errors, 102 old panics that are errors here). Encoding 3,000 images (692 decoded real images and 2,308 seeded synthetic ones in all eight color types, 1x1 to 300x200, noise, runs and gradients, with random ICC profiles and eXIf) against png's Writer: 3,000 byte comparisons, 0 differences. Measured on-CPU (getrusage, the Hand at load 11 to 15): decoding 40 large PNGs 365 -> 520 ms, of which inflate is 222 -> 330 ms (fdeflate's PNG-tuned double-literal tables against zlib-rs's port, which the rule to inflate with nanocode-compression keeps), CRC-32 over the file 2 -> 22 ms (crc32fast uses PCLMULQDQ; our slicing-by-16 is scalar) and the row work (unfiltering with png's stb-style Paeth, expansion) about equal; encoding 204 decoded RGB/RGBA images 1.38-1.73 s -> 1.76-2.07 s (the fast compressor alone is equal to fdeflate's on 64 MB, 111-124 ms against 111-145 ms, the adaptive filter's four trial filters and the CRC are the rest). `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-png`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-png --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata` packages 424 -> 425.
- nanocode-compression's `adler32` sums 32 lanes per step, so the compiler vectorizes it (2026-11-12): crates/core/compression/src/checksum.rs keeps the byte loop for inputs under 16 bytes and the tail, and for each run of up to 173 chunks of 32 bytes (5,536 bytes, under zlib's 5,552-byte bound before a sum can overflow 32 bits) keeps per-lane byte sums and per-lane prefix sums in `[u32; 32]`, then folds them into the two halves in 64 bits (high += low * length + 32 * prefixes + (32 - lane) * sums) and reduces modulo 65,521 once. Results are the same integers: output/checksum-bench compares it with simd-adler32 0.3.10 on 200,000 seeded slices (lengths 0..20,000, random offsets and random starting checksums) and on all-0xFF inputs of every length 0..11,999: 212,000 checks, 0 differences. Measured: 100 MB went from about 51-104 ms to 18-21 ms (simd-adler32's AVX2 path: 5-9 ms), which the PNG encoder (one Adler-32 over all filtered rows) and every zlib stream nanocode-compression writes or checks (Python's zlib, gzip and zip members, nanocode-http's gzip) share. `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-compression`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-compression --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata` packages unchanged.
- nanocode-http's `gzip` writes flate2's gzip bytes with nanocode-compression's `miniz` (2026-11-12): crates/core/http/src/coding.rs puts flate2 1.1.9 GzEncoder's header itself (1f 8b, method 8, no flags, mtime 0, XFL 2 at level 9 and 10, 4 at levels 0 and 1, else 0, OS 255), then `miniz::compress(bytes, level, Format::Raw)`, then the CRC-32 (checksum::crc32) and the length modulo 2^32, little-endian. flate2 leaves nanocode-http (it stays in the lock for the codex client and tower-http until their commits, and for png). Not equal: a level above 10 is an `InvalidInput` error instead of flate2's silent 10 (11 to 255) or 1 (above 255); callers pass 2 (GZIP_LEVEL). Equal: output/http-equal gzip compares flate2's GzEncoder (write_all + finish) with `nanocode_http::gzip` over 600 seeded random inputs (0 B to 4 MiB, text, JSON, runs, random bytes) at levels 0 to 10 and 862 real files (repository sources, ~/media-corpus images, /usr/bin) at every level: 11,941 checks, 0 differences. Speed is that of `miniz` (previous entry): level 2 within 3% of flate2. Commands: cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli, cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-http, cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-http. Packages 424 → 424.
- nanocode-compression gets a miniz_oxide-compatible DEFLATE compressor, `miniz` (2026-11-12): crates/core/compression/src/miniz/ (mod.rs: `Level`, `Format`, `Writer`, `compress`, `compress_sync_flush`; compressor.rs, dictionary.rs, block.rs, huffman.rs, bits.rs, tables.rs) writes the bytes flate2 1.1.9's write::DeflateEncoder and write::ZlibEncoder write over miniz_oxide 0.8.9, so gzip request bodies, permessage-deflate messages and PNG text chunks can leave flate2 without changing a byte. It has miniz's hash chains, probe counts per level 0 to 10 (0 stored blocks only, 1 the trigram parser, 2 and 3 greedy, 4 to 10 lazy), block splitting, Huffman construction and zlib header per level, and flate2's writer around it: a 32 KiB output buffer per call, `write_all` as repeated writes, `flush` as one sync call then draining calls, `finish` as finish calls. The buffering is part of the output: when a block does not fit the space a call has, miniz stops; level 1 then refills its 4 KiB lookahead at a different point, and a sync flush interrupted while lookahead remains never completes (flate2 then returns the stream without the trailing empty stored block), so `Writer` simulates the space of each call. The core started from psh's copy (crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-utils/src/deflate.rs: one-shot, levels 1 to 9, modelled on compress_to_vec); psh keeps it because psh is a vendored workspace of its own, and this copy adds streaming input, levels 0 and 10, sync flush and flate2's buffering. Not equal: `Level::new` refuses levels above 10 with `LevelError`, where flate2 compresses 11 to 255 as 10 and anything above 255 as 1. Equal: output/miniz-equal runs flate2 and the new code on the same operation sequences (one write, random and fixed write sizes from 1 byte, flushes between writes, ending in finish or flush; raw and zlib): 34,231 checks on seeded random inputs (9.4 GB, 0 B to 4 MiB, levels 0 to 10), 33,111 checks on 11,081 real files (3.0 GB: repository sources, /usr/bin, ~/media-corpus, serde_json and tokio sources), 72 checks on 8 to 32 MiB inputs: 0 differences, including 33 sync flushes that flate2 left incomplete. Benchmark (output/miniz-equal bench, thread CPU time, best of 9 interleaved runs on the shared Hand, flate2 → new): JSON 1 MiB level 2 387 → 375 MB/s, level 2 sync flush 367 → 363, level 6 zlib 96 → 93, level 1 795 → 713, level 9 46 → 44; Rust sources 8 MiB level 2 181 → 181, level 6 41 → 39, level 1 279 → 254, level 9 19.7 → 19.4. The dictionary tables are fixed-size boxed arrays so masked indexes need no bounds checks, and the bit writer's two argument checks are `debug_assert!`: as `assert!` they cost 3 to 20% at level 2 in the same benchmark. Commands: cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli, cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-compression (and --target wasm32-unknown-unknown), cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-compression. Packages 424 → 424 (nothing calls it yet).
- base64 0.22 (already in the tree through hyper-util and nine nanocode crates) does what base64-simd did in nanocode-image, nanocode-audio, nanocode-code-mode-engine, the Codex backend and nanocode-computer-repl, and base64-simd, vsimd and outref leave (2026-11-12). `STANDARD` is the same dialect (padding required, canonical padding only, non-zero trailing bits refused); `Uint8Array.fromBase64` in code mode decodes its already-cleaned alphabet-only input with a `GeneralPurpose` engine that allows trailing bits and missing padding, which is what `forgiving_decode_to_vec` did with it; computer-repl decodes a CUA image or audio payload once instead of `check` plus a 16-character header decode, and reads the signature from the first 12 decoded bytes, which are the same bytes. Error texts that reach a model or a script (`invalid base64: Base64Error`, `generated image was not valid base64: Base64Error`, a CUA payload's `Base64Error`) keep base64-simd's text through a `BASE64_ERROR` constant. Equal: output/base64-equal (base64-simd 0.8.0 beside base64 0.22.1): 32,768 encodings (every length 0..4095, 8 seeded buffers each) byte-identical with equal encoded lengths; 9,801,520 decode checks over 3,000,000 seeded strings (alphabet, padding in any place, invalid bytes, mutated valid encodings): `STANDARD` decode result and accept/reject, `check`, the forgiving path on cleaned input and the CUA signature bytes, 0 differences (934,441 accepted). Not equal: speed. base64-simd's AVX2 paths ran 8 MiB at 3.2-12 GB/s encode and 4.9-10 GB/s decode against base64's 1.3-2.9 GB/s and 0.9-2.7 GB/s (5 interleaved rounds of 10 runs on the shared Hand, noisy); a 10 MB image data URL now costs about 6 ms more to encode, against tens of milliseconds to decode and re-encode the image, and SIMD would need unsafe intrinsics, which only nanocode-sys may hold. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo clippy --locked` on the five crates, `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` for nanocode-image, nanocode-audio and nanocode-code-mode-engine. `cargo metadata` packages 427 -> 424.
- The ruff parser bounds its nesting instead of growing its stack, and parses on a long-lived parser thread with a stack sized for that bound; stacker, psm, ar_archive_writer and object leave (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-ruff_python_parser/src/parser/mod.rs: `with_recursion` (the parser's recursion points for expressions, patterns, statement blocks and format specs) counts depth against `RECURSION_DEPTH_MAX` = 20,000; the first time it is exceeded the parser records the current token's range and the number of errors so far and ends the token stream (the lexer jumps to the end of the source with no open brackets, f-strings or pending indentation, so every recursion returns at the end-of-file token), and `finish` drops the errors that recovery produced after that point and reports `ParseErrorType::NestingTooDeep`, which rustpython-compiler (`CompileError::from_nesting_too_deep`, also used by `_ast.parse`) turns into the same `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded during compilation` its AST depth check raised for deep trees. On native targets the parse runs on a per-calling-thread worker (`thread_local!`, started on first use, jobs and replies over std mpsc channels, panics carried back and resumed) whose stack is `RECURSION_DEPTH_MAX * STACK_BYTES_PER_RECURSION_MAX` (12 KiB, from the measured maximum of 9,351 bytes per level: nested f-strings in a debug build on aarch64-apple-darwin; release needs at most 4,173), 240 MiB of reserved, lazily committed address space; a worker that cannot be started is a typed `ParserThreadUnavailable` parse error. On wasm32 the parse runs in place with the same bound, as it did under stacker, which never grows the stack there. rustpython-vm's native stack check reads the stack position from the address of a local instead of `psm::stack_pointer`. Measured on gak-9 with the bound lifted and an 8 MiB parser stack (output/stackmeasure), the deepest parse that fits per construct (debug/release): unary minus 2,786/6,319, `not` 2,785/6,319, conditional expressions 4,365/10,927, lambdas 5,238/7,493, `**` 4,224/11,160, lists 1,489/2,747, calls 916/2,776, nested `if` blocks 1,919/6,100, f-strings 896/2,009; each costs one parser level per source level. Equality: output/e2e's deep corpus (532 programs: 14 constructs at depths 50 to 100,000 in eval and exec mode plus `ast.parse`, and with recursion limits 3,000 and 20,000 at depths 2,000 to 15,000; each program in its own process), old e86dae0d8 against this change on gak-9: 529 byte-identical (including the old crash at depth 15,000 with the limit raised, which still overflows codegen's stack, and every depth-100,000 case), 1 a 166 s run that timed out under the harness's 60 s alarm on one side only (both give the same RecursionError when run alone), and 2 differ: `await` chained 100,000 deep, where old parsed it and reported `SyntaxError: await expression cannot be used here` and the parser now stops at depth 20,000 with the RecursionError. Not equal: a source nested deeper than 20,000 parser levels now raises RecursionError even when it also has a syntax error that old reported (old parsed the whole tree first), and even when `sys.setrecursionlimit` was raised above 20,000 with a thread stack big enough for codegen to walk such a tree (old accepted those); a source nested 1,000 to 20,000 deep behaves as before. Cost: compile() of a 3-line source goes from 19.4 to 33-35 us on gak-9 (two thread handoffs per parse; release, 20,000 compiles, 3 interleaved rounds), and each thread that compiles keeps one parked parser thread; spawning a thread per parse cost 73-88 us and was not kept. TigerStyle departure, bounded to the vendored parser: the worker uses std channels. `cargo metadata` and the `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` counts are in the commit's check log; `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` on Linux and `cargo check -p nanocode-python` on aarch64-apple-darwin pass.
- pyexpat parses with rustpython-stdlib's own XML pull reader, and xml 1.3.0 (xml-rs) leaves nanocode-cli and Cargo.lock (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-stdlib/src/pyexpat/reader.rs is an `EventReader` over any `Read` specialised to the one configuration pyexpat's removed `create_config` built (comments and CDATA as their own events, whitespace reported as characters, character data not coalesced, root-level whitespace dropped, several root elements allowed). It decodes one byte at a time from the source exactly as xml-rs's `CharReader` did (byte order mark sniffing for UTF-8 and UTF-16 LE/BE, the `encoding` declaration matched by common prefix against utf-8/utf8, iso-8859-1/latin1, utf-16/utf16 and ascii/us-ascii with the same conflict rules, UTF-8 errors detected only after four bytes or at the end), so the parser thread pulls the same bytes at the same moments and the `NeedMore` handoff across `Parse()` chunks, `LineTracker`'s byte indices and the synchronous backend's replay are unchanged. A lexer (markup tokens, unread characters, `]]>` and `--` handling, the DOCTYPE lexing context) feeds a state machine that splits character data at markup, expands predefined and numeric references, keeps internal DTD general and parameter entities (first definition wins, external ones empty) and re-lexes them in content and in the internal subset (depth 10, 1,000,000 pending characters), resolves namespaces (first binding per element wins, the default namespace, the xml and xmlns rules, unbound prefixes), rejects duplicate attributes, applies the XML 1.0 or 1.1 character classes and the limits xml-rs had by default (names over 256 KiB, more than 65,536 attributes, 1 GiB of text, DOCTYPE or attribute value), and keeps the 16-slot event position queue that decides `CurrentLineNumber` and `CurrentColumnNumber`. pyexpat.rs builds the reader instead of `xml::ParserConfig` (the config parameter and field are gone) and reads `TextPosition` and `QualifiedName` from it. Not equal, and not observable: pyexpat never surfaced xml-rs's errors (both backends stop dispatching at the first one), so `ReaderError` is a fieldless kind without xml-rs's message text or error position, and events no longer carry what pyexpat ignored (prefixes, the namespace map, `StartDocument` and `Doctype` fields); the point where an error stops the stream (the events before it and the bytes consumed) is equal. Equality: output/xml-equal links xml 1.3.0 beside reader.rs and compares per document every event (names with namespace, attributes in order, text), the position after it, the bytes pulled from the source when it is returned, and the error point, once over a counting slice reader and, for documents up to 200 KB, once through a 64-byte `BufReader` over a source returning random 1 to 97 byte reads. Seeds 11 to 15, 150,000 generated documents each (half leaning well-formed, half noisy: declarations with odd versions, encodings and standalone values, DOCTYPEs with general, parameter and external entities, entity chains up to 14 deep, billion laughs, namespaces, CDATA, comments, PIs, byte order marks, UTF-16 LE/BE and Latin-1, names past 256 KiB, 65,535 to 65,537 attributes), each also mutated (truncations, byte flips, inserted markup and bad UTF-8, deletions) plus every prefix of every tenth short one: 9,249,874 documents, 47,852,738 checks, 0 differences. 60,003 real XML, plist, SVG, XSD, sdef and other files from macOS (/System/Library, /Library, /usr/share, /Applications, /opt/homebrew, /private/etc), each as is, with 4 mutations and a random prefix, twice (seeds 21, 22): 720,036 documents, 87,440,363 checks, 0 differences. On the Linux Hand the same harness passes seed 41 (240,324 documents, 1,245,790 checks) and 3,139 files from /usr/share, /usr/lib/python3 and /etc (18,834 documents, 2,045,059 checks) with 0 differences. End to end: 146 Python programs over 3,643 documents (2,810 generated and mutated, 800 real macOS files, 33 edge cases), each through xml.parsers.expat whole and in 1, 5, 7 and 64 byte `Parse()` chunks with and without a namespace separator and `ordered_attributes`, recording every handler with `CurrentLineNumber`, `CurrentColumnNumber` and `CurrentByteIndex`, then xml.dom.minidom, ElementTree `fromstring`/`tostring` and `XMLPullParser` fed 13-byte chunks, and xml.sax: the old (xml 1.3.0) and new e2e binaries print byte-identical 38,776,186-byte outputs (an old binary first resolved xml 1.4.0, which normalises line ends, and differed; pinned to the workspace's 1.3.0 it matches). Benchmarks on gak-9, interleaved: the reader alone over four macOS documents of 1.6 to 2.8 MB, 7 rounds, twice: xml 1.3.0 33.5 and 34.1 MB/s, new 49.3 and 50.0 MB/s; through Python, best of 5, three interleaved rounds: `ElementTree.fromstring` of 2 MB 153 to 161 ms before, 138 to 144 ms after; expat with handlers 360 to 388 ms before, 359 to 375 ms after; minidom 505 to 518 ms before, 507 to 516 ms after (the VM dominates). `cargo metadata` 484 to 483 packages; `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 291 to 290 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 292 to 291 (aarch64-apple-darwin). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-stdlib` pass.
- rg's `-E`/`--encoding` and its BOM sniffing decode with psh-utils's own WHATWG Encoding Standard decoders instead of encoding_rs 0.8.44; encoding_rs, core_detect, multiversion_no_op and simdutf8 leave nanocode-cli (2026-11-12). Where: `crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-utils/src/searcher/encoding/`: `mod.rs` (label lookup trimming the five ASCII whitespace bytes and lowercasing ASCII, without the replacement encoding's labels as `for_label_no_replacement` did; `for_bom`; the `Decoder` with encoding_rs's BOM-removal life cycle, BOM bytes held back across buffers, and its U+FFFD loop; the `Transcode` cursor and the block-compressed `Index`), `unicode.rs` (UTF-8 over `std::str::from_utf8`, UTF-16LE/BE with a four-units-per-word ASCII path), `legacy.rs` (one two-byte machine for the 28 single-byte encodings, Big5, EUC-KR and Shift_JIS; x-user-defined), `gb18030.rs` (gb18030 and GBK), `japanese.rs` (EUC-JP, ISO-2022-JP) and `data.rs`, generated by output/enc-gen/generate.py (then rustfmt) from indexes.json and encodings.json of whatwg/encoding 1d519bf8e5555cef64cf3a712485f41cd1a6a990, the revision encoding_rs 0.8.44's README names, fetched from GitHub; NOTICE carries the WHATWG BSD-3-Clause notice; `decode.rs` and `searcher/mod.rs` change only their imports. Each decoder keeps encoding_rs's control flow so every call reports the same result, bytes read and bytes written as well as the same text: the output room checked before each step (3 bytes; 4 for UTF-8, UTF-16, Big5 and gb18030, and x-user-defined checks 3 even for ASCII), the ASCII runs, the `< 60` punctuation shortcut of the single-byte and EUC-KR decoders, the bytes gb18030, EUC-JP and ISO-2022-JP carry between calls and re-emit (gb18030's pending ASCII digit, ISO-2022-JP's prepended escape byte), and UTF-16's `(OutputFull, 0, 0)` at the end of input. Tables: 138,152 bytes (16-pointer blocks stored as a u16 base plus byte offsets when their code points span under 255, else as u16s, identical blocks shared; Big5's plane-2 code points as a 2,360-byte pointer bitset; the 207 gb18030 ranges) against 169,474 bytes as plain trimmed u16 arrays; stripped release probes that decode stdin under a label are 346,528 bytes with no decoder, 536,528 with encoding_rs and 530,704 with these decoders; psh release binary 14,737,120 -> 14,729,624 bytes. Not here: the replacement encoding's decoder, which psh cannot reach (its labels are unknown to `-E` as before and no BOM names it), and encoders, which psh never used. Equal: output/enc-equal links encoding_rs =0.8.44 beside the module included by path: every label of encodings.json plus case, whitespace, prefix, suffix, Unicode look-alike and 2.2M random labels, and `for_bom` over every 0..5-byte string of an 8-byte alphabet plus 1M random prefixes, 3,295,073 checks; one-shot decodes of every 1- and 2-byte sequence alone, before `A`/`\n` and after `a`, every EUC-JP `8F xx yy`, every ISO-2022-JP two-byte tail after each escape, every gb18030/GBK four-byte form `[81-FE][30-39][00-FF][00-FF]`, UTF-8 three- and four-byte forms, UTF-16 surrogate pairs and halves, and every scalar value encoded by encoding_rs (or as UTF-16) both as one stream and one by one, 232,179,607 checks over 3.1 GB; seeded random streams of 20 MB per encoding (random bytes, encoded random text with byte flips, deletions and insertions, byte-class mixes, BOM and partial-BOM starts) decoded in lockstep with random input chunks (1 B-64 KB) and output sizes (1 B-8 KB, at least 4 for the last call as decode.rs guarantees), comparing result, read, written and output after every call, 1,119,045 calls over 885 MB, and again with 1-16-byte chunks and outputs, 54,649,808 calls over 219 MB: 0 differences. A copy with three injected bugs (EUC-KR's room check at 4 bytes, gb18030's pointer 7457 mapped to U+E7C8, ISO-2022-JP's repeated-escape error dropped) shows differences in all three. rg: output/enc-rg-equal/run.py runs release psh of e86dae0d8 and of this tree (the new build carried an interim UTF-8 valid-prefix scan, a shift DFA, that this tree replaces with `std::str::from_utf8`; both versions pass output/enc-equal call for call, and rg sees only the decoder's per-call results) as `psh -c 'rg ...'` over 93 files (15 legacy encodings in short, long and corrupted forms, 5 MB UTF-16LE/BE with BOM, UTF-16 without BOM, odd lengths and lone surrogates, UTF-8 BOM in front of UTF-16, BOM-only and partial-BOM files, invalid UTF-8, random and escape-heavy bytes) with 27 `-E` choices (no `-E`, auto, none, utf-8, UTF-16, utf-16le/be, latin1, windows-1252, sjis, shift_jis, euc-jp, iso-2022-jp, gbk, gb18030, big5, euc-kr, koi8-r, macintosh, ibm866, windows-874, iso-8859-8-i, x-user-defined, ` Windows-1251 `, replacement, a bogus label), 10 flag sets (-n, -c, --json, -o, -a -n, -U -c, -b --vimgrep, --count-matches, -v -c, -C1 -n -m 3) and 12 patterns, from files and pipes: stdout, stderr and exit status byte for byte equal in all 26,386 cases (10,951 with output, 1.72 GB of stdout; statuses 0 x9,344, 1 x15,088, 2 x1,954), 0 differences. Benchmark (output/enc-equal bench, release, 8 KB input chunks into a 64 KB output as decode.rs feeds them, median of 15 interleaved rounds, MB/s encoding_rs -> new; the shared Hand was loaded, so read ratios): UTF-16LE 222 -> 193, UTF-8 14,066 -> 397 (encoding_rs validates with simdutf8's AVX2; std's validator is what safe code has, and a shift-DFA validator tried here was not faster, so it was not kept; UTF-8 decoding only runs for an explicit `-E utf-8`, since a UTF-8 BOM keeps the undecoded path), windows-1252 50 -> 40, Shift_JIS 226 -> 185, GBK 79 -> 97, EUC-KR 209 -> 198, Big5 182 -> 108, EUC-JP 216 -> 180, ISO-2022-JP 248 -> 168, x-user-defined 1,056 -> 567; the four-units-per-word UTF-16 path and checking Big5's four two-code-point pointers only where its index is null were adopted from a first round (UTF-16LE 317 -> 216, Big5 165 -> 118 before them). The trait has the bstr `ByteSlice` methods the wtf8, vm and parser crates resolved to bstr (found by removing the imports and compiling): `find`, `rfind`, `find_iter` (memchr's `memmem`, as bstr's were), `find_byte`, `find_byteset`/`rfind_byteset` (memchr, memchr2, memchr3 up to three bytes, a 256-entry table past that, none for an empty set), `contains_str`, `starts_with_str`, `ends_with_str`, `split_str`/`rsplit_str`/`splitn_str`/`rsplitn_str` (bstr's iterators ported, so an empty separator splits at every byte with an empty piece at each end and a limit of 0 yields nothing), `replace`/`replacen`, `trim`/`trim_start`/`trim_end` (Unicode White_Space by `char::is_whitespace` on each decoded character, where bstr ran its regex-automata DFA for `\s+`) and `trim_with`/`trim_start_with`/`trim_end_with` (the predicate sees each character decoded as bstr decodes it: forward by maximal invalid subparts through `utf8_chunks`, backward by bstr's `decode_last`, which steps back at most three continuation bytes and else takes one byte, each invalid part as U+FFFD). vm's bytes, bytearray, str, bytes_inner, frame and `_io` import it from `rustpython_common::wtf8::byte_slice`; `Wtf8Buf::insert_wtf8` splices where it called `ByteVec::insert_str`; the parser's one call (`find_non_ascii_byte`) is `bytes().position(|byte| !byte.is_ascii())`, so it needs no trait. - jiff leaves RustPython: the time module's code for targets that are neither Unix nor Windows (wasm32) uses its own calendar and a jiff-compatible strftime, and the build script dates the commit with nanocode-platform's zone reader; jiff, jiff-core, jiff-static, jiff-tzdb, jiff-tzdb-platform, portable-atomic-util and defmt (with defmt-macros and defmt-parser) leave the lock (2026-11-12). On Linux and macOS time.localtime, gmtime, mktime, strftime, asctime, ctime, timezone, altzone, daylight and tzname never reached jiff: they go through libc in rustpython-host_env and are unchanged; jiff was compiled into nanocode-cli only because rustpython-vm depended on it unconditionally and its build script used it. crates/patches/rustpython-vm/src/stdlib/time/civil.rs (non-Unix, non-Windows only) is a civil DateTime over nanocode-platform's civil_from_days and days_from_civil (now public, and days_from_civil no longer Unix-only), with jiff 0.2.39's limits (years -9999..=9999, Unix seconds -377705023201..=253402207200, the same OverflowErrors), weekday, day of year and ISO week date, and a strftime that reproduces jiff's lenient Display: flags _ 0 - ^ #, widths up to 255 (integer padding capped at 20, the space-padded negative case uncapped), colons, %C %y %g of negative years, %c %x %X %r as jiff's locale-free "%Y M%m %-d, %a %H:%M:%S" family, %f %N %.Nf, and a directive it cannot format (%Z %z %:z %Q %s on a zone-less time, unknown letters, a dangling flag, width or colon, a width past 255) written back literally from its percent sign. The system zone on those targets is what jiff's TimeZone::system() returned on wasm32-unknown-unknown without its js feature, Etc/Unknown, which behaves as UTC with abbreviation "UTC": tm_zone "UTC", tm_gmtoff 0, mktime as UTC. The current time comes from std's SystemTime (it panics on wasm32-unknown-unknown, as jiff's Timestamp::now did with its own message; nanocode's boot.py routes time.time, localtime(), gmtime(), ctime() and strftime without a tuple through the host clock, so only asctime() without arguments reaches it) or, with the wasmbind feature, from JavaScript's Date.now as jiff's js feature did. build.rs takes nanocode-platform as a build dependency: git's commit time (or the clock) is shifted by utc_offset_seconds in the build host's zone (TZ, then /etc/localtime) and printed as "%b %e %Y" and "%H:%M:%S" by hand. nanocode-platform now parses a POSIX rule in TZ with the extended (TZif v3) syntax, rule times from -167 to 167 hours, as jiff and glibc do; before, such a TZ was refused and /etc/localtime used. What is not equal: (1) on wasm32-wasi, which nanocode does not build, jiff read a zone from TZ in the WASI environment; this code uses UTC there as on wasm32-unknown-unknown; (2) with the wasmbind feature, which nothing in nanocode enables, jiff took the browser's zone from Intl and its bundled tzdb; this code uses UTC; (3) for a TZ of the permanent-DST form DST from Jan 1 0:00 to Dec 31 25:00 (EST5EDT,0/0,J365/25), jiff 0.2.39 shows standard time in the five hours after each new year and nanocode-platform (like glibc) stays in DST, which can change the build host's date string within those hours; (4) an invalid TZ falls back to /etc/localtime's zone in nanocode-platform where jiff used UTC (the same on hosts whose /etc/localtime is UTC); (5) a now() reading outside jiff's range is an OverflowError instead of a panic. Equality: output/time-equal links jiff 0.2.39 beside civil.rs (included by path) and compares DateTime::new over random and out-of-range fields, Unix seconds to civil time over the whole range and past both ends with random nanoseconds, to_unix against jiff's to_zoned(Etc/Unknown) (and Etc/Unknown against UTC), the struct_time fields, strftime of every directive under every flag, 18 widths and 0 to 4 colons on boundary and random times, the dot forms, edge strings and random format strings mixing directives, flags, digits, colons and non-ASCII: seeds 1, 2, 3 at 20,000 cases give 724,131, 724,703 and 723,493 checks, seeds 11, 12, 13 at 200,000 cases 5,996,811, 5,996,356 and 6,000,562, 0 differences; build_date runs the old build.rs (jiff) and the new one side by side with git's timestamp stubbed, once per TZ: all 454 files of /usr/share/zoneinfo, 21 TZ values (POSIX rules with southern-hemisphere, half-hour, 45-minute, negative-DST, +13/+14, extended negative and 25-hour rule times; ":name", an absolute path, empty, invalid, "localtime") and TZ unset, each at every transition jiff lists (first 4,000) +-1 s and 900 random times: 2,124,379 checks, differences only in the two permanent-DST strings (6,002 each, case 3). End to end, output/time-e2e builds nanocode-python for wasm32-unknown-unknown from e86dae0d8 and from this tree into a cdylib run by Node with a fixed host clock: four programs (78,126 lines: gmtime, localtime and ctime of 738 timestamps including infinities, NaN and out-of-range values; mktime, asctime and strftime of 1,772 tuples including invalid fields and DST-gap and fold times; 8,817 format strings, every directive under every flag, width and colon count plus random ones, on 8 tuples including years -9999, -50, 1 and 9999; the module constants, struct_time, strptime and error cases) run as 42 slices: 78,258 lines of output, byte-identical. The same corpus was not run natively old against new: on Linux and macOS this change compiles none of the time module's code it edits (only build.rs, whose equality build_date shows), and the scope asked for no more release builds of RustPython on the shared Hand. Speed (release, interleaved, 7 rounds, best): strftime "%a %b %e %H:%M:%S %Y" 150 ns jiff against 203 ns, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S" 98 against 156, every directive 1,089 against 2,008; seconds to civil fields 7.0 against 27.5 ns; mktime 5.5 against 9.2 ns: slower, and only wasm32 builds run this code. cargo metadata 489 -> 480 packages; nanocode-cli on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu 299 -> 297 and on aarch64-apple-darwin 300 -> 298 packages (cargo tree -e normal,build), nanocode-python on wasm32-unknown-unknown 115 -> 113 (jiff, jiff-core, jiff-tzdb and jiff-tzdb-platform leave; the build script's nanocode-platform brings tokio and getrandom for the host). Commands: cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli, cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown, cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-vm (native and wasm32), cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-platform (native and wasm32), civil 1|2|3 20000, civil 11|12|13 200000, civil bench, zones.sh, e2e.sh.

- RustPython's lock types are built on rustpython-common's own port of the lock_api layer, and parking_lot, parking_lot_core and lock_api leave nanocode-cli (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-common/src/lock/api.rs carries what RustPython used of lock_api 0.4.14: the raw-lock traits (`RawMutex`, `RawRwLock` with its `is_locked_exclusive` default, `RawRwLockDowngrade`, `RawRwLockRecursive`, `RawRwLockUpgrade`, `RawRwLockUpgradeDowngrade`, `GetThreadId`), the `GuardSend`/`GuardNoSend` markers, and `Mutex`/`RwLock` with their guards, mapped guards (`map`, `try_map`), `upgradable_read`/`upgrade`, `downgrade`, `read_recursive`/`try_read_recursive`, `get_mut`, `into_inner`, `raw`, `data_ptr` and the same `Send`/`Sync` bounds and `Debug` output (`Mutex { data: .. }`, `<locked>`). Without the `threading` feature (nanocode's build) every PyMutex/PyRwLock is still the Cell-based raw lock of lock/cell_lock.rs, so locking behaves exactly as before; with `threading`, lock/parking.rs adapts parking_lot's raw locks to the new traits and parking_lot becomes an optional dependency of rustpython-vm and rustpython-stdlib that only their `threading` feature enables (it is on rustpython-host_env only for Windows). The places that took a parking_lot lock outside `threading` now use std: the csv dialect registry and field limit, the interpreter-admission gate (vm/runtime.rs, gc_state.rs) and the `_interpqueues`/`_interpchannels` registries take a `rustpython_common::lock::BlockingMutex` (a `std::sync::Mutex` whose `lock` ignores poisoning, as parking_lot has none), `_interpchannels`' blocked `send()` waits on a `std::sync::Condvar` (`wait`, and `wait_timeout` to the deadline in place of `wait_until`), host_env's `AppendLog` uses `std::sync::Mutex` the same way, hashlib's per-object state is a `PyMutex`, and `_functools`' lru_cache reentrant lock is, without `threading`, a depth counter (parking_lot's reentrant mutex on one thread only ever counted). TigerStyle departure, bounded to the vendored interpreter: these are blocking std locks and a condition variable rather than nanocode-sync primitives, because RustPython's object model hands out guards from shared references everywhere and porting it to an owner-and-mailbox design is a rewrite of the interpreter; the new lock layer uses the same unsafe as lock_api (cells handed out under a held raw lock), which the vendored crates already rely on. The `threading` feature did not build before this change either (`dyn Limiter` is not `Send + Sync` in vm/runtime.rs, _thread.rs and thread.rs, checked at e86dae0d8 on gak-9) and still does not. Equality: in nanocode's configuration the raw locks, guard order and unlock points are unchanged and nothing runs on a second thread, so lock behavior is identical; the end-to-end corpus (output/e2e) exercises every object access through these locks. `cargo metadata` 481 packages before and after (the optional dependency keeps parking_lot in Cargo.lock); `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 287 to 284 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 288 to 285 (aarch64-apple-darwin). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-common -p rustpython-host_env -p rustpython-vm -p rustpython-stdlib` on Linux and `cargo check -p nanocode-python` on aarch64-apple-darwin pass.
- rustpython-host_env loses the modules nanocode's Python never compiles a user of, and its remaining system calls go through the libc calls the crate already makes; nix, memmap2, memoffset and cfg_aliases leave (2026-11-12). nanocode builds rustpython-vm and rustpython-stdlib without their `host_env` feature, so the stdlib and vm modules that called host_env's faulthandler, grp, mmap, multiprocessing, pwd, select, shm, syslog, socket (Unix), resource, posix, posix_unix_like, fcntl and thread modules (os, posix, socket, select, mmap, fcntl, grp, pwd, resource, syslog, faulthandler, _multiprocessing, posixshmem, _thread with threading) are compiled out, as the earlier termios deletion was; those 14 host_env files are deleted, and the five `ToPyException` impls in vm/src/exceptions.rs for their error types now also require `feature = "host_env"`. `builtins.input`'s session-leader test (`getsid(0) == getpid()`) moves from host_env::posix to host_env::os unchanged. What nanocode does compile is ported: time.rs's `clock_gettime`/`clock_getres` on Unix use the libc bodies the file already had for WASI, `clock_settime` and `nanosleep` build a `libc::timespec` (seconds that do not fit `time_t` are an InvalidInput error where nix's `as` cast wrapped), fileutils' `StatStruct`/`fstat` are `libc::stat`/`libc::fstat`, io.rs's directory test is `st_mode & S_IFMT == S_IFDIR` with EISDIR, `page_size` is `sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE)`, `set_errno` writes `__errno_location()` (Linux) or `__error()` (Apple), and `copy_file_range` (only the compiled-out os module used it) is gone. These are the same system calls nix and rustix made, through the same libc the crate already calls with unsafe elsewhere (the vendored interpreter is outside the workspace's forbid(unsafe_code)). rustix leaves rustpython-host_env (it stays in Cargo.lock for nanocode-process and nanocode-tui until those move). Not equal: the `host_env` features of the vendored vm and stdlib no longer build (nanocode never enables them); `time.sleep`'s error for a failed nanosleep other than EINTR reads `nanosleep: Invalid argument` (strerror) where nix printed `nanosleep: EINVAL: Invalid argument`, a path a valid `timespec` cannot reach. Equality: nothing that was compiled into nanocode's interpreter changed behavior besides the ports above, which call the same functions; the end-to-end corpus (output/e2e, old e86dae0d8 against the branch head) covers time.monotonic, perf_counter, process_time and clock_gettime. `cargo metadata` 484 to 481 packages; `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 291 to 287 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 292 to 288 (aarch64-apple-darwin). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` pass on Linux, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python` on aarch64-apple-darwin (gak-9).

- nanocode-telemetry carries a server host's telemetry on nanocode-observability's own span model, batch processor, OTLP exporter and subscriber, and opentelemetry, opentelemetry_sdk, tracing-subscriber, sharded-slab, thread_local, futures-executor, rand 0.9.5, rand_chacha 0.9.0, ppv-lite86, zerocopy and zerocopy-derive leave the workspace (2026-11-12; nanocode-telemetry was their last user and is not in nanocode-cli's tree; imbl stays for nanocode-sync, nanocode-durability, code mode, subagents and the Claude backend, lazy_static for x509-parser). crates/integrations/telemetry now depends on nanocode-observability, nanocode-sync, serde_json and tracing: `GenAi<E: nanocode_observability::SpanExporter>` renames spans, adds the gen_ai.* attributes, folds content events and reports `Exported` exactly as before, with opentelemetry's `Value::as_str` reproduced (bool, i64 and f64 through Display, a string array as `["a","b"]`); `Held<P: nanocode_observability::SpanProcessor>` keeps the holding, slow/error/one_in export decision, `most` limit, expiry and `Ended` callbacks, with imbl::Vector replaced inside the same `Atom` (copy-on-write, lock-free) by nanocode-sync `Map`s keyed by (trace, position) with a per-trace length and a due queue keyed by sequence number; `Lines` and `Counters` are `subscriber::Layer`s (`Counters::layer` returns a `Filtered`), `line(event)` is unchanged, `Exports::filter` returns `filter::FilterFn`, and `METRICS_TARGET` re-exports nanocode-observability's (same value). Public API changes: nanocode-observability now exports `Event`, `KeyValue`, `Resource` (with `Resource::detected()`, the SDK's default detectors, plus `insert`/`merge`), `Scope`, `SpanContext` (public fields, `INVALID`), `SpanData`, `SpanKind`, `Status`, `Text`, `Value` with public fields, the `SpanExporter` and `SpanProcessor` traits, `BatchConfig` (SDK defaults 2,048 / 5 s / 512; `with_env()` lets set and parseable OTEL_BSP_* values win, batch size capped at the queue size as the SDK does), `BatchSpanProcessor::new(exporter, config)`, `OtlpSpanExporter::build(endpoint, &resource, &scope)`, `Tracer::new(processors)`/`shutdown_with_timeout`, `OtelLayer::new(tracer)`/`OtelSpan`; `subscriber::LAYER_SLOTS` goes from 3 to 8 and `Registry::new` takes `[Option<Filtered>; N]` for any N up to 8 (slots in a boxed slice; table entries stay 128 bytes, 8 data slots of 8 bytes). nanocode-telemetry: `GenAi::export` is synchronous; `Held` implements only `on_end` and `shutdown_with_timeout` (which still releases held traces first), so `on_start`, `force_flush` and `set_resource` go. pyramid-core's crates/kernel/src/telemetry.rs migrates as follows: `Resource::builder()` plus `with_service_name("pyramid")` becomes `Resource::detected()` merged with `Resource { attributes: vec![KeyValue::new("service.name", "pyramid")], schema_url: None }` when OTEL_SERVICE_NAME is unset; opentelemetry-otlp's `SpanExporter::builder().with_http().with_protocol(HttpBinary).build()` becomes `OtlpSpanExporter::build(&endpoint, &resource, &Scope { name: "pyramid".into(), version: None })` with endpoint OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT as given, else OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT without a trailing `/` plus `/v1/traces` (headers still from OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_HEADERS/OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS; any compression variable is refused with `OtlpError::Compression`); `GenAi::new(exporter, Some(AGENT), exported)` and `Held::new(processor, holding, ended)` keep their signatures; `BatchSpanProcessor::builder(exporter, runtime::Tokio).with_batch_config(batch_config()).build()` becomes `BatchSpanProcessor::new(exporter, BatchConfig { max_queue_size: 65_536, max_export_batch_size: 2_048, scheduled_delay: Duration::from_secs(1) }.with_env())`; `SdkTracerProvider::builder().with_resource(..).with_span_processor(held).build()` becomes `Tracer::new(vec![Box::new(held)])` (sampler and span limits still from OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER/_ARG and OTEL_SPAN_*_COUNT_LIMIT) and `Traces(Option<Tracer>)` calls `tracer.shutdown_with_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10))`; `tracing_opentelemetry::layer().with_tracer(provider.tracer("pyramid")).with_filter(exports.filter())` becomes `Filtered::new(OtelLayer::new(tracer.clone()), exports.filter())`; `tracing_subscriber::registry().with(product).with(export).with(Lines(log).with_filter(filter_fn(sqlx_warning))).with(Lines(log).with_filter(filter_fn(kernel_line))).with(Counters(..).layer()).try_init()` becomes `nanocode_observability::init(Registry::new([product, export, Some(Filtered::new(Lines(log), FilterFn(sqlx_warning))), Some(Filtered::new(Lines(log), FilterFn(kernel_line))), Some(Counters(..).layer())]))` (or `tracing::dispatcher::set_global_default(Dispatch::new(..))` to skip the log bridge `init` also installs), where the product layer implements `subscriber::Layer` and comes as an `Option<Filtered>` (an unfiltered one takes `FilterFn(|_| true)`). What is not equal: the span model has no remote-parent flag, so a request root is a Server span without a parent (opentelemetry also counted a Server span with a remote parent; neither nanocode-observability's layer nor pyramid-core creates remote parents), and attribute arrays of bool, i64 or f64 are not representable (only string arrays are); pyramid's default tracing-opentelemetry context activation has no counterpart (there is no OpenTelemetry `Context::current`; parents come from tracing's span tree, the nearest exported entered span); the batch processor exports one batch at a time with blocking reqwest on its own thread instead of the Tokio-runtime processor with 4 concurrent exports, and has no force_flush; an OTEL_BSP_* variable that is set but unparsable now keeps pyramid's value where pyramid's code kept the SDK default; only http/protobuf is sent (OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL is not read); a registry holds at most 8 layers. nanocode-cli is unchanged: its tree is 261 packages before and after (`cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`), and its install path builds the same 3-slot registry and the same batch configuration from the environment. Proven with output/telemetry-equal (old = crates/integrations/telemetry at e86dae0d8 renamed, with opentelemetry 0.32.0, opentelemetry_sdk 0.32.1, tracing-subscriber 0.3.23 and imbl 7.0.2, beside the new crate; 10 seeds): GenAi over 200,000 random batches (0 to 11 spans: model.call, tool.call, tool.execute, agent and other names, renamed and provider attributes of every value type, code.module.name and target prefixes, content events of every kind with prompts, item lists, output items, reasoning, malformed JSON and non-string content, failing and succeeding inner exporters, 4 agent settings) comparing every exported span as canonical JSON, the batch results and the Exported sequence: 1,751,776 checks, 0 differences; Held over 200,000 seeded sequences (up to 39 spans over 1 to 5 traces, Server roots and children with known, unknown and missing parents, durations around a 1 h `slow` and before start, error statuses, one_in 0, 1, 2, 3, 7, 100 and u128::MAX, most 0 to 11 and 8,192, string, number, bool and array targets against holding targets, `slow` 0 for expiry at the next span and 1 h for none, then shutdown) comparing what reaches the inner processor and the Ended callbacks: 8,007,999 checks, 0 differences; Exports::filter over 400 random configurations against 3,000 random metadata each (16 targets plus random text, 5 levels, event, span and hint kinds, content_kind field presence): 1,200,000 checks, 0 differences; Lines (sqlx and kernel filters as pyramid sets them, plus an all-pass one) and Counters in one registry each over 200,000 events from 400 callsites with spans: 223,190 lines and counters, 0 differences. output/otel-equal (old opentelemetry-based stack against a copy of this crate, `python3 drive.py 20 500 40` and `20 520 40`): 280 checks over 40 scenarios, every trace, span-header and stdout check equal, 16 differing metric files all in threaded scenarios whose gauges race (old against old on the 5 threaded scenarios of the first run differs on 8 of 35 checks). `cargo metadata --locked` 462 -> 451 packages. Checks: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-telemetry -p nanocode-observability` native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-telemetry -p nanocode-observability` (no warnings); nanocode-cli is the only other workspace crate depending on either.
- nanocode-observability formats and filters tracing with its own subscriber, and tracing-subscriber leaves it (2026-11-12). `subscriber::Registry` implements `tracing_core::Subscriber` with the three ordered filtered layer slots `install` builds (fmt, OpenTelemetry spans, metrics), reproducing `registry().with(fmt).with(otel).with(metrics)` of tracing-subscriber 0.3.23: per-layer filter bits per slot (two for the metrics layer's nested `MetricsFilter` inside `scope(otel).and(filter_fn)`) set in `enabled` and consumed by `did_enable` as `FilterState` does, the combined callsite interest and `max_level_hint` of `Layered::pick_interest`/`pick_level_hint` including the None-layer and `FilterMap::any_enabled` quirks (a callsite every filter rejects still gets interest sometimes and a span that reaches no layer), visibility of a span to a layer only when its filter enabled it (`Context::span`, `lookup_current` falling back through the thread's stack, `SpanRef::parent`, `scope`, `from_root`, `event_span`), per-thread current-span stacks with duplicate enters, reference counts with close at zero and parents closed iteratively. Spans live in a paged table of 128-byte-aligned entries reused in place (ids are generation << 32 | index + 1, free lists sharded by thread, metadata interned once per callsite, each layer's span data an Arc written once at `new_span`): a first version publishing an `Arc` per span through arc-swap measured 185 ns per insert/load/remove single-threaded and 625 ns with 4 threads, so span bookkeeping now does no arc-swap writes. `subscriber::Layer` (associated per-span `Span` type, `new_span` returning it, `on_record`/`on_follows_from`/`on_event`/`on_enter`/`on_exit`/`on_close` with `SpanRef`/`Context`, `Registry::data` for code outside the subscriber) carries the fmt layer, the OpenTelemetry span layer and the metrics layer; the span layer keeps `OtelData` and its timings behind a per-span nanocode-sync `Sequencer` turn and `Slot` (its lazy start needs exclusive mutation with a synchronous result; a contended turn parks on `Sequencer::enter`), and `span_context`/`add_link` reach it through `Dispatch::downcast_ref::<Registry>()` and `Registry::data`. `format.rs`, `pretty.rs`, `json.rs` and `style.rs` reproduce the compact (no ANSI), pretty (ANSI unless NO_COLOR is set non-empty) and JSON (span list, no current span) formats byte for byte with NEW and CLOSE span events and their `time.busy`/`time.idle`, escaping, error source lists, `r#` and `log.` field rules and the RFC 3339 timestamp from `nanocode_platform::system_time` (so a simulated host's clock shows); `filter.rs` and `env_filter.rs` port `Targets`, `EnvFilter` (its directive state machine with every quirk, dynamic span and field matching, the static-max-level warning) and `scope`; `log_bridge.rs` replaces tracing-log's `LogTracer` and `NormalizeEvent` (log records become events with the record's target, file and line); `pattern.rs` matches field-value patterns with a Pike VM over the regex syntax nanocode's regex-automata build accepts (no Unicode Perl classes or case folding there), with the DFA's unanchored leftmost-first match-at-end semantics and its `x+`/`(x+)?` compilation of repetitions. Public type change: `ObservabilityError::Filter` holds `filter::ParseError` (same Display texts) instead of tracing-subscriber's; no caller matches on it. What is not equal: span ids (opaque) are numbered differently; a directive whose untrimmed text puts a multi-byte character where tracing-subscriber's trimmed byte offsets land mid-character makes tracing-subscriber panic and us return `invalid filter directive` (3,609 and 3,502 of two runs of ~285k random filter strings); field-value patterns using flag groups, class set operations (`&&`, `--`, `~~`) or negated nested classes are rejected (`invalid field filter: error building NFA`, the text regex-automata prints for its own errors) where regex-automata accepts them, and patterns needing more than 65,536 instructions are rejected; a span whose last reference drops inside another span's `on_close` on the same thread is closed and freed here while tracing-subscriber's `CLOSE_COUNT` never frees it (nor closes its parent), and a parent is closed through this registry rather than `dispatcher::get_default`; the fmt layer's busy/idle use atomics, so a span entered on several threads at once may split an overlapping instant differently (single-threaded identical), and its debug-only assertion that a closing span is not entered is gone. Proven with output/obs-subscriber (each stack installed as the global dispatcher in its own process, old = tracing-subscriber 0.3.23 with the old install code and a FormatTime printing tracing-subscriber's own datetime.rs, new = this code with a platform host returning the same fixed time; seeded sequences over 50 event and 150 span callsites across 10 targets and 5 levels: every primitive field type, strings needing escapes, Debug, Display and error values with source chains, failing Debug, empty spans, records after creation, explicit, contextual and root parents, out-of-order exits and closes, duplicate enters, follows_from, log-crate records, 1 to 3 threads in lockstep, `Span::current`/`is_disabled` markers, random timestamps from year -95,000 to 14,000): 3,640 runs of 900 random filter strings plus DEFAULT_FILTER, `DEFAULT_FILTER,nc_metrics=info`, `trace`, `info` and the empty filter in compact, JSON, pretty and pretty with NO_COLOR, 16,064 sequences, 868,126 lines, 0 differences after replacing only busy/idle values; 1,810 runs of three recorder layers in all 8 presence combinations with random filters (two of them with a filter_fn `and`), 8,272 sequences, 420,676 lines of callbacks, visibility, parents, scopes and current spans, 0 differences; 569,730 random filter strings parsed, 0 differences in Ok or error Display beyond the panics above; 450,000 random patterns against matchers 0.2.0, 18,000,000 string and Debug matches, 0 differences; 1,500,000 timestamps identical; output/otel-equal (agent 39's end-to-end OTLP harness, old pre-OpenTelemetry-port stack against this tree): 80 scenarios, 560 checks, every trace, span-header and stdout check equal, 34 differing metric files all in threaded scenarios whose gauge values race (old against old differs on 8 of 10 of them too). Interleaved benchmark, compact layer to a discarding sink, filter `warn,nanocode=info`, median of 3 rounds, ns per op old -> new (load average ~11 on 5 cores): spans created, entered, exited and closed with the layer enabled 5,212 -> 4,401 (4 threads 9,920 -> 7,912), filtered out 456 -> 173 (819 -> 715), events in a span 1,432 -> 1,279 (2,339 -> 1,627), filtered-out events 98 -> 66 (75 -> 138; this 4-thread row moved between -22% and +85% across three runs), nested span plus event 7,600 -> 6,717 (12,425 -> 12,031). `cargo metadata --locked` 469 -> 462 packages (aho-corasick, matchers, nu-ansi-term, regex-syntax, tracing-log, tracing-serde, valuable leave; tracing-subscriber, sharded-slab, thread_local and lazy_static stay for nanocode-telemetry, regex-automata for bstr); nanocode-cli reaches 261 packages instead of 270 (`cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`: tracing-subscriber, matchers, regex-syntax, nu-ansi-term, sharded-slab, thread_local, tracing-log, tracing-serde, lazy_static leave). Checks: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-observability`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-observability` native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- Our own argument parser replaces clap (2026-11-12; Georgios reversed "clap stays"). crates/core/arguments (nanocode-arguments, std only, native and wasm32) declares a command line as const tables (`Command`, `Group`, `Argument`, `Choice`, `Parser`) and reproduces clap 4.6.2 as nanocode used it: lexing (long `=` values, short clusters with attached and `=` values, `--`, non-UTF-8 arguments), pending values and their resolution order, env fallbacks read when parsing (empty values included, flags take only `true`/`false`), defaults, global arguments propagated down and their values merged up (a deeper level wins ties, a command-line value beats env), required, required-unless, requires and conflicts, the help subcommand and `help <path>`, `-h` and `--help` (long help with possible-value lists and next-line layout at clap's fixed 100 columns, since wrap_help was off), `-V`, bin names from argv[0], and every error clap could produce here with its usage line (including the derive's per-struct argument groups that showed up in the `unexpected value` usage), `tip:` lines, strsim's Jaro suggestions above 0.7 and `For more information, try '--help'.`. Output is built styled with clap's ANSI styles and written as anstream did: raw when the stream is a terminal and NO_COLOR, CLICOLOR_FORCE, CLICOLOR, TERM and CI allow it, otherwise through a port of anstyle-parse's VT state machine that strips escapes (the stream variant keeps parser state across printable runs, the `Display` variant the TUI's /runner uses resets it, as anstream's two strippers do). bin/nanocode/src/cli.rs keeps every struct and enum with the same fields (so Debug is unchanged) and builds them from `Matches`; commands.rs's `RunnerCommand::try_parse_from` and app.rs's reload_args (now over `COMMAND.arguments()`) keep their shape. Downstream: `nanocode_observability::ObservabilityOutputArgs` keeps its name and `log_file`, `log_filter`, `enabled` and `builder`, and gains `ARGUMENTS` and `from_matches`; its clap `Args`/`FromArgMatches` impls are gone, so `#[command(flatten)]` over it no longer compiles; tempoxyz/pyramid and tempoxyz/pyramid-core reference neither it nor nanocode-observability (GitHub code search, default branches). `CuaCommand::BrowserHost::args` gets `#[allow(dead_code)]`: clap's generated reader was its only reader. Not equal: on Windows consoles without VT support anstream translated styles through wincon and we write ANSI; on targets other than unix and Windows a non-UTF-8 attached value (`--cd=<bytes>`) is an invalid-UTF-8 error, since std has no safe way to split such an OsStr there. Equality (output/clap-equal: clap 4.6.2 with the verbatim origin/master definitions beside the new tables, in-process): 24,806,166 checks, 0 differences over seeds 2 to 10 (1.62M argv cases from the real flag set with typos, `=`/separate values, repeats, `--`, non-UTF-8 bytes, 9 argv[0] forms and random env for all 20 env-backed arguments; each compares styled bytes, Display bytes, stream, exit code and parsed Debug, plus reload_args twice, /runner parses and errors, and 8.1M fuzzed strings through both strippers against anstream; seed 1 found the stream stripper's state carry-over, fixed); a pty harness running the old and new parsers as binaries under pty, pipes and mixed stdout/stderr with 12 env sets (NO_COLOR set/empty, CLICOLOR_FORCE=1, CLICOLOR=0/1, TERM=dumb/unset, CI, COLUMNS=40, escape bytes in env values) and 3 argv[0]: 6,480 runs (2,310 styled), run before and after rebasing, 0 differences. Commands: cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli, cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-arguments (also --target wasm32-unknown-unknown), cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-arguments, -p nanocode-observability --lib and -p nanocode-cli (clean). clap, clap_builder, clap_derive, clap_lex, anstream, anstyle, anstyle-parse, anstyle-query, anstyle-wincon, once_cell_polyfill, colorchoice, is_terminal_polyfill, utf8parse and strsim leave; heck stays for sqlx-macros-core. Packages 484 -> 471. `cargo metadata` 484 -> 471 packages at 1f10a22ea, 482 -> 469 on deps2-obs after the OpenTelemetry change (the 14 crates in the title leave, nanocode-arguments joins; heck stays for sqlx-macros-core).
- nanocode-cli keeps mimalloc and libmimalloc-sys (2026-11-12, measured for the ~0-dependencies round, left to the coordinator as asked: the system allocator is not within noise). output/alloc-bench links the nanocode crate (no default features, local-cells, as nanocode-cli does) in a release build twice, with and without `mimalloc::MiMalloc` (0.1.52, no_thp) as the global allocator, on a 4-worker Tokio runtime; medians of 7 interleaved rounds on this 5-core Linux Hand at load 12-17, system -> mimalloc: 400 Code Mode cells on each of 8 concurrent tasks (a cell builds, stringifies and parses 400 objects in djs, then the task round-trips an agent transcript item through serde_json) user CPU 1.313 -> 1.149 s (-12.5%), wall 1.743 -> 1.364 s, max RSS 11.8 -> 14.3 MB; 4 tasks serializing and parsing 200 batches of 500 transcript items each and freeing them on another task user 2.713 -> 2.025 s (-25%), wall 4.412 -> 2.770 s, max RSS 97.9 -> 93.1 MB; process start (runtime built, then exit, 140 runs) 28 ms wall and 11.3 MB for both. This agrees with the 2026-11-10 entry (20,000-agent swarm user CPU 61.3 -> 54.6 s, resident 2.6-2.9 -> 2.1-2.2 GB) and the no_thp entry's start-up numbers. Dropping it would cost 12-25% CPU on allocation-heavy agent work for 2 packages and a C build (libmimalloc-sys through cc, which ring already needs); replacing it means writing an allocator, which this round was told not to do.
