- nanocode-observability records spans and metrics with its own OpenTelemetry model, and opentelemetry, opentelemetry_sdk and tracing-opentelemetry leave nanocode-cli (2026-11-12, Georgios: "make this ~0 deps"). What the three did for the CLI is now in crates/integrations/observability: model.rs (values, span context, status, events, resource, scope, `ExportError`), trace.rs (the tracer: ParentBased(AlwaysOn) sampling and `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER`/`_ARG`, the 128 attribute, event and link limits and their `OTEL_SPAN_*_COUNT_LIMIT` variables, span and trace ids from a per-thread xoshiro256++ seeded by `nanocode_platform::fill_random`, start, record, end and shutdown), layer.rs (the tracing layer: tracing-opentelemetry 0.33's builder-then-started span lifecycle, `otel.name`/`otel.kind`/`otel.status_code`/`otel.status_description`, location, thread and target attributes, events, error fields and exception attributes, follows_from links, busy_ns/idle_ns), metrics.rs (the `monotonic_counter.`/`counter.`/`histogram.`/`gauge.` instruments, instrument name validation, sum, last-value and explicit-bucket aggregation with the default bounds, the 2,000 attribute-set cardinality limit and its overflow set, cumulative, delta and low-memory temporality, one periodic reader thread per exporter with `OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL`) and batch.rs (the batch span processor with the `OTEL_BSP_*` variables), all lock-free (`nanocode_sync::Atom` and `Map`, atomics, channels); otlp.rs, protobuf.rs, otlp_http.rs and file.rs now encode that model (typed.rs's integer restoration moved into the HTTP exporter). Public API: `ObservabilityError::OTelSdk` carries `nanocode_observability::ExportError` (the same Display texts as `OTelSdkError`), and `SpanContext`, `span_context(&Span)` and `add_link(&Span, SpanContext)` replace `OpenTelemetrySpanExt::context`/`add_link` in bin/nanocode/src/telemetry.rs; tempoxyz/pyramid-core and tempoxyz/pyramid do not use nanocode-observability (GitHub code search). nanocode-telemetry still depends on opentelemetry and opentelemetry_sdk for its public `GenAi`/`Held` (used by pyramid-core), so both stay in Cargo.lock; tracing-subscriber stays for now (its registry holds the per-span state). bin/nanocode names futures-util's `async-await-macro` feature for `futures_util::join!`, which futures-executor under opentelemetry_sdk used to switch on by feature unification. Proven equal with output/otel-equal, which links the old crate (a copy of 1ca10117c's nanocode-observability with opentelemetry 0.32.0, opentelemetry_sdk 0.32.1, tracing-opentelemetry 0.33.0 at the locked versions) beside a copy of the new one: (1) the JSON and protobuf encoders over 40,000 seeded random batches (escapes, unicode, integer-looking strings, NaN/inf/-0.0, string arrays, events, links, every kind and status, both schema URLs): 199,414 checks, 0 differences; (2) end to end, 164 seeded scenarios each run as two processes (old, new) through `ObservabilityBuilder::install` with the local OTLP directory and a mock OTLP/HTTP collector, driving random span trees (explicit, contextual and rootless parents, records before and after a span starts, 140-event and 140-record bursts past the limits, follows_from, `span_context`/`add_link`, error fields and error values with sources, every metric prefix including invalid names, case-colliding names and u64 above i64::MAX) under 7 filters, both telemetry levels and 12 environments (limits, the samplers, OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES and OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, delta and LowMemory temporality, small batches); timestamps, busy_ns/idle_ns and process.pid normalized, ids renamed by first appearance, resource attributes and data points sorted: traces.jsonl, metrics.jsonl, the protobuf trace and metric requests and stdout all equal in every single-threaded scenario (1,148 checks), and every span equal in the scenarios with two extra threads; the metric differences left in threaded scenarios (racing gauge last values) appear at the same rate between two runs of the old stack (26 of 126 checks on the same 18 seeds, against 26 of 126 old against new). Not equal, by design: resource attributes and metric data points are written in insertion order (the old SDK iterated a HashMap, so its order changed from process to process); a data point's attributes are its first measurement's field order (the old SDK exported either that or the sorted order, whichever key its HashMap met first); metric attribute sets compare f64 values by bit pattern (old: a NaN attribute never matched itself, so each NaN measurement took a new set up to the cardinality limit, and 0.0/-0.0 hashed apart); duplicate keys in one attribute set keep the first by a stable sort (old: unstable); ids are random either way but come from a different generator; a span that follows itself is linked to itself (tracing-opentelemetry deadlocked on its own mutex; the harness avoids that case); the batch processor does not join its thread after it acknowledges shutdown; the resource still reports telemetry.sdk.name/language/version opentelemetry/rust/0.32.1 and the meter scope tracing/tracing-opentelemetry 0.33.0, so collectors see what they saw. Invalid OTEL_* values are ignored as before, because the OpenTelemetry specification requires that and the variables are shared with other programs. Hot path, release harness, 200,000 iterations, 5 interleaved rounds at load 12-14, median ns per operation old -> new: a span with a field, an event inside and a record 6,283 -> 5,071; a parent entered with a child 8,663 -> 8,127; a span and event filtered out 518 -> 535; a metrics event with a histogram and a counter 308 -> 1,022 (each measurement is a copy-on-write `Atom` update with one allocation instead of the SDK's atomic add or mutex; the CLI emits these per terminal frame and loop wakeup, about 0.1 ms a second at 60 frames). `cargo metadata` 489 -> 487 packages (tracing-opentelemetry, web-time); nanocode-cli's tree (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and aarch64-apple-darwin) loses futures-executor, opentelemetry, opentelemetry_sdk, ppv-lite86, rand, rand_chacha, tracing-opentelemetry and zerocopy. Commands: cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli; cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-observability; cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-observability; cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-cli; in output/otel-equal: target/debug/otel-equal encode 20000 7 and 20000 99, python3 drive.py N SEED ROOTS, target/release/otel-equal bench old|new DIR 200000.
- `nanocode-turnlog` (crates/core/turnlog) and `nanocode_agent::OneLog` make one append-only log per scope, with one writer, the host's only durable store: `nanocode_log (seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, scope, body)` and `nanocode_snap (scope PRIMARY KEY, seq, body) WITHOUT ROWID` (2026-11-12). It replaces four writers on Durable Objects (the SessionLog event log, the RowStore checkpoint, the cell journal and the host's markers). A row body is JSON lines of `Record`s, and each durable point is one `INSERT ... RETURNING CAST(seq AS TEXT)` with no reads. A cold start reads one snapshot, then the tail after it. Rows are written only at A (admission), C (before a call of effect class External, through `EffectGate` for direct tools, `OneLogJournals` for Code Mode calls and `OneLog::effect` for in-object writes), F (finish, cancel or withdraw), a cancel request (committed before its acknowledgement), R (start of a turn that was unfinished at open, with its attempt and its open External calls reported as unknown), Floor (the first row of an incarnation) and Progress (a Durable checkpoint while the last row is a turn's R). Statuses, events, checkpoints (latest payload per state), tool results and cell journal updates are buffered and go into the next row. A snapshot is written when snapshot bytes plus tail bytes exceed 2 x the encoded fold. The rule "tail >= snapshot" wrote one on every new scope's first commit (1.28 rows/turn in the simulator against 0.14). `Policy.max_row_bytes` splits a row into parts that commit in the same tick, and a record that is too large alone is an error. `EffectClass::{External (default), Idempotent, None}`: `EffectClass::mcp(read_only, resumable)` derives MCP tools, read-only built-ins are None, and an undeclared tool is External. The checkpoint stays a record because a backend's `DurableState` cannot be derived from events. Event seqs: a reopen adds `EVENT_GAP` (1 << 14) to the last durable event seq, and the incarnation's first row carries `Floor`. Without the floor, the simulator reused a seq a client had seen in 54 of 5000 seeds (seed 1682): an incarnation that started idle published live events and crashed before any row. `Policy.restarts` caps consecutive R rows without log progress, and then the turn finishes Failed. Without Progress rows, 3479 of 38177 healthy turns hit the cap from restarts across the whole object, against 2468 with them. Exact attribution needs a durable "response arrived" marker and is not done. Gaps: no migration from SessionLog or RowStore data, hand tools are not declared Idempotent by default (their names come from each hand's catalog), and the event history lives in the fold, so a long session holds it in memory. Measured with output/turnlog-check (native Claude Code Mode against a scripted Messages mock, MemoryLog and SqlLog over SQLite, 10 turns): plain 2 rows (A+F), one External call 3 (A+C+F), one None call 2, and 0 warm reads. A crash while `charge` runs gives R+C+F, no second charge, 1 model call and "outcome unknown". A model that never answers with restarts = 3 gives A, R, R, R, then F Failed. Hosted on durable-cloudflare's workerd harness (`node output/sqlturn/run.mjs text|tool|reply 10`, nanocode-ts on this crate), a turn writes 2.0 rows with 3.0 statements and 3.0 event-loop commits, against 23.4/24.4/14.2 rows, 39.2/40.2/27.1 statements and 5.0/5.0/4.0 commits on 052f73db2. `npm run drill` passes. In the crash matrix, losing the commit in flight gives 0 double charges (as before). Rolling back two commits already confirmed can drop the C row after the charge ran, which workerd's output gate rules out. Checks: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-turnlog -p nanocode-tool-host -p nanocode-mcp-tools -p nanocode-agent -p nanocode`, the same with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `cargo clippy` with `-D warnings`.
- bin/nanocode-sim `--scenario turns` simulates a Durable Object turn host and runs a durability policy behind `TurnDurability` over a `LogHost` disk (disk.rs, one lock-free `Slot`) (2026-11-12). Each tick's appends, snapshots, workspace writes and subagent registrations commit atomically at its end. An output gate releases model requests, tool dispatches, acks and events only after that commit. A rolled-back seq is reused as SQLite's max+1 reuses it. The object crashes before commits (up to 8% per seed), after commits before output (up to 4%), at timed crashes, at deploys during long model calls, and on every attempt of a poison turn. The fault profiles add commit and read faults. The workload has multi-step scripted turns that call Read (None), Hand (Idempotent ledger), Charge (External ledger), Write (workspace) and Spawn. Clients resubmit, reconnect with after=<seq> and cancel, and client-less turns are redelivered until acked. `--policy reference` (onelog.rs) has a switch per protection (`--without admission|call_external|call_in_object|finish|progress|restart|result|snapshot`, `--live-seqs temporary|gap|reuse|floor`). `--policy turnlog` drives nanocode-turnlog through `SimHost`. tidy.rs now scans crates/core/turnlog. Invariants and canaries (`--mutation`): a charge applies at most once (`gate_releases_early`), a workspace write or spawn applies at most once (`tick_not_atomic`), every accepted turn ends durably (`recovery_skips_clientless`), a completed Idempotent call is never reported unknown (`idempotent_reported_unknown`), every event seq a client saw names that event in the durable log (`durable_seq_before_commit`, `seal_skipped`), and a turn reports one ending (`finish_before_row`). Each protection off on the reference policy (seeds 0..5000): no admission row loses turns in 4248 seeds, no C row before External calls charges twice in 1051, no C row on in-object ticks applies writes twice in 2827, no finish row fails liveness in 3780 and gives two endings in 1220, no restart row or cap crash-loops in 2133, and reused live seqs fail in 1516. Without the result row, snapshots or progress rows no invariant fails: they trade cost for fewer unknown outcomes (3667 vs 8806), cold reads (19.8 vs 25.0 rows) and fewer healthy turns capped. Results: `sweep.sh 0 100000 4 --scenario turns --policy turnlog --twice` and the same for the reference policy pass with 0 panics, and so do 20,000 seeds with `--calm` and with `--row-limit 1024`. Re-run on 2026-11-12: turnlog seeds 20000..23000 and reference 20000..22000 with `--twice` pass. Calm rows/turn are 3.11 for turnlog (A 1.00, C 1.11, F 1.00) and 3.80 for reference (with T 0.54 and S 0.14). Under faults they are 5.38 and 5.58. Turnlog writes 3.8x the bytes calm because a checkpoint rides in every row, and with no result row it reports a completed charge unknown 8987 times against 3667. Not modeled: hosts that commit each split part separately.
- smallvec leaves nanocode-types-core: `ResponseItem::AgentMessage`'s `content` is a `Vec<AgentMessageContent>` instead of a `SmallVec<[AgentMessageContent; 1]>` (2026-11-12). Both serialize as a JSON array and deserialize from one, so the wire bytes are the same; `ResponseItem` stays 184 bytes (its largest variant is another one), and a message's content now always lives on the heap instead of inline when it has one item, one allocation per agent message parsed. Public API change: the field's type; code that built the content with `smallvec!` or `SmallVec::from` builds a `Vec`, and reading it (`iter`, indexing, `len`) is unchanged; no workspace crate built one, and tempoxyz/pyramid-core and tempoxyz/pyramid do not name `ResponseItem::AgentMessage` (code search, no hits). Proven with output/types-equal, which builds nanocode-types-core as of e86dae0d8 (with smallvec 1.15.1) beside the new one: 200,000 seeded JSON documents (single items and arrays of two; `agent_message` with and without id, author and recipient, content missing, null, an object, a string, or 0 to 5 items that are input_text, encrypted_content, unknown types or missing fields, strings with escapes, surrogate pairs and non-ASCII text, extra fields), each parsed by both and compared as re-serialized bytes, error text and `serde_json::Value`: 400,000 checks, 0 differences (59,085 parsed as `AgentMessage`, the rest as errors or `Other`). `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-types-core` natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-types-core`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata --locked` stays at 489 packages: smallvec stays in the lock through hyper, icu_normalizer, idna and parking_lot_core.
- rustix leaves the workspace's crates: nanocode-process, nanocode-tui and nanocode-sandbox make their system calls through nanocode-sys's `unix` module, and nanocode-chatgpt-extension locks with std's `File::lock` (2026-11-12). crates/core/sys/src/unix.rs holds safe libc wrappers for what rustix did: `read` (an `io::Error` from errno, so callers match `WouldBlock` and `Interrupted` where they matched `Errno::AGAIN` and `INTR`), `set_close_on_exec` (`F_SETFD` to `FD_CLOEXEC` or 0, as `fcntl_setfd`), `status_flags`/`set_status_flags` (`F_GETFL`/`F_SETFL`), `set_nonblocking` (`FIONBIO`, as `ioctl_fionbio`), `duplicate_close_on_exec` (`F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC`), `redirect_input` (`dup2` onto stdin), `inherited_descriptor` (adopts a descriptor named on the command line after `F_GETFD` confirms it is open), `reap_children` (`waitpid(-1)` until `ECHILD`), `readable_now` (a zero-timeout `poll` for `POLLIN`), `Termios` with `terminal_attributes`/`set_terminal_attributes` (`tcgetattr`, `tcsetattr(TCSANOW)`), `make_raw` (rustix's linux_raw `cfmakeraw`, the same flags written out, so no unsafe) and `end_of_file` (`VEOF`), `window_size`/`set_window_size` (`TIOCGWINSZ`/`TIOCSWINSZ`), `open_pseudoterminal` (on Linux `/dev/ptmx` opened `O_RDWR|O_NOCTTY|O_CLOEXEC` with `ENOSPC` reported as `EAGAIN`, `TIOCSPTLCK`, `TIOCGPTN` and `/dev/pts/N`, as rustix's `openpt`, `unlockpt` and `ptsname`, `grantpt` being a no-op there; on Apple `posix_openpt`, `FD_CLOEXEC`, `grantpt`, `unlockpt` and `TIOCPTYGNAME`), `lead_session` (the `pre_exec` hook: the given signals back to `SIG_DFL`, `setsid`, `TIOCSCTTY` on stdin), `open_file_limit`/`set_open_file_limit` (`RLIMIT_NOFILE`, `RLIM_INFINITY` as `None` as rustix maps it) and on Linux `send_descriptor`/`receive_descriptor` (one byte with an `SCM_RIGHTS` control message, flags 0 on send and `MSG_CMSG_CLOEXEC` on receive; the first descriptor is kept and any others closed, as draining rustix's buffer did). Group and process kills use the existing `nanocode_platform::unix::signal_group`/`signal_process` with `SIGKILL` (the `killpg`/`kill` rustix made), a zero pid skipped as `Pid::from_raw` did. nanocode-process loses its `unsafe_code = "deny"` exception and takes the workspace's `forbid`: its `pre_exec` hook and `OwnedFd::from_raw_fd` moved into nanocode-sys. Unsafe code added to nanocode-sys (unix.rs), each a libc call on descriptors borrowed through `AsFd` or owned by the function: `read` into the caller's buffer with its length; `fcntl` (`F_SETFD`, `F_GETFL`, `F_SETFL`, `F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC`, `F_GETFD`), `dup2`, `ioctl` (`FIONBIO`, `TIOCGWINSZ`, `TIOCSWINSZ`, `TIOCSPTLCK`, `TIOCGPTN`, `TIOCPTYGNAME` into a 128-byte buffer, `TIOCSCTTY`) and `poll` with pointers to locals of the type each request writes; `tcgetattr` into a `MaybeUninit` read only after success and `tcsetattr` from a `termios` we hold; `waitpid` with a null status; `getrlimit`/`setrlimit` with local `rlimit`s; `open`/`posix_openpt`/`grantpt`/`unlockpt` on NUL-terminated paths; `OwnedFd::from_raw_fd` only on descriptors a successful call just returned (`open`, `F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC`, `recvmsg`'s `SCM_RIGHTS`) or that `inherited_descriptor` confirmed open and that the parent handed over on our command line (its one caller, handover.rs's reader, owns them alone); `signal`, `setsid` and `ioctl` inside `pre_exec` (async-signal-safe calls between fork and exec); and in `send_descriptor`/`receive_descriptor` a zeroed `msghdr` pointing at a local one-byte `iovec` and a `u64` control buffer of `CMSG_SPACE(4)` bytes, `CMSG_FIRSTHDR`/`CMSG_NXTHDR`/`CMSG_DATA` walked within it and the descriptors read unaligned. Not equal: `TIOCSCTTY` gets the argument 0 where rustix passed the address of a zero (which Linux reads as a nonzero steal flag), so only a privileged process taking a terminal that is already another session's controlling terminal would differ, and `lead_session` opens a fresh terminal that no session has; handover's reader skips a descriptor argument that is not open instead of adopting it, and clears `O_NONBLOCK` with the same `F_GETFL`/`F_SETFL`; sandbox's `channel` no longer has a "no room to pass a descriptor" error, since the buffer is sized for the one descriptor it sends; `open_pseudoterminal` exists for Linux and Apple only, the platforms nanocode builds for. Proven with output/sys-unix, linking rustix 1.1.4 beside nanocode-sys and running both on the hosted Hand (Linux 6.x): 200 rounds of pipe reads (empty nonblocking reads, readiness before and after data, counts and bytes), `FD_CLOEXEC`, `O_NONBLOCK` through `FIONBIO` and through `F_SETFL`, `F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC` at 50 lower bounds; 100 pseudoterminal pairs from each (descriptor and status flags, the controller's target, window sizes set and read crosswise, `tcgetattr` fields, raw mode applied and read back, restore, echo through the pair); `RLIMIT_NOFILE` read, set to four values and refused above the maximum (same errno); 200 descriptors passed over socket pairs with every mix of our and rustix's send and receive (close-on-exec set, same pipe, data through); a message without a descriptor; a child made session leader with a controlling terminal by our hook and by the rustix one; children reaped until `ECHILD`: 4,614 checks, 0 differences, in three runs. `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-process -p nanocode-tui -p nanocode-sandbox -p nanocode-chatgpt-extension`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-process -p nanocode-tui --target aarch64-apple-darwin`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata --locked` stays at 489 packages: rustix and linux-raw-sys remain in the lock through the vendored rustpython-host_env, which the python scope owns.
- arc-swap leaves the workspace: `nanocode_sync::Swap`, `SwapOption`, `Guard` and `Atom`'s storage are nanocode-sys's own lock-free Arc swap, on native and WASM alike (2026-11-12). crates/core/sys/src/swap.rs keeps arc-swap's design, a debt list: each thread claims a node (leaked, 128-byte aligned, reused after the thread exits; found in a push-only list) with 8 guard slots (arc-swap's `DEBT_SLOT_CNT`) and one transient slot for `load_full`; a load publishes the pointer it read in a free slot and confirms the storage still holds it, so a `Guard` costs no reference count; a writer that swapped a value out walks every slot, pays each debt on that value by adding a reference and marking the slot paid, and only then lets its own reference go; dropping a `Swap` pays the debts on its value (guards may outlive it), dropping an `Atom`'s `Enclosed` does not, since its `with` and `load_full` never let a debt escape (as the patched arc-swap's `Enclosed` did). Two places differ from arc-swap on purpose. (1) When the confirm fails and the debt was already paid, arc-swap keeps the paid reference as its value, but the writer that paid it may hold a different object that reused the address (even of another type, from another storage); here the payment names the paid object's type (`Releaser::<T>::RELEASE`, a `&'static` release function written into the slot), the reader gives that reference back through it and retries on (2) a pending load instead of arc-swap's generation-tagged helping slot: the reader announces the storage's address in the slot, reads the pointer and turns the announcement into a debt with one compare-exchange; a writer of that storage that meets the announcement first replaces it with a reference to a value it loads at that moment, so the reader returns a value the storage held during its call. (3) A paid slot stays paid until its guard drops, where arc-swap frees it at payment and lets a later guard's drop take over another guard's debt. `nanocode_sync`'s `Swap`/`SwapOption` keep arc-swap's API that the workspace calls (`new`, `from_pointee`, `empty`, `const_empty`, `load`, `load_full`, `store`, `swap`, `compare_and_swap` with `&Arc`, `&Option<Arc>`, `&Guard` or a raw pointer, `rcu`, `into_inner`, `Default`, `From`, `Debug`, `Display`; `Guard::into_inner`, `from_inner`, `Deref`); the WASM build drops its take-and-put wrapper (sync's swap.rs) and nanocode-types-core, nanocode-tui and the patched rustls-platform-verifier use nanocode-sys's types; crates/patches/arc-swap and its `[patch.crates-io]` entry are deleted. Public API change: `nanocode_sync::Swap`, `SwapOption` and `Guard` are `nanocode_sys::Swapped`/`Guard` instead of aliases of arc-swap's types (arc-swap's `map`, `Access`, `Cache`, strategies and weak pointers, which nothing used, are gone); tempoxyz/pyramid-core does not name them (code search for arc_swap, SwapOption, nanocode_sync::Guard: no hits) and tempoxyz/pyramid uses its own arc-swap. Unsafe code added to nanocode-sys (swap.rs): `Arc::from_raw` in `Raw::from_raw` for `Arc` (asserts non-null) and `Option<Arc>`, called by `Guard::owned`, `Swapped::{into_inner, load_full, swap}` and `Enclosed::{load_full, swap, compare_and_swap}` on a reference the caller owns (from `into_raw`, a storage's own reference, a paid debt or a load that added one); `P::from_raw` inside `ManuallyDrop` in `load_guard` for a confirmed debt, which keeps the value alive until the guard drops and is never dropped unless the debt was paid; `Arc::increment_strong_count` in `increment` (the value is kept alive by a debt or the storage's reference the caller holds); `Arc::from_raw` in `release` (the caller owns one reference); the dereference in `release_paid_debt` (slots tagged as paid debts are only written by `pay` with the address of a `&'static Release`); `ManuallyDrop::take` in `Guard::into_inner` (the guard is never dropped) and `ManuallyDrop::drop` in `Guard`'s drop (only when the guard owns its reference). Not equal: strong counts while a paid guard is alive (point 3: arc-swap's is one higher until another guard on the slot drops; final counts equal), `Debug` of a WASM `Swap` prints `ArcSwapAny(..)` as the native one did instead of `Swap(..)`, and the corner cases of points 1 and 2. Proven with output/sys-swap, linking arc-swap 1.9.2 (crates.io; the vendored copy differed only by `Enclosed`) beside nanocode-sys: 200 seeds of 20,000 random operations over three `Swap`s, two `SwapOption`s and up to 40 held guards (load, load_full, store, swap, compare_and_swap matching and not, rcu, guards dropped or turned into `Arc`s in random order) comparing every value, plus the strong count of every object whenever no guard is held and after everything is dropped: 6,616,429 checks, 0 differences; a stress run of 2, 4, 8 and 16 threads x 400,000 operations over shared storages, `Enclosed`s, short-lived `Swap`s, guards passed between threads and up to 12 guards held per thread, each value checked for a live canary on every read: 3,615,185 objects created and dropped exactly once; a monotonic run (4 readers alternating `load` and `load_full`, a writer storing 1..2,000,000 and publishing each after its store returns): no reader saw a value go back or fall below a published one; the same harness under AddressSanitizer (nightly, 541,406 objects) clean, and under Miri (weak memory, preemption rate 0.1, 20 runs: harness seeds 1 and 2 under 4 and 16 Miri scheduler seeds) with no undefined behaviour or data race. Benchmarks (release, single thread, 60 interleaved rounds of 1M operations, min/median ns on the loaded 5-core Hand): `load` and read 12.2/34.1 arc-swap against 12.1/37.5; `load_full` 26.3/69.9 against 24.9/73.4; `Atom::read`'s `with` 12.2/34.9 (arc-swap `load`) against 10.9/35.0; `store` 102.6/286.5 against 25.3/80.0; new and drop of a `Swap`'s storage 173 to 347 ns against 31 to 79 ns for `Enclosed`. `cargo check --locked --workspace`, `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p nanocode-sync -p nanocode-types-core -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-sync -p nanocode-types-core -p nanocode-tui` (and the first three for wasm32), `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata --locked`: 490 -> 489 packages (rustversion stays through encoding_rs).
- crossbeam-utils leaves nanocode-sync: `Slot`, `Mailbox`'s desk and the slow-wait holders keep their values in nanocode-sys's owned atomic pointers (2026-11-12). crates/core/sys (nanocode-sys) is new: the one workspace crate whose lints allow unsafe code (with `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` denied), holding only what needs it, each unsafe block minimal and behind a safe API; every other crate keeps `unsafe_code = "forbid"` (or the deny it had). Its first module, atomic.rs: `AtomicBox<T>` (an `Option<Box<T>>` in an `AtomicPtr`: `new`, `empty`, `swap`, `take`, `store`, `Sync` for `T: Send` as crossbeam's `AtomicCell` was), `AtomicArc<T>` (the same for `Option<Arc<T>>`, which the WASM `Swap` holds) and `AtomicStatic<T>` (an `Option<&'static T>`: `load`, `store`). Its unsafe code: `unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for AtomicBox<T>` (shared access only moves whole boxes in and out and never lends a `&T`); `Box::from_raw` in `reclaim_box` and `Arc::from_raw` in `reclaim_arc` (every non-null pointer in a cell came from `Box::into_raw` or `Arc::into_raw` and is owned by the cell alone, and `swap` and `drop` take it out exactly once); `as_ref` in `AtomicStatic::load` (only null or a pointer made from a `&'static T` is ever stored). Orderings are crossbeam's for pointer-sized cells: swap `AcqRel`, load `Acquire`, store `Release`, and a store into an owning cell is a swap that drops the old value, as `AtomicCell::store` does for types that need dropping. Equal: output/sys-atomic links crossbeam-utils 0.8.22 beside nanocode-sys: 200 seeds of 50,000 random swap, take and store operations on `Option<Box<_>>` comparing every returned value and the drop counts, 200 seeds of 20,000 `&'static Location` stores and loads, and 2, 4 and 8 threads swapping 500,000 values each through either cell, where every value must come out exactly once: 23,329,284 checks, 0 differences. Benchmarks (release, interleaved, 5 rounds): take and store 10.0 to 10.5 ns with crossbeam against 9.8 to 11.0 ns; 4 threads of 2M swaps 228 to 261 ms against 234 to 276 ms. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sync -p nanocode-sys` natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-sync` on both targets, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata --locked`: 489 -> 490 packages, since crossbeam-utils stays in the lock through rustpython-vm and rustpython-stdlib and nanocode-sys is a new workspace package.

The crate's `binascii` feature no longer names `dep:base64`. base64 0.23.1 stays in Cargo.lock for other workspace crates. Equality: output/base64-equal compares base64 0.23.1 with the new function, with and without the newline, over 3,000,000 seeded inputs of 0 to 69 bytes plus one of 4,096 bytes every 1,000 rounds: 6,000,000 checks, 0 differences. `cargo metadata` 484 packages before and after; `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 292 to 291 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 293 to 292 (aarch64-apple-darwin). The three changes from here down to the bit sets were checked together with `cargo check -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-ruff_python_ast -p rustpython-common`.

- RustPython's bit sets are plain structs in its own code, and bitflagset, radium, ref-cast and ref-cast-impl leave (2026-11-12). The `bitflag!`/`bitflagset!`/`atomic_bitflagset!` invocations become `#[repr(u8)]` enums and small structs over the same integer with only the operations their callers use, with bitflagset 0.0.4's semantics: rustpython-compiler-core's `MakeFunctionFlags` (u8: `new`, `insert`, `contains`, `bits`, `|`, `From<[MakeFunctionFlag; N]>`) and `CoFastFlags` (u8: `from_element`, `from_slice`, `from_bits_retain`, `contains`, `bits`, `ARG`), rustpython-host_env's `FileMode` (io.rs and io_unsupported.rs), `AccessMode` (`from_bits` is `None` for bits outside X, W and R, as bitflagset's `from_bits` was) and `ChFlags`, rustpython-vm's `EvalBreaker` (an `AtomicU8`: `insert`/`remove` are `fetch_or`/`fetch_and` with AcqRel, `contains`/`is_empty` relaxed loads, as before), the `_stat` permission bits and `PyTypeFlags` (u64 with its bit positions as `u8` constants, `from_bits_truncate` keeping only the named positions, `contains`/`insert`/`remove`/`from_element`/`from_slice` asserting the position is below 64 where bitflagset panicked) with `AtomicPyTypeFlags` (`repr(transparent)` over `AtomicU64`, which `__flags__`'s atomic member read relies on; `insert`/`remove` AcqRel read-modify-writes returning whether the bit changed, `contains` relaxed). Debug, Display, iteration and the other set methods nobody called are not reproduced. num-integer stays in Cargo.lock for num-bigint (image) but bitflagset was its only path into nanocode-cli. Equality: output/bitflag-equal links bitflagset 0.0.4 with the old invocations beside the new definitions (extracted from the edited sources) and compares 2,000,000 rounds of random u64 bit patterns through truncate, retain, contains, insert, remove, superset, disjoint, `&`, `|`, `-`, the atomic set's insert/remove/contains and resulting word, `CoFastFlags` and `AccessMode::from_bits` over random bytes, every element constant, every `MakeFunctionFlags` subset and every `CoFastFlags` byte: 36,002,361 checks, 0 differences, in both debug (with `_CREATED_WITH_FLAGS`) and release. `cargo metadata` 489 to 485 packages. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-compiler-core -p rustpython-host_env -p rustpython-vm` (no warnings in the changed files) pass.
- `Ledger` (19e65d550, the entry that stood here) is removed again (2026-11-12): on Durable Objects it saved no commits and moved a tool result past the next model call. workerd's `transactionSync` is a savepoint, and workerd commits once per event-loop turn that wrote and holds every outgoing request, response and socket send until that commit is confirmed (`ActorSqlite::startImplicitTxnImpl` and the output gate in actor-sqlite.c++). Counting event-loop commits instead of `transactionSync` calls on the durable-cloudflare harness (`node output/sqlturn/run.mjs text|reply 10`), a one-tool-call turn made 5.0 commits before and 5.0 with the ledger, a plain reply 4.0 and 3.9; what fell from 21 to 11 was savepoints. Which writes matter was measured by crashing a turn that calls a side-effecting `charge` tool before each of its commits (14 with the ledger, 22 without), rolling the object's SQLite back offline to the last commit or to the one before it, and restarting (`output/crash/run.mjs`, 70 runs): losing the admission before its 202 loses the turn; losing the cell journal's call record before the tool runs charges twice; losing the tool result before the next model call tells the model a completed charge's outcome is unknown and costs one model call; losing the model's response costs one model call; losing the start status, the background and reset markers, event batches or the post-finish cleanup changed nothing observable. With the ledger the tool result waited for the next durable write, which came after the second model call, so a crash during that call gave the unknown outcome where the direct path had written it. Both builds also report an unknown outcome for a call that had not started when the crash hit between the journal header and its call record.
- Carrying inline caches across recycled Code Mode cells was measured and not built (2026-11-12). Each cell runs on an instance restored from the prepared snapshot (`Instance::reset_written`), so the bootstrap glue's cache sites start cold every cell. Temporary counters in `step_once` (by whether the template is in the image) over the corpus replay (`output/durability-ledger` corpus binary, last week's nc cells) showed the glue taking 26 slow-path steps per `text('ok')` cell, 51 per one-`Bash` cell and 60 per average real cell, of which cache sites (get_global, get_field, get_method, define_field) were 7, 23 and about 26; the rest are `await`, async start and return, and calls of host functions, which leave the hot loop whatever the caches hold. An upper bound, skipping the restore between cells so every cache stays warm (and the restore's own 1.8% is saved), removed 6 and 21 of those steps but no instructions: `text('ok')` 197.1k -> 197.5k and 197.3k -> 198.5k per cell, one `Bash` call 490k -> 503k (the unrestored heap grows and collects). By the profile the cache-miss path (`lookup_ic`) is 0.8% of a trivial cell and the extra steps about 0.5%, under the 3% a change to the restore path would need to be worth its risk.
- The lexer steps over plain runs of template parts and string literals with a byte table (2026-11-12): `scan_template` and `scan_string` advance through ASCII bytes that can't end or escape the literal (`TEMPLATE_PLAIN`, `STRING_PLAIN`) in a tight loop instead of the full per-byte `match`. Compiling 2,000 real Code Mode cells sampled from last week's nc sessions (5 rounds through `new AsyncFunction`, djsrun): 1,628M -> 1,496M instructions (-8.1%; the template table alone -4.9%, an `iter().position` with a `matches!` instead of the table only -1.3%). In the full corpus replay through `CodeModeRuntime` the gain is -0.25% (97.62G -> 97.40G over 77,743 cells, two interleaved runs each): there the scanners are under 1% of instructions, so the djsrun loop overstates the lexer's share and is not a proxy for cell cost. Outputs identical on 5,981 sampled cells; test262 39,325/39,365.
- A Code Mode tool call encodes its result once (2026-11-12). `ToolOutput::from_json` already serializes the structured result into the output text; Code Mode then serialized `structured_result` again in `send_completed_call` (and again in `journaled_call` for journaled cells) to hand it to the cell. `from_json` now records the address and length of the text it made, and the hidden `ToolOutput::structured_json` returns that text only while `output` still holds that exact string (a replaced, regrown or cloned output falls back to encoding, so callers that rewrite the public `output`, such as codex's served builtin tools, are unaffected); `with_structured_result` clears it. Measured with the corpus replay (`output/durability-ledger` corpus binary, now driving cells from a spawned task as nc does), interleaved: a cell with one `Bash` call 531k -> 490k instructions (-7.7%), `text('ok')` flat; outputs byte-identical on 5,981 sampled real cells, `cells.rs` and the edge-case set. The same harness change showed most futex time in the earlier profile came from driving cells from `block_on` on the main thread (wall -30 to -36%, context switches 3.0 -> 1.8 per trivial cell); the remainder is Tokio waking another worker for the spawned cell actor.
- Code Mode's per-cell glue does less work (2026-11-12). Measured by replaying last week's real nc cells (86,188 unique cells from 543 sessions on gak-9, 77,743 without timers) through `CodeModeRuntime` against stub tools in `output/durability-ledger/src/bin/corpus.rs`: a cell costs about 0.12 ms natively, and the fixed cost per cell, not user code, dominates (a `text('ok')` cell was 219k instructions, one tool call 576k, the average real cell 1.38M). Three changes: `finish` waits on a promise settled by the cell's promise or `stopped` instead of `Promise.race` (whose combinator, species and iterator protocol were most of the glue's built-in calls); the terminal record skips `Object.fromEntries` when nothing was stored; and `tools` keeps the declared tools as its own frozen properties with the Proxy as its prototype, so `tools.Bash` is a plain property read and only other names reach the trap (keys, `in`, `then`, freezing, missing tools and `mcp__` routing unchanged). Instructions per cell, interleaved runs: `text('ok')` 219k -> 183k (-16%), one `Bash` call 576k -> 516k (-10%), the whole timer-free corpus -5.7% (107.2G -> 101.1G). Outputs identical on 5,981 sampled real cells, the 43 cells of `cells.rs` and an edge-case set, except the bootstrap's own line numbers in stack frames. What remains, by the same profile: inline caches start cold in every cell (each cell runs on an instance restored from the prepared snapshot, so the glue's first property reads take the slow path, about 50 per trivial cell), compiling the cell (13%), cross-thread wakeups (13% in futex) and serializing each tool result about three times.
- Run `/re/.test(x)` without creating the RegExp when the literal is only the call's receiver: on the slow path a literal's `call_intrinsic %RegExpCreate` already takes, when the code after it is `get_method key; get_loc | get_arg; call1`, `key` resolves on %RegExp.prototype% to the original `test`, `exec` is the original and `x` is a string, the match runs on the literal's compiled program with lastIndex 0 and pushes the boolean, skipping the four instructions. The fresh RegExp could not be observed: nothing else references it, and the `lastIndex` write a `g` or `y` match makes goes to an object that is about to die. Any other code, a non-string argument, a patched prototype, or a match that runs out of steps falls back to creating the object as before. `RegExp.prototype.test` became an `@intrinsic` so the check can name it. Measured against ff718269e (instructions, 1 round): a 500k loop of `/TODO:/.test(s)` -47% (1,961M -> 1,039M, below the 1,369M of hoisting the literal by hand), agent cell -7.2%, kernel suite flat (strings kernel -2.8%), compute and strings cells flat. Output identical on all workloads and on an edge-case script (overridden `test` and `exec`, a getter on `test`, `g`/`y` flags, non-string and missing arguments, ropes, catastrophic backtracking, a `lastIndex` accessor on the prototype). Rejected: handling the literal (creation alone, or creation plus this check) in the hot loop's `call_intrinsic` arm or in `intrinsic_hit`: creation alone made `/TODO:/.test` -11%, but either placement changed `run_hot`'s code and cost +1.5 to +5% on the kernels that run no regexps (loop +5.4%, fib +4.8%, dispatch +3.9%).
- Size a new property-values block by the shape tree: when the shape an object grows into has a single chain of transitions below it (objects built by the same literal or constructor went on to add those properties), allocate exactly the count at the end of the chain (at least len + 1) instead of twice len (at least 4). A two-property literal now takes 32 bytes of values instead of 48. Measured against ceba3f966 (instructions, 1 round, max RSS): compute cell loop -2.1% instr, RSS 24.0 -> 17.4 MB; 300k six-property literals pushed into an array -6.2% instr, RSS 47.4 -> 37.7 MB; 1M `{i, s}` objects pushed into an array went from OutOfMemory at the 64 MB heap cap to finishing in 0.27 s; strings cell and agent cell flat (+0.0%, +0.2%). Kernels flat except objects (class constructor adding x then y) +0.9%: the chain walk on each first allocation costs more than the smaller block saves when nothing survives. Rejected alternatives: caching the prediction in Shape (no spare field; Shape stays 24 bytes). Output identical on all workloads; test262 39,325/39,365.
- djs's hot loop keeps generator resume and `yield` on its decline path (2026-11-12): running them from `iter_next_loc` and `yield` arms of `run_hot` (one out-of-line call each, then the frame reloaded in the loop) took `for (const v of g(1000))` x2000 from 3,696M to 3,434M instructions (-7%), but added 2-4% to the call, loop, object and dispatch kernels, the register-pressure cost of new arms seen before (D2441); copying the suspended frame value by value instead of with `copy_within` took 4,050M. Not adopted.
- djs keeps its collector without a card table or promotion (2026-11-12): both were built and measured and are not adopted. A card table over the old region (marked by the arena's write barrier, by `Arena::wrote` for the hot loop's Box writes and by inline cache fills for their template; a minor collection walking only marked cards plus the roots, stack and interpreter cells, a card staying marked while it references a young cell) gave the same results but +1.4% instructions on the workerd compute cell's loop: `Marker::mark_old`'s 10% of that run's cycles is the trace of the young cells its old slots reach, not the walk over old cells. Promotion on top of it (what a minor collection leaves becomes old, the card table growing over it clean): with the existing thresholds, compute -7.6% instructions but peak RSS 23.7 MB -> 47.0 MB (promoted garbage counts as live); with minor thresholds that allow a full collection's growth and a full collection once promoted data passes its threshold (the live bytes of the last full collection kept in the roots cell), compute +0.8% at 36.5 MB, 300k objects +18.5%, 1M objects -18%; with that and `LIVE_GROWTH` 1, compute +16.6% at 28.6 MB. What is live at a collection in those runs is mostly temporaries that die soon after, so promoting them only moves garbage into the old region. `LIVE_GROWTH` 1 alone: compute 23.7 -> 17.4 MB at +13% instructions.
- `${!a[@]:2}`, `${!a[@]-x}` and the other operator forms indirect through the value of `a[@]` (an unset array is an invalid indirect expansion, several elements an invalid name), as bash does; only the plain form and the default operators on an empty array list keys (2026-11-12). The subscript of a nameref or `unset 'a[…]'` is expanded as one text, so `a[$(echo 2) + 1]` keeps its spaces. A parse error whose message has several lines (the `[[ ]]` ones) gets the `name: line N:` prefix on each, followed by the source line when the last is `syntax error near`. psh-spec: oils 2409->2413, brush 2941/3171 (12 more cases also match stderr). Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/eval.rs, expand.rs, lib.rs.
- A builtin whose first argument is `--help` prints what `help NAME` prints and returns 2, quietly when stdout can't be written, through `builtin` and `command` too (not echo, test, [, true, false, :, let, kill) (2026-11-12). `cd` takes combined option letters (the last of -L and -P wins), rejects unknown ones with its usage (status 2), returns 2 for too many arguments, follows CDPATH (printing the directory it found), and with -P resolves `..` physically; `pwd` reads -L/-P only before its first operand, the last one winning. The psh binary keeps an inherited absolute PWD that names the working directory (a symlinked path) as bash does. psh-spec: oils 2406->2409, brush 2923->2941. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/command.rs, builtins/declare.rs, builtins/help.rs, builtins/mod.rs, exec.rs, now.rs; psh lib.rs.
- `declare -fx`/`+x` exports or unexports functions and `declare -ft` sets the trace attribute (the function then sees the DEBUG and RETURN traps); `declare -F` shows `-fx`/`-ft`, and `-F -x`/`-F -t` filter on them (2026-11-12). `+f`, `+F` and `+g` turn their modes off, so `declare +F f` declares a variable. A subscript in a declaration is expanded once more when declare reads it (`declare 'a[$i]=x'`, `declare m[$key]=v` as bash), a subscript may contain `=` (`'m[a=b]=1'`), text after the closing bracket is an invalid identifier, and a compound value to an array element assigns the whole array. `-a` with `-A` warns and lets `-A` win. `export -f` without names lists the exported functions; `export -n` of a missing name creates nothing and its assignment is not exported under `set -a`; `set` shows a lone `'` as `\'`; associative keys quote `@` and not `=`; FUNCNAME is empty when only `source` frames are on the stack; DIRSTACK starts as an array. The subscript reparse (and declare's compound reparse) took the first command its parse listed, which is the innermost command substitution: it now takes the outer one. psh-spec: oils 2403->2406, brush 2898->2923. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/declare.rs, builtins/trap.rs, exec.rs, expand.rs, lib.rs, state.rs.
- `shopt -s extdebug` implies functrace and acts on the DEBUG trap's status: 1 skips the command, 2 inside a function returns from it (2026-11-12). The DEBUG trap runs at function entry, once per pipeline stage in the parent (without functrace or extdebug), and before an arithmetic for's init, condition and step; the RETURN trap sees the status of the function's last command; BASH_COMMAND shows a simple command as bash prints it (redirections normalized, here-documents kept); `declare -F name` under extdebug prints the definition's line and file. psh-spec: oils 2397->2403, brush 2871->2898. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/declare.rs, builtins/trap.rs, exec.rs, state.rs.
- `unset` of a variable that is local to a calling function restores the value it shadowed (bash's dynamic unset), and `unset -f -v` is an error (2026-11-12). `unset 'A[@]'` leaves an associative array, empties an indexed one (which stays declared), and on a scalar says it is not an array; `unset x[0]` on a scalar unsets it and other subscripts fail; an invalid name in plain `unset` is silent. `local` and `local -p` without names list only the current function's locals in declare form, and `local -p NAME` for a non-local reports not found. psh-spec: oils 2390->2397, brush 2866->2871. Upstream delta: psh-engine arrays.rs, builtins/declare.rs, builtins/mod.rs.
- In `$(( ))`, `(( ))`, `for (( ))`, substring offsets and indexed subscripts single quotes stay literal, so `$(( '1' + 2 ))` is an error as in bash, while associative subscripts keep word quoting and arithmetic unquotes associative keys (2026-11-12). Under `set -u`, reading an element of an unset or declared-only array is an unbound-variable error, and `let` on an unset name ends the shell. `getopts` clamps OPTIND past the end to n+1 and still parses before failing on an invalid variable name (status 1). psh-spec: oils 2381->2390, brush 2864->2866. Upstream delta: psh-engine arith.rs, builtins/mod.rs, exec.rs, expand.rs.
- HostInfo gains `release` and `version` (empty by default; filled from `uname(2)` on unix, empty on Windows, read from the embedder after `hosttype` in psh-wasm, whose ABI_VERSION goes 6->7), and `uname -r`/`-v` print them, `unknown` when empty (2026-11-12). Before, they always printed `unknown`, which scripts that branch on the kernel release misread. `zip -v` without operands now refuses through `lacks` (status 127, as other utilities refuse what they lack) instead of `zip error: Nothing to do!` (12), so a script probing for Info-ZIP's version table falls back. psh-spec unchanged (oils 2381, brush 2864); utils 1001/1001. Upstream delta: psh-engine host.rs, psh-os unix/mod.rs and windows/mod.rs, psh-utils small.rs and zip.rs, psh-wasm lib.rs and shell.rs.
- `printf %q`, `declare -p`, `set` and `${x@Q}` quote bytes that are not valid in the locale (any byte ≥ 0x80 in the C locale) as `$'\ooo'`, as bash does, and keep valid UTF-8 as is under a UTF-8 locale (2026-11-12). `shift`, `break`, `continue` and `return` with too many arguments abandon the line with status 1 and accept `--`; `$'…'` stops at an embedded NUL; `for ((  ; ; ))` with only blanks as its condition loops. psh-spec: oils 2366->2381, brush 2862->2864. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/declare.rs, builtins/hash.rs, builtins/mapfile.rs, builtins/mod.rs, builtins/printf.rs, builtins/set.rs, exec.rs, expand.rs.
- `coproc [NAME] command` runs the command as an in-process background job connected by two engine pipes, with `NAME` (default COPROC) an array of the read and write descriptors (chosen downward from 63) and `NAME_PID`; reaping the job unsets both while `NAME_PID` still names it (2026-11-12). Before, `coproc` stopped the script as unsupported. The coproc's future is built behind a boxed call so `run_command_with`'s frame stays the size it was (the 1000-level recursion test in debug builds overflowed otherwise). psh-spec: brush 2857->2862 and the 51 coproc cases kept for later now pass. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/jobs.rs, exec.rs, jobs.rs.
- `type`, `command -v` and `command -V` report the program found on PATH when a psh utility stands in for it (`cat is /usr/bin/cat`), as bash does on the same machine; with no such program they still report the utility (2026-11-12). `type -P` uses the hashed path, and `type -a` lists only executable files (a missing file a utility stands for still counts, so hosts without the programs keep listing them). `type -a` keeps its utility line, which psh's own `utils` listing reads. psh-spec: oils 2359->2366, brush 2848->2857. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/command.rs.
- A background job whose one command is a nested `bash`/`sh` runs it as the forked process itself, and `kill $$` in a forked copy signals the shell (2026-11-12). Since forked background jobs, such a job ran the nested shell in-process inside the copy, so signals sent to its pid hit the copy's own handling and waiting on it lost the signal it died of; `kill $$` in the copy killed the copy. The job now starts the nested shell with `process` set (its own signal handling as a shell, `died_of` from the core), waiting skips `or_signal` for it, a forked copy's ProcGuard releases its procs on drop, and `$$`'s pid in the copy is the real shell's. psh-spec (upstream psh's oils, brush, agent and utils suites, bash 5.3 goldens, run against the vendored crates): brush 2843->2848/3171, agent 726->727/727 (nested-shells/15, wait/14-17, background_jobs/20 were regressions from forking). Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/jobs.rs, exec.rs, util/nested.rs.
- perf(djs): an Error records its stack lazily (`Exec::capture_stack`, interp/run/stack.rs): an internal ValueArray of each shown frame's function and `pc * 2 + construct`, formatted into the default string only when the stack is first read (`ErrorStack`, `Vm::error_stack`), which then replaces it in the slot. The walk is shared with the eager path (`raw_frames`, `describe_frame`), so the text is the same; with `Error.prepareStackTrace` set, and for a parse error's `<input>` frame, the stack is made at once as before. `CaptureStack` returns whether the stack is pending, so RecordStack no longer reads it back. A builtin frame's name is read when the stack is formatted rather than when it was captured. 100,000 `new Error('x')`: 1,161.7M->951.0M instr (-18.1%, qjs 637M); 1M-iteration try/catch with a throw every 10th: 1,866M->1,602M (-14.1%); agent, compute and strings scripts flat.
- perf(djs): a string's chunk iterator keeps its first piece out of its stack, so iterating a flat string (`push_str_to`, `str_units`) allocates nothing; before, every iteration allocated a one-element Vec. 100,000 `new Error('x')` (trace text): 1,174.9M->1,161.7M instr (-1.1%); agent script -0.2%; compute and strings cells flat.
- perf(djs): a callback loop's next index is made with `Value::int` instead of through `conv::number`'s float round trip, and the search modes test a boolean result before calling `to_boolean`, with the mode read once per step. `a.find(x => x.id === k % 1000)` over 1,000 objects x30,000: 14,505M->13,815M instr (-4.8%).
- perf(djs): ErrorConstruct calls InstallErrorCause only for an object `options`, and RecordStack calls FinishErrorStack only when the captured stack is pending (an `Error.prepareStackTrace` set), so a plain `new Error(msg)` makes two fewer prelude calls. 100,000 `new Error('x')`: 1,228M->1,175M instr (-4.4%); throw and catch of a new Error: 1,294M->1,240M.
- perf(djs): a generator's `yield` hit pops its frame and jumps to the resuming `iter_next_loc`'s target itself instead of going through `do_return` and `gen_step_return`, which read the caller's iterator again and checked the generator it had just suspended; the `iter_next_loc` decline tries the generator resume before the Array Iterator done check. `for (const v of g(1000))` x2000: 4,178M->3,696M instr (-11.5%), 0.176->0.148 s; kernels flat.
- `tr` builds its byte table straight from its sets, without random-keyed hash maps (2026-11-12). Since the table of what becomes of each byte was added, every `tr` run filled 256 entries through `HashMap`/`HashSet` lookups seeded by `RandomState` (SipHash), which made the setup most of a small run: through nanocode-ts's glue `for i in $(seq 1 10000); do x=$(echo $i | tr 1 2); done` took 118 to 124 ms against 81 to 82 ms with the module of nanocode 5e15e341f. The sets and the map are now `BTreeSet`/`BTreeMap`, and without -c the table starts as the identity and takes the map's pairs, the deleted bytes and the squeeze flags directly (later pairs of SET1 win, as with the map's inserts). The same loop now takes 81 to 84 ms (three interleaved rounds against 5e15e341f's module: 82 to 88 ms); large inputs keep the table's gain (`seq 1 1000000 | tr 1-5 a-e`: 18 to 20 ms against 119 to 123 ms). Same output as before on 33 tr scripts compared with GNU coreutils 9.4 (ranges, classes, equivalence classes, repeats `[x*]` `[z*2]`, -c -d -s -t and their mixes, escapes, bytes ≥ 0x80) and on the 727 agent cases and 150 tool scripts run through the glue. Upstream delta: none.
- `xxd -l`, `od -N`, `hexdump -n` read only the range they print, and `fold` writes as it reads (2026-11-12). The dump tools read every input whole before cutting it to the length asked for, and fold read its whole input before folding, so `xxd -l 4 /dev/zero`, `od -N 4 -An -tx1 /dev/zero`, `hexdump -n 4 -C /dev/zero` and `cat /dev/urandom | tr -dc 0-9 | fold -w 4 | head -2` read until the module's memory budget ended the script (126 after 0.3 to 19 s), where GNU, vim's xxd and util-linux print and exit. `slurp` takes the end of the range (skip plus length; none for `xxd -r` or without a length) and stops reading there, and fold keeps its line and column across 64 KiB blocks and writes each block's output before reading the next; a file fold cannot open or read now makes it exit 1 after folding the others, as GNU's does, where it exited 0 when another input had data. Found running nanocode-ts's glue over psh-wasm-core: `od -N 4 /dev/zero` worked with nanocode-ts's TypeScript od. Checked with 27 scripts against GNU coreutils 9.4, vim's xxd 9.1 and util-linux 2.39 hexdump (fold with -s, -b, tabs, backspace and CR, a missing file, a file without a newline, 200,000-byte lines; od -j -N, hexdump -s -n, xxd -s -l -p -r on files, pipes and devices): the same output except `hexdump -s` on a pipe, which util-linux refuses with 'Illegal seek' and psh skips; 727 agent cases and 123 tool scripts unchanged through the glue. Upstream delta: none.
- A host can authorize what an agent asks of a Hand, and a Hand reports its version in its catalog (2026-11-12). `HandAuthorizer` (code-mode's remote module, re-exported by nanocode beside `HandToolSelection`) has two async methods, each given the session id and the Hand's name: `authorize_request` sees a `hands` request for a capability with its reason and answers `HandRequestDecision::Allow`, `Pending(reason)` (the tool answers `permission: prompt` with that reason and the Hand is not asked) or `Deny(reason)` (the tool fails with that reason and nothing is requested); `authorize_call` sees one call routed to a Hand (tool name and input, `hand` already taken out) before dispatch and answers `HandCallDecision::Allow` or `Refuse(message)`, which becomes the call's error output with nothing dispatched. Both default to Allow. `CodeModeExecutors::set_authorizer` installs it for the `hands` tool and for `call_on`, so for scripts on the brain, a remote Hand's callbacks naming another Hand and a registry routing through `CodeModeExecutors::calls`; it is asked only for an attached Hand, so naming an unattached one still fails as before. `ToolsBuilder::hand_authorizer` installs it where a registry routes a nested call naming `hand` to the installed `HandCalls`, for a host whose `hand_calls` lead elsewhere (a Hand forwarding to its brain); a host that installs it in both places for one path is asked twice. Selecting an executor (`select`, `set_default`) is the host's own synchronous decision, not the agent's, so it is not authorized. Unset, every path runs as before. The catalog frame, `RemoteCatalog`, `HandDescription` (what `hands` shows in `about`) and `ExecutorOptions` carry `version: Option<String>`, set by an embedder with `Hand::version`; it is written only when set and read with a default, so an old Hand's frame decodes as None and an old brain ignores the field. Checked with output/hand-hooks: `hooks` (a denying authorizer stops `call_on`, a call through `calls()`, the `hands` request and a registry-routed call with the Hand never called or asked; pending answers prompt; allow and unset pass through; catalog frames round trip with and without version, a frame without the field decodes as None, and `HandCore::catalog` writes the version it was given and omits an unset one) passes 20 of 20 and does not build at 21eec9a9b (the API is missing); `compat` at 21eec9a9b decodes a frame carrying `version` but describes the Hand without it (1 of 4 fails), and passes 4 of 4 after. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-tool-host -p nanocode-tool-runtime -p nanocode`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `cargo clippy --locked -p` the same crates `-- -D warnings`. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode/src/remote/{executors,mod,frame,hand}.rs, crates/runtime/tool-host/src/{selection,runtime/registry,runtime/execution}.rs, crates/integrations/tool-runtime/src/remote/{hand,native}.rs, crates/nanocode/src/lib.rs.
- nanocode-cli drops the third-party crates outside the async baseline, scope by scope, each in its own commit with its own entry below (2026-11-12, Georgios: "make this ~0 deps. Get rid of basically everything outside of baseline async stack like Tokio/reqwest"). The scopes and their entries: the TUI (ratatui, crossterm, syntect and onig, pulldown-cmark, unicode-width, unicode-segmentation, wide), the nanocode crates (thiserror, async-trait, nix, tower, unicode-normalization, schemars, tungstenite; regress, fluent-uri, email_address, num-cmp, appendlist, foldhash, tempfile, the digests, uuid, httpdate, subtle, proc-macro-crate), RustPython (vendored, then malachite, num-*, the compression, hash, Unicode and helper crates) and psh (its hashes, JSON, command line, diff, deflate, libm, jq, grep, regex, walker, hasher and byte helpers). Each was proven equal to the crate it replaced by a harness under output/ linking both, with the differences that remain listed in its entry. What stays and why is DEPENDENCIES.md: the async baseline (tokio, reqwest, hyper, rustls, ring, futures, serde, tracing, url and idna, libc, memchr, getrandom), image and png (kept at 0.25.6), clap (kept), opentelemetry's SDK (public types), imbl, RustPython's remaining crates, encoding_rs and rustix, and the crates whose replacement needs unsafe code or a public type change (crossbeam-utils, arc-swap, smallvec, futures-channel). Measured on the 5-core hosted Hand from fresh target directories, 4248aa710 (this request's start) against 4e73b1875 (other threads' commits between them included): `cargo metadata --locked` 710 to 489 packages; on Linux nanocode-cli reaches 299 packages instead of 514 (`cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`); `cargo build --release --locked -p nanocode-cli --timings` 5m42s to 4m44s wall, 758 to 453 units, 1,275.2 to 1,031.1 s of summed unit time; the release nanocode 102,406,152 to 99,701,256 bytes; `cargo bloat --release -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode --crates` (unstripped) 62.6 to 59.4 MiB of .text, file 147.6 to 143.2 MiB. Costs: safe code without SIMD or SHA instructions makes SHA-1 and SHA-256 2 to 10x slower (psh checksums, Python hashlib), BLAKE3 about 12x slower at 1 MiB, crc32 and LZ4 decoding slower in Python, unanchored JSON Schema patterns over long strings slower than regress's memchr start search, and some psh regex patterns 20 to 35% slower; terminal rendering, Markdown, highlighting, the WebSocket receive path, RustPython's parser and small integers got faster.
- perf(djs): a plain generator's `yield` back to the for-of loop resuming it (the frame's continuation is `GenStep`) and that loop's `iter_next_loc` resume of it run from the hot loop's out-of-line decline path (`yield_hit`, `resume_hit` in suspend.rs) instead of `step`, whose generic dispatch and fuel lookups were a fifth of a generator loop's cycles. Both allocate or reserve before changing anything (`suspend_frame`, `generator_resume`), so a failure leaves the instruction to `step` as before. `for (const v of g(1000))` x2000: 4,986M->4,367M instr (-12.4%), cycles -11.8%; generator micro -12.1% instr; other scripts and kernels flat.
- perf(djs): a short `padStart`/`padEnd` of a flat one-byte string with the default or a one-unit filler fills and copies straight into the new string (`alloc_str_uninit`, a fill, an in-arena `copy_within`) instead of building it on the stack for `alloc_latin1` to copy, whose wide loads read bytes just stored one by one. Compute cell loop (`String(i).padStart(8, '0')` per object) -0.36% instr, cycles -1.5% (same path, interleaved); padStart micro -0.6% instr, cycles neutral.

Two behaviors were found by the harnesses and kept: ignore's Walk keeps the previous root's parent chain alive, so a parent ignore file shared by consecutive roots is compiled and its errors reported once (walk.rs looks parents up in the previous root's chain), and a later root under a directory the visitor skipped stays hidden (search/walk.rs keeps the path filter and, without -L, now also skips reading the directory, which ignore's Walk could not). - psh's regular expressions are its own crate psh-pattern (parser, HIR, Unicode tables generated from regex-syntax 0.8.11's by output/unicode-gen/gen.py, Thompson NFA, PikeVM, lazy DFA, literal prefilters and the grep matcher), used by fd, diff, rg/grep (`search/matcher.rs` implements psh's own matcher interface, `crate::matcher` of the searcher change, over it, and grep's `regex_matcher.rs` adapter from grep-regex is gone), jq, git grep/log, the git excludes-file reader, expr and search/posix's existing tests; regex, grep-regex and grep-matcher leave psh-utils, and regex leaves the root lock too (regex-automata and regex-syntax stay in the psh lock only through globset, ignore and bstr) (2026-11-12). Behaviour copies regex 1.13.1 / grep-regex 0.1.14 where psh can see it: a set parses every pattern before translating any (which error wins), `\x{..}` is a codepoint under `(?-u)`, class union, negation and difference follow regex-syntax's interval sets (including its U+D7FF/U+E000 negation quirk), the matcher's capture_count is explicit groups + 1, and the NFA is built in regex-automata's state order with its literal trie, its bounded UTF-8 caches (10,000 and 1,000 FNV slots) and the reverse NFA's unanchored prefix, so `rg --regex-size-limit` fails exactly where it did (probe: smallest passing limit equal on every pattern tried); a pattern whose optimized prefix literals are exact (regex-automata's Pre strategy) builds no full NFA, has no size limit and is searched as that literal set; a RegexSet's size counts all patterns without capture states. The grep matcher picks line candidates from inner literals exactly when grep-regex did, which depends on whether regex-automata calls the regex accelerated: never for a regex anchored at the haystack start (it builds no prefilter), always for one anchored at the end (its reverse anchored strategy), else when a prefix prefilter exists; the first port ignored the anchors, so with a NUL line terminator `grep -z '^\./src'`, `grep -z '^b'`, `grep -z '[a-z]*o$'` and `rg --null-data '\Ab'` judged records in the whole buffer instead of one by one and differed (`matcher.rs`). Speed, in safe Rust: a packed prefilter (`literal.rs` Packed) tests up to three bytes of up to 8 literal groups (literals equal after ASCII lowercasing share a group and test case pairs with one mask) over 64-byte blocks written so the compiler vectorizes them, used instead of memchr2/memchr3 when the rarest byte set's worst frequency rank exceeds 230 (measured: uppercase sets such as R/O/V stay faster on memchr3, lowercase ones such as e/E, f/l/i on the packed scan; block sizes 16, 32, 64 and 128 measured, 64 kept); a regex whose matches cannot start with an ASCII byte skips ASCII a word at a time (NonAscii prefilter, `\p{Greek}`, `\p{Han}`, `[α-ω]`); the lazy DFA's forward loop runs untagged transitions four at a time (`dfa.rs`). Not equal: `shortest_match` values (the end of some match; regex's depends on which internal engine ran; psh only uses whether one exists and the line holding it); word boundaries next to a custom line terminator that is a word byte (psh never sets one); and with a line terminator other than \n, regexes whose acceleration regex-automata decides by its reverse-suffix, reverse-inner or Teddy choices (which also differ between its native and wasm builds) can still have `(?m)^`/`$` judged per record by one side and in the whole buffer by the other; output/nul (seeded random rg --null-data and grep -z command lines with ^, $, (?m), \A, \z, \b over NUL-, LF- and CRLF-separated files) found none: 7,000 cases, 0 differences (the first port: 2 in 1,000).
