- nanocode-digest (crates/core/digest) hashes SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, BLAKE3 and XXH64 from scratch, and sha1, sha2, blake3 and xxhash-rust leave every nanocode crate (2026-11-12). The crate has no dependencies and forbids unsafe code: src/sha1.rs, src/sha256.rs (SHA-224 and SHA-256) and src/sha512.rs (SHA-384 and SHA-512) follow FIPS 180-4 with its constant tables, compress whole 64- and 128-byte blocks straight from the input slice (`as_chunks`, no copy) with every round unrolled and the message schedule computed inline (src/unroll.rs), and share src/pending.rs for the partial block and the length padding; src/blake3.rs follows the BLAKE3 spec for the keyless hash: the message schedule is computed at compile time from the spec's permutation, the incremental `Blake3` compresses 64-byte blocks straight from the input and keeps chaining values on a fixed stack of 54 levels (64 bits of input length less the 10 of a 1,024-byte chunk), and a one-shot `blake3` of at most one chunk skips the stack; src/xxh64.rs is the XXH64 spec. The API is what callers used: `Sha1`..`Sha512` with `new`, `update`, `finalize` (taking `&self`, so a hasher held in a struct can be read) and `digest`, each returning a byte array (so `.into()` after `digest` and `finalize` went away), and `OUTPUT_BYTES` where `Sha256::output_size()` was; `blake3`, `Blake3` (`update` chains as blake3's did), `Hash` (Copy, Eq without an early exit as blake3's, Hash, `as_bytes`, `to_hex`, Display and Debug as blake3 prints them) and `Hex` (`as_str`, Display) for blake3's `ArrayString`; `BLAKE3_OUTPUT_BYTES` for `blake3::OUT_LEN`; `xxh64(bytes, seed)`. Switched: store-jsonl, mcp-tools, chatgpt-extension, code-mode, code-mode-engine (WebCrypto's SHA-1/256/384/512 digest), tool-host, agent, backend-codex, codex client, claude client (its kept `Hash`/`Blake3` values and XXH64 seeds), home, image, audio, mcp and durability-core (imports and calls only). What is not equal: a message past FIPS 180-4's 2^64 bits (2^128 for SHA-512) or past BLAKE3's 2^64 chunks panics where the upstream crates wrap; the upstream crates pick SIMD and SHA-NI at run time and ours is portable. Proven with output/digest-equal, which links sha1 0.11.0, sha2 0.11.0, blake3 1.8.7 and xxhash-rust 0.8.19 (the lock's versions) beside nanocode-digest: the FIPS 180-4 examples (`abc`, the 448- and 896-bit messages, a million `a`, the empty message) against their published digests, BLAKE3's 35 test_vectors.json lengths (0 to 102,400, the repeating 0..250 input) one-shot, byte by byte and in 64 random splits each, and 3,000,000 seeded random inputs (lengths up to 20,000, 30% of them within 4 bytes of a multiple of 32, 64, 128 or 1,024, some of one repeated byte, 0 and random seeds for XXH64) hashed one-shot and in up to 200 random `update` pieces, with a mid-stream `finalize` and a clone, and BLAKE3's hex, Display and Debug compared: 57,124,494 checks, 0 differences. Throughput on the hosted Hand (AMD EPYC 9255, CPU time of the thread, three interleaved rounds, upstream against ours, MB/s, 64 B / 1 KiB / 1 MiB): against the soft backends (`--cfg sha2_backend="soft" --cfg sha1_backend="soft"`) SHA-1 ~450/~940/~960 against ~475/~955/~965, SHA-256 ~195/~380/~470 against ~215/~400/~440, SHA-512 ~375/~585/~705 against ~340/~570/~710, so even; against the default build, where sha2 and sha1 take SHA-NI on this CPU, SHA-256 is ~3.7x faster upstream (~845/~1,800/~2,010 against ~230/~405/~510) and SHA-1 ~2x, while sha2's SHA-512 (AVX2) is even with ours; BLAKE3 ~700/~735/~9,500 upstream against ~695/~845/~800 ours, so even up to a chunk and ~12x slower on 1 MiB, where blake3 hashes chunks in parallel with AVX-512 (the largest callers hash request bodies of tens to hundreds of KiB, under a millisecond each); XXH64 even (~8,200/~19,600/~21,700 against ~7,900/~20,100/~20,400). `cargo metadata --locked` 677 to 676 packages: blake3 and xxhash-rust leave and nanocode-digest joins; sha1 (tungstenite) and sha2 0.10.9 and 0.11.0 (sqlx, postgres-protocol, scrypt and the crates/patches psh and RustPython crates, by their own pins) stay in the lock. Checks: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` and the touched crates, `cargo clippy --locked --lib` for nanocode-digest and every touched crate (no new warnings), and `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` for the same crates, all of which built for WASM before.

- nanocode-schema checks the `email` and `idn-email` formats with its own address parser, and email_address leaves (2026-11-12). crates/core/schema/src/email.rs is what `EmailAddress::from_str` of email_address 0.2.9 did with its default options, the only ones the validator passed: an optional display name before " <" ending in ">", the last "@" splitting local part and domain, a dot-atom or quoted local part of at most 64 bytes, a domain of at most 254 bytes made of labels of at most 63 bytes that start and end alphanumeric, or a bracketed literal; it returns the domain the format check then validates as a hostname or IP literal, as before. Kept as it was, on purpose: email_address treats a non-ASCII character as valid only when its code point's four big-endian bytes happen to read as UTF-8 (so U+00E9 is refused and U+C3A9 accepted); that quirk is reproduced so no address changes verdict, and the IDN path that masks non-ASCII characters is unchanged. Only what the validator used is kept: whether the text parses and whether it has a scheme. - nanocode-schema matches JSON Schema `pattern` and `patternProperties` with its own ECMAScript regex engine, and regress leaves (2026-11-12). crates/core/schema/src/regex/ is regress 0.12.0's `u`-flag dialect rebuilt from the grammar and regress's documented behavior: parse.rs accepts exactly what regress accepts with the same error texts (groups, named groups with duplicate names in separate alternatives, `(?i:)`/`(?m:)`/`(?s:)` modifiers, lookahead and lookbehind, `\k<name>`, `\p{…}` with General_Category, Script, Script_Extensions and the 53 binary properties of ECMA-262, `\u{…}` and surrogate-pair escapes, regress's 65,535-group, 65,535-loop and 256-level nesting bounds); program.rs compiles to a backtracking program whose loop, capture-reset, lookaround and one-character-loop steps are the ones regress's executor takes, simplifies what regress's optimizer removes (empty alternatives and loops, failing alternatives, a lone surrogate in a one-character loop that therefore never matches) and starts matching only where regress's start predicate would (anchored, a literal prefix, a set of first bytes found eight bytes at a time); machine.rs runs it over UTF-8 positions. The Unicode data (properties, simple case folding, ID_Start/ID_Continue) is generated from the Unicode 17.0.0 UCD files regress was built from by output/regex-tables.py into unicode-properties.bin (176 KB, 22,127 ranges in 367 tables), unicode-folds.bin (1,512 pairs) and the name tables in properties.rs. Not equal on purpose: nothing observable; regress's unbounded backtracking stays as it was, so a pattern that backtracks catastrophically or loops on a zero-width body with a huge minimum (`(?:a|){99999999999999999999}`, `((?m:\p{ASCII}{0,2})?-{0}|^){0,2}b\|[^]`) still exhausts memory in both, as the fuzzing shows; a cap there would change which patterns match and is left to its own change. Proven with output/regex-equal, which links regress 0.12.0 beside the module: every property, value and alias name of PropertyValueAliases and PropertyAliases (in four spellings each, under every `\p` form) and the case fold of all 1,114,112 code points, 1,181,114 checks, 0 differences; 2,300,000 seeded random patterns (five seeds) over literals, case-folding pairs, classes, escapes, groups, lookarounds, modifiers, back references, quantifiers and syntax errors, each also anchored as `^(?:…)$`, 1,605,707 of the 4,600,000 compiled and 19,268,484 `is_match` results, the last 600,000 run again after the final change, 0 differences in compile result, error text or match (the 11 patterns that exhausted memory did so in both engines on the same texts); and the 9,324 pattern strings of regress's own test suite, plain and anchored, 423,168 matches, 0 differences. Interleaved runs on the loaded Hand (three rounds, ns per match): `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$` 249–319 regress against 311–760, `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` 205–332 against 259–321, an email-like pattern 815–1,107 against 819–1,033, `^\p{L}[\p{L}\p{N} ]*$` 853–1,908 against 410–570, compiling two such patterns 52–92 µs against 26–41 µs; an unanchored `(?:foo|bar|baz)\d+` over 10.8 KB is 150 ns against 1.7–21 µs, regress's start search being SIMD memchr. `cargo metadata --locked` 710 to 709 packages. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-schema`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-schema --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- perf(djs): JSON.parse's lexer is inlined into its call sites. `Parser::next` returned the 48-byte `Result<Token, Fail>` through memory: `lex` stored the token field by field (and its padding in odd-sized pieces), and the caller copied it right back with 16-byte loads, each spanning several of those stores, so the load could not be forwarded and waited for them to retire. `perf annotate` put over half of `next`'s and `parse`'s samples on those copies. With `lex` and `next` `#[inline(always)]` the token stays in registers. 10 parses of a 1.36 MB array of 20,000 five-key records 71.7→51.0 ms (−29%; 347→269M cycles for the whole script, instructions −4%; QuickJS ≈212 ms); the workerd compute cell's script 136.8→127.8M cycles; json kernel 216.0→213.6M instr; the native djsrun binary +86 KB; test262 39,325/39,365.

- A host sets how long a cell runs before it yields when its call names no `yield_time_ms` (2026-11-12). exec waited `INITIAL_YIELD` and wait `DEFAULT_WAIT_YIELD`, the 10 s of the protocol's tool descriptions, and no host could change either: an eval host whose tasks build for minutes got "Script running" and one more model request for every 10 s of every build from a model that named no yield. `CodeModeRuntime::set_default_yield` replaces both for that runtime. A host reaches it through `ToolsBuilder::cell_yield` (`LocalCells::default_yield` for local cells), and `nanocode hand --cell-yield-ms MS` sets it for a hand. The runtime that has the policy tells the model: `model_specs` restates "Defaults to N ms" in exec's description and builds wait's description and schema with the same number (`exec_spec_yielding`, `wait_spec_yielding`). The protocol's 10 s stays the default and is now written once (`spec::DEFAULT_YIELD`); the policy adds no constant. A `yield_time_ms` in the pragma or in wait's arguments still wins, and wait reads an absent `yield_time_ms` as absent rather than as 10000. Not carried: a brain whose cells run on a remote hand describes its own default, since a hand does not announce its policy, and Claude's exec schema keeps its fixed sentence. Measured through a hand (harness case `cell-yield`: a cell without a pragma whose nested exec_command runs `sleep 13`): by default the cell answered "Script running with cell ID 2" after 11.0 s; with `--cell-yield-ms 30000` it completed after 13.9 s with the command's status 0. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-tool-host`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`; `node harness.mjs --hand=BIN --tool=exec_command --only=cell-yield --hand-args='--cell-yield-ms 30000'`. - A hand that ends on SIGINT, or because its brain ended it, leaves a reader for what its commands left running, and the reader reaps (2026-11-12). 43e077ff3 made a hand stopped with SIGTERM become `nanocode read-outputs`; a hand ended with Ctrl-C, or one whose run returned (the brain revoked it, another hand took its name), still exited with the read ends of those outputs, so a server left with `&` stayed alive and answered nothing. Decided for each end. SIGTERM keeps the exec in place: the pid stays the stopper's to watch, and sessions still running go on. SIGINT and an end by the brain start `read-outputs` as a process of its own (`leave_reader`: its own process group, the null device as its stdio) and then end as before: whoever started the hand gets the terminal or the exit status back, commands still running end with the hand as they did (their guards stop their groups when the runtime stops), and what finished commands left behind keeps a reader. `read-outputs` also waits for the children it inherited (a thread in `wait` until none is left), so a shell that ends under it does not stay a zombie until the reader exits. Measured with output/d1-background/harness.mjs: after `--signal=SIGINT`, `python3 -m http.server PORT &` left by a Bash call and by an exec_command call answered 200 before and 200 after (before the change 200, then curl's 52), `nohup` and plain `&` sleeps and a `while` loop stayed, and a session still running was stopped as before; after SIGTERM the reader had 1 child and no zombie where it had 2 children, 1 a zombie. Not run: an end by Revoked or Replaced, which takes the same `leave_reader` call as SIGINT, and macOS. `cargo clippy --locked --offline -p nanocode-cli -p nanocode-process` reports nothing, for this and for 43e077ff3's handover. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-process`; `cargo build --locked --offline --release -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode`; `node harness.mjs --hand=BIN --loader=/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 --tool=Bash --signal=SIGINT --only=server-amp-holds-pipes,…`. Files: crates/integrations/process/src/{handover,lib}.rs, bin/nanocode/src/lib.rs.
- exec's refusal of a JSON-wrapped source says how to write the JSON string, and no longer advises `String.raw` (2026-11-12). 5d5a57b95's message told the model to send the JavaScript "with no JSON around it and no JSON escaping" and to quote with `String.raw` template literals. A model reads that message only where its exec tool is a JSON function, since only there can an `{"input": …}` wrapper reach the runner, and there the source is the value of a JSON string whatever the message says. A gateway engineer's measurement on gpt-6-luna with exec offered as such a function (15 commands and file contents full of quotes and backslashes, four repetitions, 60 calls an arm): 44 of 60 inputs arrived exactly with the gateway's plain hint, 40 with the `String.raw` advice added to it, 48 and 52 with a hint that says to write each double quote as `\"` and each backslash as `\\`, and 60 of 60 with the free-form tool; the engineer reports the unescaped quote inside the template literal ending the JSON string early, which is how the cut cells come back. The message now says that nothing ran, to send the JavaScript itself, and, where the call's arguments are a JSON object, that the source is one JSON string in it and the arguments must parse: every double quote of the source as `\"`, every backslash as `\\`, the object ended after that string. Not measured: the new message in a session, which needs a model behind such a gateway. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`. File: crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/mod.rs.
- A background job that is not one program runs in a forked copy of the shell and outlives it, as in bash (2026-11-12). psh ran `( … ) &`, `{ …; } &`, `while …; done &`, a function, a builtin and its own utilities (`sleep 300 &`, `tail -f log &`) as a task of the shell's own process: the job ended when the script did, its `$!` was a number no process has, and a later command could not signal it; bash forks for each of these, and agents write exactly these forms. On a host whose shell is its own process (`Host::forks`: the standalone psh on Linux, through `UnixConfig::fork_jobs`; off for embedders, on Windows and wasm, and on macOS until it is run there) `run_background` now forks. A job that is not one simple command forks when its task first runs. A job that is one simple command expands its words first: a program runs as the job's process as before, now also where a utility of psh has its name and `PATH` has the program (`sleep`, `tail`: the process has the program's name and pid, as under bash); a function, a builtin, a shell psh runs itself (`bash script.sh &`) or a utility without a program forks. The parent waits for the copy as for any external, so `$!` is its pid and `wait`, `kill %1`, `jobs`, `disown` and the release at the script's end need nothing new. In the copy the job's vproc is the shell: it takes the process's signals, ignores INT and QUIT as bash's jobs do without job control, has `$BASHPID`, and the process ends with the job's status or by the signal that ended it; the parent's other tasks are forgotten, not dropped (a dropped task would signal the parent's externals). `( … ) &` runs its list in the job's own vproc, as bash forks once for it. A job with a descriptor that is a pipe between two vprocs of the same shell (inside `$( … )` or a pipeline of builtins) stays a task as before, since a copy would not share that pipe. Forking a process that has threads: the host holds what its threads share across the fork (`Host::prepare_fork`: the waiter pool, the escalation count, the readiness registrations and the timers; the engine then holds its wake queue and the embedder's waker) and the copy starts with them empty, with a readiness thread, a signal pipe and a signal watcher of its own. The helper threads of psh-os and the workers of blocking utilities (`Host::thread`) are now threads of the system's own instead of std's: std keeps a table of its threads behind a lock that a starting and an ending thread take, and a copy forked while a waiter thread held it could never start a thread (found by running a script of five jobs again and again: about one copy in 150 hung on that lock). A second hang at about the same rate was the copy's own: a job that ended within the scheduler round in which it forked left the copy parked, since that round still waited for the parent's script; `Shell::step` now leaves the round as soon as the process is a copy. After both, 3,000 runs in a row of a script with six jobs (a subshell with a pipeline of programs, a brace group, a function, `while read …; done < <(seq 20)`, a utility and a program, `wait`, and a job started after it) ended without a hang and with every job's output (debug build, Linux 6.18, glibc 2.39). Measured through a hand started the way an eval slot starts it (the dynamic loader, `nanocode hand --listen`, a scripted Responses endpoint, `nanocode exec --runner-connect`: `output/d1-background/harness.mjs`, and `reference.py` for the same commands under bash 5.2 on pipes and on a terminal), counting what is alive, or has had its effect, at the end of the turn: Bash 12 of 20 ways to leave a job before (130e7f0dc) and 20 of 20 after, bash 20 of 20; exec_command 13 of 21 before, 21 of 21 after, bash 21 of 21; exec_command with `tty: true` 6 of 21 before and after, bash 2 of 21 (on a terminal a job in the shell's group is hung up when the shell exits, under psh as under bash; psh's `nohup`, `setsid` and `disown` jobs get a session at once and stay, where bash's `nohup x &` loses the race with the hangup). The eight that were dead and are alive: `sleep N &`, `tail -f f &`, `(/bin/sleep 1.5; touch f) &`, `(sleep 1.5; touch f) &`, `{ sleep 1.5; touch f; } &`, `f() { sleep 1.5; touch f; }; f &`, `while true; do date > f; sleep 0.2; done &`, `seq 1 40 | while read n; do echo $n > f; sleep 0.2; done &`. No call took longer than its command (Bash at most 323 ms, for a command that sleeps 0.3 s). The standalone psh against bash on 13 scripts (`wait $!` giving a subshell's status 7, `kill %1` giving 143, a later `kill $(cat pid)` stopping a loop, a shell variable read by the job, `bash -c … &`, `true & wait`, `cd /tmp &`): the same files and statuses, psh back in 20 to 40 ms where the script does not wait. The tests of psh, psh-engine and psh-os pass (15, 136, 39), and psh and psh-os check for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu and aarch64-apple-darwin; neither was run there. Not like bash still: on macOS and Windows such a job stays a task and ends with the script; so does a job inside `$( … )` or a pipeline of builtins; the copy has every descriptor the process had open at the fork, also another vproc's private pipe end if one existed at that instant, where bash's copy has the shell's own only; `ps` shows the copy under the shell's command line; rg's own search threads are std's, so a fork in the instant one of them ends could still leave a copy unable to run a parallel rg (not seen). Commands: `cargo build --locked -p psh --bin psh`; `cargo test --locked -p psh-engine -p psh-os -p psh`; `cargo check --locked --lib -p psh-engine --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`; `cargo build --locked --offline --release -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode`; `node harness.mjs --hand=BIN --loader=/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 --tool=Bash|exec_command|exec_command_tty`; `python3 reference.py cases.json pipes|tty DIR`. Files: crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-engine/src/{exec,fd,host,lib,sched,state,util}.rs and util/blocking.rs, psh-os/src/{lib,timer}.rs and unix/{mod,ready,signals,spawn}.rs, psh/src/lib.rs.

With string-keyed reads going through it, an object of 50 keys filled a fifth of the 256 slots and about one key in five shared its slot with another, the two evicting each other on every pass. 1,024 slots (20 KB, still allocated on the first polymorphic fill): `o[ks[j]]` over 50 keys 590.0→492.5M cycles (44.7→38.0 ms, qjs 45.7), `ks.forEach(k => n += o[k])` 740.9→640.2M (57.5→50.9 ms), `Object.keys(o).forEach(...)` 1,078.8→965.7M (82.5→78.5 ms, qjs 77.7); kernels unchanged in instructions; test262 39,325/39,365.
- Our own RFC 6455 WebSocket, crates/core/websocket (nanocode-websocket, native only like nanocode-tls), does what tokio-tungstenite and tungstenite 0.30 did for the Codex Responses socket and the tool-runtime remote and attachment sockets, and both leave (2026-11-12). It keeps their shape so call sites changed only paths: `WebSocketStream` (futures `Stream`/`Sink`, inherent `close`), `client_async_with_config`, `client_async_tls_with_config`, `connect_async_tls_with_config`, `accept_hdr_async(_with_config)` with the same `server::Callback`/`ErrorResponse` rejections, `MaybeTlsStream`, `Connector`, `Message`, `CloseFrame`, `CloseCode`, `Error` with tungstenite's `Display` texts for every variant that can occur, and http 1's `Request`/`Response`. protocol.rs is tungstenite's state machine (Active, ClosedByUs, ClosedByPeer, CloseAcknowledged, Terminated; the queued pong/close reply and when it is flushed; the server ending after its close reply; reset and send-after-close errors) over a `std::io` adapter that turns `Pending` into `WouldBlock`, with tokio-tungstenite's waker proxy so a split reader and writer both wake; frame.rs parses and writes headers (reserved opcodes rejected once the header is complete, as before), masks client frames with keys drawn 64 at a time from one getrandom call and unmasks in 8-byte words without unsafe; message.rs reassembles fragments with the same incremental UTF-8 check and the same error strings (`incomplete string: Incomplete { buffer: .., buffer_len: .. }`, the lossy invalid sequence); handshake.rs writes the request exactly as tungstenite (Host, Connection, Upgrade, Sec-WebSocket-Version, Sec-WebSocket-Key, then caller headers with `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` and `Origin` recased), parses with httparse (124 headers, 4 KiB reads, the 64 KiB / 512-read attack bounds) and checks the response or request the same way; sha1.rs is a 70-line SHA-1 for Sec-WebSocket-Accept (agent 7 had no SHA-1 crate to share; sha1 stays in the graph through nanocode-audio). Limits are tungstenite's defaults where callers used defaults (64 MiB message, 16 MiB frame, 128 KiB read buffer and write threshold, masked client frames required) and the remote runner's own policy where it set them (`WebSocketConfig::frame_bytes_max`, `message_bytes_max`, `read_buffer_bytes`). Codex keeps its permessage-deflate as it was: the same offer header, `InflateStream` inflating server frames below the socket, and requests sent as one rsv1 text `Frame`. What is not equal: payloads are `Vec<u8>` and `Utf8Bytes` holds a `String` (no unsafe, so no Bytes-backed str); a frame larger than the bytes buffered is read straight into its own buffer instead of through the read buffer (same frames, fewer copies); a getrandom failure is `Error::Io` where rand panicked; a handshake write of 0 bytes is tokio's `WriteZero` error where tungstenite asserted; `Connector` is no longer optional (tool-runtime passes `Connector::Plain` for ws:// where it passed `None`; tungstenite's `None` with wss:// built an empty root store, which no caller reached); unreachable variants are gone (`WriteBufferFull`, unknown control/data opcodes, `accept_unmasked_frames`); `MessageTooLong.size` is u64; `connect_async` in nanocode-backend-codex-client keeps its signature over the new types. output/ws-compare links tokio-tungstenite and tungstenite =0.30.0 beside the new crate and compares them over a scripted stream that splits input at random points and returns random partial writes and `Pending`: sha1 against the sha1 crate on 200,000 inputs and 100,000 client keys (0 differences); 20,000 client handshakes (random URLs, caller headers, keys, methods and versions; 101 responses with frames behind them, wrong accept, missing headers, rejected statuses with bodies, HTTP/1.0, malformed lines, too many headers, truncation, subprotocols, 64 KiB headers) comparing request bytes, outcome, the messages after it and the frames written back: 84,964 checks, 0 differences; 20,000 server handshakes (methods, versions, Connection/Upgrade/version/key variants, bearer callback with 401 and 200 rejections, junk after the request, truncation) comparing response bytes and outcome: 80,000 checks, 0 differences; 20,000 sessions in both roles of random frame streams (fragmented text and binary, UTF-8 split across fragments, invalid and incomplete UTF-8, pings to 140 bytes, fragmented control frames, close codes allowed and not with valid and invalid reasons, 1-byte closes, stray continuations, reserved opcodes and bits, wrong masking, non-minimal lengths, frames to 200 KB, small limits, truncation) interleaved with sends to 2.2 MB, feeds, flushes, pings, pongs, rsv1 frames, closes and sink closes: with non-blocking I/O 60,000 checks and 0 differences (61,929 messages and 87,169 errors observed), with blocking I/O 60,000 checks and 4 differences, all in the server role at 40 % `Pending`, where tungstenite itself decides by whether a write would block (a queued pong or close reply goes out before or after the next frame, and the server reaches Terminated only once its close reply is written, so a later read reports `Remote sent after having closed` or `Sending after closing` instead of the end or `Trying to work with closed connection`); interop over TCP of our client with a tungstenite server, a tungstenite client with our server and ours with ours, 30 runs of 40 echoed messages to 400 KB plus a 1000 close: 90 checks, 0 differences. Throughput on the hosted Hand (TCP loopback, interleaved, 7 rounds, medians): receiving 1 KiB text 0.151 s against 0.171 s for 200,000 messages (1,359 against 1,197 MB/s), 1 MiB 0.232 against 0.236 s for 400; sending 1 MiB 0.335 against 0.353 s; sending 1 KiB 0.608 against 0.500 s end to end, while the same client path into a discarding stream encodes 310 to 373 ns per message against 329 to 416, so the gap is not in our framing (the Responses socket sends one request per turn). Each calls `UnicodeNormalization::nfc` or `nfkc` on a `&str` or a `char` iterator and iterates the result, and that trait and `Recompositions` are all the crate has; nfd, nfkd, the quick checks, stream-safe text, CJK variants and the `char` helpers are not written because nothing here calls them. The crate keeps the name and version 0.1.25 so the patch satisfies the parser's `^0.1.23` and stringprep's `0.1`; it is a workspace member with the workspace lints (unsafe code forbidden) and no dependencies. src/tables.rs is generated by output/nfc/generate.py from UnicodeData.txt and DerivedNormalizationProps.txt's Full_Composition_Exclusion: combining classes as a two-level table (3,915 blocks of 32 code points indexing 138 distinct blocks, 8,331 bytes), the 2,081 full canonical decompositions and the 3,849 full compatibility decompositions that differ from the canonical one as sorted arrays searched by code point, and the 961 primary compositions grouped under their 72 second characters; Hangul syllables are decomposed and composed by the Unicode arithmetic (src/lookup.rs), and a character below U+00C0 (U+00A0 for NFKC, both generated) with nothing pending passes through without a lookup or a buffer, so ASCII text allocates nothing. src/decompose.rs orders each run of non-starters by combining class with a stable sort when the next starter (or the end) arrives, and src/compose.rs composes each character with the last starter unless the last uncomposed non-starter's class blocks it, the streaming order of 0.1.25. What differs: the narrower API above; `Recompositions` is not `Clone`, `Display` or `FusedIterator` (unused); the buffers are `Vec`s that allocate on the first decomposed or reordered character rather than past four inline entries; a run of non-starters is held whole as before, bounded by the input. - perf(djs): a computed read with a string key goes through the megamorphic cache. `o[k]` has no cache slot of its own, so every read of a string key interned it and looked it up. Now the slow `GetElem`/`GetElem2` path (`lookup_elem`) writes an own or prototype data property it finds into `mega_ic` (`mega_fill`, with `own_words` shared with `ic_own_fill`), and the hot loop's element case, for a string key whose atom `memo_atom` already knows, tries that slot before declining (`keyed_hit`, out of line so the dispatch loop's code is unchanged; slots check their key and shape as named sites' do). `o[ks[j]]` over 50 keys ×20k 58.2→44.7 ms (qjs 41.4), groupBy `reduce` with `acc[x.g] ??= []` 37.2→28.4 ms (qjs 28.8), `ks.forEach(k => n += o[k])` 67.2→57.5 ms, `Object.keys(o).forEach(...)` 90.5→82.5 ms; kernels unchanged (±0.1% instr); a getter/prototype/proxy/typed-array/String/array/delete/freeze script prints the same as QuickJS; test262 39,325/39,365.
- fix(djs): megamorphic cache slots check their key. A get slot of a shape-mode receiver is a shape and a value slot, which only a site's own slot (whose key is fixed) can trust: in the shared `mega_ic`, two keys whose hashes meet in one slot for the same shape and prototype read each other's values (24 keys on 6 shapes through `new Function('o', 'return o.' + k)` sites, ×30: 673 wrong reads; dictionary entries were safe since `data_at` checks the key). The slot's last word, unused by get slots, now holds the key (`MEGA_KEY`), written with the slot and compared before `get_hit`. dispatch kernel 1,783.3→1,787.3M instr (+0.2%), others unchanged; the script reads 0 wrong values; test262 39,325/39,365.
- perf(djs): the atom memo holds 2,048 strings and is allocated on first intern. 256 slots missed whenever a loop read keys from more distinct string cells than that, as `acc[x.g]` over 1,000 records does; 4,096 (32 KB, all of L1) cost 10% in cycles on `o[k]` loops over 50 keys, and an inline array would put the table in `Heap::over`'s frame, so it is a `Vec` like `mega_ic`, emptied in place. Against the 256 slots: `a.reduce((acc, x) => { (acc[x.g] ??= []).push(x.v); return acc }, {})` over 1,000 records ×300 45.4→37.4 ms (qjs 30.5), `o[ks[j]]` 62.5→57.4 ms, `ks.forEach(k => n += o[k])` 73.4→68.4 ms; kernels unchanged; test262 39,325/39,365.
- perf(djs): interning remembers the atoms of the last strings it saw. `Heap::intern` and `find_string_atom_of` first look in `atom_memo`, 256 slots of string cell → atom indexed by a Fibonacci hash of the offset, filled on every intern and emptied whenever cells move or the arena shrinks (collections, compaction, `release_top`; a restored image starts a fresh heap). A computed key read with strings that are already keys (`o[k]` over `Object.keys(o)`, `for in` bodies, `acc[x.g]`) skipped the array-index parse, flatten check, hash and probe. `o[ks[j]]` over 50 keys ×20k 74.5→62.5 ms (qjs 47.6), `Object.keys(o).forEach(k => n += o[k])` 112.8→102.5 ms, trycatch kernel 1,111.6→1,088.6M instr; other kernels unchanged; test262 39,325/39,365.
- nanocode-tui highlights code with its own syntect port and its own Oniguruma-compatible regex engine, and syntect leaves with onig, onig_sys, bincode, fnv and pkg-config (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md's syntect row). crates/tui/src/highlight/syntaxes.rs is generated by output/syntect-gen from the same default newlines dump `SyntaxSet::load_defaults_newlines` read (75 syntaxes, 4,460 linked contexts, 8,156 match patterns, 3,639 regex sources, 4,556 scopes over 1,391 atoms; includes resolved by syntect's linker, the two it left unresolved in MATLAB skipped as its `MatchIter` skips them; `first_line_match` and `hidden` are not emitted because nothing in nanocode reads them); grammar.rs holds the data types, the lazily compiled regexes (one `OnceLock` per source, like syntect) and the per-context flattened pattern lists, parser.rs ports `ParseState::parse_line` (earliest match over prototypes, the context and its includes, syntect's tie-breaking, per-line search cache, non-consuming push and pop loop protection, the 100-deep push limit, with_prototype, captures-ordered ops, clear_scopes and restore, backreference substitution escaped as regex-syntax's `escape` did) and highlighter.rs ports `Highlighter`, `HighlightState` and `HighlightIterator` for the eight single-scope theme rules (scores `len * 2^(3 * depth)` as f64, the default style when the style stack underflows, the line cut short where a restore finds nothing cleared). regex.rs and regex/ are an Oniguruma 6.9.10 work-alike for `Syntax::default()` (the Oniguruma syntax, not Ruby's: `(?m)` is dot-all, `(?s)` is an error) with `REGEX_OPTION_CAPTURE_GROUP`: a parser that follows regparse.c token by token (option-only groups take the rest of the alternation, `\1`-`\9` are always backreferences, invalid intervals are literals, `{n,m}` with n>m is possessive, nested quantifier reduction, string splitting before a quantifier, class set operations and nested negation), the regcomp.c tuning that changes results (adjacent string merging, ignore-case unravelling of strings and classes with multi-character case folds, look-behind length checks, division of different-length alternatives and reduction of leading quantifiers, empty checks, quantifier expansion limits, automatic possessification, head-exact and peek-next pushes) and a backtracking machine with onig's stack discipline (marks, cut-to-mark voiding, capture restore, repeat counters, `\b` with onig's Latin-1 word table that counts ² ³ ¹ ¼ ½ ¾ as word characters for `\w` and `\b` but not for `[\w]`); regex/unicode.rs is generated by output/unicode-gen from UCD 16.0.0 (onig 6.9.10's version). Search bounds backtracking with `RETRY_LIMIT_IN_MATCH` (10,000,000 per start position, onig's `DEFAULT_RETRY_LIMIT_IN_MATCH`) and returns `SearchError::RetryLimitInMatch`; the parser treats that error as no match at that position, exactly as syntect's regex wrapper treated onig's retry-limit error, because a line hitting it in real Rust windows-sys code and Makefiles would otherwise lose its highlighting; a substituted backreference regex that fails to compile is `ParseError::Regex` (syntect panicked) and the line falls back to `code_style`. Equality: output/regex-harness compares every regex source against onig 6.5.3 (all 3,639 compile or fail alike) over corpus lines of 75 extensions, seeded random strings with non-ASCII, case-fold and ligature characters, and mutations of matching lines, at three start offsets each: three seeds of 26,336,760, 26,342,412 and 10,936,584 searches, every capture group compared, 0 differences once onig's and our retry-limit errors count as no match (the 35 raw differences are both sides failing on the same line, or our required-byte check returning no match where onig spends its 10,000,000 retries; syntect saw no match in both). output/e2e-harness runs `highlight::line` from master (syntect) and from this commit over real files of the 33 syntaxes that have files on this Hand (repository, ~/.cargo/registry/src, /usr/share, /usr/include, /usr/lib/python3) plus 700-line corpus documents for each of the 75 syntaxes, carrying state across lines and resuming through `state()`/`from_state` with a half line in between as markdown.rs does, plus line-edit, line-shuffle and random-line mutations: two seeds of 762 documents and 381,470 lines with 1 difference and 2,232 documents and 844,524 lines with 0 differences, and syntax_for_token and syntax_for_path over 82,850 names, extensions, paths and random strings with 0 differences. The one difference is not equal on purpose: Makefile's nested-parenthesis look-ahead (the "level 0 ... level 4" pattern, also in Rust) takes about 3 s per search on a corpus line in both engines, onig gives up at its 10,000,000th retry and we finish the search under it with a match, because our retry count is close to but not identical with onig's bytecode (its optimizer merges and skips pushes we do not), so lines that drive a pattern to within a few percent of the limit can highlight differently. Speed, from output/e2e-harness's bench on the shared Hand at load 15 to 23, old and new interleaved: highlighting 156 real files of 33 syntaxes (46,166 lines, 1.4 MB) took five rounds at 9,992 to 21,911 lines/s before and 21,102 to 45,972 after (2.0 to 3.1x); first use (assets, theme, the Rust lookup and one highlighted line in a fresh process, 15 runs each) has a median of 5,429 us before and 3,730 us after; compiling all 3,639 regex sources takes 278 to 298 ms against onig's 372 to 376 ms; searches that run into the retry limit are about 1.5x slower than onig's (regex-harness totals 61.5 s against 42.2 s, dominated by them). `cargo metadata --locked` 645 to 639 packages (710 to 704 on the master it was written against); the port uses the terminal layer's `ui` styles and the Unicode 17 width and grapheme functions where it was written against ratatui and unicode-width. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-tui` (no warnings) and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.

Width walks the text from its end as unicode-width does, through one enum of what follows the character (`Following`: a line feed, emoji presentation, modifier, ZWJ, keycap, tag-flag and regional indicator sequences, variation selectors 1 to 3, 15 and 16, and the Arabic lam-alef, Hebrew, Buginese, Tifinagh, Lisu, Old Turkic, Khmer coeng and Kirat Rai ligatures, whose leftover selector bits are three flags); an ASCII text is its length less its CR LF pairs and an ASCII run inside other text is measured at once. Exact equality is the requirement (every event's byte range reaches the renderer), so the algorithm is pulldown-cmark's own; crates/tui/NOTICE.md and bin/nanocode/NOTICE.md carry its MIT license. Its names are whole words, its limits are named constants (`LINK_DESTINATION_PARENTHESES_MAX` 32, `LINK_LABEL_CODE_POINTS_MAX` 1,000, `TABLE_FILLED_CELLS_MAX` 2^18, `LINK_REFERENCE_EXPANSION_BYTES_MIN` 100,000, the spec's 4-column code indent, 9 list digits, 7 decimal and 6 hex entity digits, 2 to 32 byte URI schemes and 63-byte email labels), no function recurses (the iterator's recursion past tight paragraphs is a loop), and no unsafe code is needed since pulldown-cmark's only unsafe code is its SIMD scanner, off by default. Three tables are generated by output/commonmark-tools/gen_tables.py: entities.rs (the 2,125 named references ending in `;` from WHATWG's entities.json), case_fold.rs (full case folding, statuses C and F of Unicode 18.0.0 CaseFolding.txt, which link labels compare with as unicase's `UniCase` did) and punctuation.rs (general categories P and S of Unicode 15.1.0 UnicodeData.txt, the set pulldown-cmark's table holds). Not equal: where pulldown-cmark 0.13.4 panics on an empty tight paragraph in `OffsetIter` (`unwrap` at parse.rs:2199; 14 of 5,000,000 random documents and 2 of 2,000,000 more, all with footnote definitions in set A, such as `1) [^x]: '1990s\r            \r`), which crashed the TUI, the new parser skips that paragraph and goes on; pulldown's plain `Parser` iterator ended the stream there instead, and no input of set B reached it.
