- A template literal (the `concat` instruction) of up to 16 parts whose strings are flat and shorter than `APPEND_START_LEN` (256 units) together is written into one new string (`Heap::concat_flat`, `CONCAT_FLAT_PARTS`) (2026-11-12). It joined the parts two at a time, and below `ROPE_MIN_LEN` each join copied everything so far into another new string: six parts were six allocations and copies. A rope part, a longer result or more parts take the pairwise joins as before, so an accumulator that grows by `out += …` keeps its append buffer (a 4,096-unit cap instead slowed such a loop by 11%). The template micro benchmark went from 50.2 to 40.5 ms (QuickJS 2021-03-27: 44.6 ms; djsrun minimum of 5, hosted Hand), the strings, lines and str_concat benchmarks did not move, and the instruction counts of the kernels did not change. A script of 12 templates run twice (numbers, -0, 1e21, booleans, null, undefined, Latin-1 and two-byte strings, lone surrogates, empty parts, 200- and 300-unit parts, slices, ropes, objects with toString in order, a Symbol, 18 parts, a 300-line accumulator) prints what it printed before and what Node prints. test262 stays at 39,325 of 39,365.
- GetIterator and IteratorClose of an Array or String Iterator cache their prototype lookups (`Exec::iterator_method` and `Exec::lacks_return` in ic.rs, `Heap::iterator_ic` and `Heap::return_ic`) (2026-11-12). Each array destructuring and for-of looked up @@iterator from the Array (its own properties, then Array.prototype's table) and `return` along the iterator's chain (the iterator, %ArrayIteratorPrototype%, %IteratorPrototype%, Object.prototype). The @@iterator read now keeps a prototype-read slot as a get site does (D1621, built by `proto_words`, the part of `ic_proto_fill` that computes it), and the absence of `return` keeps the iterator's prototype and the prototype epoch, after marking the chain `OBJ_IS_PROTO` as an addition cache does, so adding `return` or changing a prototype on that chain misses. Both are emptied by every collection, as `mega_ic` is, and the iterator's own properties are still looked up. Instructions per run (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, djsrun, hosted Hand): `closures` 4,398.0M to 4,033.7M, `maps` 1,947.5M to 1,886.8M, others unchanged; djsrun minimum of 5: 300,000 `const [c, d] = [1, k]` 67.8 to 53.4 ms, `for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(o))` over 50 keys 6,000 times 69.4 to 56.4 ms (QuickJS 2021-03-27: 83 ms), micro benchmarks entries 235.6 to 187.7 ms, destructure 230.0 to 204.9 ms and map_set 84.4 to 77.4 ms. A script that adds and removes `return` on each object of the chain (a method, a getter, null), replaces Array.prototype's and String.prototype's @@iterator, gives an array its own or an inherited one, swaps %ArrayIteratorPrototype%'s prototype and collects in between, with warm caches before each step, prints what it printed before and what Node prints. test262 stays at 39,325 of 39,365.
- Spreading a plain object into an empty one copies its shape and values block (`Heap::clone_plain_props`, from `copy_data_props` for `{...o}` and from Object.assign's native entry), and an object rest of a plain object builds the rest from its entries in one step (`Heap::plain_entries` and `new_object_from_entries` in `rest_props`) (2026-11-12). A plain object (`Heap::plain_shape`) is an ordinary non-prototype object in shape mode without elements or indexed properties whose every descriptor is a string key with writable, enumerable and configurable data flags: CreateDataProperty of each of its keys, in order, into an empty extensible ordinary object ends in the same shape and values, so the target takes the shape and a copy of the values (shapes are shared and never change). Object.assign only gets there after its existing check that no key meets a setter or a read-only property on the target's chain. Anything else (a symbol, accessor, non-enumerable or read-only key, elements, a dictionary-mode object, a target with properties) takes the per-key loop as before. djsrun minimum of 5 (hosted Hand; QuickJS 2021-03-27 in brackets): 300,000 `{...base}` of five keys 92.3 to 19.3 ms (100), 300,000 `Object.assign({}, base)` 149.3 to 79.9 ms (104), 300,000 `const {a, ...rest} = {…four keys}` 157.6 to 132.4 ms (160); micro benchmarks spread 56.4 to 38.8 ms and destructure 259.9 to 225.0 ms. A script of 26 cases run twice (`__proto__` keys from JSON.parse, symbols, non-enumerable, getters, index keys, frozen and read-only sources, class instances, prototypes, nullish, strings and arrays spread, keys before and after a spread, rests with symbols, getters and `__proto__`, setters on the target's chain, a Proxy, a function, 80 keys, deleted keys, mutation of either side afterwards) prints what it printed before and what Node prints. test262 stays at 39,325 of 39,365.
- Array.prototype.flat of a plain Array is native (`array_flat` and `flatten_into` in fast.rs, `@fast` on ArrayPrototypeFlat) (2026-11-12): with depth undefined or a primitive, and the Array's species the plain Array, each element present in dense storage is pushed or, while depth remains and it is an Array, flattened in turn, and the result is one new Array. A hole, an element that is a Proxy while depth remains, an Array-like `this`, an object depth (its valueOf is observable) or nesting past `FLAT_MAX_NESTING` (64) leaves the call to the builtin as before. 20,000 calls of `[[1,2],[3,[4,5]],[6]].flat(2)` went from 35.7 to 8.2 ms (4.2 ms of it building the literal), and the flat_concat micro benchmark from 42.4 to 12.7 ms (QuickJS 2021-03-27: 29.2 ms; djsrun minimum of 5, hosted Hand). A script of 15 cases run twice (depths undefined, 0, −1, 2, '2', 1.7, NaN, null, true, Infinity and a valueOf object, holes, undefined elements, a subclass, a Proxy element, an Array-like, a removed constructor, a cycle, 100 levels, a getter, an index on Array.prototype) prints what it printed before and what Node prints. test262 stays at 39,325 of 39,365. scripts/gen-intrinsics.py and scripts/bgen.sh regenerated builtins/gen.
- JSON.parse gives an object the shape the previous object at the same depth got when their keys match, in order (`Heap::new_object_from_entries_like`, `Heap::shape_is`, one shape per depth in the parser) (2026-11-12). An array of records repeats one key list per depth, and each object walked the shape tree from the root again, one descriptor scan and one transition search per key. A match compares the shape's descriptors with the keys and their flags, so duplicate keys, a different order or another key set take the walk as before, and the values block is allocated and filled as the walk would leave it. Allocation never collects, so a shape stays put for the whole parse. Instructions (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, djsrun, five runs, hosted Hand): parsing 20,000 records of five keys with a nested object five times 7,487.7M to 6,627.8M (−11.5%), 20,000 pushed, stringified, parsed, filtered and joined 1,133.2M to 1,081.1M, the `json` kernel 226.6M to 216.1M, other kernels within 0.6%. A script of 8 inputs parsed twice (duplicate keys, `__proto__`, index keys, empty and nested objects, reordered keys, a reviver, 70-key objects past the shape limit, 50 alternating key sets, mutation and freezing afterwards) prints what it printed before and what Node prints. test262 stays at 39,325 of 39,365.
- djs collects after the arena grew by twice the live data instead of once (`LIVE_GROWTH`, heap/gc.rs `next_threshold_cheap`; still at least `MIN_GROWTH` and never past half the headroom below the limit) (2026-11-12). Every collection marks and slides all the young live data (a minor one leaves only the builtin prefix), so a run that builds up data paid for it about twice as often as it grew. Instructions per run (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, djsrun, hosted Hand): the `json` kernel 277.1M to 226.6M (12.50 to 10.26 ms), `maps` 2,021.9M to 1,949.2M, `objects` 4,818.7M to 4,774.5M, the others within 1.2%; 20,000 objects pushed, stringified, parsed, filtered and joined 12.4 to 10.2 ms; the workerd `compute` cell 478.0M to 456.9M instructions per turn, other cells flat. Peak RSS stayed within 2 MB on runs that keep 100,000 to 400,000 objects (14 to 49 MB) and on every kernel, and the workerd harness's RSS did not rise (305/296/299 to 292/294/293 MB). test262 stays at 39,325 of 39,365.
- `grep` and `wc` reuse their read buffers across files (2026-11-12). `Run::search` allocated a zeroed 96 KiB buffer for the first read of every file and `wc` a 64 KiB one per operand; grep now keeps one in `Run` and passes the bytes read as a borrowed slice to the searcher, and wc allocates once before its loop. `grep -rn needle src` over 2,000 files (14 MB): wasm 15.5 → 14.1 ms (30 runs each, alternated), native 14.8 → 13.1 ms; `wc -l $(find src -type f)` wasm 12.6 → 12.3 ms. Same output as before and as GNU grep on recursive searches with binary, unreadable and large files, -l -L -c -q -C, --binary-files and stdin, and on the wc case file. Upstream delta: none.
- `head` leaves standard input from a seekable file just after what it printed (2026-11-12). It reads 64 KiB at a time, so `{ head -n 2; cat; } < f`, `while read l; do head -n 1; done < f` or `head -n 1 <&3` twice lost the rest of the block; GNU head seeks back on such input, and bash scripts rely on it. After the last block of `-n N`/`-c N`, and after `-n -N`/`-c -N` printed all but the end, `head` seeks standard input back by what it read and did not print (`UtilCtx::seek_stdin`, a no-op on pipes and on hosts whose files cannot seek). Named files and pipes are unchanged: GNU head cannot give back to a pipe either. 12 bash-compared scripts (two heads in a row, -c, -n -N, -z, a descriptor opened with exec, read loops, pipes) now match; before 9 differed. Upstream delta: none.
- Plain `sort` of lines shorter than 8 bytes sorts on exact keys (2026-11-12). Such a line's first 8 bytes, zero padded, with its length in the last byte, order exactly as the line does (a prefix sorts first because its padding is zero and its length smaller), so the whole-line path sorts `(key, line)` by key alone and never compares the lines themselves; a reverse sort reverses the result as before. `sort` of `cut -c1-2` of 1,000,000 lines (about 100 distinct values): wasm 22.5 → 19.6 ms, native 37.9 → 34.6 ms. Writing the output straight from sorted u64 keys was tried and was slower in wasm (25.3 ms: the extra pass to rebuild the lines costs more than the smaller records save). Same output as GNU sort under LC_ALL=C on NUL bytes, empty lines, bytes ≥ 0x80, -r, -u, -z, a last line without newline, and as before on the three sort case files. Upstream delta: none.
- djs sorts by a difference, order or localeCompare comparator natively: `%SortByKey` (array.rs, called by SortList before the merge sort) takes a comparator whose bytecode is exactly `(a, b) => a - b` or `b - a`, an order ternary `a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0` (either direction, either operand order), or `a.localeCompare(b)` while String.prototype.localeCompare is the original, each also over one property of each element (`a.k - b.k`) (2026-11-12). Such a comparator is consistent, so any stable sort gives the merge sort's order: Numbers other than NaN are compared numerically and strings by code units (Latin-1 strings only for localeCompare, which djs implements as a code-unit compare), each from an element or an ordinary object's own data property, sorted with `crate::sort::sort_by` and written back. Anything else (another comparator, NaN, mixed types, undefined, a getter, an inherited key, a replaced localeCompare) leaves the list to the merge sort, which calls the comparator through its resume points. The `sort` kernel (100,000 integers, `(p, q) => p - q`) went from 1,990.3M to 347.3M instructions (77.0 to 18.7 ms); micro benchmarks (djsrun minimum of 5, hosted Hand, QuickJS 2021-03-27 in brackets): 1,000 integers 200 times by difference 83.2 to 15.3 ms (44.5), objects by a string field with the ternary 105.6 to 21.4 ms (74.8), 1,000 strings 100 times by localeCompare 67.9 to 7.1 ms. Two scripts of 18 and 30 sorts, run twice so the comparators are compiled (signed zeros, infinities, NaN, undefined, mixed types, holes, by a property ascending and descending, a getter, an inherited key, a replaced localeCompare, non-Latin-1 strings, ties, `toSorted`), print exactly what djs printed before. test262 stays at 39,325 of 39,365. scripts/gen-intrinsics.py and scripts/bgen.sh regenerated the table, natives and builtins/gen.
- awk reads `$1`…`$8` of an unsplit record in place and runs rules without a future until they wait (2026-11-12). With FS blanks or one byte (not paragraph mode), `field_at` finds field i by scanning to it, so `field_num`, `field_text` and `get_field` no longer split the whole line into the field list when a rule reads only a few fields; any other access still splits it once. `exec` is now `exec_now` (push the frame, `step` until done or until it waits) and `exec_wait` (the old loop from the waiting step), and the record loop calls `exec_now` for patterns and actions, so a rule that needs no input or output never builds the async state. `awk '{s+=$1} END {print s}'` over 1,000,000 lines: native 67.6 → 51.1 ms (918 → 875 M instructions), wasm 63.4 → 54.2 ms; `awk '{}'` wasm 35.1 → 30.2. Same output as before on 46 field, FS, paragraph, getline, exit, next, range, function and error scripts, the awk case file and 727 agent cases. Upstream delta: none.
- `${#x}`, `${x#p}`, `${x%p}` (and `##`, `%%`) and `${x:-w}`, `${x:+w}` expand synchronously (2026-11-12). `expand_part_now` handled only a bare `$x`, so any parameter operator sent the whole command to the async path. `param_op_now` covers a plain scalar or positional (no subscript, nameref, computed value, `$@`/`$*`/`$$`/`$!`), operands of literals, quotes and plain parameters, and patterns of the same plus double quotes; `params_now`/`part_static` let `now::command` take such words. `remove_affix_with` strips `L`, `*L` and `L*` with a byte search when L is ASCII without pattern characters, instead of matching every prefix of the value. Native `for ((i=0;i<20000;i++)); do f=dir/file$i.txt; b=${f##*/}; e=${b%.txt}; n=${#e}; d=${x:-def}; done` 82.7 → 34.3 ms; wasm 141 → 58 ms. Same output as before on 40 bash-compared operator scripts (globs in values and operands, IFS, set -u, extglob, nocasematch, namerefs, -i, arrays, UTF-8, quoted patterns), on the 727 agent cases and the tool case files. Upstream delta: none.
- Code Mode's bootstrap parses a nested tool call's result and settles the caller's promise in the pump, from `[resolve, reject, name]` kept per call, instead of chaining `.then(jsonParse, …)` on the call's promise (2026-11-12). Each call made one promise and one reaction job fewer; a result that is not JSON, or a failure payload `toolFailure` cannot turn into an error, still rejects the caller's promise with the thrown error. Measured with `perf stat -e instructions:u` on the hosted Hand (jsbench from output/durability-ledger, real `CodeModeRuntime` on djs, per-cell instructions from 200- and 1,200-cell runs, against 38c7cbefa): one call per cell went from 425,884 to 417,666 instructions, 16 sequential calls from 2,579,202 to 2,468,924 (−4.3%), 16 parallel calls with 100-character strings from 2,995,432 to 2,879,742 (−3.9%) and four calls in try/catch from 890,265 to 860,035.
- `read` and assignments in front of a builtin take the synchronous path (2026-11-12). `now::command` adds read to its builtins, and runs a builtin with prefix assignments (`IFS= read -r line`) when each target is a plain variable (no nameref, -i, case attribute, readonly or computed value) and none appends: the values expand after the words, as in `prefix_assigns`, are set exported for the builtin and put back in reverse order afterwards, as `run_builtin` does. Native `while IFS= read -r l; do n=$((n+1)); done` over 100,000 lines from a file 202 → 152 ms (260 before the previous entry). Same output as before on 19 bash-compared scripts of prefix assignments (repeated names, values that use earlier ones, exported, readonly, -i, -l, unset, arithmetic errors, set -u, functions) and on the read scripts and 727 agent cases. Upstream delta: none.
- read reads ahead from engine pipes and seekable files and gives back what follows the line (2026-11-12). It read one byte per poll, each through `or_signal`, so a line of n bytes cost n+1 reads (n+1 syscalls on a file). `Input` now reads up to the first delimiter already in an engine pipe's buffer (`PipeReader::line_len`), or 128 bytes from a file whose offset can be read (doubling to 4 KiB while no delimiter comes), and `give_back` returns the rest before anything else can read the descriptor: pushed back onto the pipe (`PipeReader::unread`) or sought back on the file. Terminals, FIFOs and other unseekable files still go one byte at a time, as in bash. Before → after, `while read -r l; do :; done` over 100,000 lines: native from a file 236 → 173 ms, from a pipe 154 → 133 ms; WASM `while IFS= read -r l; do n=$((n+1)); done < file` 293 → 188 ms (with the next entry). Same output as before on 29 scripts compared with bash: read then cat, head or sed on the same file or pipe, -n, -N, -d, -u, -a, -r and backslashes, NUL bytes, CRLF, multibyte characters cut by -n, no last newline, empty input, break out of a loop then read the rest, here-strings and here-documents. Upstream delta: none.
- A hand that is stopped with SIGTERM hands what its commands left running to a process that only reads their output (2026-11-12). `nanocode hand` had no SIGTERM handler, so a stop ended the process at once and with it the read ends of every pipe and the controller of every terminal it held. A server the agent left in a `tty: true` exec_command session was hung up at that moment; one left in a session without a terminal, or started with a plain `&` in a call that had returned, stayed alive but failed at its next line of output: a Python `http.server` then closed each request's connection without a response (curl status 52). An eval harness stops the hand before its verifier runs, so that the agent cannot see the tests: in the Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of 2026-11-12 a package index served from a terminal session was dead when the verifier asked for it. Now nanocode-process keeps a duplicate of the descriptor of every session output and of every pipe a discarding task reads (`output::Open`, in an `Atom`; the embedded shell's streams have none), `hand_over(command)` runs the given command with `read-outputs` and those descriptors in place of this process (`exec`: the same process id, so its children stay its children, and nothing of the hand is left to run a cell or reach the brain), and `read_outputs_if_requested` is that program: one thread per descriptor reads until end of file or the terminal's EIO, then it exits with 143, the status a SIGTERM leaves. With nothing to read `hand_over` returns 143 and the hand exits as before. The hand is not dropped first, because dropping a session terminates it; so a command in flight is left running too, as it was when SIGTERM killed the hand, but its pipe is not read. `nanocode_psh::program()` is the command that starts this executable again, through the loader when one started it. Checked with output/d1-background/harness.mjs (hand started through the loader, Linux x86_64), HTTP requests to the server two at a time before and after the stop: a server left in a session answered 200/200 then 52/52 without a terminal and 200/200 then connection refused with one before this change, and 200/200 then 200/200 in both after it; a server started with `python3 -m http.server PORT &` in a Bash call 200/200 then 52/52 before, 200/200 then 200/200 after; the reading process was the hand's process id, ended with 143 within 1.5 s of the last such process being killed, and a hand with nothing left exited with 143 at once. With a cell in flight at the stop (`sleep 4; touch a` then a second call), the command finished and the second call never ran. Not done: the reading process does not reap the children it inherits, so those that end stay zombies until it does; a second SIGTERM ends it at once (the default action), which hangs up what it read for; a hand the brain disconnects (`Revoked`, `Replaced`) or that ends on SIGINT still ends as before. Not checked: macOS.
- djs builds an object rest (`const {a, ...rest} = src`) natively when `src` is a non-proxy object without enumerable getters and the excluded keys are strings (2026-11-12). `%CopyDataPropertiesExcluding` ran as bytecode, comparing every key with every excluded key through `Get` and `SameValue`; `call_intrinsic` now takes those cases itself: each excluded string becomes the atom it already is (an index string its integer atom; a string never interned names no key), and the enumerable data properties of `src` not among them are defined on a new object from %Object.prototype%. Anything else (a primitive or Proxy source, a getter, a computed numeric or symbol key) still runs the builtin. `const {a, ...rest} = {a: k, e: 3, f: 4}` 300,000 times went from 395.3 to 115.7 ms (QuickJS 2021-03-27: 100.5 ms), and the micro-benchmark mixing it with an array pattern from 587.0 to 236.3 ms (djsrun minimum of 5, hosted Hand). A script of 15 patterns (index and computed keys, string, Array, Proxy and class-instance sources, a getter, symbols, a `__proto__` own key, non-enumerable and absent keys, parameters) prints the same as QuickJS, and test262 stays at 39,325 of 39,365.
- djs's `Object.assign` has a native entry (builtins/fast.rs, `@fast` on `ObjectAssign`) for an ordinary target when every source is null, undefined, a non-string primitive, an empty string or a non-proxy object without enumerable getters, and every enumerable key a source copies is a writable data property on the target or its prototypes, or absent from an extensible target (2026-11-12). It checks all of that before writing anything, then copies source by source, reading each value when it writes it, with the heap's own-value write or CreateDataProperty, which is what [[Set]] does in those cases; anything else declines to the builtin. As bytecode it was 3.8x QuickJS: `Object.assign({}, {a: 1, b: 2}, {c: k})` 200,000 times went from 301.9 to 106.2 ms (QuickJS 2021-03-27: 81.7 ms; djsrun minimum of 5, hosted Hand). A script of 21 cases (a `__proto__` key from JSON.parse, inherited and own setters, read-only, frozen and non-extensible targets, an inherited read-only key, getters, string, number and symbol keys, the target as a later source, an Array target, a Proxy source, a class instance) prints the same as QuickJS, and test262 stays at 39,325 of 39,365. builtins/gen is regenerated by scripts/bgen.sh.
- jq parses strings, numbers, blanks and object keys from its buffer in bulk (2026-11-12). `Reader::string` copies each run without a quote, backslash or control byte at once, `literal` takes a token that ends inside the buffer as a slice (falling back to the byte loop for errors and for tokens at the buffer's end, so messages and positions are unchanged), `skip_ws` skips a run of blanks with its line and column, and `key` returns a key without escapes from a 256-slot cache of `Rc<str>`, so an array of objects allocates each key name once. Before → after, `jq -r '.[].name'` over a 2.7 MB array: native pshm 37.5 → 35.1 ms CPU; WASM wall jq workload 50.4 → 47.0 ms. Same output and status as before for nine inputs (escapes, surrogate pairs, raw control characters, invalid literals, unfinished input, several values per line, huge and tiny numbers, UTF-8 keys) under `.`, `-c`, `..|strings`, `input_line_number` and `tostream`, and on the big file. Upstream delta: none.
- sort -n keeps a 32-byte record per line instead of 48 (2026-11-12). `Num` holds its rank as two u64 and its line as a u32 (inputs of 2^32 lines or more take the general keyed path), so it no longer has a u128's 16-byte alignment, and a key without fraction digits skips the 18-step fraction fold. Most of the native time was the kernel faulting in fresh pages for the records. Before → after, `sort -n` over 1M lines: native pshm 57 → 41 ms CPU; WASM wall 34.0 → 31.7 ms. Same output as before on the three sort case files (79 cases: -n with -r, -u, -k, -t, -s, signs, fractions, blanks, huge numbers). Upstream delta: none.
- The prompt cache lifetime of API-key Claude sessions stays five minutes; a one-hour lifetime would cost more than the misses it removes (2026-11-12). Measured on the exported event streams of one Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of the Claude harness (89 tasks, 1,182 model calls, 26.05M input tokens of which 24.39M were cache reads): 15 calls followed a gap of more than 300 s since the previous call (none more than 3,600 s), and 11 of them read only the 6,664-token static prefix from the cache and wrote the rest of the conversation again (14k to 44k tokens each). Priced in base input tokens, with a five-minute write at 1.25, a one-hour write at 2 and a read at 0.1, the run's input cost 4.51M units as it ran; those 11 misses account for 0.21M of it (4.6%). Writing every cache entry with the one-hour lifetime instead would have removed the 11 misses and made every other write dearer: 5.42M units, 20% more. So `cache_one_hour` stays off by default, and the lever for these gaps is the refresh 6f49aa8cf added for a session that waits past the lifetime: one read of the prefix per five minutes of waiting, 0.04M units over the same 11 gaps, a net saving of about 0.17M units (3.7% of input cost) if it runs on such a session. Not verified: that the refresh runs on an API-key session behind a gateway, and its effect on a live run; the provider reported no cache-write counts in this run, so writes are taken as the uncached input of each call. The script is a pass over each task's `model.call.completed` events (input tokens, cached tokens, time since the previous call ended). No code changes.
- A nanocode that the dynamic loader starts runs psh through the loader too (2026-11-12). `nanocode_psh::shell()` named `current_exe()` as psh's program. A host that carries nanocode with a loader and libraries of its own starts it as `ld.so --library-path DIR nanocode …` (nanoeval's slots do, so that one build runs in every task image), and `/proc/self/exe` is then the loader: every command the embedded shell did not run in place was started as `ld.so psh-shell -c …` and ended with status 127, so a hand of today's master could run almost nothing in such a slot. On Linux `shell()` now compares `/proc/self/cmdline` with the arguments the program itself was given: the words the loader consumed (its options) stay in front, then the program by its canonical path, then `psh-shell`, all run by the loader. nanocode-cli asks for the shell before it hides a prompt from its argument area (6989c41d0), which empties that file. Checked with output/d1-background/harness.mjs `--loader=/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2` (the hand started as the loader's argument, Linux x86_64): on f9c53fe29 all 14 Bash cases ended with status 127; with this change 12 of 14 through Bash and 13 of 15 through exec_command are alive at the next call, as without the loader. Other systems keep `current_exe()`. Not covered: a `--library-path` relative to a directory the process has left since (the loader's words are passed on as given), and nc-lite with a prompt hidden before it asks (it does not hide one).
- `hands` lists the machines a call can name, not the runner that only executes scripts (2026-11-12). A host that runs cells in the brain's own process (`LocalCells`, which a Worker registers as the fallback beside its sandbox hand) has no tools and answers every call that names it `this host cannot run X for another hand`, yet `hands` listed it by name with no `about`, and models took it for a second machine: in each arm of the Terminal-Bench 2.1 run three calls probed `hand: "local"` and failed, and one model went on to reason about a brain machine it could not reach. `LocalCells` now describes itself, with no tools and no capabilities, and `hands` leaves out a described hand that has neither unless the script is running on it, in which case `here` names it and `about` shows its empty tool list. A host that gives no description is listed as before, since nothing says it takes no calls. The tool's description gains one sentence saying so. Checked with output/code-mode-lab `hands` (a hand serving `hand_tools` over a loopback WebSocket registered as the default, `LocalCells` as the fallback): before, `hands = ["local","slot"]` with `about` for slot only; after, `hands = ["slot"], here = "slot"`, and with the session placed on the runner `hands = ["local","slot"], here = "local"` with `about.local: tools = []`; a call naming the runner fails as before without running anything. Not run: a model. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-tool-host`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `-p nanocode-code-mode --features local-cells --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode/src/{code_mode/local.rs,remote/executors.rs}.
- A command that ends leaves what it started in the background running, and a call returns when its shell exits, not when its pipes close (2026-11-12). nanocode-process killed the process group of every command once its shell had exited: the reaper sent SIGSTOP and SIGKILL to the group before it reaped the leader (`prepare_to_reap`), and `Session::wait_for_output` asked for it again. `server &`, `nohup server > log 2>&1 &` and `bash start.sh` were therefore gone when Bash or exec_command returned, where Claude Code's Bash and a shell leave them running, and `setsid nohup x &` usually lost the race with the kill. In the Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of 2026-11-12 on the build nanoeval pinned, 12 of 87 Claude-harness trajectories start a shell background job; four rows were lost to it, three of which Claude Code passed, and one agent measured it itself (a `nohup` launch left no process and no log, `Popen(start_new_session=True)` survived). Under psh, `nohup`, `setsid` and disowned jobs already left the group (psh gives them a session), plain `&` jobs did not. Now the group is killed on a timeout, a cancelled call, a terminated session and a dropped `ProcessChild`, and never because the shell exited: `prepare_to_reap` is gone and the reaper only reaps. A background process may hold the command's stdout or stderr, so reading to end of file would wait for it. `run_bash` and the session drains stop reading when the shell exits, take what the pipe holds at that moment without waiting (`Ready::ready`: a non-blocking read of the descriptor for pipes, `try_recv` for the embedded shell's streams; everything the shell and the commands it waited for wrote is in the pipe by then, so no grace period is needed), and give a pipe that a process still holds to a task that reads and discards until it closes, so that process does not die of SIGPIPE at its next line of output. A terminal session's reader is a blocking read that nothing can interrupt: `finish_drains` aborted it after `DRAIN_GRACE` and then awaited it, which never returned while a process held the terminal, so exec_command with `tty: true` did not return (11 s to the cell's yield, with the session left behind); it now leaves that reader after the grace. Checked with output/d1-background/harness.mjs on Linux x86_64: a scripted Responses endpoint drives `nanocode exec --runner-connect` against `nanocode hand --listen`, one call per case, and reads the process table when the next model request arrives, at the end of the turn, and after SIGTERM to the hand. Three builds, 14 cases through Bash and 15 through exec_command (`nohup x > log 2>&1 &`, `x &` with the pipes held, `setsid nohup x &`, `x > /dev/null 2>&1 &`, `(cd d && x &)`, Python's `Popen(start_new_session=True)`, a nohup'd HTTP server, `x & disown`, `bash -c 'x &'`, `bash start.sh`, `x & echo; sleep; echo`, an HTTP server started with a plain `&`, psh's own `sleep &`, a compound `( … ) &`, and for exec_command a server left running in a session): processes alive at the next call were 1 of 14 and 2 of 15 on the released CLI of 2026-11-06 (Python's own session only, and the session), 5 of 14 and 6 of 15 on master 89d826753, 12 of 14 and 13 of 15 with this change; the plain-`&` HTTP server answered 200 to two requests after its call returned; no call took longer than its command (17 to 110 ms; 364 ms for the case that sleeps 0.3 s). With `tty: true`: 2, 6 and 6 of 15, the two cases that hung now return after 2.1 s. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-process` and clippy pass on Linux, and the check passes for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu. What still ends with its command: a background job that runs inside psh's own process, which is psh's own utilities (`sleep 300 &`) and compound jobs (`(sleep 2; touch done) &`): bash forks for those and psh has one process, so they end when the script does; and under `tty: true` a plain `&` job, which is in the terminal's foreground group and is hung up when the shell exits, as under bash on a terminal. Not checked: macOS (the change is the same code there, not run), and a model arm.
- A cell that ends with nested calls still out says so, and says which (2026-11-12). A rejected nested call fails the script as soon as it is awaited, and through `Promise.all` that is while its siblings still run: the cell ended, the siblings were dropped, the event log recorded each as `Code Mode cell ended before the tool returned; execution outcome unknown` (39 Read and Bash results of that kind in the Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of the Codex harness), and the model was shown only the one rejection, as if nothing else had been started. The script error now ends with the calls that had not returned, by tool and count, that whether each took effect is unknown, and that `Promise.allSettled` or a `try` around each call lets the others finish; a script that completes with a call it never awaited gets the same list with the advice to await what matters, in place of the silence the exec description promises for unawaited promises. A cell whose calls all returned is unchanged, and so are the records of the abandoned calls. Claude's Code Mode instructions said `use Promise.all for independent calls`; they now say to use it for calls that must all succeed and `Promise.allSettled` when one may fail, with the reason (+173 bytes of system prompt). Checked with output/code-mode-lab `cells all` against `hand_tools`: `Promise.all` over two Bash calls and a Read of a missing file printed only `Error: path: No such file or directory` before, and now adds `Nested calls that had not returned when the script failed were abandoned: 2 Bash. Whether each took effect is unknown. …`; the same three calls through `Promise.allSettled` return one fulfilled result and one rejection after 2.0 s; an unawaited Bash is listed after the script's own output; a cell that awaits its call prints what it did before. Not run: a model. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-backend-claude`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/mod.rs, crates/backends/claude/prompts/code_mode.md.
- nanocode-observability exports OTLP/HTTP and writes its metric lines itself, and opentelemetry-otlp and opentelemetry-proto are gone (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md's former rank 1; Georgios approved changing `ObservabilityError::Otlp`'s payload). `cargo metadata` resolves 687 packages to 677, the ten ae326a70f predicted: opentelemetry-otlp, -proto, -http, prost, prost-derive, const-hex, anyhow, proptest, rand_xorshift and unarray. `cargo tree --duplicates` gains nothing. opentelemetry, opentelemetry_sdk and tracing-opentelemetry stay for nanocode-telemetry's public `GenAi` and `Held`, and `http` becomes a direct dependency, already in the graph through reqwest. protobuf.rs encodes `ExportTraceServiceRequest` and `ExportMetricsServiceRequest` the way prost 0.14 does: fields in tag order with a oneof at its lowest tag (so a number point's `as_int`, tag 6, comes before its exemplars, tag 5), proto3 defaults left out (a 0.0 `zero_threshold`, not a NaN one), proto3 `optional` sums, mins and maxes written when present, repeated numbers packed, and each nested message's length prefixed in place by moving its bytes once. otlp_http.rs posts it as opentelemetry-otlp 0.32 did with the blocking reqwest client lib.rs gave it: `Client::new()`, so reqwest's 30 s timeout applies, and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT` and the per-signal timeouts never applied and still do not. It posts to the `--otel-endpoint` URL with `/v1/traces` or `/v1/metrics`, parsed as an `http::Uri` so the same endpoints fail with the same message, with `content-type: application/x-protobuf` and `user-agent: OTel-OTLP-Exporter-Rust/0.32.0`, then the headers in `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_HEADERS` or `_METRICS_HEADERS`, else `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`, split, percent-decoded and filtered as before. An entry that does not parse is still skipped: this departs from "surface invalid states" so that the variable means what it means to every other OpenTelemetry SDK on the machine. Any `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_COMPRESSION`, `_METRICS_COMPRESSION` or `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_COMPRESSION` still fails `install`, gzip and zstd included, since the old crate was built with neither. `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_TEMPORALITY_PREFERENCE` is parsed by the SDK's own `Temporality::from_str` and fails with the same message. The protocol and endpoint variables stay ignored, as the explicit endpoint and protocol made them. The response body is read and dropped, since partial-success logging was compiled out. What changed: `ObservabilityError::Otlp` carries `nanocode_observability::OtlpError` (`Endpoint`, `Compression` naming the variable, `Temporality`) instead of `opentelemetry_otlp::ExporterBuildError`. A failed export says what reqwest reported, without the URL (`HTTP export failed: HTTP status server error (500 ...)`), where the old one always said `network error`. The metric exporter's shutdown is an `AtomicBool` rather than a `Mutex<Option<client>>`. Spans with different scopes go out in first-seen scope order, where the old `HashMap` order changed with its random seed. otlp.rs: the three proto enums are named constants (`SPAN_KIND_*`, `STATUS_CODE_*`, `SPAN_FLAGS_*`, with `AGGREGATION_TEMPORALITY_*` and `DATA_POINT_FLAGS_NONE`). file.rs's metric lines, which serialized `ExportMetricsServiceRequest` through a `serde_json::Value`, are written by hand: camelCase names in field order, 64-bit integers and `asInt` as strings, hex exemplar IDs, null for a missing min or max and for a non-finite float, every point kind. The field order is what the CLI wrote, since nanocode-cli turns on serde_json's `preserve_order`; a host without it got keys sorted alphabetically before and gets the CLI's order now. Two old behaviors stay for byte identity: a u64 value past i64::MAX goes out as `asInt` 0 (opentelemetry-proto's `unwrap_or_default`), and a scope with a NaN attribute equals no scope, itself included, so each of its spans gets its own ScopeSpans. Proof, in output/otel-proof: a crate with its own workspace that compiles the new protobuf.rs, otlp_http.rs, otlp.rs and typed.rs by path next to opentelemetry-otlp 0.32, opentelemetry-proto 0.32 and the base otlp.rs, with serde_json's `preserve_order` as in the CLI. `otel-proof spans <seed> 300` for 20 seeds encodes 6,000 random batches (474,449 spans) through `group_spans_by_resource_and_scope` with prost and through protobuf.rs. The batches cover IDs, trace flags, trace states, remote parents, every attribute type and array, NaN, ±0, infinities, subnormals, control and non-ASCII text, empty and 25 KB strings, times before 1970 and after 2554, events, links, dropped counts, up to four scopes and empty batches. All 1.56 GB match: byte for byte, and the 905 batches with several scopes as sets of ScopeSpans, since the old order is random. Each span's JSON and each trace line from the base otlp.rs and the new one match too (4,399 lines). `otel-proof metrics <seed> 12` for 40 seeds runs 480 `SdkMeterProvider`s: cumulative, delta and low-memory; u64, i64 and f64 counters, up-down counters, gauges, histograms with default, custom, empty and view bounds, exponential histograms, observable counters and gauges, random attribute sets, and resources with schema URLs. Their 3,685 exports (98,817 points) give identical protobuf (68.2 MB) and identical metric JSON (97.4 MB) against `ExportMetricsServiceRequest` with prost, and with serde plus the old `metric_integers`. SDK 0.32.1 never fills exemplars (aggregate.rs builds them empty and `Exemplar` has no public constructor), so their encoding follows the proto but no corpus reaches it. `e2e.sh` runs the old exporters, built as lib.rs built them, and the new ones against `otel-proof capture`, a recording HTTP server: 63 trace and 35 metric requests a side. The bodies are byte-identical (two batches with several scopes are equal up to ScopeSpans order), and the request lines and header sets are identical. That holds with `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` holding percent escapes, empty values, keys without values, an invalid name, a bad escape, duplicates, and overrides of user-agent and content-type; with a signal's variable set empty; against a 500, where both fail every export; and against a server slower than `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT=200`, where both succeed, the variable ignored like the protocol and per-signal endpoint variables. `otel-proof build` builds both under 17 environments and endpoints: compression gzip, zstd, bogus and empty, also per signal; temporality DeLtA, lowmemory and bogus; an endpoint with a space, not a URI, empty, IPv6, upper case, port 99999. All 34 builds agree on success or failure and on temporality. Last, the release nanocode before and after, side by side: `nanocode --otel-endpoint <capture> --telemetry all exec --model mock hello` against the capture server, which lists a mock model and refuses the turn, sends one trace request from each build. The two carry the same headers and the same spans, kinds, flags, statuses, and attribute names and types, in two runs of each build. Measured on the hosted Hand (5 vCPUs, shared, `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=2`): `cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-cli --timings` took 10m57s before and 10m52s after, 758 units to 748 and 1,262.8 s to 1,258.4 s summed. The removed units summed 6.8 s: opentelemetry-proto 2.1, opentelemetry-otlp 1.3, prost-derive 0.9, anyhow with its build script 0.9, opentelemetry-http 0.7, prost 0.5, const-hex 0.4. nanocode-observability took 7.5 s and then 7.8 s. A clean `cargo build --release -p nanocode-observability --timings`, interleaved, took 62.0 s and 39.9 s before against 48.0 s and 36.5 s after, 195 units to 182 and 120.2 s and 74.2 s summed to 89.8 s and 66.7 s. The release nanocode went from 102,710,344 to 102,468,168 bytes (236 KiB less), and `.text` from 65,668,032 to 65,528,416 bytes (136 KiB less, `size -A`). Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-observability` (and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`), `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-observability`, `cargo metadata`, `cargo tree --duplicates`. - cut and uniq take buffered lines without a future, and a utility asks whether stdout is a terminal once (2026-11-12). `LineReader::buffered` returns the next complete line already in the buffer as a range, synchronously; `next_ref` reads more and returns a borrowed line, so cut and uniq copy no line (uniq copies a line only when its group changes). cut builds its output in one 64 KiB buffer (written per line on a terminal). uniq checks the budget every 256 lines instead of every line, and `Key::of` returns the line at once without -f, -s or -w. `UtilCtx::write_now` and `write` asked `is_terminal(1)` (an ioctl on the native host) for every line with a newline; `UtilCtx::stdout_tty` caches it. Before → after, native pshm: `cut -c1-2` over 1M lines 27 → 12 ms, `uniq -c` over 1M sorted lines 22 → 10 ms, the cutsort pipeline 75 → 54 ms; WASM wall cutsort 77 → 48 ms. Same output as before on the cut case file and on uniq with -c -d -u -i -D --group --all-repeated -f -s -w -z, files and stdin. Upstream delta: none.
- sed runs a program of plain `s` commands line by line from its read buffer (2026-11-12). When every command is an `s` without an address, `w` or `e` flag, `Run::run` takes the complete lines already read (`Reader::buffered_line`) in a synchronous loop (`Run::batch`) before falling back to the general cycle for the next line, so the cycle's futures, the copy into the pattern space and the per-line drain checks go. A single `s` without `p` under autoprint substitutes straight from the buffer into the output; a literal pattern (psh-regex's `Regex::literal`, new) is found with one `memchr::memmem::Finder` built per run (building one per line was 60% of the time). Substitution is one function (`replace_into`) shared with the general path. Before → after, `sed 's/1/one/g'` over 1M lines: native pshm 70 → 25 ms CPU (GNU sed 86 ms); WASM wall 79.9 → 42.9 ms. Output identical to before and to GNU sed for ten programs (g, N, groups, anchors, empty matches, p with -n, two commands) over a file without a last newline and over big.txt, plus several files, stdin, UTF-8 and empty input. Upstream delta: none.
- djs's `String.prototype.repeat` writes a one-byte result of up to 4,096 bytes by doubling a byte buffer (2026-11-12). It built a list of `n` pieces of the same string and joined them, which checked each piece's kind and view and copied it on its own, so `'x'.repeat(2000)` cost about 2,000 piece visits. Measured with `perf stat -e instructions:u` on the hosted Hand (jsbench from output/durability-ledger, per-cell instructions from 200- and 1,200-cell runs, against 761c330f7): a Code Mode cell sending 16 tool calls with a 2,000-character string each went from 10.11M to 4.07M instructions through the real runtime and from 6.97M to 0.93M on djs directly, a loop of 400 `repeat`s up to 2,000 characters from 41.4M to 1.33M, and the 16-call cell with 100-character strings (the 128-byte stack path) and the strings, chars and json kernels did not move. test262 stays at 39,325 of 39,365.
- Claude's conversation keeps each retained Code Mode round's size with the round (2026-11-12). `retain_code_calls` summed `bounded_json_len` over every retained round (up to 256 rounds of 64 nested calls) each time a Code Mode cell finished, so a round's JSON was walked again on every later turn and a session's cost per turn grew with its length; `CodeRound` now measures its value once into a `OnceLock<usize>` beside its record. Measured in Miniflare's workerd 5.20261110.1-beta on the hosted Hand with nanocode-ts built the way `scripts/build.mjs` builds (wasm-opt -O3), counting `perf stat -e instructions:u` on the workerd process over each call, three interleaved rounds of two 75-turn sessions per cell against bd63acec5: a cell with 16 nested tool calls went from 44.94, 45.11 and 44.78M instructions a turn to 43.85, 43.81 and 44.24M, and turns with no cell, a trivial cell and a two-call worker cell stayed within 0.5%. In one 250-turn session of the 16-call cell the turns after the 50th took 49.2M instructions each instead of 53.2M (twice, identical counts).
- `text()` does not print the base64 of a data URL (2026-11-12). `image(await tools.Read({ file_path }))` shows an image file in one step since 209406cc3 and 925471e46 (checked here: output/code-mode-lab `cells image` returns the image item), but a model that prints the same value with `text` got the whole file as base64 in its transcript: in the Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of the Codex harness one such cell took the next request from 11k to 43k input tokens, and nothing in that text is of use to a model. The cell's text sink now replaces the payload of each `data:<type>/<subtype>;base64,` URL with `[N base64 characters not printed as text; pass the value to image() to see it]` (`audio()` for audio types, and for any other type the advice to write it to a file), wherever the URL sits in the text, so the JSON of a Read result keeps its shape around it. Only a payload longer than its own note is replaced, so the output never grows, and a string that merely mentions `data:` or carries a short URL is printed as written. The media type is matched by the bound RFC 6838 gives a type or subtype name (127 characters), which also bounds the look-ahead, and the scan is one pass in Rust over the bytes. Values a cell passes to `image`, `audio`, a tool or `store` are untouched. Checked with `cells image` against `hand_tools`: `text` of a Read result printed the PNG's base64 before and now prints `"image_url":"data:image/png;base64,[96 base64 characters not printed as text; pass the value to image() to see it]"`; an 80,000-character URL prints as its note; `data:text/plain;base64,QUJD` and `"data:image/png;base64,"` print unchanged. Cost, in an unoptimized build: 9.2 MB of text with 400,000 occurrences of `data:` and no URL goes through `text` in 197 ms including the cell's own string handling, and 8 MB made of 1,000 URLs in 89 ms. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode-engine -p nanocode-code-mode`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`. File: crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/cell.rs.
- `$(cmd)` with one plain simple command runs it on the cloned vproc in place instead of as a task (2026-11-12). `subst` tries `now::command` on the subshell (`subst_now`), reading the pipe while a continuation waits, then runs the EXIT trap and drops the subshell to read to the end; anything else still goes through `spawn_sub`. Saves the task spawn and the scheduler round trips: WASM wall for 3000 `x=$(echo $i)` 10.9 → 8.2 ms; native subst workload 3.1 → 2.8 ms CPU. Same output and status on the agent cases and on bash-compared scripts covering status, set -e, return, printf errors, nested and 70,000-byte substitutions. Upstream delta: none.
- psh runs a plain simple command or `((…))` without a future when it can (2026-11-12). `now::command` (psh-engine/src/now.rs), tried by `run_list` and `run_andor` before `run_command`, takes a command with no redirections, traps, xtrace, pending signals or killed job: assignments only, or one of echo, printf, test, [, true, false, :, let, shift, return, break, continue (not shadowed by a function or `enable -n`), whose words are literal text, quotes, plain `$name`/`$1`/`$@`/`$?` (set scalars, no glob chars when unquoted) and literal `$((…))`. Everything that decides to hand the command back is checked before any side effect; then it expands synchronously (`expand::words_now`, `single_now` over `expand_part_now`), assigns, or polls the builtin's future once with a no-op waker, and returns a future only for what must wait (a full pipe, an error message, errexit). `$_`, `PIPESTATUS`, `$LINENO`, the budget (`Sched::pass`) and errexit are kept as `run_command_with` keeps them. `for ((…))` evaluates literal condition and step the same way (`now::arith_word`). `run_list` reaches `run_background` and `run_andor` through plain functions, so its poll frame stays under the 16 KiB per level embedders size stacks for (debug deep_recursion needs 19,281 KiB for 1000 levels, was 19,585). Before → after, hosted Hand, median of 7: native pshm CPU loop 14.7 → 10.3 ms, strbuild 3.4 → 3.0, func 11.0 → 10.1; WASM wall loop 20.6 → 12.7 ms (1.6x), strbuild 2.43 → 1.58 (1.5x), func 9.2 → 7.5, smallpipe 0.39 → 0.24; utilities unchanged. Same output and status as before on 727 agent cases, the per-utility case files and 55 errexit/nounset/IFS/PIPESTATUS/`$_`/return/break/let/printf/arith-for/trap/xtrace scripts compared with bash. Upstream delta: none.
- A background Bash job on a hand or a runner reports its end in the result of the next `exec` or `wait` that returns (2026-11-12). A session's own tools bind their jobs to the agent, which is told when one ends; a hand's and a runner's tools (`hand_tools`, `runner_tools`) have no agent to tell, so every job a command started there, or a foreground command moved there at its timeout, answered `Nothing notifies you when the command finishes` (16 times in 12 of 89 tasks in the Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of the Claude harness, where every tool lives on a hand), and a moved job was stopped after its 10 minutes in the background without a word to anyone. `CodeModeToolset` and `CodeModeToolPolicy` gain `session_notices(session_id)`, which a cell's observation appends as notifications to whatever it returns, a yield or a result; Claude's tool selection installs a policy over its job table that hands out, once, the `<task-notification>` of each finished job the asking session started (the same text an agent-bound session receives: completed with exit code 0, failed with its code, or stopped at its background time limit with the note on restarting). A job knows its session from the call that started it, so a hand serving several sessions reports each job only to its own. An agent-bound job table is untouched: its notices still go to the agent at once. The start message now says `Its end is reported with the result of the first exec or wait call that returns after it finishes; nothing interrupts you before then`, and for a moved command also that it is stopped after 10m in the background and that this is reported the same way. Not changed: the time limit itself, and nothing reaches a session that makes no further call. Checked with output/code-mode-lab `remote background` (a hand serving `hand_tools`, a brain over a loopback WebSocket): a 3 s job's completion arrives appended to the result of a 4 s cell that ended after it, a job that exits 3 arrives as `failed with exit code 3`, one past its `timeout` as `was stopped after reaching its background time limit` inside the yield of a cell still running, each once, and a later cell carries none; before, the three start messages said nothing would notify and no later result mentioned the jobs (`cells background`). Not run: a model. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-tool-host -p nanocode-backend-claude`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `-p nanocode-tool-runtime -p nanocode-backend-codex` both ways. - Bash takes a `timeout` above its maximum and runs with the maximum, as Claude Code does (2026-11-12). The pinned upstream schema says `timeout` is `max 600000 for a foreground command`; Claude Code accepts a larger value and applies the maximum (in the Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of Claude Code 2.1.318 a call with `timeout: 900000` ran and reported `did not complete within its 600s timeout`), while `ClaudeBash` rejected it with `timeout must be 1 to 600000 milliseconds`, five times in the same run of the Claude harness, one model call each. A `timeout` above the maximum now becomes the maximum, for foreground commands (600,000 ms) and for `run_in_background` (7,200,000 ms, the SDK's own bound) alike; zero is still an error. The bound is not hidden: a command that reaches it is moved to the background with `did not complete within its 600s timeout` as before, and the one case that fails instead, a command that starts with `sleep`, now names the time it ran (`Bash command timed out after 600s`, before `Bash command timed out`). Options the schema does not have (`stdin`, `yield_time_ms`) are still rejected by name, as an unknown argument should be. Checked with output/code-mode-lab `cells timeout clamp` against `hand_tools`: `echo ok` with `timeout: 900000` was `rejected: Error: timeout must be 1 to 600000 milliseconds` and now returns its result; `sleep 700; echo late` with `timeout: 900000` ends after 600.0 s of wall time; `sleep 5` with `timeout: 2000` ends `timed out after 2s`; `timeout: 0` is rejected. - A cell result over the connection's frame budget arrives cut, with a marker that says what was cut, instead of not at all (2026-11-12). When a hand's reply to `exec` or `wait` exceeded `max_frame_bytes`, `reply_text` first dropped the nested calls' inputs and outputs from the reply, as it still does, and when that was not enough replaced the script's whole output with `remote frame of N bytes exceeds the connection's max_frame_bytes policy of M bytes; the script's output was not sent` and marked the cell failed, although every tool call in it had run and succeeded: 20 cells in the Terminal-Bench 2.1 runs (3 in the Claude arm, 17 in the Codex arm, under a 1 MiB budget) ended that way and their work was repeated blind. The reply now keeps the head and the tail of the output's text and puts between them how many of how many bytes were cut, the budget that cut them, and what to do instead; the cell keeps its own success flag. The cut is exact rather than estimated: the frame is serialized, the overshoot is taken from the kept text, and that repeats until the frame fits, so JSON escaping cannot leave it over. Images and other media in a result that must be cut are dropped and counted in the marker. Only when even an empty output does not fit (the notifications alone exceed the budget) does the old replacement apply. Checked with output/code-mode-lab `remote big`, a hand serving `hand_tools` and a brain over a loopback WebSocket with `max_frame_bytes` 1,048,576: a cell printing 2,990,068 bytes was `success=false` with only the message before; after, `success=true`, 1,002,557 bytes delivered with `FIRST LINE` and `LAST LINE` present and `…[1987725 of this output's 2990068 bytes were cut here: the result exceeded the connection's max_frame_bytes policy of 1048576 bytes. Print less, or write large results to a file and read the part you need.]…` between; a 600 KB result and a small one are byte-identical to before. Not changed: the default cell output budget stays unlimited, so a host that wants replies far below its frame budget sets `max_output_tokens`. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`. File: crates/runtime/code-mode/src/remote/hand.rs.
- exec refuses a source that is a JSON wrapper of the tool input and says how to call it (2026-11-12). A gateway that maps the free-form exec tool to a JSON function `{input: string}` hands the arguments over raw when the model's JSON does not parse, and the cell runner compiled whatever arrived: in the Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of the Codex harness through such a gateway 8 cells had a source starting with `{"input":"const r = await tools.Bash({command:"` followed by up to 45,215 characters of whitespace (two of those model calls emitted 32,768 output tokens over 181 s and 202 s), and each answered `SyntaxError: expecting ';'` at a position inside text the model never meant as JavaScript, which says nothing about the cause. `parse_exec_source` now refuses a source whose first token opens an object keyed `"input"` or `"code"`, the two names under which adapters carry the source: no JavaScript program can start that way, because a block statement cannot hold `"input":`, so nothing valid is refused. The error says the input is a JSON object wrapping the source, that nothing ran, to send the JavaScript itself, and to quote shell commands and file content with `String.raw` or single quotes instead of escaped double quotes. A source of only whitespace was already refused with its own message. The wrapper is not unwrapped and run: when the arguments were cut or mis-escaped upstream the inner text is not what the model wrote, and running a guess is the silent fallback the rules here exclude; recovering the input is the gateway's part. Not done here: the model's own call, with its whitespace, stays in the history later requests carry; the Codex driver keeps model items as the provider returned them. Checked with output/code-mode-lab `cells junk`: before, `Script error: SyntaxError: expecting ';' at <input>:1:9`; after, the message above, in 0.0 s with no nested call. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/{spec.rs,mod.rs}.
- A yield with nothing printed says what the cell did: how many nested calls returned, the latest result's tail, and which calls are still running (2026-11-12). A cell that loops over nested calls and prints only at its end gave every `exec` and `wait` that yielded on it `Script running with cell ID N` and an empty output: in the Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of the Claude harness one `wait` of 901 s and one of 788 s on such a loop returned nothing while the Bash results inside it, 36 in the first, already showed that the job the loop polled had ended with an error. When the script printed nothing since the last yield, the yield now carries one text item: the count of nested calls that returned since then and how many failed, the latest one's name and the tail of its output under the bound a terminated cell's output already has (`TERMINATED_OUTPUT_BYTES`), and the names of the calls still running. It counts every call, also those past the per-tool logging limit, and a `max_tokens` on the wait bounds it like any output. A yield with printed output is unchanged, as is a cell's final result. Checked with output/code-mode-lab `cells tail` against `hand_tools`: a six-step Bash loop yielding every 3 s shows `2 nested call(s) returned since then, 0 of them failed. The latest, Bash, returned: {"exit_code":0,…,"stdout":"tick 1\nSTILL_RUNNING\n",…}` and `Nested calls still running: 1 Bash.`; during one 8 s call it shows only the running call; a cell that prints each step yields exactly what it did before. Before, every one of those yields was empty (`cells loop`). Not run: a model, so whether it ends such loops earlier is not measured. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`. File: crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/mod.rs.
- Claude's exec takes `yield_time_ms` and `max_output_tokens` as arguments, and `wait` reads the numbers models send (2026-11-12). The Claude adapter gives exec a JSON schema with `code` only and read only `code`, so a `yield_time_ms` a model passed beside it was dropped without a word and the cell yielded after the default 10 s; only the `// @exec:` pragma inside the source worked. In the Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of the Claude harness 184 of 1,182 model calls (15.6%) were `wait` calls. The schema now declares both fields with the pragma's own wording, and the adapter passes them through `code_mode::source_with_options`, which writes them as the pragma line the cell runner already parses, so a hand of an earlier build honors them too. A value given both ways, or one that is no non-negative safe integer, is an error that says so. `wait` parsed `cell_id` as a string only and `yield_time_ms` and `max_tokens` as JSON integers only: `{"cell_id": "3", "yield_time_ms": "3000"}` and `{"cell_id": 3}` each cost a model call (`invalid type: string "3000", expected u64`). `cell_id` now reads a number, the two integers read a numeric string or a whole float, and `max_tokens: null` means none. Checked with output/code-mode-lab `cells yield loop` against `hand_tools`: a cell that sleeps 14 s yields after 11.0 s and needs a second call when the argument is ignored, and completes in one call in 14.0 s with `yield_time_ms: 20000`; `"3000"` yields after 3.0 s; both forms of `wait` that failed to parse now wait 3.0 s. - bin/nanocode-sim runs the subagent runtime: `--scenario agents` drives a `nanocode_subagents::Registry` with hibernation on through the simulated host, and its seeds reproduce the CLOSE hang f5aa344a5 fixed (2026-11-12). The store workload stays the default and is unchanged (`--seeds 0..2000 --twice --verbose` prints the same seed digests, md5 `caba4b81`, and the same RESULT line before and after; `--tidy` clean; both store mutations still caught). agents.rs: each seed builds a Registry with `channel`, `set_hibernation(true)` and `set_max_resident` of 0 to 4 (`RESIDENT_MAX`), a store, and a root `AgentHandle`, starts 1 to 64 flat children with `start_agents`, sleeps a seeded virtual time up to the longest turn its script allows, then calls `close_all` or, in a quarter of seeds (`CANCEL_PPM`), `cancel_all`. It judges: the call returns `Ok` in less virtual time than the runtime's stop deadline (`RUNTIME_STOP_TIMEOUT`, the 30 s of `AGENT_STOP_TIMEOUT`); after one more such deadline no scripted turn is running, after Close no agent is open (every one was shut down, so none holds a resident harness), and the directory lists every child Closed (after Cancel: Interrupted, Completed or Failed; a child whose turn ended before the cancel fails with MissingResult because scripted turns never call `submit_result`). scripted.rs: an `AgentFactory` and `LifecycleBackend` whose turns take 1 to 8 steps (`TURN_STEPS_MAX`), each a model call that lands after 50 ms (`STEP_LATENCY_MS_MIN`, output/durability-ledger's mock latency) to a seeded maximum up to 20 s (`STEP_LATENCY_MS_MAX`) on the virtual clock; with parking on a step parks as the Claude backend's does (`parked` resolves, `park` claims the call and shuts the agent down, `unpark` lets the resumed turn adopt it), `checkpoint` and `restore` round-trip the session (restore takes up to 2 s, `RESTORE_LATENCY_MS_MAX`, and shutdown up to 1 s, `SHUTDOWN_LATENCY_MS_MAX`, as a real backend's journal read and flush do), and a store over `MemorySubagentStore` answers `pending_turn` from the turns the script has open, as the durable store does. Everything runs on the executor: spawns, sleeps and time go through the installed host, nothing reached Tokio's runtime, and a seed's trace digest covers every turn, step, park, unpark, restore and shutdown with its virtual time. The result of publishing a step's ModelCallStarted event is dropped: a closed event stream only means the harness already let the agent go. Measured on the hosted Hand (5 vCPUs, shared): `--scenario agents --seeds 0..10000 --twice` passes 10,000 of 10,000 with identical digests (2m32s wall, release; 7,476 closes, 2,524 cancels, 326,977 children, 666,084 parks, 591,548 restores; the slowest stop 2,416 ms virtual); on the final stack (rebased on a59ed408e with the spawn routing, tidy and journal writer entries below) `sweep.sh 0 100000 3 --scenario agents --twice` passes 100,000 of 100,000 with identical digests, 0 panics (8m48s wall, 26m20s user), and the reverted build fails 1,743 of `--seeds 0..10000`, 68 of them timing out. Canary: f5aa344a5's runtime.rs hunk hand-reverted (`git show f5aa344a5 -- crates/runtime/subagents/src/runtime.rs | git apply -R`, built into a separate binary) fails 1,743 of `--seeds 0..10000` (1m19s), all of them Close seeds (1,743 of 7,476): 1,675 leave a restored child resident with no one to close it (`N children still hold a resident harness after Close`, the wake installed after close collected harnesses and settled hibernated turns), 65 are the hang itself (`close_all failed: timed out waiting for subagent turns to stop` after 30 s of virtual time, the woken child's turn resumed on a harness nobody closed; seed 625 replays it), and 3 time out waiting for harnesses to close; over `--seeds 0..2000` 354 fail (343, 9, 2). The delays matter: with restores and shutdowns that take no virtual time, close ran from its request to settling hibernated turns in one instant and only 2 of 300 seeds took the reverted path, neither caught. - The subagent journal writer's wait (runtime.rs, `journal_writer`, the completion fill loop) is a `biased` `tokio::select!` that takes a finished fill first, then a revision change, then a journal request, then the retry timer (2026-11-12). Unbiased, Tokio drew the branch order from its own thread-local RNG, which bypasses the platform host, so the simulator could not replay it, as the earlier host entry noted. The order cannot starve anything: the fill is one-shot (taking it empties the slot and the loop goes on waiting), and the other three branches all leave the loop for the same thing, a journal save, whose loop top drains every queued request and whose save reads the current revision, so which of them wins only decides whether one later wake is redundant. Decided on a measurement: in the interleaved runs of the spawn-routing entry below (gak-9, `matrix.sh <swarm> 10000 1000 memory jsonl sqlite rows`, two rounds) this commit settled memory 4.77, 4.94 (user CPU 19.5, 19.6 s), jsonl 3.67, 3.86 (20.2, 20.1), sqlite 6.27, 6.16 (22.4, 22.3), rows 6.25, 6.35 (21.9, 21.4) against the commit before it, memory 5.18, 4.86, jsonl 3.68, 4.35, sqlite 6.22, 6.20, rows 6.20, 6.22, with the same commits and bytes per agent, so the fixed order costs nothing measurable and makes the writer replayable. With it and the cancel-order fix above, `stopcheck.sh <swarm> 2000 50 1000 jsonl sqlite memory` settles every CANCEL and CLOSE with and without hibernation, as base does (CLOSE with `MAX_AWAKE=0` in 0.099, 0.125, 0.127 s against 0.066, 0.104, 0.122 s), `treecheck.sh <swarm> 20 50 1000` with `MAX_AWAKE=0 LATENCY_MS=300` completes all 1,020 (jsonl 2.09 s, sqlite 2.39 s; base 2.08, 2.39), and `killresume.sh <swarm> 3000 1500 1000 jsonl sqlite rows` resumes all 3,000 to completed (settled 1.61, 1.81, 1.68 s; base 1.88, 1.85, 1.97). - bin/nanocode-sim's commits sometimes blank an inherited record and write it again, read the rewritten records back through the store that wrote them, and judge a blank read wrong, with the canaries `cache_keeps_blank` and `staged_refuses_rewrite` (2026-11-12). In content mode each inherited record has a 25% chance (`REWRITE_INHERITED_PPM`) of being written as a blank followed by its content, as Code Mode's cell journal does when a resumed cell writes its journal again; after such a commit succeeds the process reads those records through its own store (plain, cached or staged), and each must answer its content: a blank is wrong (a blank only removes a record), and none is wrong unless the store was damaged. `Model::plan` ignores blanks; `Stats` counts `rewrites`. The two fixes below are what this found: on master (277079c8e) `nanocode-sim --seeds 0..2000` failed 1,476 seeds (622 blank reads back through CachedStore or StagedStore, 854 refused staged commits). Canaries, each a new invariant's mutation: `--mutation cache_keeps_blank` makes a cached process's read back answer blanks, as RecordCache did, and `--mutation staged_refuses_rewrite` makes a staged commit with a rewrite fail with StagedStore's old refusal; on `--seeds 0..2000` `cache_keeps_blank` is caught by 1,417 seeds and `staged_refuses_rewrite` by 1,463 (both need content mode's rewrites, so with `--records slots` neither is caught), and the four store mutations are caught as before (in content mode `record_insert_overwrites` rewrites the same content under a content key and is not caught there, on master too). With both fixes, on the 5-core hosted Hand shared with other builds: `sweep.sh 0 100000 3 --twice` passed 100,000 of 100,000 with identical digests, 0 panics (8m58s wall, 15m32s user); `sweep.sh 0 100000 3 --records slots --twice` passed 100,000 of 100,000, 0 panics (9m47s wall); rerun on the final stack (with the agents scenario and the spawn routing above), content and slots each passed 100,000 of 100,000 `--twice` again (5m03s and 4m03s). Commands: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sim`, `cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-sim`. Files: bin/nanocode-sim/src/{workload.rs,model.rs,store.rs,simulate.rs}.
- The paying proxy encodes its trust bundle a whole base64 group and a PEM line at a time (2026-11-12). `x509::base64` built each 4-character group in a loop over the group's length with a padding test per character, and `x509::pem` pushed the encoded text one character at a time with a modulo per character: 10.6M instructions for the 122 roots of Ubuntu's bundle, a fifth of the proxy thread. Full groups now go through `as_chunks` with fixed shifts, the last partial group through the old loop, and `pem` copies 64-character lines into a string sized up front. The bundle is byte-for-byte the same apart from the per-process CA (the 121 system roots hash equal from both builds, and the CA parses with openssl x509). callgrind (hosted Hand): bundle encoding 10.57M to 4.27M instructions, proxy thread 48.4M to 42.2M. On the EPYC 4245P box, interleaved with the commit before in the run of the entry below: first-frame CPU 11.3 to 11.0 ms, first frame 3.43 to 3.42 ms, one-shot CPU 9.16 to 8.96 ms, one-shot wall 6.90 to 6.91 ms.
- The paying proxy makes its certificate authority on its own thread, not on the main thread before the TUI's first frame (2026-11-12). `ForwardProxy::bind` generated two P-256 keys with nanocode-tempo's curve and self-signed the CA: 7.5M instructions on the main thread, about half of what it runs before the first frame. `bind` now only takes the port, the token and the bundle path, which are all `environment()` needs, and `spawn`, which already runs on the `nanocode-paying-proxy` thread, generates the CA before it writes the bundle with the CA's root first, as before. A CA that cannot be made now fails `spawn` with the warning a failed root load gave ("shell commands pay no Tempo services: the paying proxy did not start") instead of failing `bind`. Measured on an AMD EPYC 4245P box (Ubuntu 24.04, release builds, bench/cli `suite.mjs --parts=firstframe,oneshot,idle --rounds=30` under netguard, c311bbedb and this commit interleaved in every round): first frame 3.81 to 3.43 ms (first byte 2.80 to 2.44), first-frame CPU 11.1 to 11.3 ms, one-shot wall 8.89 to 6.90 ms (reply end to exit 2.73 to 1.78), one-shot CPU 8.76 to 9.16 ms, RSS 1 s after the frame 39.3 to 38.9 MB, idle CPU unchanged. callgrind on the TUI up to Ctrl-C (hosted Hand): main thread 15.94M to 8.41M instructions, proxy thread 40.9M to 48.4M.
