- psh expands literal text, quotes, a plain parameter that is set and an arithmetic expansion without expansions in it without making a future (2026-11-12). Every part of every word went through `expand_part`, an async fn of 1,992 bytes held inside each `expand_pieces` and `expand_parts` future, so expanding `s=$((s+i))` built, boxed and copied about 2 KB per word (memmove was 12% of an arithmetic loop's samples). `expand_part_now` does those parts at once: text through `expand_text` (the arms moved out of `expand_part`), `$name` and `${name}` of a scalar that is set and is neither a nameref nor dynamic, positional and special parameters other than `$!` that have a value, and `$((…))` whose word is a cached literal. Anything else, an unset parameter (`set -u`) and every operator still go to `expand_part`, now boxed so that the callers' futures stay small; an arithmetic error is reported as before (`arith_failed`). Measured as in the sort entry above, before to after: native `for ((i=0;i<20000;i++)); do s=$((s+i)); done` 15.3 to 14.4, 500 `x=$(echo $i)` 3.5 to 3.4, a string built over 2,000 iterations 4.5 to 3.8, 3,000 function calls 12.5 to 11.4; wasm 20.4 to 20.1, 12.1 to 10.1, 5.6 to 5.3, 16.7 to 15.6. psh-engine's and psh-syntax's tests pass, and the 727 agent cases of output/psh-path through `-c` give the same output before and after all three changes (two print their temporary directory's name). Upstream delta: psh-engine expand.rs.
- psh-wasm is built with WebAssembly SIMD (2026-11-12). crates/patches/psh/.cargo/config.toml adds `-C target-feature=+simd128` for wasm32-unknown-unknown, which cargo joins with the root config's flags when the module is built from crates/patches/psh, as nanocode-ts's scripts/psh.mjs does (its archive of crates/patches/psh carries the file); native builds and the workspace's own wasm32 builds (nanocode, nanocode-shell) are unchanged. memchr and the regex crates then take their simd128 paths instead of searching a byte or a word at a time. SIMD is in every engine nanocode-ts runs on (V8 since 9.1, so Node 16 and later and workerd; Firefox 89; Safari 16.4); an engine without it refuses the module when compiling it. Measured as in the sort entry above (wasm), before to after: `grep -c e` over 6.9 MB 1.63 to 0.58, `wc -l` 2.20 to 1.33, `cat | wc -c` 2.69 to 2.10, `rg -n 'fn [a-z]+_7' src | wc -l` over 2,000 files 21.2 to 16.3, `grep -rn needle src | wc -l` 28.7 to 24.5; the shell loops, awk, sed and jq within noise. The module is 8,742,759 bytes instead of 8,831,245. Upstream delta: .cargo/config.toml (new).
- psh's sort orders whole lines by their first 8 bytes before comparing the rest, without a stable merge, and ranks -n keys in u64 arithmetic (2026-11-12, Georgios: "make it 10x more performant in both the Rust and every other environment esp the WASM ones"). A sort with one whole-line text key and no -d, -f or -i (plain `sort`, `sort -r`) compared lines through `Sorter::cmp` in a stable `sort_by`; such a key is the whole line, so lines that compare equal are the same bytes and their order cannot show: each line is now paired with its first 8 bytes big-endian and the pairs sorted with `sort_unstable_by` (prefix, then the bytes), reversed for -r. `rank` folded the integer and fraction digits of a -n key in u128, which on wasm32 is a software multiply (`__multi3`, 19% of `sort -n` in psh-wasm); both fit u64 (at most 18 digits each), so they are folded in u64 and joined into the same u128. Measured on the Linux x86_64 hosted Hand with output/psh-wasm-bench (psh-wasm under Node 24.22 through nanocode-ts's Bash glue at fdf14e8 with its ABI check moved to 6, over its MemoryFileSystem; CPU median ms of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 runs) and output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/pshm (`psh::run_with` with mimalloc, as `nanocode psh-shell` runs it; CPU median of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 `-c` runs), before to after: wasm `sort -n` of 1,000,000 numbers 104.2 to 36.6, `seq 200000 | sort -r | head -1` 17.3 to 12.5, `cut -c1-2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3` over 1,000,000 lines 92.9 to 75.1; native 62.4 to 58.0, 12.8 to 13.5 (within noise), 83.4 to 75.6. output/psh-perf/sortcases.json, sortcases2.json and sortcases3.json (79 invocations) give the same bytes before and after. Upstream delta: psh-utils sort.rs.
- What replacing the OTLP export would take, measured, nothing changed in code (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md's opentelemetry row). Only opentelemetry-otlp and opentelemetry-proto can leave: nanocode-telemetry's public `GenAi<E: SpanExporter>` and `Held<P: SpanProcessor>` are opentelemetry_sdk's traits, and tempoxyz/pyramid-core builds its tracer from them around its own opentelemetry-otlp exporter (crates/kernel/src/telemetry.rs), so opentelemetry, opentelemetry_sdk and tracing-opentelemetry stay; tempoxyz/pyramid does not link either nanocode telemetry crate. Without -otlp and -proto `cargo metadata` drops 10 packages (opentelemetry-otlp, -proto, -http, prost, prost-derive, const-hex, anyhow, proptest, rand_xorshift, unarray); without all five it would drop 16. Removing the two needs, in nanocode-observability: otlp.rs's three proto enums (span kind, status code, span flags) as named constants; file.rs's metric lines, which serialize `ExportMetricsServiceRequest::from(&ResourceMetrics)` with serde, written by hand to the same JSON (camelCase names, hex IDs, 64-bit integers as strings, every data point kind); and, for `--otlp-endpoint`, a `SpanExporter` and a `PushMetricExporter` that encode `ExportTraceServiceRequest` and `ExportMetricsServiceRequest` as protobuf the way prost does and POST them with the blocking reqwest client to `<endpoint>/v1/traces` and `/v1/metrics` with the headers, timeout and environment variables opentelemetry-otlp 0.32 reads; each proven byte-identical against the crates over a corpus of spans and metrics. It also changes a public type: `ObservabilityError::Otlp` carries `opentelemetry_otlp::ExporterBuildError`, so the variant's payload would become nanocode's own error, which no host names today (nanocode-cli builds through `install` and matches no variant).
- image stays at `=0.25.6`, and with it png 0.17 and bitflags 1 (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md's image row, now kept on purpose). Why it was pinned is not written down: af9179d88 (2026-10-14, the commit that made nanocode-image) moved it from 0.25.9 to `=0.25.6` and says only that image and codec compatibility was checked with probes; `git log -S'=0.25.6'` finds nothing else. What 0.25.6 is: the last image before moxcms. Measured on the hosted Hand with throwaway crates over image's own API, the workspace's features (bmp, gif, jpeg, png, pnm, webp), 0.25.6 against 0.25.10 (the current one, with png 0.18.1, zune-jpeg 0.5.15, gif 0.14.2, moxcms 0.8.1 and pxfm 0.1.30): the graph goes from 23 to 25 packages (bitflags 1 leaves, moxcms and pxfm join); summed release build time 23.2 to 40.5 s (moxcms 8.0 s, pxfm 2.6 s); a decode, thumbnail and PNG and JPEG encode as a size-optimized cdylib grows from 547,019 to 624,178 bytes as wasm32-unknown-unknown and from 894,240 to 971,536 natively. And the images change: output/image-equal decodes 270 files made by Pillow 13 (noise, gradients and checks from 1x1 to 800x600 as RGB, RGBA, gray, gray-alpha, palette and 16-bit PNG, baseline, 4:4:4, progressive, gray and CMYK JPEG, GIF, lossy and lossless WebP, BMP, PPM and PGM) with both and hashes the pixels, a Lanczos3 resize and image's PNG, JPEG (quality 85) and WebP encodes: 10 of the 75 JPEGs (every 4:2:0 baseline and progressive one of 64x48 and 800x600) decode to other pixels, and so resize and encode differently, and 69 PNG encodes give other bytes; the 2026-11-09 entries hold nanocode-image's prepared images to the same bytes, so moving would change what models are sent. Nothing landed; moving needs those differences accepted and moxcms's cost with them.
- The five crates that used both base64 and base64-simd use base64-simd alone (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md's base64 row): nanocode-audio, nanocode-image, nanocode-backend-codex, nanocode-code-mode-engine and nanocode-computer-repl. base64-simd is the one to keep because it is the fast path: output/b64-bench on the hosted Hand (x86_64, 64 MiB per size, two rounds) encodes at 5.2 to 15.1 GB/s against base64's 1.4 to 3.6 and decodes at 4.7 to 11.3 against 1.1 to 3.3, about 4x on a 1 MiB screenshot either way. Dropping base64-simd instead would have taken base64-simd, vsimd and outref out of the graph (3 packages) at that cost; dropping base64 takes none out, since reqwest and hyper-util need it and ten other crates keep it for small encodes, so `cargo metadata --locked` stays at 710. The base64 fallbacks after a base64-simd decode (`decode_to_vec(..).or_else(|_| BASE64_STANDARD.decode(..))` in audio, image and the engine's audio, `check(..).or_else(..)` in computer-repl) are gone because they never ran: output/b64-bench's `fuzz` gives base64's STANDARD and base64-simd's STANDARD 10,000,000 inputs (encodings of random bytes, some with one symbol changed, and random strings of the alphabet, `=`, whitespace, `-`, `_` and other bytes, padded and not) and they accept the same 2,783,304, decode them to the same bytes, reject the same 7,216,696 and encode identically. The engine's `__nanocodeBytesFromBase64` decodes its cleaned symbols with `base64_simd::forgiving_decode_to_vec` where it used base64's engine with trailing bits allowed and no padding: equal on all 10,000,000 cleaned inputs. Its `__nanocodeBytesToBase64`, Codex's served `read_file` data and credential forms, and the image-generation result decode are base64-simd's STANDARD. What changes: a rejected payload's message now ends in base64-simd's `Base64Error` instead of base64's description of the offending symbol (`invalid base64 payload: …` from nanocode-image, `generated image was not valid base64: …` from Codex's image generation, and computer-repl's CUA image and audio errors); the engine's decode error cannot happen for cleaned input. Checks: `cargo clippy --lib` for the five crates natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown` (only the existing codex-client warning) on Linux, and natively on gak-9.
- nanocode-observability writes its log lines through its own writer thread, and tracing-appender leaves with crossbeam-channel and symlink (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md's tracing-appender row). crates/integrations/observability/src/writer.rs is what `NonBlockingBuilder::default().buffered_lines_limit(4_096).lossy(false)` was, on std's bounded `sync_channel`, as the crate's OTLP file exporters already are: `LineWriter` is the `MakeWriter`, and each formatted event is one message that waits while `LOCAL_LOG_BUFFERED_LINES_LIMIT` (4,096) lines are queued, so nothing is dropped; the owning `nanocode-log-writer` thread writes every message it can take without waiting, then flushes; dropping `WriterGuard` queues a close behind the lines already sent, waiting up to 100 ms for room, then up to 1,000 ms for the thread to write and flush them, tracing-appender's two bounds, and prints its message if the close could not be queued. A failed write or flush of one batch is dropped as before (the output is the log itself; the last flush reports its error on stderr). A thread that cannot be spawned is now `ObservabilityError::Output` from `install` instead of a panic. Compared with output/log-writer-old and -new, one binary each linking nanocode-observability before and after (`output/log-writer-compare.sh`, timestamps and span busy and idle times removed): one thread's 20,000 events with spans give byte-identical files in the compact, JSON and pretty formats (60,000, 60,000 and 240,000 lines); 8 threads of 25,000 events give the same 600,000 lines in compact and JSON; 4 threads to stderr 40,000 events each; a FIFO whose reader starts after 0.5 s (so writers wait on the full queue) gets all 40,000 events before and after; 4 threads of 50,000 events to a file, three interleaved rounds, 951, 799 and 780 ms before against 852, 782 and 874 ms after, with the guard's drop under 5 ms in each. `cargo metadata --locked` 713 to 710 packages. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-observability` (only the existing otlp.rs warning) and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-observability --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- chrono and iana-time-zone leave the workspace: nanocode-platform reads the local time zone itself (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md's chrono row). `nanocode_platform::local_date(at)`, `utc_date(at)`, `utc_offset_seconds(at)` and `time_zone_name()` replace `chrono::Local` in the Claude backend's `current_date`, the Codex backend's `ExecutionEnvironment::local` and the Code Mode engine's per-cell time zone offset, and `iana_time_zone::get_timezone` in the Codex environment; the dates now come from `nanocode_platform::system_time`, so an installed host's clock (the simulator's) dates them too. On Unix, crates/core/platform/src/zone/tzif.rs ports chrono 0.4.45's own lookup: TZ read as chrono reads it (empty is UTC; `localtime`; `:name`; a file under /usr/share/zoneinfo, /share/zoneinfo, /etc/zoneinfo or /usr/share/lib/zoneinfo or by absolute path; else a POSIX rule), otherwise /etc/localtime, then the zone the system names under /usr/share/zoneinfo, then UTC; TZif versions 1 to 3 with leap seconds and the footer rule (Julian, zero-based and month-week-day days, version 3's extended hours) under chrono's validation; kept per thread and checked again at most once a second against TZ and /etc/localtime's modification time, as chrono did. The name is read as the workspace's patched iana-time-zone did: on Linux /etc/localtime's link under a zoneinfo directory, then /etc/timezone, then OpenWrt's /etc/config/system; on macOS the link's path after /zoneinfo/; on other Apple systems CoreFoundation's system zone, the one unsafe module of nanocode-platform, whose lints therefore deny rather than forbid unsafe code, as nanocode-process's do. WASM keeps the UTC date and Etc/UTC. Windows and other non-Unix targets now get UTC and no name where chrono and iana-time-zone asked the system; the workspace does not build for Windows today (`cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` stops in ring's C code on gak-9). The UTC fallbacks are chrono's and the Codex environment's own, kept so that no date changes, and the offset of a clock reading beyond the years a rule can compute (|year| near 2^31) panics as chrono's did. Proven with output/tz-equal, which links chrono 0.4.45 (with the patched iana-time-zone) beside nanocode-platform: a child process per TZ value compares the offset and the local date at three instants of every day from 1900 to 2100 and around every offset change it finds by bisection (one second and one hour either side), the zone name and `Local::now`. Linux (hosted Hand, tzdata 2026e): 594 values (the 447 zone files, 63 of them also with `:` and 40 by absolute path, TZ unset, and 43 POSIX and malformed strings: southern-hemisphere and Julian rules, `/26` and `J365/25` that only version 3 allows, out-of-range fields, names too short or long, a rule without its end) 262,225,956 checks over 57,846 transitions, 0 differences; macOS (gak-9, 25.3): 728 values, 321,511,612 checks over 83,926 transitions, 0 differences; and 15 /etc layouts in a mount namespace (`unshare -rm`: links absolute, relative and into /etc/zoneinfo, a copied file with and without /etc/timezone, /etc/timezone alone and empty, nothing at all, OpenWrt with zonename, with timezone only and with a broken quote, a link outside zoneinfo, broken and dangling links, a garbage file), each with TZ unset and with an invalid TZ, 0 differences. The offset of now costs what it did (2,000,000 calls, three rounds on the loaded Hand: 70 to 174 ns against chrono's 106 to 245 ns). `cargo metadata --locked` 722 to 713 packages: chrono, iana-time-zone, iana-time-zone-haiku, android_system_properties, windows-core, windows-implement, windows-interface, windows-result and windows-strings leave, and crates/patches/iana-time-zone goes; chrono took 4.07 s of release build time on the Hand (`cargo build --release -p chrono --timings`), nanocode-platform with the reader takes 1.7 s. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-platform -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-codex -p nanocode-code-mode-engine` natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown` on Linux (no new warnings), and on gak-9 for macOS and, for nanocode-platform, `--target aarch64-apple-ios`.
- `RecordCache` (behind `CachedStore` and `RecordCache::remember`) never caches a blank record; a blank removes the key from the cache (2026-11-12). `put` inserted every written record, blanks included, and an insert keeps the first value of a key, so after a commit that blanked a key and wrote its content again the cache answered an empty value for that key until it was evicted, though the store held the content; after a commit that only blanked a key, the cache went on answering the old content although stores that apply blanks (`MemoryStore`, `JsonlStore`) had removed it. `put` now forgets a blanked key (`Records::forget`, which gives back its bytes) and inserts only content; the key's place in the eviction order stays until it is popped, which then frees nothing. With only the StagedStore fix (previous entry), bin/nanocode-sim's rewrite workload (the simulator entry above) failed 1,212 of `--seeds 0..3000`, every one a cached read back of a rewritten record answering blank; with both fixes none fail. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability` (and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`), `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability`. File: crates/runtime/durability/src/record_cache.rs.
- `StagedStore` takes a commit's records by the last write of each key and treats a blank record (an empty value, which removes a record) as no content, so a commit that blanks a key and writes its content again stages that content (2026-11-12). Code Mode's cell journal does this when a resumed cell writes its journal again (`DurableCellJournals::save` blanks the replaced cell's links, then stages the new chain, whose link has the same content key when the update is the same). `staged_write` compared every record with what was already staged, so the blank differed from content an earlier staged commit wrote under that key and the commit failed with "a staged record already has different content"; when the key was not staged yet, `or_insert` kept the first record, the blank, so the content was dropped and a read through the store answered an empty value. The records are now folded into a map from key to its last value (a blank then content is content; content then a blank is a blank, the order `MemoryStore` applies them in), a staged blank conflicts with nothing and content replaces it (and is put again, as `stored` forgets the key), different non-empty content still fails as before, and a read of a staged blank answers no record instead of an empty value. The map borrows the commit's keys and values: one allocation per staged commit beside the key and value copies each staged record already makes. Found by bin/nanocode-sim's rewrite workload (the simulator entry above): on master `nanocode-sim --seeds 0..2000` failed 1,476 seeds, 854 of them on a refused staged commit; with only the CachedStore fix (next entry) `--seeds 0..3000` still failed 2,204 seeds, 1,366 refused staged commits and 838 blank reads back through a StagedStore, and with this change none of those. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability-core` (and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`), `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability-core`. File: crates/core/durability/src/staged.rs.
- psh is the only shell of the agent's commands: `--shell` and `NANOCODE_SHELL` are gone, and nothing hands a command to the system's bash (2026-11-12, Georgios: "Everywhere default - delete everything non psh"). nanocode and nc-lite serve psh from their own executable (`nanocode psh-shell`, `nc-lite psh-shell`), choose it and embed it before anything else runs; off Unix both refuse to start, since psh is served on Unix hosts only. `nanocode_home::shell::Shell` is psh's program and arguments only (the zsh, bash, sh, PowerShell and cmd types, shell detection and PATH search are gone); `chosen()` answers the shell a host chose, and Claude's `Bash` and Codex's `exec_command` fail with "this host has not made psh its shell" when none was chosen, instead of falling back to a machine shell. A `shell` the model names in `exec_command` is ignored: psh speaks bash, and `default_shell_name` is always `bash`. Removed with it: `nanocode_psh::plan` and its `Plan`/`Reason` classifier (coproc, interactive builtins, `set -o posix`, `set -r`, `enable -f`, macOS-only signal numbers went to /bin/bash; psh now reports `not supported yet` and exits 2), the forked-zsh command server (server.rs, server/direct.rs, 2,446 lines), the warm bash loader and `export_secrets_after_profile` (a bash or zsh login shell only); warm processes are psh's alone. What stays from the machine: the user's login shell (`login_shell()`: zsh, bash or sh from passwd, else /bin/zsh on macOS or /bin/bash elsewhere) still reports its environment once per startup-file change for login commands, since psh cannot read .zshrc; it runs `-lc "printf …; /usr/bin/env -0"` and no agent command. output/psh-path (`compat psh fg|exec` with PSH_PATH_EMBED=1, HOME and TZ fixed) over the 727 agent cases on the Linux hosted Hand: run_bash output is byte for byte the same before and after; exec_command differs in 5 cases only by the order stdout and stderr of a child process arrive, and two base runs differ the same way. Six cases the classifier used to delegate now end in psh's `not supported yet` (coproc, bind, set -o posix, set -r, enable -f); a .bash_profile export still reaches login commands. Workspace `cargo check --locked`, the wasm32 check, clippy on nanocode-home, nanocode-process, nanocode-psh, nanocode-psh-embedded, nanocode-cli and nc-lite (no new warnings) and the dependency boundaries pass; Cargo.lock drops psh-classify and psh-syntax from nanocode-psh and nanocode-psh from nanocode-process, and nc-lite gains psh.
- clap stays (2026-11-12, Georgios chose to keep it; DEPENDENCIES.md's clap row moves to Kept on purpose). An earlier attempt at a parser over `std::env::args_os` found what it would have to reproduce exactly: nanocode-cli's about 60 flags over 7 subcommands, with `env` fallbacks, roughly 1,200 lines of generated help and clap's context-dependent errors and suggestions, which scripts and users read. Against that, clap brings 12 packages, 4.7 s of build for clap_builder and 275 KiB of .text (measured at 7b0586574, the DEPENDENCIES.md baseline), so a rewrite would trade a stable interface for a small saving.
- 2026-11-12: a Code Mode nested call builds its `JournaledCall` (a deep copy of the input) only when the cell's status record or a persisting journal will keep it, moves it into the record's `Arc` instead of cloning it there, and copies it a second time only when both need it; `journaled_call` takes it as an `Option`. Before, every call cloned the input once for the journal entry and again for the record, and without persistence the copy was dropped unused. Measured on the real `CodeModeRuntime` (output/durability-ledger's jsbench `qjs` engine, now djs underneath: `perf stat -e instructions:u jsbench qjs 1 N tools`, N = 300 and 2,300, interleaved, two rounds): a 16-call `Promise.all` cell 3.006M → 2.975M instructions (−1%).
- 2026-11-12: the djs compiler's per-unit buffers (`resolve::Scratch`: instruction, line, handler, code and peephole vectors) live on the heap between compiles (`Heap::compile_scratch`, outside the image, carried over by `restore_image` like the normalization tables), so a compile starts with their capacity instead of growing and freeing them again; Code Mode compiles one unit per cell. Measured with output/durability-ledger's jsbench (`perf stat -e instructions:u jsbench djs 1 N trivial`, N = 3,000 and 33,000, interleaved, two rounds): a trivial cell 70.1k/69.1k → 64.7k/64.7k instructions (−7%); wall time per cell (5 µs trivial, ~62 µs tools, ~12.7 ms compute) and max RSS unchanged within noise. test262 active group unchanged (39,325/39,365, ratchet OK).
- nanocode-cli pays Tempo services with its own MPP client, and mpp leaves the workspace with alloy, aws-lc, bundled SQLite, commonware and tempo-primitives (2026-11-12, Georgios: "a from-scratch implementation of mpp/tempo-alloy, without any deps", DEPENDENCIES.md rank 1, after the nanocode-tempo entry below). bin/nanocode/src/tempo/ replaces each mpp piece the CLI used (mpp at tempoxyz/mpp-rs 65fe50a, features client, tempo, sqlite, forward-proxy): protocol.rs parses WWW-Authenticate Payment challenges, builds credentials, reads Payment-Receipt and ranks Accept-Payment as mpp does; mcp.rs carries MCP challenges and credentials with an RFC 8785 canonicalizer; charge.rs, tx.rs, signing.rs and keys.rs build, sign and submit Tempo charge transactions (fee payer and unsponsored, keychain access keys from the Tempo wallet) over nanocode-tempo; session.rs with channel, wire and recovery opens, tops up, vouches and closes escrow channels; store.rs keeps channels in channels.json in the wallet directory and imports the old channels.db once, read-only, with its WAL (store/sqlite.rs reads the SQLite file format itself); rpc.rs is JSON-RPC over the workspace reqwest with alloy's RetryBackoffLayer policy (20 retries, 10 ms initial, 1,000 compute units); proxy.rs and x509.rs are the forward proxy, terminating TLS with a per-host certificate it signs itself (P-256, RFC 6979), on hyper, hyper-util, tokio-rustls and rustls-native-certs, already in the graph (hyper gains its server feature); events.rs, flow.rs, provider.rs, payer.rs and error.rs are the provider, events and errors around them. nanocode-tempo gains TempoTransaction::encode_fee_payer_envelope. nanocode-cli's serde_json takes preserve_order, which mpp alone turned on, so every JSON the CLI prints keeps its key order. Proven against mpp in throwaway harnesses under output/ that link both: protocol-equal over 20,000 seeded cases, 135,831 checks, 0 differences (2,371 challenges mpp parses, credentials, receipts, MCP, Accept-Payment, RFC 3339, JCS); charge-equal, 43 charge cases against a recorded RPC and the store fixtures, 352 checks, 0 differences (validBefore is wall-clock seconds, so a run that crosses a second differs there); session-equal, 938 cases (fee payer and unsponsored, open, top-up, voucher, close, recovery, and importing 394 synthetic rows and real WAL files), 0 different; proxy-equal 53 of 53 equal; tempo-equal primitives 9,829 checks over 300 rounds equal. Not equal: v1 escrow sessions fail with the error mpp gave for access keys; sessions whose challenge sets machineTokenEnabled fail with a clear error; mpp APIs the CLI did not call are gone (max deposit, with_http_client, hint client, bootstrap, WebSocket); the PaymentFailed, CredentialCreated and ChallengeReceived events, which nothing listened to, are gone, and Deposit and PaymentUpdate are emitted synchronously; a channel the tempo CLI or an older nanocode writes to channels.db after the import is not seen, so it may open another channel; proxy certificates are signed deterministically instead of with random nonces (the same fields and extensions); errors for malformed hex, ABI and RNG failures word their detail differently; a missing home directory reads "IO error: home directory is unavailable"; lock expiry waits in whole seconds. Measured on the 5-core hosted Hand, each from a fresh target directory, 7322f1059 against this commit: `cargo metadata --locked` 966 to 722 packages (244 leave, none join: mpp, tempo-alloy, tempo-primitives, tempo-contracts, every alloy crate, commonware-cryptography, aws-lc-rs and aws-lc-sys, rusqlite and libsqlite3-sys, k256, dashmap, sha3-asm); `time cargo build --release --locked -p nanocode-cli --timings` 5m48s to 4m44s wall (user 18m15s to 15m53s), 966 to 768 units, 1,297.4 to 1,048.0 s of summed unit time (aws-lc-sys's 43.5 s gone); the release nanocode 108,097,480 to 103,071,496 bytes; `cargo bloat --release -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode --crates` (unstripped) 66.6 to 63.0 MiB of .text, file 155.1 to 148.5 MiB, mpp's 1.5 MiB and tempo_alloy's 225.3 KiB gone, nanocode_cli 2.2 to 3.3 MiB. Checks: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-cli` clean in bin/nanocode/src/tempo, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-tempo` native and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- psh's grep stops reading a file at its first match when its output is /dev/null, as GNU grep does (2026-11-12). `grep … > /dev/null` (the exit-status idiom, `if grep -r pat dir >/dev/null 2>&1`) read every file to its end and formatted every matching line for the null device, where GNU grep notices that standard output is /dev/null and treats each file as with -l: done at its first match, nothing printed, no binary-file notice, the same exit status, and every file still searched so that errors are reported. Host files now say whether they are the null device (`HostFile::is_null`, false by default; on Unix a character device whose device number is /dev/null's), `UtilCtx::discards` asks it of a descriptor, and grep sets `discard` from descriptor 1, which stops the sink at the first match and turns off context lines and match spans. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/grepqb.json (CPU median ms of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU grep 3.11 in brackets): `grep -rn needle src > /dev/null 2>&1` over 2,000 files 15.4 to 8.9 (8.8), `grep needle 17MB > /dev/null` 8.9 to 2.4 (4.3), `grep -rn needle src | wc -l` unchanged at 16 (20.6). The cases of output/psh-perf/grepq.json and a run of -r, -l, -c, -v, -m1, missing files and `>&3` to /dev/null in the data directory give the same output and status before and after, except that a binary file's match no longer prints `binary file matches` when the output is /dev/null, which now agrees with GNU grep. Upstream delta: psh-engine host.rs, util.rs (`discards`); psh-os unix/file.rs; psh-utils grep/mod.rs, search.rs, sink.rs.
- psh's wc counts an ASCII byte without turning it into a char first (2026-11-12). Every byte became an `Option<char>` and went through a match on characters with `char::is_control` and a separate whitespace test, which held `wc` to about 500 MB/s. A byte below 0x80 now takes one match on the byte that does the same: a newline counts a line and ends a word, space, tab, CR, VT and FF end a word (tab, CR and FF move the -L column as before), other controls do nothing, and anything else widens the line and may start a word; bytes from 0x80 keep the character path, so UTF-8, C1 controls and invalid bytes count as before. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/wc.json (CPU median ms of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU wc 9.4 in brackets): `wc` of 17 MB 35.4 to 20.6 (31.8), `wc -w` 35.1 to 21.0 (31.4), `wc -m` 35.0 to 20.5 (31.2), `cat | wc` 36.3 to 21.7 (35.2), `wc -L` of 4 MB 9.8 to 6.0 (9.5). 5 invocations (output/psh-perf/wccases.json: several files, -w, -m, -L, -c, every ASCII control, NUL, UTF-8 text, U+0085 and U+2003, invalid bytes, reads split across chunks, a gzip stream in UTF-8 and C locales) give the same bytes before and after; GNU differs where it counts U+2003 as a space and in -L of non-ASCII text, as before. Upstream delta: psh-utils wc.rs.
- psh's sort compares several keys through a 128-bit summary of each key before its bytes (2026-11-12). With more than one key, or one key that is not numeric, each comparison compared the key slices with memcmp (51% of `sort -k2,2 -k3,3n` over 100,000 lines) and the numbers digit string by digit string, and the last resort compared whole lines. Each line's keys (`KeyPart`) now also carry, for a numeric key, the same u128 rank the lone-numeric path uses (`rank`, shared with `Num`) and, for a text key without -d, -f or -i, its first 16 bytes big-endian (`prefix`); keys compare by those first and only an equal prefix compares the slices, ranks that do not fit (more than 18 integer or fraction digits) fall back to the digit strings, the last resort compares the first 8 bytes of each line before the rest, and with the last resort the line order sorts with `sort_unstable_by`. -d, -f, -i, -g, -M, -V, -h and -R keys keep their comparison. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/sort.json over 100,000 lines (CPU median ms of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU sort 9.4 in brackets): `sort -k2,2 -k3,3n` 87.6 to 45.2 (83.8), `sort -k2` 31.9 to 29.4 (43.2); the lone-numeric and plain sorts unchanged. 31 invocations (output/psh-perf/sortcases3.json: the 27 earlier cases plus two-key sorts with r on either key, global -r, -s, -u, character positions, -t, -f, -d, keys longer than 16 bytes that share their first 16, NUL and UTF-8 bytes, and n, g, M, V and h keys mixed with text keys) give the same bytes before and after and the same as GNU sort. Upstream delta: psh-utils sort.rs.
- `RowStore` lists a state's record keys in key order (2026-11-12). `record_keys` (its `StateStore::list_records`) gathered the held and sealed keys into a `HashSet` and returned them in its random order, which reached decisions: `RowStore::unreachable` orders `Unreachable.keys` by it, `manifests_by_content` keeps the last key of two that share a content key, and staged writes append to it. The keys now go through a `BTreeSet`, so two runs of the same seed list the same order. The audit of every hash-ordered iteration in crates/core/durability and crates/runtime/durability (HashMap, HashSet, nanocode_sync's `Map` and `AtomMap`) found no other that reaches bytes, the wire or a decision: `Index::evict`'s `min_by_key` has unique `used` stamps except empty placeholders, `MemoryStore`'s queries sort through a top-k heap on unique keys, and the rest are membership, sums or independent per-item work; everything persisted is already ordered (`OrdMap`, `BTreeMap`, sorted staging). Listing is a cold path (garbage collection and manifests). Commands: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability-core`, `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p nanocode-durability-core`. File: crates/core/durability/src/row.rs.
- bin/nanocode-sim installs a simulated `nanocode_platform::Host` and checks the simulated crates for calls that bypass it (2026-11-12). `host.rs`: `SimulatedHost` answers `now` with an `Instant` taken once per seed plus the seed's virtual clock, `system_time` with `SIMULATED_START_UNIX_SECS` (1,794,441,600, 2026-11-12T00:00:00Z, the simulator's date: positive and inside UUIDv7's 48-bit millisecond range, like any timestamp a real run writes) plus the virtual clock, `sleep` with the executor's `Clock::sleep`, `fill_random` with the seed's `host` splitmix64 stream, and `spawn` by queueing the task for the executor; it is installed once at start and `simulate` points it at each seed's clock (`host::enter`), so a sweep runs many seeds in one process. The executor adopts queued tasks before each step as background tasks: `run` ends when its own tasks have finished, and background tasks (a store driver waiting for commands) are dropped with the run, as a process's are when it exits. `nanocode-sim --tidy` scans crates/core/durability, crates/runtime/durability and crates/runtime/subagents for `SystemTime::now`, `Instant::now`, `thread::spawn`, `thread::Builder`, `getrandom`, `tokio::time`, `tokio::spawn` and `Handle::try_current` (as tempoxyz/zempo's tidy determinism_banned list does), with an allowlist of {path, call, why}, and also fails on an allowance no longer used; the four allowances are the native defaults of the previous entry (SharedStore's driver thread, and `Handle::try_current` in memory.rs, session.rs and child_journal.rs, each reached only without a host). Checked on the hosted Hand: `nanocode-sim --tidy` prints `TIDY determinism: clean`; `--seeds 0..1000 --twice` passes 1,000 of 1,000 with identical digests, and the first 50 seeds' digests are the same with and without the host (md5 of their `--verbose` seed lines `b2eb9dcb`), since the store workload reads no host time or randomness into its trace; user CPU for that sweep 8.21, 8.30, 8.23 s before and 8.67, 8.84, 8.60 s after, the host's thread-local reads. Commands: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sim`, `cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-sim`. Files: bin/nanocode-sim/src/{host.rs,tidy.rs,executor.rs,main.rs,simulate.rs}, bin/nanocode-sim/Cargo.toml.
- nanocode-platform has a native installable `Host`, and the durability and subagent runtime spawn tasks and read time through it, so bin/nanocode-sim can run them on its own executor and virtual clock (2026-11-12). Until now `host.rs` was wasm-only and natively the crate re-exported std and tokio. Natively `Host` (`Send + Sync`: `now`, `system_time`, `sleep`, `fill_random`, `spawn`, futures as `HostFuture`) is installed once per process with `install(&'static dyn Host)` into a `OnceLock`; `host()` is one acquire load, and with no host every function calls exactly what it called before: `std::time::Instant::now`, `SystemTime::now`, `tokio::time::sleep` and `timeout`, the buffered `getrandom` and `tokio::spawn`. New on both targets: `now()` (the monotonic `Instant`, still `std::time::Instant` natively, so the type and its callers are unchanged) and `spawn` (`spawn_local` on wasm). `sleep` and `timeout` are functions that choose tokio's future or the host's when called, so a deadline still starts at the call as tokio's does; `Elapsed` is the crate's own type on both targets (natively it was tokio's re-export, which nothing named) with tokio's `From<Elapsed> for io::Error`; `uuid_v7` reads `system_time()`, so `uuid_v4`, `uuid_v7` and `OwnerId::new` follow an installed host's randomness and clock. Through the host now: `SharedStore`'s `spawn_driver` gives drivers to an installed host and otherwise keeps the process-wide current_thread runtime on its own thread (entry (11) of the 2026-11-03 store pipeline: the store pipeline is never queued behind agent tasks, and `SharedStore::new` needs no Tokio runtime), `spawn_operation`, `MemoryStore`'s and durable sessions' drivers, claim acknowledgements and the child journal writer (each of these keeps its `Handle::try_current` default), the queue timestamps behind `queue.duration_ms` in shared_store.rs, and the subagent runtime's spawns, sleeps and stop deadlines (subagents platform.rs and the seven `Instant::now` in runtime.rs). tokio's `rt` feature on nanocode-platform adds no package. Two `tokio::select!`s that drew a random branch are `biased`: `DurableOwner`'s release checks completion before the closed command channel (both end the wait, and completion first reports a release that did happen), and the child journal writer settles finished writes before taking the next write (settling only frees in-flight slots and in-flight writes come only from earlier writes, so neither branch can starve the other). The other `select!`s in durability were already biased; subagents runtime.rs:1333 (completion fill) is not yet. Measured on the hosted Hand (Linux x86_64, 5 vCPUs, other agents building), the commit before this one against this one: output/platform-bench (10,000,000 calls, current_thread runtime, three interleaved runs, ns per call) `uuid_v7` 65.0, 62.2, 64.7 to 62.0, 62.6, 69.5; `uuid_v4` 34.8, 36.0, 37.9 to 38.2, 37.2, 42.9; `unix_millis` 32.0, 31.3, 33.2 to 31.9, 31.6, 34.5; `timeout` around a ready future 45.2, 50.4, 45.7 to 53.0, 52.8, 54.5 (the enum and async block around tokio's `Timeout`; `timeout` wraps model, MCP and tool waits, not per-record work); `std::time::Instant::now` 44 to 48 in both. output/durability-ledger `matrix.sh <swarm> 10000 1000 memory jsonl sqlite rows`, two interleaved rounds, settled s and user CPU s before / after: memory 10.51, 9.93 (27.0, 25.0) / 10.18, 10.93 (26.5, 27.0); jsonl 10.07, 10.16 (29.0, 28.8) / 8.36, 9.20 (25.4, 26.9); sqlite 15.10, 10.74 (36.6, 30.1) / 11.19, 11.76 (31.2, 33.1); rows 14.65, 14.79 (30.9, 31.1) / 13.86, 14.12 (29.3, 29.4); commits and bytes per agent within 0.5%. `stopcheck.sh <swarm> 2000 50 1000 jsonl sqlite memory` settles every CANCEL and CLOSE, with and without hibernation; `killresume.sh <swarm> 3000 1500 1000 jsonl sqlite rows` resumes all 3,000 to completed (settled 2.00, 2.91, 4.26 s before, 2.36, 3.15, 4.53 s after); `treecheck.sh <swarm> 20 50 1000` with `MAX_AWAKE=0 LATENCY_MS=300` completes all 1,020 (jsonl 2.45 to 2.65 s, sqlite 3.30 to 3.41 s). The swarm binary's text grows from 52,610,712 to 52,778,768 bytes (`size`). Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib` and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib` for nanocode-platform, nanocode-durability, nanocode-subagents and the 17 other crates that use nanocode-platform. Files: crates/core/platform/src/{lib.rs,native.rs}, crates/runtime/durability/src/{shared_store.rs,memory.rs,session.rs,child_journal.rs}, crates/runtime/subagents/src/{platform.rs,runtime.rs}.
- psh writes to an anonymous pipe on macOS in pieces of up to 64 KiB less what the pipe holds, not 512 bytes (2026-11-12). After poll says a shared pipe is writable, a write was cut to `PIPE_BUF` so that it could not wait, which is 512 bytes on macOS: `cat 17MB` into the pipe of the program running psh took 34,000 polls and writes, and macOS pipes never grew past their first 16 KiB. On macOS an anonymous pipe (a FIFO whose device is 0) reports in `st_size` how much it holds and grows to 64 KiB when a write needs it, so `UnixFile::room` allows 64 KiB minus that; a named FIFO (whose size reads 0 however full it is) and every other stream keep `PIPE_BUF`, so a FIFO read by a background job of the same shell cannot block the engine (tested: with 64 KiB for FIFOs that job hung). A pipe the kernel cannot grow makes the write wait for its reader, as Windows does for shared pipes (D1077). Linux is unchanged (its `PIPE_BUF` is 4,096). output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/io.json over a 17 MB file on macOS (M1 Max; CPU median ms of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs, stdout a pipe to the harness), before to after (/bin/bash with BSD tools in brackets): `cat` 35.6 to 8.2 (6.1), `grep -n e` 85.4 to 52.0 (89.0), `seq 1 300000` 9.9 to 6.7 (47.8), `awk '{print $1}'` 49.3 to 44.8 (426). The FIFO case, `seq 1 300000 | cat | wc -l`, `yes | head -c 5000000`, a slow reader (`sleep 1; wc -l`) and `| head -2` give the same results before and after. Upstream delta: psh-os unix/file.rs, unix/ready.rs.
- psh writes to /dev/null and other character devices that are not terminals without asking poll first (2026-11-12). A shared descriptor that may wait (a pipe, FIFO, socket, terminal or character device) was polled for room before every write and each write was cut to `PIPE_BUF`, which is 512 bytes on macOS, so `> /dev/null` and `2> /dev/null` cost a poll and a write per 512 bytes there (4,096 on Linux). A character device that is not a terminal never makes a writer wait, so `UnixFile` keeps a separate `write_waits` (a stream, and a terminal or not a character device) for writes; reads still poll as before. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/io.json over a 17 MB file (CPU median ms of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs), before to after (the system's bash running its own tools in brackets): macOS (M1 Max, BSD tools) `cat > /dev/null` 36.2 to 4.7 (4.8), `tr a-z A-Z > /dev/null` 42.6 to 10.8 (713), `head -n 300000 > /dev/null` 30.3 to 6.7 (21.5), `sed s/a/b/ > /dev/null` 74.6 to 43.1 (108.8); Linux x86_64 (GNU coreutils 9.4) `cat > /dev/null` 3.9 to 3.4 (4.8), `head -n 300000 > /dev/null` 4.4 to 4.1 (8.6). A FIFO read by a background job of the same shell, pipelines through cat, `yes | head -c` and psh-os's own tests behave as before on both systems. Upstream delta: psh-os unix/file.rs.
- psh's line reader (paste, uniq, nl, comm, cut) looks for the end of a line in its first 16 bytes and then with memchr (2026-11-12). `LineReader::next` compared every byte with the delimiter through `position`. memchr alone made a long run of short lines slower (`seq 1000000 | paste -sd+` 30.7 to 33.5 ms, a call per 7-byte line), so a line's first 16 bytes are still compared in place and only a longer line goes to `memchr::memchr`. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/lr.json (CPU median ms of 5 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU coreutils 9.4 in brackets): `uniq` of 400,000 lines 27.0 to 20.8 (33.6), `nl` of 100,000 11.3 to 9.8 (16.6), `paste -d,` of two 100,000-line files 12.0 to 11.0 (23.1); `paste -sd+` of 1,000,000 numbers 30.5 to 30.5 (24.1), `uniq -c` and `comm` within noise. 5 invocations (output/psh-perf/lrcases.json: paste -s, -z and a missing final newline, uniq -c, -d, -i, nl -ba, comm, a 300 KB line) and the 19 of cutcases.json give the same bytes before and after. Upstream delta: psh-utils textio.rs.
- psh's head -n N finds line ends with memchr (2026-11-12). It compared every byte of each 64 KiB read with the delimiter in an enumerate loop until N lines were seen. It now steps from delimiter to delimiter with `memchr::memchr_iter`. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/head.json over a 17 MB file (CPU median ms of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU head 9.4 in brackets): `head -n 300000 > /dev/null` 11.1 to 4.9 (9.7), `head -n 200000 | tail -1` 10.2 to 6.1 (13.9), `head -n 1000 | wc -l` 2.2 to 2.0 (5.3). 4 invocations (output/psh-perf/headcases.json: -n 0, counts past the end, several files, -c, -z, no final newline, pipes from cat, seq and yes, -n -N and -c -N) give the same bytes before and after and the same as GNU head. Upstream delta: psh-utils head.rs.
- psh's tail and head -n -N find the last lines by searching back from the end with memrchr (2026-11-12). `cut_last_lines` collected the start of every line of the input into a vector and then indexed it, so `cat file | tail -1` of 17 MB built a vector of 400,000 offsets for one line, and `head -n -5` the same. It now walks the delimiters backwards with `memchr::memrchr_iter`, skipping a final delimiter, and stops at the Nth, which is the same offset. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/tailp.json (CPU median ms of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU coreutils 9.4 in brackets): `cat 17MB | tail -1` 20.2 to 8.7 (14.7), `cat 17MB | tail -n 5` 19.4 to 9.0 (16.7), `head -n -5` of 17 MB 27.6 to 16.3 (17.0), `cat 4MB | tail -n 1000` 6.3 to 3.5 (9.2). The 27 tail invocations of output/psh-perf/tailcases.json (including head -n -N and -n -0) give the same bytes before and after, and head's unit cases still pass. Upstream delta: psh-utils head.rs.
- psh's tr translates a buffer in place when nothing is deleted or squeezed, and deletes without a branch per byte (2026-11-12). Every read was copied into a new Vec and each byte went through a lookup of `Option<(u8, bool)>`, a squeeze check and a push. When the sets are bytes (no UTF-8 operands) and there is no -s, a translation with no deletion now maps the read buffer in place through a 256-byte table and writes it; a deletion writes each byte's translation to the next output slot and advances by one only when the byte is kept. -s and UTF-8 sets keep the loop they had. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/tr.json and tr2.json over a 17 MB file (CPU median ms of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU tr 9.4 in brackets): `tr a-z A-Z > /dev/null` 17.6 to 8.4 (9.9); with `| tail -1` 33.3 to 24.4 (20.8), `tr -d aeiou | tail -1` 34.0 to 26.2 (28.8), `tr -cd 'a-z\n' | wc -c` 22.4 to 18.4 (24.2); `tr -s ' '` unchanged at 37.5 (31.5). 8 invocations (output/psh-perf/trcases.json: ranges, classes, -d, -c, -s, -ds, -t, all 256 bytes of a gzip stream, NUL bytes, UTF-8 sets, invalid bytes, errors) give the same bytes before and after. Upstream delta: psh-utils tr.rs.
- psh's seq writes integers with its own digit loop instead of i128's to_string (2026-11-12). Integer operands are kept as i128 so that they stay exact, and each number went through `i128::to_string` (a 128-bit division per digit) into a new String, then `zero_pad`. `int_text` now writes the digits backwards into a 48-byte buffer on the stack, dividing as u64 once the value fits, then the zero padding of -w and the sign, and `emit!` copies the bytes. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/seq.json (CPU median ms of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU seq 9.4 in brackets): `seq 1 1000000` 20.0 to 12.0 (7.5), `seq -w 1 1000000` 41.6 to 22.6 (151.0), `seq -s, 1 300000` 7.9 to 5.5 (7.9), `seq 1000000 | paste -sd+` 39.9 to 30.5 (19.9); fractional `seq 0.5 0.5 200000` unchanged at 73 (63). 5 invocations (output/psh-perf/seqcases.json: negative steps, -w with negatives, -s, values around 2^63, 2^64 and 2^127, fractions, -f, errors) give the same bytes before and after. Upstream delta: psh-utils seq.rs.
- psh's sort ranks a lone numeric key as one 128-bit integer and sorts the lines' records in place (2026-11-12). With one `-n` key, every comparison compared the sign, integer and fraction digit strings (`cmp_parts`) and, among equal numbers, the two whole lines, through an index into two other vectors; a profile of `sort -n -k3` over 100,000 lines with 1,000 distinct numbers spent 79% of its time in memcmp. When the only key is numeric, each line now gets a record (`Num`) with its number as one u128 (sign, then up to 18 integer and 18 fraction digits; longer numbers keep the digit-string comparison), the first 8 bytes of the line big-endian, and its index; records compare by rank, then by the prefix and the whole line for the last resort (reversed by -r as before), and sort with `sort_unstable_by` when the last resort makes only identical lines equal, else the stable `sort_by` (-s, -u). Other keys keep their path. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/sort.json over 100,000 lines (CPU median ms of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU sort 9.4 in brackets): `sort -n -k3` 126.5 to 25.8 (41.8), `sort -t: -k3,3n` of 20,000 lines 5.3 to 5.3 (8.4); two-key `sort -k2,2 -k3,3n` unchanged at 87 (82). 27 invocations (output/psh-perf/sortcases2.json: the 21 earlier cases plus negatives, -0, fractions, numbers of 18 to 28 digits, empty and non-numeric keys, leading blanks, +5, 1e3, 3,000, -r, -rn, -s, -u, -b, -c, -z, NUL bytes and runs of equal keys) give the same bytes before and after and the same as GNU sort. Upstream delta: psh-utils sort.rs.
- psh's diff numbers lines by their bytes in place, with foldhash (2026-11-12). Every line of both files was copied into a new Vec to be its key (`Differ::key`) and hashed with SipHash in a `HashMap<(Vec<u8>, bool), u32>`, 100,000 allocations and hashes for two 50,000-line files. `key` now returns the line itself when no option rewrites it (-i, -w, -b, --strip-trailing-cr) and the rewritten copy otherwise (`Cow`), and the ids live in a foldhash map (`LineIds`, `Differ::line_ids`). output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/diff.json over 50,000 lines (CPU median ms of 4 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU diff 3.10 in brackets): 7,516 lines changed 13.6 to 9.2 (10.5), the same with -u 14.8 to 10.3 (12.2), one line changed 11.6 to 7.5 (5.7), identical files 5.1 to 5.1 (5.5). 96 invocations (output/psh-perf/diffcases.json, including -b, -w, -i, -B and -I) give the same bytes before and after. Upstream delta: psh-utils diff.rs.
- psh's diff marks the lines that appear only in one file as changed before it looks for the shortest edit script (2026-11-12). Myers' search ran over every line of both files, so many scattered edits (a 50,000-line file with 7,516 lines changed by `sed s/needle/pin/`) took about 75 ms in `middle_snake`. A line whose content never occurs in the other file cannot be part of any common subsequence, so `diff_algo::diff` now marks those lines changed, runs the same search on the lines that are left, maps the result back and slides runs with `compact` as before; the script stays minimal, which GNU's fuller discarding of frequent lines (also tried) does not promise and did not make closer to GNU's output here. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/diff.json over 50,000 lines (CPU median ms of 3 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU diff 3.10 in brackets): 7,516 lines changed 86.2 to 14.4 (13.0), the same with -u 86.5 to 14.8 (13.7), one line changed 11.7 to 12.3 (7.8), identical files 5.5 to 5.3 (5.9). Over 96 invocations (output/psh-perf/diffcases.json: 300 generated pairs, from random lines and from edited Rust sources, with and without final newlines, in normal, -u and -c form, plus large pairs, -b, -w, -i, -q, -y, -e, -B and -I) the output is the same before and after except one 30,000-line deletion of every third line, where an equally short script places two deletions differently; GNU differs from psh in 13 of them before and in those 13 and that one after. Upstream delta: psh-utils diff_algo.rs.
- psh's base64 encodes three bytes and decodes four symbols at a time (2026-11-12). The encoder looked at each chunk's length and checked the wrap column before every symbol; the decoder sent every symbol through `Decoder::push` with a match per character. Encoding now turns each whole three-byte group into four symbols with one shift per symbol, pads the last group on its own, then cuts the symbols into lines with one copy per line, keeping the column across reads. Decoding takes four symbols at once through a 256-byte table (`DECODE`) when a group starts and all four are alphabet symbols, and gives anything else (newlines, `=`, garbage, a group split across reads) to the decoder as before. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/b64.json over a 17 MB file (CPU median ms of 4 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU coreutils 9.4 in brackets): `base64 | tail -1` 46.2 to 30.8 (30.7), `base64 -w0 | wc -c` 30.8 to 16.8 (22.0), `base64 -d` of the 23 MB encoding 113.3 to 52.0 (65.1). 10 invocations (output/psh-perf/b64cases.json: -w 0, 1, 4, 7, every length from 0 to 6 and around a line, padding errors, symbols after padding, -i with garbage, random bytes round-tripped, CRLF, -o and a missing file) give the same bytes before and after. Upstream delta: psh-utils base64.rs.
- psh's checksums and git's object hashes come from the RustCrypto md-5, sha1 and sha2 crates (2026-11-12). psh's own MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-2 compressed one block at a time in portable Rust, which held sha256sum to about 370 MB/s against GNU's 1.3 GB/s; sha1 and sha2 pick the CPU's SHA instructions at run time (SHA-NI on x86_64, the SHA2 extension on aarch64) and keep a portable path elsewhere, including wasm32. They are the versions nanocode already builds (0.11.0, default features off), so the nanocode build adds no crate; psh's own Cargo.lock gains them and their dependencies. `Digest` keeps its API (`new`, `update`, `finish`) over the crates' hashers, and the specifications' vectors in sum_hash.rs still pass. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/sum.json over a 17 MB file (CPU median ms of 4 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand, AMD EPYC 9555), before to after (GNU coreutils 9.4 in brackets): sha256sum 47.2 to 11.3 (13.4), sha1sum 34.6 to 11.7 (13.1), sha512sum 33.4 to 22.0 (19.4), md5sum 31.9 to 28.2 (24.5), sha224sum of 4 MB 13.3 to 4.2 (6.0). 10 invocations (output/psh-perf/sumcases.json: every algorithm, an empty file, stdin, --tag, -c with good, missing and bad lines, every length around the padding boundary, git add, commit, status and hash-object) give the same bytes before and after. Upstream delta: psh-utils Cargo.toml (md-5, sha1, sha2), sum_hash.rs.
- psh's tail reads only the end of a regular file for `-n N` and `-c N` (2026-11-12). It read the whole file into memory and then cut the last lines out of it, so `tail -n 5` of a 17 MB file read and scanned 17 MB. Host files can now move their offset (`HostFile::seek`, `None` by default; Unix, std and Windows regular files implement it, pipes and terminals do not), and tail seeks to the end and reads back in blocks of 64 KiB and up, doubling, until the block holds more delimiters than lines asked for or reaches the start (`read_last`); `-c N` reads exactly the last N bytes. Stdin, pipes, `+N` and anything that cannot seek keep reading everything; a file that shrinks while read falls back to that too. With `-f`, following starts from the size found at the seek. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/tail.json (CPU median ms of 5 interleaved rounds of 5 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU tail 9.4 in brackets): `tail -n 5` of a 17 MB file 18.3 to 1.9 (2.3), `tail -c 1000` 7.1 to 1.7 (2.5), `tail -n 3000` 18.4 to 1.8 (4.5); `cat | tail -n 5` unchanged at 3.1 (5.3). 27 invocations (output/psh-perf/tailcases.json: -n 0, counts past the file, -c, no final newline, empty file, several files and -q, -r, -z, stdin and pipes, /dev/null, a missing file, a directory, +N, a 300 KB line, obsolete forms) give the same bytes before and after. Upstream delta: psh-engine host.rs, std_host.rs, util.rs (`UtilFile::seek`); psh-os unix/file.rs, windows/file.rs; psh-utils tail.rs.
- A hibernated subagent whose wake loses the race with a close is not made resident again, so closing every agent with hibernation on settles (2026-11-12). In output/durability-ledger's stop check (`stopcheck.sh <swarm> 2000 50 1000 jsonl sqlite`: 2,000 flat agents, mock latency 50 ms, `close_all` 1 s in, `MAX_AWAKE=0`, which turns hibernation on) CLOSE never settled, on master too: `close_all` failed after `AGENT_STOP_TIMEOUT` (30 s) with "timed out waiting for subagent turns to stop", with 93 to 462 children still holding a turn, every one Closing, resident and with a harness task. A trace of each harness (temporary prints, not kept) showed the same history for all of them: the child hibernated before the close, and its wake (`Registry::hibernated`'s task, then `rehydrate`) installed a restored harness after the close request. `rehydrate` checks that the child is not Closing in one state call (`missing_runtimes`) and installs the harness in a later one (`restore_missing`), after `journal_snapshot` and `restore_runtime` await; `request_close_all` ran between the two, marked the child Closing and collected the harnesses resident at that moment, which did not include it, and `settle_hibernated` then found nothing to settle because the install had taken the hibernated turn and resumed it on a harness nobody closed. That turn did not finish while `close_all` held the scope: its `TurnFinished` came after the timeout in every trace, so close waited out its deadline. The install now checks the child's status in the same state call: a child that began closing is left as it was, its hibernated turn to close's `settle_hibernated` (or already settled by it), and the restored harness is closed, which shuts its agent down; this is what `missing_runtimes` already did for a child that was Closing when the wake began. Measured on the hosted Hand (Linux x86_64, 5 vCPUs, shared with other builds), master against this change: the stop check's CLOSE with `MAX_AWAKE=0` timed out (60 s) on jsonl and sqlite before and now settles on jsonl, sqlite, rows and memory (close in 0.29 to 0.66 s, settled 1.33 to 1.85 s, all 2,000 closed; the same flat run of three in a row closed in 0.44, 0.56 and 0.66 s); CANCEL and CLOSE without hibernation unchanged. `matrix.sh <swarm> 10000 1000 memory jsonl sqlite rows`, two interleaved rounds, settled s master/fix: memory 14.99, 14.52 / 16.91, 16.46; jsonl 15.95, 19.86 / 23.04, 16.83; sqlite 16.87, 21.22 / 21.53, 17.54; rows 21.62, 24.60 / 21.39, 17.54 (noise from other builds on the machine; commits and bytes per agent within 0.5%, all 10,000 completed in each). `killresume.sh <swarm> 3000 1500 1000 jsonl sqlite rows` resumed all 3,000 to completed on both; `treecheck.sh <swarm> 20 50 1000` with `MAX_AWAKE=0 LATENCY_MS=300` on jsonl and sqlite and without hibernation on jsonl completed all 1,020 on both (jsonl 3.70 to 3.37 s, sqlite 4.83 to 4.63 s, off 1.53 to 1.32 s). The Result of closing the discarded harness is logged at debug: the agent was never installed, so a failure to shut it down leaves nothing the scope tracks. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-subagents` (and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`), `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-subagents`. File: crates/runtime/subagents/src/runtime.rs (`restore_missing`).
- 2026-11-12: djs's `conv::rem` takes the i64 remainder for every integral double below 2^63 in magnitude, not only safe integers: those are exact in i64, and so is their remainder (an fmod result is always representable). `checked_rem` covers a zero divisor and i64::MIN % -1, and a conversion that saturates to i64::MAX (2^63 and up, +Infinity) falls back to fmod. LCG-style code such as `(x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2147483648` passes 2^53 and went through `djs_libm::fmod`'s bit loop. Interleaved `~/w/cmp.py` (3 rounds, perf stat), two runs: sort (its setup is that LCG) 86.3 → 76.4 and 84.8 → 78.0 ms (−1.1% instructions; the division loop was latency, not instructions); loop +0.5% instructions (3,179.0 → 3,193.7 M; time 110.1 → 111.6 and 112.6 → 112.2 ms); chars unchanged. A script of `a % b` over ±0, ±1, 2^53..2^64, ±1e18, 9.2e18, 1e300, fractions, NaN and ±Infinity pairs prints the same as QuickJS. test262 active group unchanged (39,325/39,365, ratchet OK).
- 2026-11-12: a new djs error's stack reads the realm's Error constructor once (`realm::error_constructor`) and gives it to both `stack_trace_limit` and `prepare_stack_trace`, which each looked it up in the constructors record before. Interleaved `~/w/cmp.py` (3 rounds, perf stat): trycatch 1,136.9 → 1,118.5 M instructions (−1.6%), 70.2 → 67.3 ms; fib unchanged. test262 active group unchanged (39,325/39,365, ratchet OK).
- The tool crates stay on schemars 0.8 (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md's schemars row, now kept on purpose). It was ranked as a second schemars beside gakonst/cua's 1.x, which left with cua (2d2d81dc4), so 0.8 is the only one built. Moving to 1.x would change the bytes models are sent: output/schema-check renders the same types with schemars 0.8.22 and 1.2.3, under the settings `nanocode_tools::schema_for` and the Codex web search use (draft 2019-09, inlined subschemas; 1.x has no `option_add_null_type`) and through `schema_for!` as the Claude host tool TaskOutput uses it, and every schema differs: an unsigned integer's `minimum` is `0.0` in 0.8 and `0` in 1.x (TaskOutput's timeout, the web search's ids and line numbers), `required` is sorted in 0.8 and in field order in 1.x, an `Option` field adds `"null"` to its type in 1.x (41 differences in the web search commands), a serde-tagged enum's tag is `enum: [..]` in 0.8 and `const` in 1.x (which `plain_schema`'s flattening reads), and `schema_for!` names draft 2020-12 instead of draft-07. Keeping the bytes on 1.x would take a pass that rewrites its output into 0.8's. The public API names the trait too: `nanocode_tools::schema_for<T: JsonSchema>`, `__private::schemars` behind `#[tool]`, and `FunctionTool::typed<Args: JsonSchema>`. Hosts, by GitHub code search on 2026-11-12: tempoxyz/pyramid (backend/ and hands/) derives schemars 1 for its own tools and calls none of these; tempoxyz/pyramid-core derives schemars 1 and calls `FunctionTool::typed_with_parameters` with its own schema (crates/kernel/src/tools/mod.rs) because `typed` takes 0.8; gakonst's repositories use none. So no host breaks either way, but a move buys no package (1.x brings ref-cast and ref-cast-impl beside the same dyn-clone, schemars_derive and serde_derive_internals) and changes model-facing bytes, and writing the two in-tree schemas as pinned JSON would not drop schemars, which the public APIs keep. Revisit when a host wants 1.x for `typed`, with the rewrite pass and a byte diff of every tool schema.
- nanocode-tui keeps syntect's Oniguruma regexes (`regex-onig`) rather than `regex-fancy` (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md's syntect row, now kept on purpose). `regex-fancy` highlights the same: output/hl (one binary per build, nanocode-tui at 3c16e6c8e with each feature, `highlight::line` over every line of a file with a fresh `HighlightLines`, 5 rounds a run, before and after interleaved over 3 runs) wrote identical styled spans for Rust (crates/backends/claude/src/agent.rs, 9,096 lines), C (secp256k1's tests.c, 7,841), Go (cua's fleet_sdk.go, 7,098), JavaScript (cua_driver.mjs, 3,447), Python (argparse.py, 2,677), YAML (1,087), CSS (one 100 KB line), HTML, JSON (840 KB) and two files the default syntaxes take as plain text (TOML, TypeScript). It is slower, median ms per file on gak-9 (macOS arm64, quiet), Oniguruma to fancy-regex: Rust 202 to 658 (3.3x), C 216 to 859 (4.0x), JavaScript 210 to 615 (2.9x), Python 82 to 224 (2.7x), Go 84 to 213 (2.5x), YAML 15.5 to 148 (9.6x), CSS 71 to 342 (4.8x); the loaded hosted Hand gives the same ratios (Rust 3.7x, C 2.8x, YAML 12x, CSS 5x, JSON 1.05x). The interface highlights as replies and diffs are drawn, each line once (markdown keeps and resumes its highlight state), so fancy-regex costs every session on every code line (a line of Rust 72 µs instead of 22 µs on gak-9, a 500-line diff 36 ms instead of 11 ms) to save onig_sys's C build once per clean build: 40.8 s of unit time in this measurement's loaded `cargo build --release -p nanocode-cli --timings` (onig_sys's build script 38.0 s, onig 1.7 s; 11.5 s on a quiet Hand per DEPENDENCIES.md). Switching would have taken onig and onig_sys out of `cargo metadata` and brought fancy-regex 0.16.2.
- nanocode-process opens a terminal session's pseudo-terminal itself, with rustix, instead of through portable-pty (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md's portable-pty row). `spawn_pty` opens the controller with `openpt`, `grantpt` and `unlockpt` and the terminal by `ptsname`, as the shell server's `own_terminal` already did, gives it the 24 rows and 80 columns portable-pty was asked for (the VT100's size) with `tcsetwinsize`, and starts the shell with std's `Command` on the terminal as stdin, stdout and stderr. Its `pre_exec` does what portable-pty's `spawn_command` did between fork and exec: SIGCHLD, SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGQUIT, SIGTERM and SIGALRM back to their defaults (a disposition the host ignores would otherwise survive exec; std already empties the signal mask and resets SIGPIPE), `setsid`, and `TIOCSCTTY` on stdin so the terminal is the session's controlling one and Ctrl-C written to it interrupts the foreground group. When the session's input closes, a newline and the terminal's VEOF are written, as portable-pty's writer did when it was dropped; that write's result is dropped as it was there, since the session is ending. The exit status is the shell's code, or 1 when a signal ended it, as portable-pty mapped it. Departure from the workspace's `unsafe_code = "forbid"`: `pre_exec` and nix's `signal` are unsafe, so nanocode-process sets its own lints with `unsafe_code = "deny"` and only `lead_session` allows it, as nanocode-computer does for its AX module; it is the code portable-pty ran, now in this crate, bounded to async-signal-safe calls (sigaction, setsid, ioctl). Differences: a workdir that does not exist is now an error (`No such file or directory`), as it already was for a command without a terminal, where portable-pty silently started the shell in $HOME; portable-pty set SHELL from the password database when the environment had none, and closed every descriptor above 2 listed in /dev/fd before exec, where std's descriptors are close-on-exec (the harness lists 0-3 on Linux and 0-4 on macOS before and after); on Windows a terminal session is refused with `Unsupported`, where portable-pty used ConPTY (nanocode is not released for Windows; not checked there, as no Windows target is installed on either machine). Leave Cargo.lock and `cargo metadata` (975 to 966 packages at b1c970d0b): portable-pty, nix 0.28.0, filedescriptor, serial2, shared_library, shell-words, winreg 0.10, downcast-rs and cfg_aliases 0.1, so `cargo tree --duplicates` no longer lists nix. Build (`cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-cli --timings`, CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=2, without the build cache wrappers, at 3c16e6c8e on the hosted Hand under other agents' load: 35m38s, 4,202 s of summed unit time): the units that leave sum 9.7 s (portable-pty 4.08, nix 0.28 2.98 with its build script, serial2 0.96, shell-words 0.84, filedescriptor 0.41, downcast-rs 0.27, cfg_aliases 0.17). `cargo bloat --release -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode --crates -n 0`, before and after: portable_pty 47.6 KiB, filedescriptor 3.4 KiB, serial2 513 B and downcast_rs 220 B of text leave, nix 5.2 to 5.0 KiB, nanocode_process 513.2 to 509.1 KiB, `.text` 67.0 to 66.9 MiB. Checked with output/pty-check (one binary per build, before and after, driving `ShellSessions` with tty and /bin/bash) on Linux (the hosted Hand) and macOS (gak-9, arm64): the same output and status for output with a tab, `exit 7`, a shell ended by SIGTERM (status 1), `stty size` (24 80), `stty rows 40 cols 120` with a WINCH trap, isatty of 0, 1 and 2 and a write to /dev/tty, the shell leading its process group in the foreground (`ps` stat `s+`), Ctrl-C ending `sleep 30; echo after` (`^C`, status 1) and running an INT trap (status 3), a line read from stdin, Ctrl-D ending cat, Ctrl-C read as byte 003 in raw mode, the descriptors the shell holds, its environment, `terminate_all` killing background sleeps in the group (3 processes to 0) and a background job gone once the shell exits; only the missing workdir differs. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-process`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-process` (no warnings) on Linux and on macOS.
