Interleaved `~/w/cmp.py` (3 rounds, perf stat): trycatch (66,667 `new Error` throws) 1,194.6 → 1,136.9 M instructions (−4.8%), 72.8 → 66.4 ms; fib unchanged. test262 active group unchanged (39,325/39,365, ratchet OK).
- `StagedWrites::commit_to` checks a state's owner and revision before it acquires it, and an error after one of its states committed says so (2026-11-12). It acquired each staged state, taking the next fence, and only then compared that fence with the staged base, so a staged writer whose base was already stale fenced out the live owner before answering Fenced, and a stale revision did the same before Conflict. It now reads `owner` and `peek` first and answers Fenced or Conflict without acquiring when the fence or the revision moved since staging (`unmoved`); the acquisition and its checks stay, so an owner that acquires between those reads and the acquisition is still fenced, a narrower race that only a conditional acquisition could close, which StateStore does not offer. commit_to commits state by state, so on a store without a transaction an earlier state stays committed when a later one fails, and that failure came back as the later state's Fenced or Conflict, which say nothing was written. An error after any state, or any of a state's payloads, committed is now `Backend("staged writes committed state <ids> and then failed: <error>")`, an uncertain outcome that names what landed; an error before anything committed keeps its kind. Refusing stores without transactions would need a capability StateStore lacks, and the one in-repo caller, store-sql's `commit_staged`, runs commit_to on the caller's Postgres connection inside its transaction (`SqlxTransaction`), where a rollback undoes the earlier states and the caller sees an Err either way. Cost: an owner and a peek read per staged state before its acquisition (two more statements in store-sql's transaction). Checked with bin/nanocode-sim, which now judges every head swap of a failed commit_to: an acquisition that took a fence from a head other than its staged base is Wrong unless that head was written after commit_to began (counted as `staged_fence_races`: 403 over seeds 0..300), and a Fenced, Conflict or NotCommitted after an attempt's head landed is Wrong, while an uncertain error without an injected fault is counted as `partial_commit_to` (399). The simulator cannot change the code under test, so the canaries for these checks are hand reverts of staged.rs built beside it: acquiring before the reads, as before, fails 133 of 200 seeds (`took fence 7 of s0 from the head at fence 6 revision 1, written before it began, although it staged on fence 4 revision 0`, seed 2), and the old error kinds fail 97 of 200 (seed 3: `reported durability state owner was fenced … after one of its states committed`). Sweeps on 2026-11-12, 4 jobs on the shared 5-core Hand: seeds 0..100,000 at 1,000 ops pass (254 s), 100,000..110,000 at 10,000 ops pass (336 s), 0..10,000 with `--twice` pass with identical digests (53 s) and 0..10,000 with `--records slots` pass; the canaries over seeds 0..200 are caught by 134 (`cas_ignores_expected`), 129 (`record_insert_drops`), 106 (`power_loss_drops_acked`) and, with `--records slots`, 131 (`record_insert_overwrites`). `cargo check` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability-core`, native and wasm32, and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-store-sql`, clean.
- 2026-11-12: the djs parser takes `undefined` and `arguments` from the well-known atoms (`atoms::UNDEFINED`, `atoms::ARGUMENTS`) instead of hashing and looking them up on every `Parser::new`, i.e. every compiled cell. Measured with output/durability-ledger's jsbench (`perf stat -e instructions:u jsbench djs 1 N trivial`, N = 3,000 and 33,000, interleaved, two rounds): a trivial cell ~71.9k → ~70.1k instructions (−2%). test262 active group unchanged (39,325/39,365, ratchet OK).
- A durability record is immutable once stored, and `KeyValueStore` enforces it key by key, so a fenced-out writer can no longer change a committed state's records (2026-11-12). `replace` wrote a commit's records with `put_values` before its fenced head swap, so a stale owner's commit overwrote the records of the revision the live owner had committed and only then answered Fenced, and so did a commit whose head swap was refused as Conflict or failed after a torn or acknowledged write. Every other store already treats a record as written once: SqlStore inserts with `ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING` (one row per key across the database, held per state), RowStore's index leaves out the keys a state holds (`Index::fresh`), MemoryStore and JsonlStore refuse a different value for a held key with NotCommitted `durability record … has conflicting content`, StagedStore refuses a staged record with different content, and CachedStore never replaces a cached key; the StateStore contract above says a commit "inserts absent records". Every writer agrees: EncodedPayload's keys are content addresses, the root pool and catalog transfers copy records verbatim, and agent-host's cell journal (format 2) writes its links as EncodedPayloads, its `{cell}/{seq}` keys being only read, from format-1 journals. Its one other write is the empty value that asks a store to drop a record no head names any more (`blanked`, in the commit that drops the cell from the head), which no reader depends on: SqlStore and RowStore keep the row (both insert with `ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING`, so the 2026-11-10 entry's "SqlStore and RowStore delete such a record" does not hold; RowStore's compaction and SqlStore's `collect` reclaim it once unreachable), JsonlStore leaves it out and MemoryStore removes it, so the stores that ignore it break nothing and there is no second bug there. KeyValueStore was the one store that wrote it as a value, so a fenced-out writer's forget could blank a record the live head still names. Now each record with a value is inserted with `compare_and_swap(key, None, "record", value)`, all of a commit's together (`try_join_all`) and before the head swap as before; when the key exists its value is read: the same value passes (a retried commit, or the same content-addressed record), an empty value an older build wrote is filled by one more swap against its version, and any other value fails the commit with NotCommitted `durability record `<key>` has conflicting content` before its head swap. A record with an empty value is left out, since `KeyValue` cannot delete. The swap against absence is atomic per key, where reading first and writing after lets two writers both find a key absent. The layout is unchanged and records older builds wrote read as before (`get_values` reads values whatever their version); `put_values` stays in the `KeyValue` trait and KeyValueStore no longer calls it. Cost: one swap per record instead of one `put_values` per commit, issued together, and a read for a record already stored. Checked with bin/nanocode-sim on 2026-11-12, 4 jobs on the shared 5-core Hand: `--records slots`, whose check (every record a committed revision names holds the value of the attempt that wrote that revision) failed 133 of 200 seeds before, passes seeds 0..10,000, its refusals typed (21,585 NotCommitted conflicts over seeds 0..200), never Wrong; `--mutation record_insert_overwrites --records slots` (an insert against absence that overwrites a stored record, the old behavior) is caught by 131 of 200 seeds. Seeds 0..100,000 at 1,000 ops pass (258 s), 100,000..110,000 at 10,000 ops pass (300 s), 0..10,000 `--twice` pass with identical digests. The canary `put_drops_last` reached only `put_values`, so it became `record_insert_drops` (an insert reported as swapped that never lands), caught by 128 of 200 seeds; `cas_ignores_expected` 135, `power_loss_drops_acked` 106. `cargo check` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability-core`, native and wasm32, clean.
- 2026-11-12: djs gets a megamorphic inline cache: 256 cache slots per heap (`Heap::mega_ic`, outside the image), indexed by the key's hash, the receiver's shape word (its offset in dictionary mode) and its prototype. A get site whose filled slot misses for another receiver also writes the new slot there, and the get slow path (`lookup_ic`) checks it before the full lookup. Hits go through the same checks as a site's own slot (`get_hit`, shared by both), so a stale or colliding entry is only a miss; every collection and `compact_for_image` empties it because its slots hold arena offsets, and it is allocated on the first polymorphic fill, so monomorphic programs never pay for it. Interleaved `~/w/cmp.py` (3 rounds, perf stat, frame-pointer release builds): dispatch (method calls on three classes) 2,496 → 1,783 M instructions (98.5 → 66.9 ms), a new four-shape own-property kernel 1,748 → 1,272 M (63.0 → 44.8 ms), the other 11 kernels within ±0.2% instructions. test262 active group unchanged (39,325/39,365, ratchet OK); a cache-invalidation script (prototype method replace/delete, shadowing, setPrototypeOf, primitive prototypes, 20,000 shapes) prints the same as QuickJS.
- Member descriptors trace their class, so a dropped interpreter's modules are freed (2026-11-12). PyMemberDescriptor held its owning type without a traverse, so the cycle collector never saw that edge and every class with __slots__ kept its module graph alive after the interpreter dropped; each new interpreter in the same process inherited the garbage, so GC and drop cost grew per session. Measured interleaved base/r1/after: tracked objects after 40 sessions of import gc, json, collections 70,511 (growing ~1,654 per session) to a constant 5,322; 100 sessions of import json, re, argparse, collections: drop median 96.5 ms to 5.3 ms, wall per session 128 ms to 31 ms, max RSS 298,276 KB to 35,884 KB; single import json session new 4.41 to 3.53 ms, drop 11.9 to 4.1 ms; wasm stdlib cold 157/160 ms to 122/123 ms, memory at end 76.1/78.3 MB to 31.4 MB. drive.py 56/57 stdlib unchanged, limits.py and edge.sh outputs unchanged. Still leaking: typing generics (~2,111 objects per session) and type aliases (8 per session). The engine gets crate-private, macOS-only `running`, `open`, `observe`, `perform`, `element` and `refocus`, because cua-driver's callers act and read separately; keys and typing take the app's current focus first, since the provider does not read between a click and typing. Permissions are `AXIsProcessTrusted`/`AXIsProcessTrustedWithOptions` with its prompt and `CGPreflightScreenCaptureAccess`/`CGRequestScreenCaptureAccess`. Not ported, so lost on macOS: cua-driver's SkyLight path (`SLEventPostToPid`, focus without raise, Chromium's off-screen primer), so coordinate clicks into Chromium, Electron and Catalyst windows are untested and may not land; every window of an app but the one the engine reads (`get_window_state` ignores `window_id`); the tools outside the 15 that `cua.driver.call` reached; PNG screenshots and `max_image_dimension`; screenshots of hidden or minimized windows; regorus policy files; modifier-key clicks (refused). - nanocode-tempo holds Tempo's primitives without a dependency, and nanocode-cli reads the Tempo wallet's store itself (2026-11-12, Georgios: "a from-scratch implementation of mpp/tempo-alloy, without any deps", toward DEPENDENCIES.md rank 1). crates/core/tempo has keccak-256, SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA256, base64url, hex, a 256-bit integer, secp256k1 and P-256 over one Montgomery field type with RCB16 complete addition (Algorithm 1, general a), ECDSA signing with RFC 6979 nonces exactly as RustCrypto derives them (the prehash as bits2field, unreduced, as the DRBG nonce input; s normalized low, parity flipped with it), secp256k1 recovery that refuses high s as alloy's recover_signer does, P-256 verification, EIP-55 addresses, RLP encoding and a canonical decoder, ABI encoding, and Tempo's types: the 0x76 transaction with its signing payload, fee-payer hash (0x78), fee-payer service encoding and signed envelope, primitive, P-256, WebAuthn and keychain V2 signatures, and key authorizations with tempo-primitives' trailing(canonical) optional fields. Secret-dependent work does not branch or index on secrets: field arithmetic masks its reductions, scalar multiplication walks fixed 4-bit windows with a masked scan of the whole table and complete formulas (no special cases for doubling or the identity), and hex and base64url decode secrets arithmetically; RFC 6979 retries only for a candidate at or above n. Invalid input is a typed nanocode_tempo::Error (bad hex, base64url, lengths, keys, signatures, recovery ids, RLP, ABI). It builds natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown with no dependency. The CLI's one tempo-alloy call, TempoAccountsWallet::from_default_store()?.active_account() for the account whose gas-token balances it reads, is bin/nanocode/src/tempo/accounts.rs: $TEMPO_HOME/wallet/store.json or ~/.tempo/wallet/store.json, the tempo-cli.store root, the state envelope or a bare state, the active account by index or address, with tempo-alloy's error texts; nanocode-cli and the workspace no longer name tempo-alloy, which mpp still brings until its replacement lands. output/tempo-equal links nanocode-tempo beside alloy-primitives 1.7.3, k256 0.13.4, p256 0.13.2, tempo-primitives 1.11.0 and alloy-signer-local 2.5.0 and compares them over seeded random inputs: `cargo run --release --bin primitives 3000` reports 98,085 equal checks (keccak, SHA-256, base64url both ways and on malformed inputs, secp256k1 key validity, addresses, checksums, signatures, recovery of good and tampered signatures, P-256 public keys, signatures and verification, signed key authorization encodings, hashes and decoding, transaction signing payloads and hashes, fee-payer hashes and service encodings, keychain V2 hashes, signed envelopes and their hashes, U256 display, parsing and quantities). Checks: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-tempo` native and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-tempo` clean, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata` resolves 1,176 packages, one more than before (nanocode-tempo).
- `bin/nanocode-sim` is the deterministic simulator of the durability stores and the one home of checks (2026-11-12; Georgios approved it as the exception to "no tests", and AGENTS.md says so in one line). It drives `KeyValueStore`, `CachedStore` and `StagedStore` over `SimKv`, a `KeyValue` with a pending and a durable image, from 1 to 4 simulated processes on 1 to 6 states, crashes and power losses at random virtual times, and judges every answer against a model: no revision read goes below one acknowledged or observed, a fenced-out owner never commits, no fence is granted twice, an acknowledged head was written, a definite error (Fenced, Conflict) never follows a landed head write, an error without an injected fault is Wrong, the records a committed revision names read back, and a store reopened after a crash holds no revision past the last attempted. Faults are drawn per seed as tempoxyz/zempo's store fuzzer draws a disk's (`src/sim/store_fuzz.zig` `faults_of`): four seeds in ten clean, two with injected errors (before and after apply, a torn `put_values`, failed reads), two with asynchronous durability (writes reach the durable image at a sync; a power loss keeps the synced writes and an in-order prefix of the rest), two with a lying cache (at a power loss each of the last 32 durable writes, zempo's `cache_sectors`, reverts with 5 to 50%, zempo's `cache_lost_ppm`); latency always, its floor drawn from 20 to 120 µs (zempo's read latency) and its spread up to 2 ms (zempo's sync spread). The error rates (1,000 to 50,000 ppm per write, up to 20,000 per read), the sync rate (1 to 30% of writes), think time (up to 200 µs) and crash times (0.5 to 200 ms) are this simulator's policy, set so a 1,000-op seed meets faults and crashes: over seeds 0..2,000, 14 injected faults and 9.4 crashes a seed. Every knob is a named constant in `faults.rs`, `store.rs`, `workload.rs` and `simulate.rs`. It runs on its own single-threaded executor with a virtual clock, not tokio's `test-util`: Cargo unifies features across a workspace build, so `test-util` would reach every crate in `cargo build --workspace`, and the simulator needs no tokio at all. The executor owns non-Send tasks, each with an atomic wake flag; when several are ready the seed picks the one that runs (a scheduler fault, as zempo's VOPR has), when none is the clock jumps to the next timer, and an epoch ends at its crash time by dropping every task where it waits. The clock and the store are Send and Sync over nanocode-sync's `Slot` (taken and put back around each step, asserting it is never taken twice; no Mutex) so the platform's installable native Host (time, sleep, randomness, spawn) can route the runtime's own sleeps and spawns here: `Clock::now_ns` and `Clock::sleep` are that Host's time and sleep, the per-label splitmix64 `Rng` its randomness, and a spawned future would join the executor's task list. It is a workspace member with `publish = false` and `autotests = false`, outside `default-members`, and adds no external crate (nanocode-durability-core, nanocode-durability, nanocode-sync). Usage: `cargo build --release -p nanocode-sim`, then `nanocode-sim --seed S | --seeds A..B [--ops N] [--twice] [--mutation M] [--records content|slots] [--verbose]`, or `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh A B JOBS [args]` across processes (`NANOCODE_SIM` names the binary); a failure prints its replay command, `--twice` runs each seed again and compares trace digests, and a mutation passes when some seed catches it. Measured on 2026-11-12 at c0f750d2d on the 5-core hosted Hand while other builds ran (load 8 to 12), 4 jobs: seeds 0..100,000 at 1,000 ops all pass (333 s), 100,000..110,000 at 10,000 ops all pass (518 s), 0..10,000 with `--twice` all pass with identical digests (64 s); the canaries over seeds 0..200: `cas_ignores_expected` caught by 135, `put_drops_last` by 130, `power_loss_drops_acked` by 103. `--records slots` (records under fixed keys, as agent-host's earlier cell journal keys `{cell}/{seq}`) checks that every record a committed revision names holds the value of the attempt that wrote that revision, and fails 133 of 200 seeds: `KeyValueStore` writes a commit's records before its fenced head swap, so a fenced-out or failed writer overwrites a committed revision's record (`nanocode-sim --seed 149 --ops 10 --records slots`: slot0 of s0 revision 1 holds the value of attempt 2, whose commit was refused as Fenced). The next entry fixes it; `--mutation record_insert_overwrites` (an insert of an absent record that overwrites one already there) is that check's canary. A seed replays exactly only while the code under it reads no real time, randomness or scheduling: `OwnerId::new` (uuid_v7), `SystemTime::now` and `Instant::now` in the runtime crates, unbiased `select!` (session.rs, child_journal.rs), random hashers (nanocode-sync's `Map`, staged.rs and payload.rs `HashSet`s), SharedStore's driver on its own thread and store-jsonl's workers are the sources found; the stores simulated here avoid them (owners are named per process and epoch).
- nanocode-store-sql keeps both Postgres drivers until tempoxyz/pyramid-core moves its pipelined writes (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md rank 5). Who uses which: tempoxyz/pyramid main (50c2ec3d0; backend/crates/engine and backend/crates/store) imports only the sqlx side (`SqlxSql`, `PgConnections`, `stage_records`, `commit_staged`, `unreachable`, `collect`), and output/durability-ledger's pg and pgrows stores run `SqlxSql` over two `PgPool`s; tempoxyz/pyramid-core (9d1dc9b of 2026-11-11, on nanocode ac7b98c22) runs its locked writes on `PostgresSql::dialing` lanes (`locked`, `once`, `probe`, `available`, `PipelineError`, `Unavailable`, `collected_wakes`; crates/kernel/src/db/handle.rs), and its kernel takes tokio-postgres directly for `ToSql`, `Row` and `types` (broker/ledger.rs, threads/tools.rs, threads/messages.rs). Why both exist: `PostgresSql` sends BEGIN, the setup and advisory locks, the fenced statements, the wakes read and COMMIT on prepared statements before it reads a reply, one round trip; sqlx waits for each statement, three round trips for the same transaction (pyramid-core NOTES.md, "Locked writes in one round trip", whose budget allows two Postgres round trips on a Hand call's critical path, the admit being one of them). sqlx 0.9, and the gakonst/sqlx fork at 7667896 that both hosts patch in, pipelines only through `raw_sql`'s simple protocol, with parameters inlined as text. `PostgresSql::once` and `locked` take `&dyn tokio_postgres::types::ToSql` and return `tokio_postgres::Row`, so the type cannot move onto sqlx without new signatures and new call sites in pyramid-core, and deleting it breaks pyramid-core's next nanocode bump, against the rule to preserve public APIs. Converging takes one of two moves, each with pyramid-core's owner: `PostgresSql` over sqlx's simple protocol, sending `EXECUTE` of statements prepared once per connection with literal parameters (one round trip, generic plans kept), once pyramid-core passes literals instead of `ToSql` values; or pyramid-core keeping its pipelined lanes in its own tree, after which nanocode drops tokio-postgres, tokio-postgres-rustls, webpki-roots, percent-encoding and postgres.rs's rustls verifier (11 packages; sqlx alone is 9). Hosts that use only sqlx, Pyramid's backend among them, build the 11 meanwhile. No code changes here, so the ledger's pg and pgrows runs were not repeated. Checked: `grep` over tempoxyz/pyramid main and tempoxyz/pyramid-core main for `nanocode_store_sql`, `PostgresSql` and `tokio_postgres`, and the ledger's src/postgres.rs on gak-9.
- nanocode-zstd encodes, and the Codex client, store-jsonl and store-sql compress with it instead of the C zstd crate (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md rank 3). The three call sites: Codex request bodies under ChatGPT auth at level 3 (`zstd::stream::encode_all`: no content size, no checksum, no dictionary), on the latency path; JSONL session archives and the summaries cache at level 1 against the 41.6 KB raw-content `session.dict` (`bulk::Compressor::with_dictionary`: content size, no checksum), on the disk path at shutdown; and RowStore pages through `store_sql::Zstd::level(n)` (`bulk::compress`; tempoxyz/pyramid-core passes 3). None uses long-distance matching, a trained dictionary, a checksum or more than one frame. `nanocode_zstd::compress(content, level)` and `compress_with_dictionary(content, dictionary, level)` write one frame with its content size (a single segment when the content fits the window), no checksum and no dictionary ID (a raw-content dictionary has none), in blocks of at most 128 KiB: libzstd 1.5's parameters for levels 1 to 3 (0 is its default, 3) by source-size class from clevels.h, narrowed to the input; its fast and double-fast matchers with repeat offsets; Huffman literals (one or four streams, codes of at most 11 bits, weights written directly or FSE-compressed); FSE sequences that take the predefined table, RLE, a new table or the previous block's by their cost in bits; and a raw or RLE block wherever compressing does not pay, after which the repeat offsets and tables go back to what the decoder holds. The constants come from the format (block size, table logs, code tables) or libzstd (the level table, its 8-byte hash multiplier, kSearchStrength 8, the 64-byte literal minimum, the incompressible-literal and minimum-gain rules, FSE's rounding thresholds). Other levels are a typed error (`Error::InvalidParameter`), so `Zstd::level(n)` outside 0 to 3 now fails to pack a page where libzstd compressed it; pyramid-core, the only caller, passes 3. `StreamingDecoder::with_dictionary(options, dictionary)` decodes against a raw-content dictionary, which the decoder already followed internally; archives libzstd wrote before this change read back through it. Measured on 2026-11-12 with output/zstd-bench (`zstd-bench <mode> session.dict <out> 5 <files>`: per file, the median of 5 interleaved rounds of repeated calls, against zstd 0.14.3 with zstd-sys 2.1.2, libzstd 1.5.7, called as each site called it) on gak-9 (Apple M1 Max, load 5 to 11) over real inputs, ours against libzstd. Codex: 30 request bodies made of replay-cache's Responses request with the items of 30 real Codex rollouts appended (31 KB to 3.2 MB, 27.4 MB in all): 10.345 MB against 10.314 MB (+0.30%), 80.2 ms against 59.2 ms in all (1.35x); median per body 189 against 125 us at 36 KB, 1.00 against 0.69 ms at 301 KB, 3.10 against 2.27 ms at 1 MB, 8.98 against 6.84 ms at 3 MB. Archives: 120 real session files (0.7 KB to 6.7 MB, 202.6 MB): 48.74 MB against 49.90 MB (-2.3%), 357 against 209 ms (1.71x); median 35 against 33 us at 1 KB, 274 against 207 us at 74 KB, 2.9 against 1.8 ms at 1.3 MB, 9.1 against 5.3 ms at 6.3 MB. Pages: 52 runs of session lines of 4 to 128 KB (3.4 MB): +0.19%, 10.9 against 7.0 ms (1.55x; 229 against 148 us at 62 KB). Decoding is nanocode-zstd's existing decoder at 3.3 times libzstd's time (the archives: 324 against 97 ms), which only restoring an archive adds. The tradeoff: a request body takes 0.06 to 2.1 ms longer to compress before it is sent, beside a model's first token in hundreds of milliseconds, and is 0.3% larger; archiving and paging are off the latency path. What would close the gap: the matchers are about 60% of the encoder's cycles (perf on the Linux Hand; 1.13 to 1.32 G cycles against libzstd's 0.72 to 0.87 G at level 3 over six files), and libzstd hashes two positions per step and prefetches in both; Huffman tables are built and written every block where libzstd repeats the previous one. Checked: every output decodes with the reference CLI (`zstd -t`, with `-D session.dict` for archives; 1.5.7 on gak-9 over the 202 real outputs, 1.5.5 on the Linux Hand over a synthetic corpus of text, JSON, random, zeros, empty and one-byte inputs up to 8.5 MB), with libzstd and with nanocode-zstd, and libzstd's archives decode with nanocode-zstd; output/zstd-bench's `fuzz` round-trips 2,500 generated inputs (0 to 3 MB of random bytes, text, back-references, runs and dictionary pieces, levels 1 to 3, with and without the dictionary) through libzstd and nanocode-zstd, and 350 of them through the CLI. The output is deterministic: no hasher or clock reaches it. Dependencies: zstd 0.14.3 and zstd-safe 8.2.0 leave the graph (`cargo metadata` 1,175 to 1,173 packages); zstd-sys stays only under cua's cursor-overlay (zstd 0.13.3, rank 2), so a host without cua, such as Pyramid's backend, builds no zstd C. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `cargo clippy --locked --lib` on nanocode-zstd, nanocode-store-sql, nanocode-store-jsonl and nanocode-backend-codex-client. Files: crates/core/zstd/src/encode/ (new), streaming.rs (`with_dictionary`), sequence.rs (tables shared with the encoder), store-sql zstd.rs, store-jsonl archive.rs, codex transport/http.rs.
- ToInt32 of a Number outside int32 truncates through i64 instead of floor and fmod (2026-11-12). `conv::to_int32` (every bitwise operator and `|0` on a double, typed array stores) took a non-int32 value through `floor` and djs-libm's software `fmod` by 2^32; for a finite value strictly inside (-2^63, 2^63), `n as i64 as i32` is the same truncation modulo 2^32. Larger magnitudes, infinities and NaN take the old path. Seven operators (`|0`, `>>>0`, `>>1`, `<<1`, `~`, `&0xffff`, `^1`) over 30 values (±0, fractions, the int32 and uint32 edges, 2^53 + 1, ±2^62, ±2^63, 2^64, ±1e20, 1e300, infinities, NaN, 5e-324) and a `(h * 31 + i) | 0` loop print the same as Node. output/djs-bench, interleaved, three rounds: chars (`h = (h * 31 + s.charCodeAt(i)) | 0`) 82.2 to 69.0 ms (2,015.1 to 1,901.6 M instructions per run); fib, loop and dispatch unchanged in instructions. test262 active group 39,325 of 39,365, no new failures. Commands: the wasm32 check and clippy of djs-core and djs-embed. Files: crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/interp/conv.rs.
- Making an Error reads `Error.stackTraceLimit` and `Error.prepareStackTrace` through well-known atoms (2026-11-12). Every Error the engine or a script creates looked both names up with `Heap::atom_str`, which hashes the text and searches the atom tables: 11% of a loop that throws and catches an Error every third iteration. They are now `atoms::STACK_TRACE_LIMIT` and `atoms::PREPARE_STACK_TRACE`. The well-known list is part of `LAYOUT_HASH`, so images and parked or snapshot bytes of builds before this one are refused, as for any layout change. `image::ENGINE_ATOMS` still interns both names when an image is made; they now resolve to the well-known atoms. Output of a script that reads stack lengths with the limit at 10, 1 and 0 and with a `prepareStackTrace` hook set and deleted is the same as before. output/djs-bench, interleaved, three rounds: trycatch 78.4 to 71.1 ms (1,390.4 to 1,194.7 M instructions per run); fib and dispatch unchanged in instructions. test262 active group 39,325 of 39,365, no new failures. - `%` on Numbers that are integers but not int32 computes an integer remainder instead of calling fmod (2026-11-12). The interpreter's general path for `Op::Mod` did `x % y` on f64, which in djs-core (no_std) is compiler_builtins' software fmod, a bit-by-bit loop: 27% of a loop like `s = (s + i * i) % 1000003`, where `i * i` leaves int32. `conv::rem` now takes the remainder of the two as i64 when both are integers with the dividend within Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (exact, with JavaScript's sign of the dividend and -0 for a zero remainder of a negative or -0 dividend), and calls djs-libm's fmod otherwise. Putting the same float path into run_hot's `fast::MOD` as well took the loop to 0.52x but added 1.5 to 4.5% instructions to unrelated kernels (fib, objects, dispatch), so the hot loop still declines to the general path for non-int32 operands. Output of 27 x 27 operand pairs (zeros, ±2^53 and beyond, ±2^63, ±1e300, infinities, NaN, fractions, 5e-324) is byte-equal to Node's. A kernel suite added for this work (output/djs-bench: fib, loop, objects, arrays, strings, json, maps, sort, dispatch, chars, closures, trycatch, each run in a reused djs-embed instance, least of 7) interleaved before and after, three rounds: loop 158.2 to 117.1 ms (3,677 to 3,179 M instructions), the others unchanged in instructions (fib 504.2, objects 4,819.5, dispatch 2,496.3, closures 4,302.8). Against QuickJS 2021-03-27 (`qjs`, its startup subtracted) the suite stood at fib 1.41x, loop 1.40x (now 1.04x), objects 1.04x, arrays 1.09x, strings 0.66x, json 0.47x, maps 0.42x, sort 2.23x, dispatch 1.89x, chars 1.57x, closures 0.95x, trycatch 2.29x of QuickJS's time. test262 (upstream djs's runner at 7ab7faf over the vendored crates, active group, lazy): 39,325 of 39,365, no new failures. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p djs-embed --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p djs-core -p djs-embed -- -D warnings`. - `_ast` is imported when something first needs it, not by every interpreter at start-up (2026-11-12). RustPython's `initialize` imported `_ast` (the node types and their fields), which only `compile()` with `PyCF_ONLY_AST` or `PyCF_TYPE_COMMENTS` uses; `compile_string_object_with_flags` now imports it first on those paths, and an AST object handed to `compile()` comes from a module that imported it. `compile("x", "f", "eval", 0x400).body.id` and `ast.parse` answer as before, and `_ast` is no longer in `sys.modules` after start-up. Measured (5-core Linux Hand, interleaved): `Python::new` in output/python-bench's `phases` (CPU of the thread, medians of 25 in one process) 3.98, 4.52, 4.68 ms to 3.73, 3.98, 3.95 ms; a `py -c 'print(1)'` process (`perf stat -r 30 -e task-clock`) 18.96, 20.03 ms to 17.73, 16.19 ms; the wasm module in Node (output/python-wasm `run.mjs`, a new interpreter, `print(1)` and its drop) 39.7, 39.8 ms to 32.6, 34.6 ms. drive.py 56 of 57 as before. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python` natively and for wasm32 pass.
- `str.split`, `bytes.split`, `bytearray.split`, their `rsplit`s and the JSON scanner take a step for each piece they make, so a memory limit ends them (2026-11-12). One call made all its objects before the ceiling was looked at: under `PYBENCH_MEMORY_MB=256` the process reached 512 MB resident for `("a " * 5 * 10**7).split()`, 5.98 GB for `(b"a " * 5 * 10**7).split(b" ")`, 1.51 GB for `json.loads("[" + "1.5," * 2 * 10**7 + "1.5]")` and 415 MB for `("a,b," * 2 * 10**7).rsplit(",")` before the refusal. `VirtualMachine::step` spends a unit of fuel and asks the limiter when none is left, as the dispatch loop and `PyIter::next` do; `anystr::piece` takes one after making each piece (the split closures and `py_split_whitespace`/`py_rsplit_whitespace` now return `PyResult`), and `with_recursion`, which the JSON scanner enters for every value, takes one first. Crossing the ceiling zeroes the fuel, so the next piece asks the limiter, which refuses `Memory`. Now 253 MB, 362 MB, 295 MB and 233 MB (max RSS of the whole process with its 80 to 100 MB source, `/usr/bin/time -f %M`), each refused with status 126 and the next run printing 42. These pieces are steps too, so a step or time limit or a cancel also ends a long split or decode. workloads/limits.py ends every case as before; workloads/drive.py passes the same 56 of 57 standard-library workloads with CPython 3.14.7's output. Commands: `/usr/bin/time -f %M env PYBENCH_WARM=1 PYBENCH_MEMORY_MB=256 PYBENCH_THEN='print(6*7)' target/release/py -c '...'`, `python3 workloads/limits.py target/release/py`, `python3 workloads/drive.py NAME target/release/py`. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python` natively and for wasm32 pass.
- The psh utility's python3 takes an idle interpreter thread or starts one, so a script that loops holds only its own (2026-11-12). Every psh shell of a process sent its python3 to one `python3` thread, so `while True: pass` in one shell that nobody cancels left every other shell's python3 waiting in `recv`, where its own cancel cannot reach it. `IDLE` is a `nanocode_sync::Slot` holding the sender of the interpreter thread that is free: a call takes it or spawns a thread, and puts it back when its run ends; when another is already back, the replaced one closes and its thread drops its interpreter. Calls one at a time keep reusing the same warm interpreter as before. nanocode-python gains nanocode-sync as a native dependency (the CLI already links it). Measured with output/python-bench's `pool` (two psh shells on engine threads, the first running `python3 -c 'while True: pass'`, the second started 300 ms later running `python3 -c 'print(6 * 7)'; python3 -c 'print(7 * 7)'`): before, the second shell never returned (`timeout 20 target/release/pool`, status 124); now it prints 42 and 49 and ends 325 ms after the start while the first still loops. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-python` and the wasm32 check pass.
- python3 in nanocode-shell runs on the shell's fuel (2026-11-12). `Command` gave Python the host's `Budget`, and a host that gives no step or time bound (the harnesses and the CLI give `u64::MAX` and `Duration::MAX`) let `while True: pass` hold the session's interpreter and its shell for good: the shell's fuel bounds its own loops and the child shells `Session::run` starts, but not Python. `Session::fuel` answers what the shell has left and `Session::spend` charges what a command used, refusing `Limit::Fuel` at zero as `Session::run` does for a child shell; `Command` caps Python's steps at the shell's fuel, `Ran::steps` reports the steps a run spent (instructions, iterator steps and regex moves), and the shell is charged them. A run the shell's fuel stops says `python3: it ran more steps than this shell allows` (126) and the shell ends `Refused(Fuel)`. Measured with output/python-bench's shellpy over MemFs (`PYBENCH_FUEL` sets the shell's fuel): `python3 -c "print(1)"; python3 -c "while True: pass"; echo after` with fuel 50,000,000 ran until `timeout 30` (status 124) before, answering at once and answering later alike, and now ends after 0.31 s with `Refused(Fuel)` at fuel 50,000,002; `python3 -c "print(sum(range(100000)))"` costs the shell 111,760 fuel where it cost 1; workloads/shell.sh prints the same before and after in both modes apart from fuel counts. Commands: `PYBENCH_FUEL=50000000 timeout 30 target/release/shellpy now|later '...'`, `sh workloads/shell.sh target/release/shellpy now|later`. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-python -p nanocode-shell` and the wasm32 check of both pass.
- psh's cut copies a byte or ASCII range as one slice and a field without splitting the line into a vector, and writes a line without a future (2026-11-12). `-b` and `-c` looked up the range of every byte (or decoded character) of the line (`cut_units` with `range_of`), and `-f` collected every field of every line into a Vec before choosing; each output line was an awaited `ctx.write`. The ranges are sorted and merged when parsed, so `cut_bytes` copies each one as a slice of the line, which is what the unit walk produced, also for `-c` on a line that is all ASCII (others keep the character walk); `-f` with a one-byte delimiter checks for the delimiter, walks the fields and stops after the last range; lines go through `UtilCtx::write_now`. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/cut.json (CPU median ms of 4 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU cut 9.4 in brackets): over 400,000 lines `cut -d' ' -f2` 51.3 to 28.1 (29.1), `cut -c1-10` 56.8 to 24.0 (26.3), `cut -b3-8,12-` 76.6 to 35.2 (40.8); over 100,000 lines `cut -d' ' -f1,3` 16.0 to 9.4 (11.9) and `-f2` to stdout 13.6 to 8.3 (7.8); `cut -d: -f1,6` over 20,000 lines 4.8 to 3.5 (6.5). 19 invocations (output/psh-perf/cutcases.json: -s, --complement, --output-delimiter, open and overlapping ranges, -z, UTF-8 and invalid bytes, no final newline, a missing file) give the same bytes before and after; GNU differs only where it cuts -c by bytes. Upstream delta: psh-utils cut.rs.
- psh's sort finds each line's keys once, not at every comparison (2026-11-12). A comparison found the start of each key field again (`key_slice`) and, for `-n`, read the number again (`numeric_parts`), about 1.7 million times each for 100,000 lines. When a key is more than the whole line as text (a field, a column, -b, or an ordering such as -n), sort now keeps every line's key slices, and for -n keys the sign, integer and fraction digits, in one vector beside the lines, and sorts the line numbers with the same stable `sort_by` and the same comparisons (`Sorter::keyed`, `cmp_keyed`, `cmp_parts`); a plain `sort` keeps its path. What is left behind GNU's -n is the last-resort comparison of whole lines among equal keys (`sort -s -n -k3` takes 57 ms against 132 ms with it). output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/sort.json over 100,000 lines (CPU median ms of 5 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (GNU sort 9.4 in brackets): `sort -n -k3` 165.8 to 129.5 (41.2), `sort -rn -k3` 161.1 to 126.5 (34.1), `sort -k2,2 -k3,3n` 153.9 to 95.4 (78.9), `sort -k2` 43.0 to 34.4 (41.4), `cut | sort -nu` 75.5 to 72.8 (33.6); plain `sort` 26.5 and 27.9, `sort -t: -k3,3n` over 20,000 lines 4.6 and 5.1, within run-to-run spread. 21 sort invocations (output/psh-perf/sortcases.json: -n -r -u -s -f -b -V -h -M -g -R -z -c -o, character positions, several keys) give the same bytes before and after, and the same as GNU sort. Upstream delta: psh-utils sort.rs.

Names already found in the listing are reused. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/ls.json (CPU and wall median ms of 6 interleaved rounds of 5 `psh -c` runs; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (bash 5.2 with GNU ls in brackets): `ls -la` of 50 files 3.97 to 1.75 CPU, 10.9 to 3.0 wall (4.3, 7.4); `ls -l` of 40 directories 3.90 to 2.00 CPU, 11.2 to 3.6 wall (5.4, 9.0); `ls -laR` of 2,040 entries 121.5 to 8.3 CPU, 464 to 17.5 wall (8.7, 12.8). - psh asks whether a descriptor is a terminal once, when it wraps it, not at every write (2026-11-12). `UtilCtx::write` and `write_now` flush at each newline when stdout is a terminal, and `UnixFile::is_terminal` answered with `isatty`, an `ioctl(TCGETS)` per call: `awk '{print $1}'` over 100,000 lines into a file or a pipe the shell did not make made 99,991 failing ioctls (strace -c), one per line. Whether a descriptor is a terminal does not change while it is open, so `UnixFile::new` asks once and only for a stream (a regular file, a directory or a block device is never a terminal), and the shell's own pipe ends (`UnixFile::private`) are not terminals; the same awk makes 4 ioctls. output/psh-perf/pb.py with output/psh-perf/out.json (CPU median ms of 4 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs, stdout a pipe; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand), before to after (bash 5.2 with GNU coreutils and mawk in brackets): `awk '{print $1}'` over 100,000 lines 18.8 to 11.7 (12.4), the same over 400,000 lines into a file 67.3 to 39.4 (40.6), `cut -d' ' -f1,3` 22.1 to 14.7 (8.2), `nl -ba` 19.4 to 12.5 (12.6); sed, cat, grep, seq, tr and echo and printf loops unchanged. `test -t 0` and `test -t 1` answer as before in a pty and in a pipe; 60 awk programs and the 727 agent cases give the same output through `psh -c`. Upstream delta: psh-os unix/file.rs (`UnixFile::terminal`).

- psh's awk does `x op= value`, `x++` and `x--` on a scalar in one instruction when the result is not used (2026-11-12). They compiled to a load, the operand, the operator and a store, four dispatches with a value pushed and popped at each. `Op::AugStore(var, op)` takes the operand from the stack and stores the result through the same `load` and `store` as before, special variables included, with one `arith` that the binary operators now share; a right side that does more than read, or a result that is used, compiles as before. `{s+=$1} END {print s}` over 1,000,000 lines 70.2 to 64.2 ms CPU (mawk 42.5), `{s+=1}` 52.7 to 46.6, `{s+=$3}` over 400,000 lines 43.8 to 41.3 (43.1); output/psh-perf/pb.py as in the entries below, with the same output for the awk programs and agent cases there. - psh's awk runs its instructions in a plain function and makes a future only to wait for input or output (2026-11-12, Georgios: "go and optimize all of them 10-100x"). `Interp::run` was one async function over every instruction, so each block (every action and pattern, once per record) built and polled a future, and every builtin call and `print` awaited through it, though only reading input, `system`, `close`, `fflush` and a write past the stdout buffer can wait. `Interp::step` now runs instructions until the block ends or one of those must wait (`Step::Check`, `Flush`, `Wait`), and `exec` loops over it; `call_builtin` is synchronous and `call_io` takes system, close and fflush; `print`, `printf` and a pattern without an action write to stdout through `UtilCtx::write_now`, which buffers what `write` would buffer without flushing and answers false where `write` would flush or fail, so the caller awaits `write` then. Upstream delta: psh-engine util.rs (`write_now`), psh-utils awk/interp.rs. Measured with output/psh-perf/pb.py (CPU median of 4 interleaved rounds of 3 `psh -c` runs each; the thread's hosted Hand, Linux x86_64, AMD EPYC 9555, 5 vCPUs), before to after, mawk 1.3.4 in brackets: over 400,000 lines of 8 fields `{print $1}` 52.5 to 41.7 ms (44.1), `{print $2, $1}` 57.9 to 47.6 (50.3), `$3 > 500` 69.0 to 59.7 (58.5), `{print $1, NF}` 77.4 to 65.6 (54.0), `{print NR": "$0}` 108.7 to 96.4 (43.4), `{printf "%s %d\n", $1, $3}` 117.2 to 103.4 (67.5), `NR%2==0` 50.4 to 38.1 (18.3), `length > 40` 74.8 to 55.4 (23.4), `/needle/` 30.3 to 27.4 (19.5); over 1,000,000 numbers `{print $1}` 88.4 to 63.4 (39.9) and `{s+=$1} END {print s}` 73.7 to 70.2 (42.5). The same stdout, stderr and status as before for 60 awk programs (output/psh-perf/awkcases.json with diff.py: every assignment operator, redirects, pipes to and from commands, getline, system, fflush, close, ranges, recursion, a reader that leaves early) and the 727 agent cases of output/psh-path through `psh -c`.

Commands: the checks and clippy above. Files: crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-embed/src/{park.rs,snapshot.rs}, djs-embed CHANGES.md.
- A host can keep a Code Mode cell's prepared snapshot and give it to a later runtime (2026-11-12, for nanocode-ts's move to djs). In local workerd (nanocode-ts's output/harness/workerd, Miniflare 5.20261110.1-beta, its `swarm/perf` djs module against master's QuickJS module, two rounds) djs is faster on every cell (CPU per turn: text('ok') 4.0 to 4.5 ms against 5.6 to 5.8, 16 tool calls 6.3 to 7.0 against 7.5 to 7.7, compute 31.8 to 32.0 against 41.8 to 42.8, strings 16.0 to 16.8 against 17.5 to 17.8) but a session's first cell costs more: `more.mjs firstcell` puts an open and a turn with one cell at 20.3 to 21.3 ms of CPU per session on djs against 17.7 to 18.7 on QuickJS, and two cells at 20.7 to 21.3 against 23.7 to 24.3. nanocode-ts instantiates its module once per session (every Durable Object, each time it wakes), so each session builds the cell snapshot again: the bootstrap, code-tools and its 95 KB prelude compiled and run, 3.9 ms natively (1.7 ms without a prelude), which QuickJS did in less. `nanocode_code_mode::code_mode::set_snapshot_store(Some(store))` (`SnapshotStore`: `load(setup)` and `save(setup, bytes)`, keyed by djs-embed's `Builder::setup_hash`) makes the engine load a snapshot from the store's bytes with `Snapshot::from_bytes` instead of building it, and save the bytes of each one it builds; bytes that do not load (another setup or build, damaged) are logged and the snapshot is built and saved again. The default is no store, which is the behavior before. The bytes hold the image of a build of djs, so a host keeps them for the same module (nanocode-ts in its isolate's memory). output/durability-ledger `firstcell` (Linux, 5 cores; one runtime per round, the same catalog, the first and second cell's wall time), interleaved runs of 30 rounds, p50 first cell without and with an in-memory store: with nanocode-ts's prelude 3.84, 3.93 ms to 1.09, 1.07 ms, without a prelude 1.85, 1.69 ms to 0.52, 0.52 ms; the second cell 0.04 ms either way. Checked in local workerd on 2026-11-12 (nanocode-ts's output/harness/workerd, three interleaved rounds of 40 sessions): nanocode-ts's module built on this commit with an in-memory store per module (its `djs/snapshot-store` branch) against the same module answering no stored bytes and master's QuickJS module, CPU per session for an open and a turn with one cell 10.0, 10.0, 10.3 ms against 18.3, 18.5, 19.8 ms (no store) and 17.0, 17.0, 17.2 ms (QuickJS), with two cells 13.5, 13.5, 13.8 against 18.3, 18.5, 18.8 and 21.0, 21.0, 21.3; per-cell CPU in later turns is the same with and without the store (text('ok') 3.67 against 3.73 to 3.80 ms, QuickJS 5.27). Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p djs-embed -p nanocode-code-mode-engine -p nanocode-code-mode`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `cargo clippy --locked --lib` on them with `-D warnings`. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/{cell.rs,lib.rs}, crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/mod.rs.
- The terminal interface loads syntect's syntaxes when a turn starts or a session is resumed, not at launch (2026-11-12). `highlight::prewarm` ran on a thread at every start, 16.6M instructions under callgrind (bincode reading the syntaxes' lazy contexts a byte at a time) and the memory they take, for an interface that may never show code; `App::launch_turn` and `App::connect` with a session to resume call it now, so the set is ready before a reply streams, and anything drawn earlier loads it on first use as before. On the EPYC 4245P (same harness, runs and date as the two entries below): first frame 4.02 to 3.86 ms with 11.4 to 10.1 ms of CPU, and one second after it RSS 41.1 to 40.2 MB and anonymous 7.49 to 7.01 MB.
- `rustls_platform_verifier::Verifier` reads the system trust roots at its first certificate check instead of when it is built (2026-11-12). reqwest builds a verifier with every client, and nc builds its clients in `Host::build` before the first frame, so every start read and parsed the roots on its main thread (the 2026-11-10 cache made it once a process, not free): under callgrind a one-shot `exec` against bench/cli's HTTP fixture retired 86.9M instructions, 60.3M of them in `rustls_native_certs::load_native_certs` (30.7M under `Tempo::claude` on the main thread, the rest in mpp's paying proxy, which loads them itself), and the terminal interface 31.0M of 95.0M in `prepare`. The verifier keeps its extra roots and crypto provider and builds its `WebPkiServerVerifier` on the first `verify_server_cert`, kept in an `ArcSwapOption`; TLS 1.2 and 1.3 signatures and the supported schemes come from the provider's `signature_verification_algorithms`, as `WebPkiServerVerifier` takes them. An empty root store is now reported by the first handshake instead of by the client's construction. A process that makes no HTTPS request (the fixture, local models) never reads the roots; one that does reads them on the worker that makes its first handshake. On the EPYC 4245P (same harness, runs and date as the entry below, release builds with and without this change): first frame 5.76 to 4.02 ms with 12.9 to 11.4 ms of CPU; a one-shot `exec` 11.0 to 8.96 ms, spawn to request 7.51 to 5.85 ms, CPU 10.7 to 9.16 ms. https://example.com still answered the 405 it answers, and self-signed.badssl.com and expired.badssl.com still failed with `UnknownIssuer` and `certificate expired`, before and after. `cargo check --locked -p rustls-platform-verifier`, nanocode-tls and nanocode-http pass.
- `nc` builds mimalloc with `no_thp` (2026-11-12). mimalloc v3 advises `MADV_HUGEPAGE` on the arenas it reserves, so on a kernel whose transparent huge pages are in `madvise` mode, Ubuntu 24.04's default, nc's heap was backed by 2 MiB pages from its first allocations: one second after the first frame the terminal interface held 24 to 37 MB of `AnonHugePages` in its `[anon:mimalloc]` mapping for a heap of a few MB, and zeroing those pages was most of its start-up CPU. `no_thp` defines `MI_NO_THP`, which in mimalloc v3 removes only that advice; `MI_DEFAULT_ALLOW_THP` stays 1, so mimalloc does not call `prctl(PR_SET_THP_DISABLE)`, which the commands the agent runs would inherit, and a kernel set to `always` still backs the heap with huge pages. `MIMALLOC_ALLOW_THP=0` gave the same memory on the release build (anonymous 28.0 to 10.2-10.8 MB) but sets that prctl. Interleaved on an AMD EPYC 4245P (12 threads, Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.8, THP `madvise`; bench/cli on the cli-bench branch, `tools/netguard.sh node harness/suite.mjs --parts=firstframe,oneshot --rounds=20` and `--parts=tools --steps=10 --toolrounds=8` with `BENCH_NC_VARIANTS`, release builds of fe57c2ff3 with and without the change, 2026-11-12, medians): one second after the first frame RSS 63.5 to 41.9 MB and anonymous 29.6 to 8.12 MB; first frame 7.25 to 5.76 ms with 29.2 to 12.9 ms of CPU; a one-shot `exec` 12.7 to 10.7 ms of CPU and 58.6 to 43.9 MB peak RSS; a 10-step shell turn 5.03 to 4.81 ms of CPU a step and 82.7 to 60.2 MB peak RSS. The 20,000-agent swarm of the mimalloc entry was not rerun.
- When the Messages API refuses a request as too large (HTTP 413 `request_too_large`, the API's 32 MB request limit), the Claude driver compacts the conversation and sends the step again, once, as Claude Code 2.1.318 does, and every prompt-based compaction now sends the summarizer `[image]` and `[document]` in place of each image and document (2026-11-12). Before, the 413 ended the turn with `Messages HTTP 413`; with up to 100 images kept (the image-history entry of the same day) a conversation of large screenshots can reach it. What 2.1.318 does, from its bundle: an API error whose details contain `request_too_large` (`H2o`, `MTe`) takes the same path as a prompt that is too long: a reactive compaction (`Qar`, transition `reactive_compact_retry`) and the request again, and only when that cannot run does the turn end with "Request too large (max 32MB). Accumulated images and attachments in the conversation pushed the request over the limit. Remove older images or compact the conversation." (`Epe`); its compaction requests pass the history through `ZV`, which turns every image block into `{type: "text", text: "[image]"}` and every document into `[document]`, top-level and inside tool results. Here the request is detected the way the driver detects the other refusals it retries (`request_too_large` in the provider's error text), the refused attempt's effect is settled with `refuse` like theirs, and the step's retry carries the `request-too-large` scope. The recovery uses the existing `ContextRecovery` compaction (the prompt-based summary, not server compaction) with `pending_continuation` off, so nothing is kept verbatim: a step refused for one huge tool result would be refused again if that result were kept. `cursor.context_recovery_attempted` bounds it to once per turn, shared with the context-window recovery; a second refusal, or a summary request that is itself refused, ends the turn with the provider's error, which is not rewritten into Claude Code's sentence. No size is checked before sending: the limit is the server's answer. Checked on 2026-11-12 with output/parity-harness: mock.py answers 413 `request_too_large` above `MAX_BYTES`, and `./big.sh` has one cell show 80 noise PNGs (1200x900, each about 650 KB of base64 after Read's normalization), with the mock answering `wait` while the cell runs. With `MAX_BYTES=15000000` (`./big.sh big4 18717 80`): the 18,367,578-byte step with 28 images was refused, the summary request that followed was 46,193 bytes with 28 `[image]` texts and no image, the step went again as 37,436 bytes (the summary alone) and the turn and the next prompt finished. The earlier run without the `refuse` failed with "cannot advance past an unsettled effect" after the summary. With the real limit (`./big.sh big2 18715 80`) no request passed 30,801,262 bytes, because the driver's own token estimate compacted first; the summary requests there also carried `[image]` texts instead of 5 and 28 images. Not exercised: a 413 at a turn's first step after a resume, and the real API's 413 body (the mock's follows Anthropic's documented error shape). Commands: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude -- -D warnings`, `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p nanocode-backend-claude` (pass).
- Claude's TaskStop also stops a subagent: given the id of an agent this session can see (the `agent_id` that `spawn_agent` and `list_agents` give the model), it closes that agent's subtree through the subagent runtime's own `close_agent` tool and answers `{"message": "Successfully stopped task: <id> (<role>)", "task_id", "task_type": "local_agent", "command": "<role>"}`, the shape Claude Code 2.1.318's TaskStop returns for a `local_agent` task (its `call` maps `dFe`'s `{taskId, taskType, command}`, where an agent's command is its description, and killing one also kills the local agents it owns) (2026-11-12). An agent that is not pending or running gets Claude Code's "Task <id> is not running (status: <state>)", and an id that is neither a Bash task nor a visible agent keeps "unknown task_id in this session". nanocode's Claude model never sees Claude Code's Agent tool or its task ids: it delegates with the SDK's `spawn_agent` family, whose numeric ids TaskStop now accepts as strings ("2"). The Claude backend may not depend on nanocode-subagents (scripts/check-dependency-boundaries.mjs), so `install_default_tools_with_providers` hands TaskStop the `list_agents` and `close_agent` tools it already receives from the runtime's delegation; Claude tools a host selects itself (`hand_tools`, `runner_tools`) have none and keep the Bash-only behavior. Pending counts as running here because a queued nanocode agent has no Claude Code counterpart and stopping it is what the call asks. TaskStop's output schema allows `local_agent`. Checked on 2026-11-12 with output/parity-harness built with the facade's default Claude tools (`NOTOOLS=1`, `./stop.sh stop1 18713` against mock.py): a cell spawned a subagent whose own cell waits 60 s, called TaskStop with its id 1.5 s later and got `{"command":"sleeper","message":"Successfully stopped task: 1 (sleeper)","task_id":"1","task_type":"local_agent"}`; `list_agents` then showed it closed, a second TaskStop failed with "Task 1 is not running (status: closed)", `task_id: "99"` with "unknown task_id in this session", and the run ended in 2.6 s rather than waiting for the subagent. Commands: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude -- -D warnings`, and `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p nanocode-backend-claude` (pass).
- Claude's `Read` sends a PDF read without `pages` whole, as a document block, as Claude Code 2.1.318 does, so it needs no Poppler, and a document crosses Code Mode: `ToolOutputContent::InputFile { file_data }` (`{"type": "input_file", "file_data": "data:application/pdf;base64,..."}`) carries it, and the Claude `exec` result surfaces the documents of the cell's `Read` calls after its text, at most 4, as Claude Code's REPL result does (2026-11-12). Before, every PDF went through `pdfinfo` and `pdftoppm` (the audit's financial-document attempts had neither and failed with "PDF helper unavailable"), and in a cell a document became `[document content is available to direct Claude tools, not Code Mode]`. What 2.1.318 does, from its bundle: with no `pages` it asks `pdfinfo` for a page count (10 s timeout) and refuses more than 10 pages ("This PDF has N pages, which is too many to read at once. ... Maximum 20 pages per request."); when `pdfinfo` is missing or fails it goes on without a count (`tengu_immutable_tide` defaults to 0); then it refuses an empty file, one over 20 MB (`bMr` = 20,971,520, "PDF file exceeds maximum allowed size of 20MB.") and one without `%PDF-`, and answers `[{type: "text", text: "PDF file read: <path> (<size>)"}, {type: "document", source: {type: "base64", media_type: "application/pdf", data}}]`; its REPL result appends inner Reads' PDFs as document blocks after the text and images, at most `ao` = 4, then "[N more PDF document(s) from inner Read calls not shown — a REPL result surfaces at most 4 documents; read fewer PDFs per call]", here with "an exec result" for "a REPL result" since nanocode's tool is `exec`. Read with `pages` still renders pages through Poppler, as 2.1.318's does. The cell gets `{content: [input_text, input_file]}` and the Read output schema names the item. Codex's function call outputs have no file item, so Codex turns one into the text "[document omitted: Codex function call outputs carry text and images]", and a function tool's MCP-shaped result into "[document omitted: function tool results carry text, images and audio]"; neither produces one today. Checked on 2026-11-12 with output/parity-harness (facade Claude agent, Code Mode only, against mock.py, no `pdfinfo` or `pdftoppm` on the machine): `./pdf.sh pdf1 18711`: a cell's Read of a 599-byte PDF printed `input_text input_file | PDF file read: .../ws/invoice.pdf (599 bytes)` and the next request's tool result was [text, text, document (application/pdf, 800 base64 bytes)]; the image read after it still carried its image block. `./pdf2.sh pdf2 18712`: five PDF reads in one cell gave four document blocks and the "1 more" note; an empty file, a non-PDF named .pdf and a 20 MiB + 9 byte file failed with Claude Code's three messages; `pages: "1"` failed with "PDF helper unavailable"; after `open_session` in a new process the first request repeated all 7 earlier messages, documents included. Commands: `cargo check --locked --workspace --lib`, `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-types-core -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-tool-host -p nanocode-backend-codex -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-claude-tools -- -D warnings` and `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` on the same crates (all pass).
- TIGER_STYLE.md says how nanocode applies TigerBeetle's TigerStyle, following tempoxyz/zempo: paired assertions and a three-way failure split (our invariant panics, bad external input and local exhaustion are typed errors), a named bound on every queue, batch, retry and depth, buffers sized and reused on hot paths, and determinism rules for the durability, runtime and store crates (time, randomness and identifiers only through nanocode-platform, storage only through the durability traits, no random-hasher order reaching bytes or decisions) so a deterministic simulator can replay a seed exactly. DEPENDENCIES.md ranks the dependencies to trim next with what each costs (2026-11-12, 5-core Linux Hand, 7b0586574): of 1,176 packages, mpp with tempo-alloy brings 216 that nothing else does, including aws-lc-sys (106.8 s of a 1,623 s release build by `cargo build --timings`) and bundled SQLite (33.5 s), and gakonst/cua's driver 189; the release `nanocode` has 66.5 MiB of text (`cargo bloat --crates`), 6.7 MiB of it rustpython-vm and 1.5 MiB mpp. Commands: `cargo metadata` exclusive-package counts over the resolve graph, `cargo tree --duplicates --target all`, `cargo shear`, `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP=false cargo bloat --release -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode --crates`.
- Two dependencies that did nothing are gone (2026-11-12): `imbl` from nanocode-agent, which no code in it named (`cargo shear`), and `opentelemetry-semantic-conventions` from nanocode-observability and the workspace, of whose 21,000 lines of constants it used two, now `SCHEMA_URL` (`https://opentelemetry.io/schemas/1.42.0`, the version the crate named) and `SERVICE_VERSION` beside the attribute names already declared there, so the exported resource is unchanged. `cargo metadata --locked` resolves 1,175 packages instead of 1,176; imbl stays for the six crates that use it. This is the first batch of DEPENDENCIES.md, which ranks the rest by measurement. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-observability -p nanocode-agent`, the same for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib` on both crates pass (clippy's one warning, `chunks_exact` in `otlp.rs`, was there before).
- Integration recheck of the Claude parity fixes and the swarm's round-4 branches on master (2026-11-12): lifecycle (5), djs-vm (8), psh-vfs (7), tools (9) and python without its last commit (6), so the CLI keeps the bundled python3 (the owner's decision: binary size is second for now). One merge change: psh-wasm-core's Shell::build takes the utility list it is given and master's policy fields (unconfigured with answers), and Session::run's child shell now takes its parent's list and policy from the Vfs instead of the full registry, so a shell built without git does not get git back through a host command. Checks on the merged tree: workspace `cargo check --locked`, the wasm32 check of nanocode, nanocode-shell, nanocode-code-mode, nanocode-backend-claude and nanocode-store-jsonl, and clippy -D warnings on nanocode-shell, nanocode-python, nanocode-backend-claude, nanocode-subagents, nanocode-agent-core, nanocode-durability, nanocode-code-mode and nanocode-cli pass. Release CLI (macOS arm64, release profile): 101,127,296 bytes; `nanocode psh-shell -c` runs python3 as RustPython 3.14 with PATH empty, awk and git in the shell, and PSH_UTILS_OFF=python3 hands python3 back to the system's. output/durability-ledger on Linux (5 cores, shared): matrix 3000 on memory, jsonl, sqlite and rows, kill/resume on the three stores, kill-twice, cross-version kill/resume in both directions against 1b57e8631 on jsonl and sqlite, and both tree checks end with every agent completed; 20,000 agents on jsonl complete with user CPU 58.6 to 63.0 s and max RSS 1,034 to 1,115 MB on either build, within the noise of the shared machine.
- Claude's TaskStop takes `task_id` when both it and `shell_id` are given, as Claude Code 2.1.318's `call` does (`task_id ?? shell_id`), instead of refusing, and the native Claude toolset no longer registers TaskOutput, which 2.1.318 removed (its settings say "the TaskOutput tool was removed. Read a background task's output file with the Read tool instead") (2026-11-12). Native background commands already write Claude Code's output file and send its notifications, so the Claude Code Mode guidance no longer says to poll TaskOutput: the model follows what the background result says. The host adapter (`host_tools`), whose background commands have neither an output file nor a notification, keeps the TaskOutput SDK extension, and its `timeout` property now says "0 to 300000, default 30000". Code Mode's TypeScript prints property descriptions as comments but not `minimum`/`maximum`, and the audit counted 15 rejected timeouts. `TaskStopRequest` for `ClaudeHostTools` deserializes through a private input struct, so a call with both ids no longer fails as a duplicate field. Checked on 2026-11-12 with output/parity-harness: `TaskStop({task_id, shell_id: 'nope'})` stopped the task and returned Claude Code's result; `tools.TaskOutput` rejected with `TOOL_NOT_AVAILABLE`; `ALL_TOOLS` lists TaskStop and no TaskOutput. Not done: TaskStop does not stop agents or team members as Claude Code's does; nanocode's subagents stop through close_agent and interrupt_agent. Commands: the focused checks, wasm32 checks and clippy above.
- `nanocode` started with a prompt on its command line (`nc "..."`, `nc exec "..."`) removes the prompt from its process arguments on Linux, so a command such as `pkill -f <words of the prompt>` cannot match the agent itself (2026-11-12). The audit's SQL-optimization attempt ran `pkill -f my-sql-query` and ended with exit 143 while that string was in nanocode's argv. Claude Code 2.1.318 does not avoid this: Bun's `process.title = "claude"` changes only comm, and `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` of `claude -p "please optimise my-sql-query now"` still held the prompt on this machine. Once clap has copied the arguments, `arguments::hide` reads `startstack`, `arg_start` and `arg_end` from /proc/self/stat, points each argv entry at a leaked copy and zeroes the area after the program name through /proc/self/mem, with no unsafe code. std's `args_os()` reads argv on every call (reload and restart use it), so it still sees the arguments, while `/proc/self/cmdline` shows only the program. If the layout is not the one exec left (argc or an argv entry disagrees), it changes nothing and says why on stderr. A job's cancellation was already scoped: each Bash command runs in its own process group, and TaskStop kills that group. In output/parity-harness, a background `sleep 301 & sleep 302 & wait` (pgid 65747: the shell and both sleeps) was gone after TaskStop, and no other process was touched. Measured on 2026-11-12. With output/argv-harness, a binary built with the same module and given the prompt "Optimize my-sql-query so it runs faster": without hiding, `pkill -f my-sql-query` from its child ended it with SIGTERM; with hiding, `args_os` was unchanged, cmdline no longer held the string, pkill matched nothing and the binary exited 0. With output/parity-harness built with the module (`HIDE=1`, no wrapper process): the agent survived, and its Bash call reported exit 143, because its own shell was killed (that shell's argv holds the command, as Claude Code's `eval` shell's does); without the module the agent was terminated. Still exposed: a launcher whose own argv carries the prompt (a `timeout` or `bash -c` wrapper) is killed, and `timeout` passes the signal on, which also ended the agent in the harness. nc-lite is unchanged. Commands: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-cli` (no warnings in bin/nanocode; with `-D warnings` it stops on nanocode-subagents' existing `fetch_update` deprecations).
- `arguments::hide` also works when the dynamic loader starts nanocode (`ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 --library-path <dir> nanocode exec -- "..."`), as the Terminal-Bench harness does to run a binary against its own glibc in task images (2026-11-12). Run as a program, glibc's loader (2.39 here) removes its own arguments by moving argv down the stack and lowering argc there (`_dl_start_args_adjust`), so argc no longer equals the arguments in the area and master refused with "the argument area does not hold the arguments exec gave", leaving the prompt in /proc/<pid>/cmdline. hide now accepts an argc smaller than the area, takes the leading arguments as the loader's, checks that each remaining argv entry points at the matching later argument, and zeroes the whole area after the first one; any other disagreement still changes nothing and says why. Checked live on 2026-11-12 in the query-optimize task image (alexgshaw/query-optimize:20251031) with the toolkit's glibc 2.39 loader, a black-holed HTTPS proxy keeping each process waiting for its first request, and the prompt "please optimize my-sql-query zebra": master 168a133dd under the loader printed the warning, its cmdline held the prompt and `pgrep -f my-sql-query` matched it; this build under the loader showed only the loader's path and pgrep matched nothing; started directly, both builds showed only the program. `cargo build --release -p nanocode-cli` built with no warnings. The harness's own `bash -c "... > stdout 2> stderr"` wrapper still holds the prompt (bash forks rather than execs a command with redirections), so the rerun passes the instruction as `exec ... -- "$(cat file)"`.
- The Claude driver keeps a conversation's images in its requests up to the Messages API's per-request image limit, 100 for a model whose context window is 200,000 tokens and 600 otherwise (Anthropic's vision documentation), instead of `DEFAULT_INLINE_IMAGES` (8) (2026-11-12). Claude Code 2.1.318 never removes an image from a conversation before compaction, which replaces each image with `[image]`, and for a many-image error it tells the user to /compact. With eight, the ninth image turned the four oldest into omission text: that moved the request's changed prefix back to the first image and took away images the model had already seen. The audit's financial-document run read invoices 89 and 208 times against Claude Code's 17, even after the cache repair 723bc13d9, which this keeps (the floors still mark the first kept image and the latest image-bearing message). A host that sets an `ImageHistory` keeps its own window. Measured on 2026-11-12 with output/parity-harness, 12 image reads (24 requests; `./run.sh new default 12` against `./run.sh old8 8 12`, analyze.py comparing each request's messages with the previous request's, cache markers aside): with the new default every request repeats the previous messages byte for byte and the last one carries all 12 images; with `ImageHistory::new(8)` the request after the ninth read rewrites from message 2 and every later request carries 4 omission texts. Across a restart (ckpt.sh: three image turns, then `open_session` in a new process over the same JSONL home and two more), the first request after restoring repeats all 11 earlier messages byte for byte, cache markers included, with the same system and tools. Not measured: server cache reads. Not exercised: compaction. Not handled: the 32 MB request limit, which large PNGs (about 1 to 2 MB each in base64) can reach before 100 images; that request now fails with the provider's error, as Claude Code's does, where eight images never reached it.
- Claude's `Read` gives Code Mode its media as `{content: [...]}`, the content array of the tool result Claude Code builds for an image (2.1.318's Read `mapToolResultToToolResultBlockParam`: `{type: "tool_result", content: [{type: "image", source}]}`), and `image()` takes such a result whole (2026-11-12). In the Terminal-Bench 2.1 audit of the frozen 0.6.7 run (`eed3f234`) the model called `.content[0]` on a Read result, the pattern the exec description teaches for MCP results (`image(result.content[0])`), failed on the bare array and only then found `[0]`. Text reads are still strings. A direct call's structured result was already the serialized content (`take_structured_result`), so events and journals carry nothing new. `image()` unwraps `content` before its array path, so the description's `image(await tools.Read({ file_path }))` still works, and its text now says it takes a tool result whose `content` is an array of image items. The host adapter's image Read returns the same shape. Checked on 2026-11-12 with output/parity-harness (the facade's native Claude agent, code-only, Opus 5.5, against mock.py, a local mock of the streaming Messages API; `./run.sh new default 12 18611`): 12 turns each read a PNG in a cell, alternating `image(r.content[0])` and `image(r)`; every cell printed `object 1 input_image` and every tool result carried its image block.
