- `nanocode psh-shell` (and `--shell psh`) runs the bundled python3 when PATH has none, and the facade re-exports the crate as `nanocode::python` off wasm (2026-11-11). `psh::run_with(args, extra)` in the vendored psh program's library puts the embedding program's utilities after psh-utils' registry, and nanocode passes `nanocode::python::UTILITY`; it is a PathFallback utility, so a python3 on PATH keeps winning and the bundled one runs when there is none or when PSH_UTILS_FORCE names it. The re-export is native only, because a wasm facade would put RustPython's getrandom requirement into every wasm host. Difference from upstream psh e5f136e: `run_with`, the `UTILITIES` cell and one line in `shell_config` in crates/patches/psh/crates/psh/src/lib.rs. Measured with target/release/nanocode (load 150-210, CPU, three rounds): 300 calls of `python3 -c "import json; print(1)"` in one `nanocode psh-shell -c` script take 0.19-0.21 s with PATH=/bin against 8.6 s with Homebrew's python3 on PATH and 12.3 s with macOS's /usr/bin/python3; `timeout 1 python3 -c "while True: pass"` ends with status 124 and the next python3 prints 42; sys.implementation.name is cpython with python3 on PATH and rustpython with PATH=/bin or PSH_UTILS_FORCE=python3. The executable is 103,987,776 bytes (44.8 MB gzip) with the untrimmed library; the last one built without python on this machine (the foundations worktree, another branch) is 66,001,024, so this is about 38 MB and not a same-tree comparison. The CLI's allocator is not `Metered`, so python3 there runs with no memory ceiling, as any program the shell starts does. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --offline -p psh` and `cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-cli` pass.
- python3 is a command of nanocode-shell: `nanocode_python::Command::new(budget, rest)` keeps one interpreter per shell session and reads and writes through the shell's own tracked files (2026-11-11). It is a `Commands` that answers python3, python, /usr/bin/python3 and /usr/bin/python and hands every other name to `rest`; two sessions never share an interpreter and nothing waits on a process-wide thread. When the host's filesystem answers at once Python uses it directly; when it answers later the working directory's subtree is copied in first, Python runs over the copy, and what differs is written back (removals deepest first, then directories, then files), because the interpreter cannot wait in the middle of an instruction; paths outside that subtree then fail. Output and file limits are the shell's; steps, time, memory, sleep and depth are the `Budget` the host gives; cancel is the shell's. A script that needs a package or a machine adds python3 to the run's missing list and exits 127, a refused one exits 126, a cancelled one 143. It is not linked inside nanocode-shell because psh-wasm is nanocode-shell and would gain 16-21 MB for a Python that is a JavaScript handler there today; a host opts in by wrapping its commands. Measured with output/python-bench's shellpy over MemFs (three rounds, CPU for the whole script, workloads/shell-bench.sh): 300 calls of `python3 -c "import json; print(1)"` take 63-77 ms against 250-270 ms through the psh utility on the process's files and 9.0 s when psh starts the python3 program; 300 here-document edits take 84-110 ms against 350-390 ms; the same loop of echo takes 2-3 ms; with every answer made to come later, 60-73 ms and 90-95 ms. workloads/shell.sh shows the change report (files written, removed and made, and the rename) correct in both modes, python3 in the missing list for numpy and subprocess, status 126 for the three limits with the next python3 printing 42, and decimal's precision carrying from one call to the next within a session. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-python -p nanocode-shell`, the wasm32 check of both and scripts/check-dependency-boundaries.mjs pass.
- A host command of nanocode-shell gets the shell it runs in: `Call::shell` is a `Session` with the shell's tracked files, its limits, its missing list and its cancel flag (2026-11-11). A command behind `Commands` had only its arguments and three streams, so one that reads and writes files had to hold the raw FileSystem and what it changed was absent from the run's change report and operation count, and one that computes inside a step could not see `Shell::cancel`. `Session::files()` is the same `Vfs` the engine uses (every operation charged, every change recorded, the file limit applied), `limits()` the shell's limits, `lacks(name)` the missing-program report with its strict refusal, and `stop()` a closure that answers whether the run was cancelled, from any thread. `Vfs` gains mkdir, remove, rename, symlink, set_mtime and lacks, which `Host` now calls instead of carrying their bodies. Difference from upstream psh e5f136e: `ControlHandle::cancelled()` in crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-engine/src/lib.rs. No measurement of its own. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-shell`, the wasm32 check, and `cargo check --offline -p psh-engine -p psh-wasm` (and psh-wasm for wasm32) in crates/patches/psh pass.
- python3 cannot outrun its caller: nanocode-python's `Limits` gain `steps`, `time`, `memory` and `depth`, `Run` gains `stop`, and a run that passes one ends `Refused(Limit::Steps | Time | Memory)` or `Cancelled` with no except, finally or with able to catch it (2026-11-11). Until now `while True: pass` held its thread for good, which on a native host is the one thread every python3 shares. The mechanism is in the vendored interpreter (difference from upstream 0.6.0, all marked "nanocode:"): vm/limit.rs (new) has the `Limiter` trait (refuel, reserve), `VirtualMachine::{fuel, limiter, stopped, recursion_cap}`, `Metered` (a global-allocator wrapper that counts the bytes each thread holds) and `with_memory_ceiling`; frame.rs spends one unit of fuel per instruction and `unwind_blocks` finds no handler once the limiter has refused; protocol/iter.rs spends a unit per `PyIter::next`, because `sum(itertools.count())` never reaches the dispatch loop; stdlib/_sre.rs and sre_engine's engine.rs make the matcher tick every 1,024 moves (a move is a step) and turn a match the limiter ended into an error; sequence.rs, vm_ops.rs, builtins/int.rs, builtins/str.rs and bytes_inner.rs call `reserve` before repetition, `bytes(n)`, padding, zfill and integer powers and shifts; vm/mod.rs counts native recursion against the recursion limit on wasm32, where the engine's stack cannot be read, and no longer prints a failed unraisable hook to the process's stdout; stdlib/sys.rs stops `setrecursionlimit` at `recursion_cap`. What each bound covers: steps are bytecode instructions, iterator steps and regex moves; time is looked at every 4,096 steps; cancel is a closure the host answers from any thread, asked at the same points; memory is the bytes the interpreter's thread holds beyond what it held when the run began, counted by `Metered`, which the program installs as its allocator (a run that asks for a memory limit without it is refused before it starts); depth is the recursion limit and its cap. What they do not cover: one native operation that takes no step (a sort, a big-integer multiplication or factorial, a codec or decompression over a large input) runs to its end; one whose result a number sizes outside the reserved sites (a format width, expandtabs, int.to_bytes) or that grows inside one call (zlib.decompress) has its memory before the ceiling is looked at; a doubling string overshoots by one doubling (537 MB resident under a 256 MB limit); sleep is bounded by `sleep` and `time` but not interrupted by cancel; on a host whose clock stands still during computation (Workers) only steps bound a loop. A refused run gets one more slice of 4,096 steps to flush what it printed, and the kept interpreter runs the next script. Also fixed: `raise KeyboardInterrupt` reached RustPython's exit path, which sends SIGINT to the process; output a refused run left buffered appeared in the next run's stdout; psh's cancel now reaches the interpreter thread (`SyncCtx::canceller`, added to the psh-engine file this branch owns). Measured with output/python-bench (load 60-200, CPU): workloads/limits.py, 54 hostile scripts, all end within the limit natively and the interpreter then prints 42; output/python-wasm/limits.mjs in Node 22, 20 of 20 scripts and 36 of 36 recursion shapes at depth 100, 200 and 300 end without a trap, while at depth 500 one shape of twelve (a __repr__ chain) overflows V8's stack and at 1,000 two do; on wasm a 64 MB limit let linear memory reach 148 MB, since freed blocks stay in the module. - The span encoder writes its bytes itself (2026-11-11). After the entry above, encoding a span through serde was 4.3 to 4.7% of a 20,000-agent swarm's samples with telemetry on: a serializer state per object, every static key (`"key"`, `"stringValue"`, `"code.file.path"`) escaped byte by byte each time, integers and timestamps through `core::fmt`, and a `Vec` collected for events and links even when a span has none. `otlp.rs` now pushes the bytes: keys and framing are literals, a string is copied a run at a time up to the next byte that needs an escape, found a word at a time with the test serde_json's reader uses for the same bytes, integers and nanosecond timestamps are written from a stack buffer sized by `u64::MAX`'s digits, and only doubles still go through serde_json so that their text cannot differ. A value kind OTLP does not define is still an error that reaches the writer and its flush result. Byte check as above with this encoder: 92,021 spans in 219 batches, 134,832,407 bytes identical, the two-scope batch equal as JSON. Measured with the queue unbounded: `otlp::span` 4.3% -> 2.2% of the samples and `on_end` 5.1% -> 3.3%; three interleaved runs, user CPU 44.3, 44.4, 43.3 s before and 43.3, 43.4, 43.1 s after.
- A span is encoded on the thread that ends it, and the trace writer only assembles lines (2026-11-11). The local trace writer took `SpanData` off a channel, cloned every span into the OTLP protobuf structs (`group_spans_by_resource_and_scope` clones each `SpanData` before converting it), serialized those to JSON and wrote the line, all on one thread, and a span kept its place in the 2,048-span queue until its whole batch was on disk. On merged master that thread was 10.0% of a 20,000-agent swarm's samples with telemetry on and could not keep up with ten workers: 132,000 to 200,000 of about 855,000 spans were dropped per run. `crates/integrations/observability/src/otlp.rs` serializes a span straight from `SpanData` to the same JSON, the restoration of integer-looking string attributes included, in `on_end` on the thread that ends it; the writer joins the encoded spans of each instrumentation scope, frames the line with the resource it encoded once, writes it with one call, and gives a span's queue slot back when it takes the span off the channel. Before it sleeps the writer yields once, so under load it comes back to a batch instead of being woken for every span (without the yield the workers' wake-ups of the sleeping writer went from 0.61% to 2.13% of the samples and the file had 130,000 lines of mostly one span). Where spans wait, measured with counters in the writer at load 180 to 340: 817,080 spans in 128,289 batches, 55% of them one span; the queue was found full on 1 to 16 wake-ups a run, after the writer thread itself had been off the CPU (longest single write 113 to 150 ms, longest drain of at most 2,048 already encoded spans 47 to 49 ms), so what is left of the drops is scheduling, which the next entry removes. Byte check: the harness's swarm with `TRACE_CHECK=1` records every span of a 2,000-agent run through tracing-opentelemetry, adds synthetic spans (every value kind including NaN and infinities, the four array kinds, strings with quotes, controls and non-ASCII, events, links, remote parents, trace state, the three statuses, a second scope with version, schema URL and attributes) and encodes each batch with the old path and the new, the new one through the crate's own otlp.rs included by path: 90,938 spans in 218 single-scope batches, 133,681,837 bytes identical, and a two-scope batch equal as JSON (the old order of scopes is a HashMap's; the new one is first seen). Measured with the queue unbounded so that no run drops spans: writer plus `on_end` 10.5% -> 7.0% of the samples; three interleaved runs, user+system 44.6+4.9, 44.3+4.4, 45.4+5.2 s before and 42.6+3.8, 44.8+4.8, 44.5+4.7 s after, so the totals do not resolve it; with the default queue, spans dropped 170,645, 200,557, 180,736 before and 61,029, 45,453, 38,455 after. Measured and left out: waking the writer by the batch-processor variables (`OTEL_BSP_SCHEDULE_DELAY` 5 s, `OTEL_BSP_MAX_EXPORT_BATCH_SIZE` 512) instead of per message brings writer plus `on_end` to 6.2% and system time down by a further 0.5 s (1,400 lines instead of 10,000 to 30,000), but a span would reach the file up to five seconds after it ended and a killed process would lose them, so it is not in.
- 2026-11-11: **The macOS accessibility reader converts no more of a name or value than the state shows.** tempoxyz/pyramid main's #3023 (CYCLOPS-5788), whose code is this crate's now: `read_node` turned every title, description and value into a whole `String` and kept it until `render`, which only then cut it to 200 characters, so one long text field or document cost a full UTF-16 to UTF-8 conversion and a copy per read. Names and values for the state now go through `ax::label_of`, which converts only `state::shown_units(len)` UTF-16 units (enough for one character past the 200 shown, never splitting a surrogate pair) with `CFStringCreateWithSubstring`; `flat` cuts while it replaces newlines instead of after. The rendered state is unchanged. `ax::text_of` still reads whole values where an action needs them (`set_value`, the selection, scrolling, the role and subrole). The bound is derived from the 200 the state shows, not a new limit; Linux already asks AT-SPI for at most 1,000 characters. Checked: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-computer` natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and for `aarch64-apple-darwin` through cargo-zigbuild on Linux with `swift` and `xcrun` stubbed and `DOCS_RS=1` (type-checked and linted, not linked or run: no Mac was used); output/clip-check takes `flat` and `shown_units` from `state.rs` and compares them with the code before on main's eight cases and 20,000 random texts of ASCII, newlines, tabs, accents, CJK and characters outside the BMP: every text is shown as before, 4,805 were read only in part, and none needed more than 402 units.
- 2026-11-11: **A sandboxed call says whether it may use the tailnet and what its proxy answers a refused host.** `run::Runner` took both for all its calls (`Reach::tailnet`, `Reach::refusal`), so a host could not treat one call differently from the next. tempoxyz/pyramid needs to: code no admin has reviewed must not reach the tailnet, whose route acts as the backend's own node, and the refusal the tool reads should say which of the two reasons applies. `Call` now carries `tailnet: bool` and `refusal: fn(&str) -> String`, and `Reach` keeps the route's address and loses the text. A call without the tailnet gets no route and its declared tailnet hosts are left out of its allowlist (`egress::tailnet_host`: a name or `*.` pattern under `.ts.net`, the suffix the proxy already dials through the route), so the proxy refuses them like any host the call does not list, in the call's own words. Checked: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sandbox` natively, for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` and (through cargo-zigbuild) for `aarch64-apple-darwin`; output/reach-check on dev-georgios runs curl through a Runner under bubblewrap 0.9.0 with a SOCKS server standing where the tailnet's is: with the tailnet a declared tailnet host and one matched by a declared pattern are dialed through it and an undeclared host gets the call's sentence; without it neither is dialed, both get the sentence the host gave for an unreviewed call, an undeclared host gets the other sentence, and a declared host off the tailnet is still reached for (8 cases).

- psh's rg gives its reader the first file's output at once and then each time as much again as it has been given, so a reader that has left stops the search (2026-11-11). psh's rg writes each file's output in walk order through a block buffer; with little output nothing reached the pipe until the search ended, so `rg -l X | head -1` searched every file after head had gone, where ripgrep's own writer hands over each file's output as it prints it. A reader that is gone is now seen after at most twice the output it took, and one that reads everything is woken a number of times that grows with the logarithm of the output. Seven invocations give the same stdout and statuses before, after and from Homebrew rg. Upstream difference: psh-utils rg/main.rs (Merge::given, Merge::held).
- psh's awk makes a value only for the fields a program reads (2026-11-11). 38% of its samples were malloc and free: each record cost five allocations before the program ran. A field is now kept as a place in the record and becomes a value on first read (a field that is the whole record shares it; assigning a field or NF settles them first, as before); the reader hands over the record as the text the interpreter keeps and reuses the terminator while RS finds the same one; a run of at most f64::DIGITS digits is a number without a float parse; the separator is found with bstr's byte search. CPU median, interleaved, same output: `awk '{s+=$1} END {print s}'` over 1,000,000 lines 237.8 to 137.0 ms on macOS (Homebrew bash with /usr/bin/awk 267.7); a two-awk pipeline over 300,000 lines 303.2 to 202.7 ms (508.0); `awk -F: '{print $1, NF}'` 374.7 to 272.0 ms (766.6). In a Linux arm64 container the first is 294.1 to 168.9 ms as a process and 152.9 ms in the Hand's process, against mawk's 121 to 127 ms: awk is still slower than mawk there. Upstream difference: psh-utils awk/interp.rs (Field, set_record, field_value, settle_fields), awk/io.rs (Record, RecordReader::rt), awk/value.rs (scan_number).

The trade: a contained script shares the Hand's memory and fate, so a host that confines commands by wrapping the programs it starts must not install the hook.

The vendored `psh::embed` (Unix) has `contained(script, env)`, true when the classifier proves every command is a builtin or a bundled utility and nothing reads the shell's own pid, `start(Command, ended)` and `Running::{interrupt, stop}`; `psh_engine::{is_builtin, uses_pid}` and a `settings(env)` shared by the standalone binary and the embedded shell keep the two from drifting. - A psh command that asks for a login shell gets the login shell's environment from one probe per process, not from startup files run per command (2026-11-11). `nanocode-process` runs `$SHELL -lc "printf '\0MARK\0'; /usr/bin/env -0"` once, in its own task behind a SingleFlight, keeps the launch environment and the reported one, and gives each psh command that snapshot with the command's own differences applied (secrets, variables it set or removed; PWD, OLDPWD, SHLVL and _ stay the command's). The probe is repeated only when a startup file's fingerprint changes; a command waits for it at most its own yield time and otherwise fails with that reason rather than running without it. The probe costs 6.1 ms CPU once (15.7 ms wall, 15 runs) where zsh -lc costs it on every command. Under `env -i HOME USER PATH=/usr/bin:/bin TMPDIR`, five cases (the 28-variable environment, the 16-entry PATH, SHLVL, tools found on PATH, a session variable) are the same bytes from `/bin/zsh -lc` and from psh; 727 agent cases through exec_command differ in 0 with and without the login environment, on macOS and in a Linux arm64 container. For a user whose shell is fish the login shell is the system fallback, as on the system path.

The heading goes before the first tool's section (after its namespace heading, if it has one), or at the end when no tool has a section; an undeclared tool, named as registered or as its JavaScript identifier, keeps its heading and description and loses its `exec tool declaration` block. The layout is not part of a pin's contract, as a heading a host's pins added was not: a changed heading alone still pins as the same contract. In the same profile `store_for` is 0.18 to 0.21%, `root_of` 0.23 to 0.27%, RunnerAgents 0.28 to 0.37%, AdmissionGate 0.34% and RuntimeGuard's drop 0.21 to 0.24%; they stay as they are.
- A durable session's driver task is sized for waiting, not for its largest command (2026-11-11). `Driver::run(mut self)` stored the 1,560-byte driver twice, as an async fn does with an argument it rebinds, and awaited `handle_command` in place, a 6,896-byte future because it embeds every command's own future (`commit_writes` 5,624, `admit_automatic` 4,856, and `DurableState`, 624 bytes, passed by value through `applied`, `persist` and `persist_settling`): 10,240 bytes per task, 12,288 from the system allocator, for every awake session, none of it in use between commands. `run` now borrows the driver from the async block that owns it and boxes each command's future while it runs (one 7 KB allocation per command, about eleven per agent in the swarm). Measured on 2026-11-11 with output/durability-ledger (5,000 children on JSONL, system allocator, `malloc_history`), bytes live per agent, each including 5.6 KB of the process's own thread stacks and up to 3.4 KB of the harness: awake and waiting on a model call 164.6 -> 144.4 KB with the entry above (durable session driver 16.0 -> 5.7 KB, its task 12,288 -> 2,048 bytes), hibernated 21.1 -> 20.9 KB, completed 17.3 -> 17.1 KB, waiting in the queue 11.1 KB. What an awake agent still holds: the last request body kept for the next request's prefix (24 KB, `WireCache::assembled`), the Claude turn's futures (`run_locked` 8 KB, `observed_response` 7 KB, `start_turn` 3.5 KB), one B-tree leaf sized for eleven 440-byte `OperationState`s (6 KB) and one for `StepState` (2 KB), four copies of the prompt (11 KB) and three event channels' first blocks (4 KB). User CPU of SWARM flat 20000 at 2,000 concurrent: 35.9, 35.5, 35.1 s before and 35.8, 35.5, 34.9 s after. The peak of that run (1.5 to 1.7 GB RSS) is not agents at rest: a heap taken mid-run holds 195 MB in 476 djs arenas of 409,600 bytes, one per running cell, of 722 MB live, under an RSS of 1.8 GB.
- `nanocode_subagents::platform::spawn` holds the future it spawns once (2026-11-11). It boxed an async block that moved the future into a second async block and awaited it there; every move of a future into a block or across an await reserves its space again, so the box was three times the future (`-Zprint-type-sizes`: `Instrumented<Harness::run>` is 3,576 bytes and its task 10,776, a 12,288-byte allocation for every awake child). The task is now `Abortable::new(future.map(send), registration).map(drop)`: one copy, the same abort and the same result. Measured on 2026-11-11 with output/durability-ledger `heapsleep.sh` (5,000 children on JSONL, system allocator, `malloc_history`): an agent awake and waiting on a model call holds 24.9 -> 15.0 KB in nanocode-subagents (its harness task 12,288 -> 4,096 bytes), a hibernated one 1.90 -> 1.61 KB; user CPU of SWARM flat 20000 at 2,000 concurrent did not move (35.9, 35.5, 35.1 s against 35.8, 35.5, 34.9 s, with the driver change below).
- Compaction and the session archive sync through `sync_journal` like the journal's commits (2026-11-11). nanocode and nc-lite compact and archive the session after `Runtime::shutdown`, after the answer is printed; compaction synced its temporary file and the directory with `sync_all` and the archive synced the directory the same way, three F_FULLFSYNCs of 6 to 10 ms each on Apple platforms (compaction predates the journal's move to F_BARRIERFSYNC and was rare then). With the barrier the rename still cannot be on disk before the data it names, and a power loss can lose the compaction or the archive, never leave a name without its content. `migrate.rs` keeps `sync_all`: it runs once per home. Measured with output/first-request on 2026-11-11 (25 alternated runs of a one-turn session, load average 160): the archive phase 81.2 -> 19.9 ms (minimum 48.0 -> 14.9), compacting a 6.5 KB journal 15 to 25 ms -> 2.4 to 3.1 ms. An archived session read through a new store has its revision and payload, is restored to be read and is archived again.
- `records/` is synced once per batch of new shared records and with the journal's barrier (2026-11-11). `Shared::put` synced the directory after every rename with `sync_all`, which on Apple platforms is F_FULLFSYNC: 6 to 10 ms on this machine against 1 ms for `fcntl(F_BARRIERFSYNC)` on the same directory (12 trials each, load average 300), and a new home writes three records (system prompt and tool catalog) inside the commit that precedes its first model request. `Shared::store` now syncs the directory once after the batch, through `sync_journal` (F_BARRIERFSYNC, `sync_all` where the filesystem refuses it and on other platforms), which orders the names before the journal entry that refers to them exactly as it orders the journal's own commits. Measured with output/first-request in a new home on 2026-11-11 (12 alternated runs, load average 300, with the ordered pool write of the entry above, worth 1 ms): the store job that holds the three records 32.7 -> 6.0 ms (minimum 22.7 -> 3.6), first request after main 53.5 -> 14.7 ms (minimum 38.2 -> 11.5).
- A record pool write is committed `Settle::Ordered`: it has to reach the disk before the continuation that names its records, not before the caller goes on (2026-11-11). `Pool::ensure` used `replace`, which on JSONL answers after the sync, and the Claude driver pools its request template inside `stage_cursor`, so the first turn of every root session waited for a third sync between accepting the prompt and sending the model request (the other two are the session's acquisition and the prompt's admission, which are promises of `spawn().build()` and `prompt()` and stay). The JSONL worker appends an ordered write, answers, and hands the file to the syncer, which syncs it before it answers any later commit, so the continuation is never acknowledged ahead of its template; if the process dies first, nothing names the records. SQL and memory stores do not tell the settles apart and behave as before. Measured with output/first-request (a new harness: the host `bin/nanocode` builds for `exec` without Tempo's clients and MCP servers, one prompt against a local mock, wall and CPU per phase, every `durability.store` operation and sync) on 2026-11-11 in an existing home, builds alternated, load average 150 to 300: syncs finished before the first request 3 -> 2, request after the prompt was accepted 1.81 -> 0.86 ms (median of 20) and 2.34 -> 0.97 ms (median of 30), minimum 1.18 -> 0.43 ms, first request after main 8.75 -> 7.20 ms. Of what remains before the request in an existing home, the main thread spends 1.1 ms (ClaudeHarness::build 0.8 ms, of which the default tools 0.4 ms and `ComputerConfig::cua_driver` 0.23 ms once per process), the two remaining syncs 0.8 ms each on an idle disk, and the rest is the store's file creation and thread hand-offs.
- nc does not have cua-driver-sdk in its dependency graph, because an executable links every `#[no_mangle]` symbol of every crate in it (2026-11-11). The merge into one nanocode-computer crate (887747809) put the driver back into the CLI's link that the nanocode-cua-driver helper had taken out: rustc's symbols object references the SDK's UniFFI scaffolding (`_UNIFFI_META_*`, `cua_driver_abi_is_compatible_v1`), the linker loads the whole driver for it and then strips the Rust code as dead (`-Wl,-map`: cua_driver_core 144 live symbols of 16,963, platform_macos 23 of 11,566), but screencapturekit's Swift objects carry metadata that cannot be stripped, so 48 dylibs loaded before main (AppKit, ScreenCaptureKit, AVFoundation, Metal, VideoToolbox, 22 libswift*); `-dead_strip_dylibs` alone removed only six. The cua_repl surface (`ComputerConfig`, `ComputerTools`, `ProviderTool`, `browser`, `browser_socket`, `embedded_driver`, the catalogs and `cua_driver.mjs`) is now `nanocode-computer-repl` (crates/integrations/computer-repl, the files moved unchanged), which nanocode-computer re-exports at its root (`pub use nanocode_computer_repl::*`), so every `nanocode_computer::` path, `driver` and `embedded` included, and `nanocode::cua` are unchanged. nanocode-agent-host's `cua` feature depends on the repl crate; nanocode-cli takes the facade with `default-features = false, features = ["local-cells"]`, turns on `nanocode-agent-host/cua` and names nanocode-computer-repl itself. The facade's own `cua` feature still re-exports all of nanocode-computer, so a host that links `nanocode` with default features on macOS still links the driver; narrowing `nanocode::cua` to the repl crate (as it was before 887747809) would fix that for every host and is a public API decision left to the owner. Measured on 2026-11-11 (release profile, load average 150 to 220, builds alternated, minimum of 15 runs): dylibs 48 -> 4 (Security, CoreFoundation, libiconv, libSystem), binary 74.9 -> 73.6 MB, `--version` 47.3 M -> 34.7 M instructions, 10.7 -> 8.0 MB max RSS and 6.7 -> 5.0 ms CPU, `sessions` 55.9 M -> 43.6 M and 16.7 -> 13.9 MB, `psh-shell -c true` 48.5 M -> 35.8 M and 11.5 -> 8.7 MB. What is left above an empty C program (8.9 M) is CoreFoundation, which costs 9.9 M instructions and 4.3 MB by itself (`cc -Wl,-needed_framework,CoreFoundation`; Security adds 0.2 M) and is linked by security-framework, system-configuration and others, and 16 M of nc's own launch.
- 2026-11-11: **Four blocks a server host builds its model clients from: a route by model, an auth with a key behind it, a subscription request that sends itself, and a kept client.** tempoxyz/pyramid-core had each of these in its own runtime, and tempoxyz/pyramid a second copy of one; they name nothing of either, so they move here and the hosts keep only their policy. (1) `nanocode_backend_codex_client::ModelRoute` is an HTTP layer for `OpenAiBuilder::http_layer`: a request whose body names one of its models goes to its URL with its authorization, keeping the last path segment, and every other request passes unchanged. The model is read from the body's first 256 bytes, where nanocode's own Responses requests put it, and by parsing the body when it is not there. `ModelRoute::bearer` builds the authorization from a key. (2) `ClaudeAuthOrKey` is a `ClaudeAuthProvider` over another one with an API key behind it: when the first fails to give headers, or to recover from a 401, requests go out on the key, for good or until `back_after` has passed, and `on_fall` hears each failure with whether a key took over and whether that switched (`ClaudeFall`). Without a key the first's error is returned. `ClaudeSubscription::settling(wait, poll)` is a provider over a subscription that, the first time its headers fail, polls the status for `wait` while another process's exchange is uncertain or validating, since a refresh in flight elsewhere ends within seconds. `ClaudeWorkloadIdentity::auth(http, base_url)` gives the federated token auth without a client, so a host can put a key behind it. Together they replace pyramid-core's `PlanThenKey` (a member's plan, then the organization's key) and Pyramid's `FederatedOrKey` with its copy of the token exchange. (3) `ClaudeSubscriptionHttpRequest::send(client)` and `SubscriptionHttpRequest::send(client, timeout)` send a subscription host's request on a reqwest client and read the answer up to the request's own byte limit (`nanocode_http::bounded_text`, whose `BoundedError` prints what reqwest, the limit or the decoding said), natively only: a host's `request` is one call, and a WASM host still implements it. (4) `nanocode_sync::Kept<K, V>` keeps at most `kept` values, each for `fresh`, and makes a missing one with the caller's function (`get_or_try`); it is `Aged`, which `Throttle` and `Recent` already use, with a synchronous make, for a host that keeps a key's client across turns. Every number (the wait, the poll, the fallback window, the counts and ages) is the caller's. Checked on 2026-11-11 on dev-georgios: `cargo clippy --locked --lib` for nanocode-sync, nanocode-http, nanocode-backend-codex-client and nanocode-backend-claude-client natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, no new warnings; `scripts/check-dependency-boundaries.mjs`; and pyramid-core built on these against the same core on its own copies, with a harness that runs turns through its runtime against one recording mock (Anthropic Messages and OAuth, the ChatGPT issuer and Codex endpoint, a routed endpoint): 44 requests in 10 scenarios (keys, a Claude plan signed in, its bearer refused once, a refresh in flight elsewhere, the plan failing over to the key and failing without one, a ChatGPT plan with a refused token and a refused model, a subagent on a routed model, sign-out) are the same before and after, headers, bodies and order, in two runs each, with the same connections opened.

Harness: `cells` and `preludecheck` identical; `cellreplay` 4 ok and the known failure; `sinkreplay` 5 ok; matrix 3000 on the four stores, kill/resume on three, kill-twice, both tree checks, release, and matrix plus kill/resume with telemetry on (`OTEL_DIR`) end with every agent completed. `metriccheck` prints the same line for the build with and without the observability change under five filters (default, `nanocode=debug`, `nanocode[span]=trace`, `warn,nanocode_durability=trace`, `off`). With telemetry on, the build without the observability change against the build with it, three interleaved runs: user CPU 46.7, 46.4, 46.7 s to 44.8, 43.9, 44.5 s, 1.0 GB of spans either way. - Telemetry at scale, and three things in how its layers are assembled (2026-11-11). output/durability-ledger never installed the CLI's telemetry, so it hid a cost `nc` pays: with `ObservabilityBuilder` as the CLI configures it (OpenTelemetry traces to a local file, no log output; the harness's `swarm` installs it when `OTEL_DIR` is set) a 20,000-agent swarm burns 50.8 to 52.9 s of user CPU against 40.0 to 40.6 s without it, writes 1.1 GB of spans (about 750,000, roughly 1 KB each: `durability.store` 37%, `subagent.journal.persist` 12%, `durability.jsonl.worker` 10.6%, `model.call`, `messages.attempt`, `tool.execute` about 6% each) and reports dropped spans 65 to 106 times a run because 2,048 are waiting. The subscriber's work on the workers was 15.1% of the samples (enter 5.6%, exit 2.9%, close 2.3%, new span 2.2%, record 1.6%) and the trace writer's thread 7.8%. Changed, none of it altering what is recorded: (1) each layer was filtered by an `EnvFilter`, which takes a read lock on its span table at every new span, enter, exit, record and close whether or not a directive names a span; a filter string without brackets (every default, and any `--log` of `target=level` pairs) is now a `filter::Targets` built from the same directives, after `EnvFilter::try_new` has parsed the string, so the accepted syntax and the errors are the ones from before, and a string with a span or field directive keeps the `EnvFilter`; (2) the target filter and the closure after it were two nested per-layer filters and are one (`FilterExt::and`); (3) the trace layer no longer attaches an OpenTelemetry `Context` to the thread on every enter and detaches it on every exit (`with_context_activation(false)`): nothing in the workspace reads `Context::current()`, a span's parent is found from the tracing span stack, and `Span::context()` is unaffected. Measured, three interleaved runs: user CPU 53.0/52.5/53.1 s before, 50.8/51.0/51.5 s with (1) and (2), 49.8/49.3/51.2 s with all three; tracing_subscriber's own frames 6.0% -> 3.2 to 3.6% of the samples, subscriber work 15.1% -> 12.1%. Checked: the traces of a 300-agent run have the same (span, parent span) pairs and attribute keys before and after (two pairs come and go between runs of either build); the harness's `metriccheck` emits spans and metric events under five filter strings (default, a span directive, mixed levels, `off`, metrics only) and master and this build record the same ones; `nc sessions --log ...` accepts and rejects the same strings (a space after a comma is an `EnvFilter` error in both); the swarm matrix, kill and resume, kill twice, trees, cancel, close and reopens pass with telemetry on and off. Measured and left for a decision, since each changes what a trace contains (scripts/otel.mjs reads these fields): idle and busy time per span (`with_tracked_inactivity`) is what is left of enter and exit, 4.5% of the samples; `code.file.path`, `code.module.name`, `code.line.number`, `thread.id` and `thread.name` are five of a span's nine or ten attributes and about half of the file; the per-call durability spans are half of all spans. Also left: the writer converts every span to the protobuf structs and then to JSON (transform 2.7%, serialization 3.2%, `restore_integers` 0.7%), which a serializer straight from `SpanData` would roughly halve; and the metrics layer's filter cannot simply reject spans (0.70% -> 0.49%), because a span directive enables metric events inside the span only if the filter saw the span.
- A `Mailbox` call that was answered inline does not spend the task's cooperative budget (2026-11-11). `Mailbox::call` runs the job on the caller when the mailbox is idle, so the reply is normally there before the returned future is first polled; the future awaited a tokio oneshot regardless, and every tokio resource poll takes one unit of the task's budget of 128. A task that makes many calls within one poll, which is what a cell awaiting hundreds of `spawn_agent` calls does (each `enqueue_child` makes several registry calls), ran out, was told Pending with its replies already waiting, and went back through the scheduler (`tokio::runtime::context::defer` under `enqueue_child`). `replied()` now takes a reply that is already there with `try_recv` and awaits only one that is not. Measured with output/syncbench `mailbench` (one worker, 64 futures of 8 calls each in a `FuturesUnordered`, thread CPU, old and new interleaved three times): 139 to 149 ns -> 69 to 70 ns per call, and the task is polled 1.00 times per batch of 512 calls instead of 8.81. In a 20,000-agent swarm the forced yields were 0.1 to 0.5% of the samples while children are being spawned and under 0.1% of the whole run, so the swarm's user CPU does not resolve it. What changes: a task whose mailbox calls are all answered inline no longer yields because of them; each such call ran its job on that task anyway, and the mailbox's own hand-off after 128 delivered letters is unchanged.
- `nanocode_sync::Map` and `Set` hash with foldhash (2026-11-11). The trie hashed every key with std's `RandomState` (SipHash-1-3), and its keys are session ids, `(session id, AgentId)` pairs and other 30 to 70 byte strings. The hasher is `foldhash::quality::RandomState` (0.2.0, already in the lock under hashbrown; a new workspace dependency for nanocode-sync only): seeded per process and per map, and the `quality` variant because the trie consumes the hash five bits at a time from the low end and needs every bit mixed (the `fast` variant measured 24 ns against 26 ns and was not taken). Measured with output/syncbench `mapbench` (thread CPU, best of 5, 36-byte string keys in an `Atom<Map>`): a lookup 39 ns -> 26 ns in 300 entries, 46 -> 33 ns in 2,000, 96 to 106 -> 73 to 88 ns in 20,000; a copy-on-write update is unchanged at 350 to 950 ns because its cost is the path copy. In a 20,000-agent swarm sampled for its whole run, hashing under `Map` and `Set` is 0.33% -> 0.04% of the samples; user CPU does not resolve it. `mapcheck` (4.4 million random operations against std's `HashMap` over string, integer and colliding keys with snapshots held across writes, now also 200,000 integers spaced 2^20 apart and 200,000 strings sharing a 24-byte prefix inserted, found and removed) prints MAPCHECK OK. Measured and left: the std `HashMap`/`HashSet` sites still on SipHash are 0.6 to 1.0% of the swarm in total but spread over dozens of call sites of at most 0.09% each (`Journal::apply`'s state map, `Driver::persist`, `refresh_dynamic_tools`, `JournalClaims`), none in this crate. The trie's fan-out stays at 32: with 16, 8 or 4 a single-threaded update moved by under 5% and a lookup in 2,000 entries got 20% slower (46 -> 57 ns); ten threads updating one `Atom<Map>` were 30% cheaper at fan-out 16 in a write-only run (5,000 -> 3,350 ns) but not in three interleaved runs with eight lookups per update (4,150/5,525/6,021 ns at 32 against 4,986/5,841/6,835 ns at 16), and the swarm's share of path copies moved inside its own noise (3.2 to 3.5% -> 2.3 to 3.1%).
- Dropping an `Atom` does not walk every thread's debts (2026-11-11). An arc-swap `Guard` is not tied to the lifetime of the storage it was loaded from, so `ArcSwapAny`'s drop calls `Debt::pay_all`, which reads the debt slots of every thread that has ever used one (14 in the swarm: ten workers, the store's three threads and main). Each of those lines is being written by its owner, so a drop costs a cache-line transfer per thread and slows that thread's next read: output/syncbench `atombench` measures `Atom::new` + drop at about 1,000 ns beside 13 threads that keep reading Atoms, against 20 ns alone, and `pay_all` under a drop was 1.00% of a 20,000-agent swarm's samples in a 9 s window (0.69% over a whole run), because an agent creates and drops dozens of small Atoms (`Arc<State>`, `Sequencer`'s `Line`, the wire cache, cell journals). The vendored arc-swap gains `Enclosed<T>` (crates/patches/arc-swap/src/lib.rs, the only addition; marked as not upstream): an `ArcSwap<T>` that never lets a `Guard` out. Its five calls (`from_pointee`, `load_full`, `with(|&T|)`, `swap`, `compare_and_swap` returning a full `Arc`) hold any debt only while they borrow the storage, so a storage that is being dropped is owed nothing and its drop gives up the stored reference without the walk. It does not matter if the same `Arc` also sits in an ordinary `ArcSwap`: that storage's own reference backs its guards and it pays them when it lets go. `Atom` is built on `Enclosed` (on WASM on a wrapper of nanocode's own `Swap` with the same five calls); `Swap`, `SwapOption`, `Inbox` and `SingleFlight` are unchanged and still pay on drop. Unsafe code stays in the patch, as with the two `pay_all` changes before it. Measured, 20,000 agents on JSONL, `sample` at 1 ms: `pay_all` under drops 1.00% -> 0.21% (window) and 0.69% -> 0.15% (whole run; what is left drops `Swap`/`SwapOption` directly), all `pay_all` 2.74% -> 2.16%, arc_swap 4.47% -> 3.66%; `Atom::new` + drop beside 13 reading threads about 1,000 ns -> 9 to 120 ns. User CPU of three interleaved runs does not resolve it (39.6/39.9/39.8 s before, 39.7/40.0/39.6 s after). Checked: output/syncbench `atomcheck` (12 threads x 3,000,000 rounds, 32 x 500,000, and 25 runs of 16 x 20,000 for thread turnover: values with a canary and a live count read, replaced, updated and dropped through shared and private Atoms; every value made was dropped once and none was read after its drop), the swarm matrix on memory, JSONL, SQLite and rows, kill and resume, kill twice, trees with and without hibernation, cancel, close, three reopens, `cells`, `preludecheck`, `cellreplay`, `sinkreplay`, `mapcheck`. What is left of arc_swap is the walk on every `update` and `set` (1.1% and 0.4 to 0.5%) and `compare_and_swap` in `Inbox` (0.3%): a write has to look at every thread, about 1.3 to 2 us beside 13 busy readers against 22 ns alone, so the lever there is fewer writes at the call sites (`executors::State` 1.55% inclusive, `Registry::enqueue_status` 0.85%, the registry's `Set<(String, AgentId)>` 0.5%, `pending_checkpoints` 0.45%), not the cell.
- Ids draw their random bytes from a per-thread kernel read (2026-11-11). Every `uuid_v7`, `uuid_v4`, candidate id and `OwnerId` asked the kernel for 8 to 16 bytes: `getentropy` was 1.05% of a 20,000-agent swarm's samples over a whole run (uuid inclusive 1.09%), almost all system time, with ten workers queueing on the kernel's generator. `nanocode_platform::fill_random` now serves a request shorter than 256 bytes from a per-thread buffer that one `getentropy` call fills; 256 bytes is the most `getentropy(2)` returns per call, which is where the size comes from. Bytes are copied out once and zeroed in the buffer, never handed out twice; a request of 256 bytes or more and a thread whose locals are already destroyed go straight to the kernel, so every byte still comes from the kernel. `uuid_v4` is built from `fill_random` on native as it already was on WASM, and `OwnerId::new` uses `nanocode_platform::uuid_v7` on both targets instead of `uuid::Uuid::now_v7` natively (which also took the uuid crate's shared v7 context lock); `nanocode-durability-core` no longer depends on `uuid` (one line out of `Cargo.lock`). Measured with output/durability-ledger, 20,000 agents on JSONL, `sample` at 1 ms: `getentropy` 1.05% -> 0.08% in a 9 s window and 1.05% -> 0.16% over the whole run, uuid inclusive 1.09% -> 0.13 to 0.23%; system CPU of three interleaved runs 4.2/4.4/4.0 s at master against 3.8/4.0/3.6 s with this and the three sync changes below, user CPU not resolved by this change alone (40.4/41.6/41.3 s before, 40.9/41.8/41.4 s after). `jsbench` `text('ok')`: 44 to 46 us -> 42 to 43 us a cell and half the system time (each cell seeds `Math.random`). Left as they are: `AttachmentRouter` draws a `uuid::Uuid::new_v4` per session in `route_workspaces` (0.02 to 0.17% of the samples, in the tool-assembly code) and `gzip_padded` asks for 259 bytes, which is two kernel calls as before. A process that forks and keeps running Rust in the child would share the unread bytes of the forking thread's buffer; nothing in the workspace does (`pre_exec` and `fork` are not used).

- djs: matchAll, Array.from and Date timestamps skip their bytecode, and atob decodes bytes (2026-11-11). What was left above QuickJS after the two passes above and is the builtins' own. String.prototype.matchAll ran three builtin-language frames before its first match (the `g` flag check through the flags getter, RegExp.prototype[@@matchAll], a RegExpCreate with a flags string): a `@fast` entry makes the iterator directly for a pristine global RegExp whose @@matchAll is the original (now an `@intrinsic`, so the entry can check it), over a copy of the RegExp that shares its program (`regexp::copy`). Array.from of a dense array, or of a string's code points, into a fresh Array copies in one `%ArraySliceDense` instead of a Get and a CreateDataProperty per element in bytecode (only for %Array% itself: another constructor's result keeps the loop, whose failures must throw). `@fast` entries for Date.now, Date.prototype.getTime and toISOString. A match array's captures are collected on the stack (up to 8 groups) instead of a Vec. atob decodes whole groups of four digits straight from a one-byte string's bytes and hands the rest (white space, padding, a partial group) to the general decoder. Measured through `CodeModeRuntime` (us per benchmark run, before -> after, QuickJS in brackets): matchAll over 2000 lines 13621 -> 9003 (5423); Array.isArray + Array.from(words) x5000 10867 -> 4688 (4397); `[...str]` + Array.from(str) x2000 9986 -> 5148 (3791); btoa+atob of 62 KB x50 15543 -> 10660 (6010); `d.toISOString()` x20000 on one Date 7822 -> 5333. - djs's String and RegExp builtins run as leaves, and a replacer function gets one frame (2026-11-11). Against QuickJS the `strings` cell was 3.3x slower (28 ms against 8.5 ms). Sampling djs-cli on one microbenchmark at a time (`sample` at 1 ms, `selff.py`/`treef.py`) showed neither the regexp engine nor the string code: `Exec::run_hot` was 37-67% of every loop, because each String method without a `@fast` entry, and all of RegExp.prototype[@@replace] with a function, ran as a builtin-language bytecode frame: `'x'.startsWith('y')` 417 ns where the `@fast` `indexOf` is 92 ns, and replace(regex, fn) 1.6 us a match (a match array, a captures array, an args array and a CallWithArray per match, all in bytecode). What changed, all in `crates/patches/djs`: (1) `builtins/fast.rs` has `@fast` entries for startsWith, endsWith, lastIndexOf, codePointAt, localeCompare, concat, toLowerCase/toUpperCase and the locale forms, trim/trimStart/trimEnd, substr, replace and replaceAll with a string pattern and a string template (GetSubstitution as pieces), Array.prototype.reverse and concat over dense arrays. (2) `FastFn::metered`: entries that run the regexp matcher, for RegExp.prototype.test/exec, %RegExpStringIteratorPrototype%.next and String.prototype.match/search/split/replace/replaceAll with a pristine RegExp (and, for replace, a string template). Such an entry takes at most `FAST_STEPS` = 16,384 matcher steps (about 50 us at 3 ns a step), charges them to the run's fuel afterwards as the other run-to-completion leaves do, and declines a longer match with nothing charged, so the builtin runs it and suspends as before. The first version drew from the remaining fuel and declined when it ran out; upstream's `vm::tests::budgets_with_collections_and_suspended_regexps` caught that (the state after a budget depended on how the fuel was sliced), which is why the bound is a constant that depends on the RegExp and the string alone. (3) RegExp.prototype[@@replace] with a function on a pristine RegExp: `%RegExpMatchSpans` (suspendable like `%RegExpSplitRaw`) finds every match, `%EachDense` mode 9 calls the replacer with (matched, position, string) in one reused frame while it returns strings (a non-string result goes back to the builtin for ToString, so the order of user-visible conversions is the spec's), a RegExp with capture groups gets its arguments from `%RegExpReplaceArgs` and CallWithArray, and `%RegExpReplaceJoin` writes the result once. lastIndex, `this`, the arguments and the call order are as the spec's loop has them. (4) The pristine-RegExp check (`builtins/regexp.rs::pristine`, moved out of the interpreter) reads %RegExp.prototype%'s properties from remembered entry slots (a static hint per property, validated by key on every read) instead of fifteen table searches and an `own_keys` Vec: it was 270 ns a call. The metered entries reuse one matcher state per heap (`Heap::regexp_state`, kept up to 4 KiB) instead of a malloc and free a match. toLowerCase/toUpperCase of ASCII and localeCompare of one-byte strings read the string in place. (5) The vendored tree gains what regenerates it: `builtins/*.ts`, `builtins/intrinsics.d.ts`, `crates/djs-bgen` and `scripts/{bgen.sh,gen-intrinsics.py}` (`cd crates/patches/djs && scripts/bgen.sh --check` passes; `python3 scripts/gen-intrinsics.py` rewrites the intrinsic table). Edits outside the text files, kept minimal: `interp/run/fastpath.rs` (try_fast_call passes `&mut self.fuel`), `interp/run/each.rs` (mode 9, about 30 lines), `interp/run/json_regexp.rs` (the new leaves; `regexp_pristine` delegates), `heap/mod.rs` (the scratch field), `heap/object.rs` (`only_own_key`), `bytecode/intrinsics.rs` (regenerated: +7 leaves, +3 `@intrinsic` builtins). Per benchmark run (`SCRIPT=... jsbench qjs 1 3 x`, the difference of 12 and 2 repetitions in one cell, us; djs before -> after, QuickJS in brackets): replace(/[aeiou]/g, fn) over 2000 lines 35611 -> 7896 (7810); replace(regex, string) 3363 -> 1839 (6214); non-global replace 7353 -> 1164 (1556); replace(string, string) 3531 -> 928 (860); replaceAll(string) 13739 -> 1933 (1811); match(/g) 12391 -> 2164 (2853); search 7534 -> 2170 (2062); regex test 2608 -> 1600 (1820); regex split 3836 -> 2188 (5685); split-reverse-join 4359 -> 2064 (2482); startsWith 9075 -> 1803 (1304); endsWith 6984 -> 1563 (965); toUpperCase 5710 -> 2604 (4413); localeCompare sort of 2000 lines 33274 -> 5960 (31468); slice().reverse().concat() 40992 -> 3668 (6765).
