The psh-vfs work reported it from a WebAssembly profile (`Counter::feed` 31% of `find src -type f -exec cat {} + | wc -l`); natively it was 6.7% of that pipeline's samples and most of its user time. Without `-w`, `-m` or `-L`, `Counter::feed_lines` adds the chunk's length and its count of newline bytes; `wc` without options and the other counts take the old path. Upstream delta: psh-utils wc.rs. Measured (ab.py, user+system CPU of interleaved `psh -c` runs, 24 each): the find, cat and wc pipeline over 2,000 files 85.9 ms before, 73.3 ms after (user 28.9 to 12.9 ms; bash with BSD tools 96 ms); `grep -rn needle src | wc -l` 80.9 to 74.4 ms; find and rg unchanged. The output of `wc -l`, `wc -c`, `wc -lc` on files, a pipe, a missing file and invalid UTF-8 is byte for byte what it was.
- 2026-11-11: **A psh subshell shares its parent's variables instead of copying them.** Every pipeline stage, `( … )` and `$( … )` is a vproc that started as a copy of its parent, variables included: a String and a value to allocate per variable and, when the subshell ends, to free. A sample of `for i in $(seq 1 500); do x=$(echo $i); done` had 27.7% in `Vp::subshell` (the table's clone) and 19.3% in dropping the subshell. `Vars` is two layers: `base`, a table shared by reference with the vprocs a vproc came from and the ones made from it and never changed while shared, and `own`, what the vproc changed since (a variable it set, or a mark for one it unset), found through an index, so every lookup is one hash and `get_mut` and `entry` no longer look twice. `exec::enter` settles the parent first (`own` moves into `base`, in place unless a subshell made earlier still holds it), so the subshell starts with a reference and copies only the variables it changes; `enter_shared` is for the one caller that only has the vproc shared, and `Shell::start` settles before it keeps the copy for a cancelled run. An assignment to a variable without a nameref, readonly, integer or case attribute skips `prepare_value`, which would return the value as it is. Upstream delta: psh-engine vars.rs (Vars), exec.rs (enter, enter_shared), state.rs (assign_with, assign_target), util.rs (one caller), lib.rs (start). Measured (ab.py, user+system CPU of interleaved `psh -c` runs, 18 each): 500 command substitutions 9.22 ms before, 6.22 ms after (bash 5.3.9 441 to 487 ms); the arithmetic loop 23.46 and 22.98 ms, 2,000 string appends 8.16 and 7.96 ms, `cd src && ls | sort | head -3` 4.23 and 4.21 ms. The first version, with the changed variables in a second map, cost the loop 3% (two lookups in `get_mut`) and was replaced by the index before it was committed. With all of today's changes, `psh -c` against bash 5.3.9 and upstream e5f136e (CPU ms, medians of 12): loop 47.65, 80.12, 22.88; substitutions 487, 9.86, 7.51; appends 53.25, 20.84, 8.61; find, cat and wc 96.3, 87.5, 83.7; grep -r 172.9, 81.1, 75.8; cut, sort and uniq 632.9, 125.1, 115.2; sed 533.9, 415.8, 400.7; jq 104.9, 65.8, 64.5; sort 85.5, 23.4, 22.2; echo 5.09, 3.90, 3.86; view 10.91, 4.52, 4.08; awk 294, 256, 264 and find 18.1, 12.8, 13.7 (unchanged within noise); rg 124.2, 139.9, 129.1.
- 2026-11-11: **`nc --shell psh` runs the agent's commands in the psh built into the binary; the default stays the system's shells.** nanocode links the vendored psh (crates/patches/psh/crates/psh) and serves it from its own executable: `nanocode psh-shell ARGS` is `psh ARGS`, answered in `run_with` before the command line is parsed. `--shell psh` (`NANOCODE_SHELL=psh`, global, so a session, `exec` and a hand take it) calls `nanocode_home::shell::choose(nanocode_psh::shell())`; `--shell system`, the default, is the machine's bash and the user's login shell as before; off Unix `--shell psh` is refused. `PSH_UTILS_OFF=all` in the environment keeps the machine's own find, grep, sed and the like under psh. Why not the default, with the measurements behind each: (1) what was compared is psh against bash on commands written for bash: 698 of 727 agent-shaped cases print what the machine's bash prints (12 of them but for the shell's name in a message) and 724 with the machine's utilities; the 26 between are psh's GNU-dialect utilities against macOS's BSD ones (`wc -l` without padding, `ls` of a missing file exiting 2, `sed -i` and `head -n -4` working where macOS's fail), which is a change of what models see on a Mac and is the owner's call; (2) `exec_command` promises the user's login shell: zsh or bash read the user's startup files and psh reads none (`-l` is accepted and ignored), so a PATH set in `.zprofile` is not there unless the Hand already has it; (3) upstream's own numbers on macOS are 91.7% of the Oils cases and 88.7% of brush's, so about one shell-language corner in ten (declare, trap, signals, type) still differs from bash 5.3 without saying so; (4) nothing here ran on Linux beyond `cargo check`; (5) a warm shell served by the 34.7 MB nanocode costs 7.0 ms of CPU to start (`--version`, 40 interleaved runs) against 3.3 ms for the 12.7 MB psh program, 4.8 ms for Homebrew's bash and 7.0 ms for nix's, so on a machine with a cheap bash psh served by nanocode itself saves wall time and utility processes but not start-up CPU; `Shell::psh(path, vec![])` takes a psh program of its own, which the release does not ship yet. The workspace lock gains psh's dependencies (argument, argument-parser, bigdecimal, crossbeam-deque, crossbeam-epoch, deser-core, deser-json, encoding_rs, encoding_rs_io, grep-matcher, grep-printer from crates/patches/psh/third_party through `[patch.crates-io]`, grep-regex, grep-searcher, ignore, jaq-core, multiversion_no_op, rust_decimal, termcolor, typed-arena and the five psh crates), and three crates move to the minimums psh declares: globset 0.4.19 to 0.4.21, libc 0.2.186 to 0.2.191, regex-automata 0.4.16 to 0.4.18; bstr gains its regex-automata dependency. `cargo check --offline` had also moved itertools for two alloy crates and getrandom for tempfile; those were put back by hand and `--locked` accepts the result. Landed on master on 2026-11-11 together with the virtual-filesystem branch (the two touch psh-engine's exec.rs, lib.rs and util.rs in different functions and merge textually); on the merged tree upstream's `psh-spec -j 4` exits 0 (the vendored sources laid over the full upstream tree with its suites), `cargo test -p psh-engine --lib` passes, psh-wasm builds to 7,095,021 bytes, and the workspace check, clippy and wasm32 checks of nanocode-shell, nanocode-psh, nanocode-home and nanocode-process are clean. A release `nanocode` with psh linked is 74,891,008 bytes against 65,670,976 before. The 15 workloads of output/psh-bench through `nanocode psh-shell -c` print what Homebrew's bash 5.3 prints in 9; the other 6 differ only in the padding of `wc -l` and `uniq -c` counts (psh's GNU dialect against macOS's BSD tools). A live `nc --shell psh exec -m claude-haiku-5-5` session ran its three Bash commands in psh (`psh 5.3.9(1)-release`, `sort is a psh utility`).
- 2026-11-11: **The warm psh runs wholly on its engine thread.** `psh --warm` read its command on the main thread, handed it to the engine thread and waited there for the result: two thread switches around every command, which cost little on an idle machine and a scheduler's turn each on a busy one. The engine thread now reads the configuration, writes the ready NUL, reads the command, catches the signals, runs the script and ends the process (`std::process::exit` once the shell is dropped); the main thread starts it, blocks the signals a script may trap in itself, so that only the engine thread takes them from its start as in the standalone shell (one that arrives while the shell waits still ends the process), and waits. Upstream delta: psh/src/lib.rs (`warm`, `warm_shell`). Measured on 2026-11-11 at load average 300 to 380 with output/psh-path/launchers.sh (`echo hi` through `run_bash`, 60 ms before each command, 10 interleaved rounds of 60 commands per launcher): the 10th percentile of a round was lower with this build in 9 rounds of 10 (0.80 ms against 0.92 ms, medians of the rounds; nix's bash 0.89 ms) and the median 2.27 ms against 2.49 ms (bash 1.91 ms at 10.1 ms of CPU a command, psh 4.6). Measured and left out: starting the signal watcher thread while the shell waits (handlers installed when the command arrives) gave 0.96 ms p10 and 3.15 ms median in the same run, worse than without it, and was reverted. What is left on a busy machine is that psh is ready only once a second thread has been scheduled, where bash is one thread: the median wait is still above bash's; running the engine on the main thread needs a 20 MiB main stack (a linker flag on macOS, the stack limit on Linux) and is not done.
- 2026-11-11: **psh expands a value without writing it out as a pattern, reads its pipes as slices, and opens an operand without a stat first.** Three places a sample pointed at. `s="$s$i,"` in a loop spent 69% of its samples in `pattern::escape`: every quoted expansion was also written out as a glob pattern, a byte at a time, though an assignment value, a here-string, a `case` word and an arithmetic word (`expand_single`) only ever use the text. `Fields` has a `text_only` mode that `expand_single` sets, `escape` copies the text between two pattern characters in one piece, and `joined` hands over a single field's text instead of copying it. `find src -type f -exec cat {} + | wc -l` spent 11.6% in `PipeReader::poll_read`, which moved a pipe's bytes out of its ring one at a time (it copies the ring's two runs as slices; a here-document's pipe takes its bytes as a Vec), and 14.4% in `stat`: `Input::open` asked whether each operand is a directory before opening it. It now opens first and asks the open file (`UtilFile::kind`, from `HostFile::kind`), and looks the path up again only where the host cannot tell or the open fails. That puts a contract on hosts: one whose `open` succeeds on a directory answers `FileKind::Dir` or `None` from `HostFile::kind`. Upstream delta: psh-engine expand.rs (Fields), pattern.rs (escape), pipe.rs, util.rs (UtilFile::kind); psh-utils common.rs (Input::open). Measured (ab.py, user+system CPU of interleaved `psh -c` runs): 2,000 string appends 18.7 ms before, 8.3 ms after (12 runs each; bash 5.3.9 51.3 ms); the find, cat and wc pipeline over 2,000 files 93.8 ms before, 82.8 ms after (32 runs each; bash with BSD tools 96 to 104 ms). Measured and left out: rg stays at ripgrep's CPU (129 ms against 124; its sample is open, read and close in the kernel and worker threads waiting on a mutex); awk is unchanged (264 ms against bash's 294; 40% of its samples are malloc and free of one Rc per record and field, which is a change to the awk interpreter's values); `sed … | tail -1` uses 401 ms of CPU against 534 but more wall time than bash's two processes, because a psh pipeline of utilities runs on one thread.
- 2026-11-11: **A host can make psh the shell of model commands; it runs as a process started ahead of each command, and what psh lacks goes to the system bash before anything runs.** Claude's `Bash` ran every command in the machine's bash and Codex's `exec_command` in the user's login shell. `nanocode_home::shell::choose(Shell::psh(program, arguments))`, called once before the runtime is built, makes `bash_shell()` and `default_user_shell()` answer psh (its name for the model is `bash`, since that is what it speaks; `system_bash_shell()` is the machine's); a shell the model names itself is still the system's. `nanocode-psh` (crates/integrations/psh, builds for wasm32 too) holds what a Hand needs without linking the shell: `ARGUMENT` (`psh-shell`), `shell()` for a host whose own executable serves psh, `serve_if_requested(psh::run)` for that executable's `main`, and `plan(script)`. Why a process and not the engine inside the Hand (0.12 ms for `echo` against about 0.9): nothing in this repository confines a command (nanocode-sandbox has no dependents; a host confines the Hand, supplies Claude's `SandboxBashExecutor`, or wraps a program with `run::Runner`), so the one thing that keeps every confinement and every promise of the tools as it is today is that the shell stays a spawned program: its own process group for the STOP-then-KILL of a timeout, Ctrl-C and `terminate_all`, pipes, an exit status from wait, a crash that is its own. The warm pool (integrations/process/src/warm.rs) keeps `PROGRAM ARGUMENTS --warm [-l]` processes exactly as it keeps `bash -c LOADER` ones (same lanes, depth and eviction; no startup files to fingerprint, since psh reads none) and writes each its session variables and script; the 4 KiB limit of the bash loader does not apply. A PTY, a script with a NUL or an empty pool start `PROGRAM ARGUMENTS -c SCRIPT`. `export_secrets_after_profile` is skipped for psh (no profile can clobber them). `plan` parses the script with psh's parser and reads psh's classification: a script that does not parse (with and without extglob), `select`, `coproc`, the builtins psh stops at (`bg`, `fg`, `bind`, `compgen`, `complete`, `compopt`, `fc`, `suspend`), `enable -f`, `set -r`, `set -o posix`, a here-document that ends with the script (bash warns and adds the newline, psh does neither) and, off Linux, `kill` or `trap` with a signal number outside the ones Linux and BSD share (psh numbers signals as Linux does) are `Plan::System(reason)`: `nanocode_process::delegated` then runs the command in the system bash and records the reason in a `tracing::info!` event; with no system bash it runs in psh, which prints `NAME: not supported yet` and exits 2. What cannot be seen in the text (`eval "$x"`) gets that loud stop at run time. Measured on 2026-11-11 (M-series Mac, load average 250 to 380, output/psh-path: `run_bash` and `ShellSessions::execute`, one process per shell, interleaved, 60 ms before each command; CPU is the Hand's plus its children's): `echo hi` 0.89 ms p10 and 1.91 ms median with nix's bash 5.3 at 10.1 ms of CPU a command, 0.92 and 2.49 ms with psh at 4.8 ms; `sed -n 40,60p f | head -5` 9.4 and 17.6 ms at 16.5 ms of CPU against 1.1 and 2.6 ms at 5.2; `cd src && ls | sort | head -3` 12.6 and 18.3 ms at 19.7 against 1.3 and 2.8 ms at 5.9. The 727 agent-shaped cases of psh's suite through both: 686 identical in status, stdout and stderr, 12 differ in the shell's name in front of a message, 26 in what macOS's BSD tools and psh's utilities print, 3 in a job notice; with `PSH_UTILS_OFF=all` 712, 12 and 3. Eleven behaviour scenarios print the same lines for bash and psh in five runs; the order of stdout and stderr lines in `exec_command`'s output varies for both. psh is not the default: see the `--shell` entry for what blocks it. Not done: the choice is one per process (a second runtime in the same process cannot differ), and `nc-lite` neither serves nor chooses psh.
- 2026-11-11: **The psh program is a library, has a start-ahead mode, and its utilities have an off switch.** A host that keeps shells waiting pays the start of a program before a command, not during it; nanocode does that for bash with a loader script (integrations/process/src/warm.rs). crates/patches/psh/crates/psh is now `src/lib.rs` (what `main.rs` was) plus a three-line program: `psh::run(args)` is what `psh ARGS` does, so a host's own executable can serve the shell. `psh --warm [OPTIONS]` (Unix) closes every inherited descriptor above 2 (`psh_os::unix::close_inherited`: std on macOS makes pipes inheritable first and close-on-exec after, so a process spawned at that moment from another thread gets the write end of another command's output, and a process that waits would hold it; the first run of the comparison harness hung two of 727 commands for 40 s this way, the bash loader closes them for the same reason), reads the configuration from the process, writes one NUL to stdout and reads its command from stdin to the end of file: `NAME=VALUE` and a NUL per variable to export, one more NUL, the script. It then runs as `psh OPTIONS -c SCRIPT` with those variables and the null device as stdin; nothing on stdin ends it; signals keep their default action while it waits. `PSH_UTILS_OFF` (`all` or a list of names; `psh_utils::OFF_VAR`, `off_names`) turns psh's own utilities off so those names run the system's programs, and like `PSH_UTILS_FORCE` it is taken out of the environment. Upstream delta: psh/src/lib.rs (new, from main.rs: `run`, `warm`, `script`, `run_script`, `finish`, `Signals::catch(control)`), psh/src/main.rs, psh-utils/src/lib.rs, psh-os/src/unix/mod.rs, and the formatting of one line of psh-engine vars.rs. Timestamps inside `psh -c 'echo hi'` (release, the quiet runs of five): catching signals 45 µs, the engine thread's start about 100 µs, the configuration 65 µs, `Shell::new` 65 µs, the script 95 µs, dropping the shell 55 µs. Starting the program (startup.py, user+system CPU, 60 to 80 interleaved runs): /usr/bin/true 2.0 ms, an empty Rust program 2.5 ms, `/bin/bash -c :` (3.2) 2.5 ms, `psh --version` 3.2 ms, `psh -c :` 3.7 ms, Homebrew's bash 5.3 4.8 ms, nix's bash 5.3 7.0 ms. Measured and left out: a fat-LTO, one-codegen-unit, stripped build of psh is 8.2 MB instead of 12.7 and starts in 3.59 ms instead of 3.73 (awk 221 ms instead of 245); that is a profile for whoever builds the program, not a source change.
- 2026-11-11: **psh's variable table hashes with FxHash, copies a name only for a new variable, and rewrites PIPESTATUS in place.** After the arithmetic change a sample of the same loop still had 7% rebuilding `PIPESTATUS` (a new BTreeMap and Vec after every command), 7% in SipHash for variable lookups, 6% in `Vars::entry`, which copied the name even when the variable existed, and 9% each in `Vp::var` and `Vp::target`, which copy the name to follow namerefs that are almost never there. `vars::NameHasher` (FxHash: the keys are the script's own names, so a keyed hash defends nothing) hashes `Vars` and the arithmetic cache; `entry` allocates only for a new name; `Vp::var` and `assign_with` take a name that is no nameref as its own target; prefix assignments borrow the name from the source; `set_pipestatus` rewrites the digits of the elements it has when their indexes are the ones it would write. Upstream delta: psh-engine vars.rs, state.rs (var, assign_with, assign_target, Code::arith's map type), exec.rs (set_pipestatus, prefix_assigns). Measured (ab.py, 12 interleaved runs each): the 20,000-iteration loop 33.9 ms before, 24.2 ms after (bash 5.3.9 44.7 ms); 2,000 string appends 22.6 to 19.5 ms. psh-spec passes as before. Measured and left out: mimalloc as the allocator of the psh program took the loop from 24.6 to 17.7 ms and jq from 64 to 50 ms at 0.24 ms more to start; nanocode links mimalloc already, so a psh served by nanocode gets it, and a psh program of its own is the integrator's build to decide.
- 2026-11-11: **psh parses an arithmetic word that is literal text once, and reads and writes a counter where it is.** The vendored psh (crates/patches/psh) ran `s=0; for ((i=0;i<20000;i++)); do s=$((s+i)); done; echo $s` 1.6 times slower than bash 5.3. A sample of the loop (macOS `sample`, 3,102 samples of the engine thread) had 37% in the arithmetic evaluator, 10% of it parsing the same text again, and 22% expanding the three arithmetic words through the field splitter to the text they already were; `arith::Env::get` and `set` copied each variable's name and value on every access and assigned through the general path. `psh-engine` now keeps, per parsed chunk (`state::Code::arith`, by the word's span), the expression of each arithmetic word made only of literal parts without a `~` (which may be a tilde prefix): `((…))`, `for ((…))` and `$((…))` skip expansion and parsing after the first round, and a word with an expansion or one that does not parse takes the old path, which reports the error. `psh-syntax`'s `ArithEnv` has a provided `load` returning `ArithValue::{Unset, Num, Text}` (`plain_decimal` is public), which the engine answers from the variable in place when it is no nameref, not computed and not `BASHPID`; `set` writes the digits into the buffer of a scalar that is no nameref, not readonly and not computed (the integer and case attributes change nothing for a decimal). Upstream delta: psh-engine arith.rs, exec.rs (arith_command), expand.rs (Part::Arith), state.rs (Code::arith) and the six `Code { … }` constructors (lib.rs, exec.rs, expand.rs, builtins/eval.rs, set.rs, declare.rs); psh-syntax arith_eval.rs, lib.rs. Measured with /tmp/swarm-psh/ab.py (user+system CPU of `SHELL -c CMD` from wait4, shells interleaved, 12 runs each, load average 130 to 330): 73.6 ms before, 36.0 ms after, bash 5.3.9 44.3 ms. psh-spec passes as before (oils 2303/2511, brush 2814/3171, agent 725/727, utils 1001/1001).
- 2026-11-11: **A hosted call's channel is one end of a socket pair that the launcher hands to the program as descriptor 3.** `run::Runner` gave a call with a `Host` a unix socket bound in its socket directory, mounted at `<root>/host.sock` under bubblewrap and named by its own path under Landlock. Under Landlock that never worked: `confine`'s seccomp filter allows only IPv4 and IPv6 TCP sockets, so the program's `socket(AF_UNIX)` is refused (pyramid-core's sandbox-landlock harness on Linux 7.0; Pyramid's built-in shell then fell back to a Hand for every command). Now the Runner makes a socket pair, serves its end as before, and the program finds the other at `confine::CHANNEL_DESCRIPTOR` (3), which `Seen` names on both arms for the host's command line. Nothing is bound, mounted or removed for a channel, the seccomp filter is unchanged and nothing new is reachable. Getting the descriptor to the program without widening anything: not `pre_exec`, which makes std `fork` instead of `posix_spawn` (output/forkcost at load 45: a spawn from a process holding 1 GiB takes 0.06 ms with `posix_spawn` and 12 to 16 ms after a `fork`, 72 ms at 3 GiB), and never a descriptor left inheritable in the host process, where any program spawned at that moment would get it too. Instead the child's stdin is the program's end of the pair (std dups it in `posix_spawn`), `confine::channel` sends the read end of the call's input pipe over the pair with `SCM_RIGHTS`, and the launcher (`launch_if_requested`, first argument `tool-channel`) duplicates the socket to descriptor 3, receives the pipe and makes it stdin, then confines itself as before (`tool-sandbox`) or executes bubblewrap, which passes inherited descriptors on. Every descriptor in the host stays close-on-exec, so no other call's program can hold a call's channel. What a host must do: a bubblewrap host now calls `confine::launch_if_requested()` first thing in `main`, as a Landlock host already did, and `Confinement::Bubblewrap` carries the `launcher`; a call without a `Host` is spawned exactly as before. The frames on the channel are unchanged. Linux only, as both confinements are; elsewhere `confine::channel` is unsupported. Checked: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sandbox` natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`; through pyramid-core's `Sandbox` with Pyramid's `runtime.ts` reading the descriptor through `fs`: under bubblewrap /home/ubuntu/dev/harnesses/sandbox-run before and after prints the same 710 lines (a channel session with an echo, a host failure, parts within and beyond the budget, a header that is not JSON) but for the variable that names the channel; under Landlock for real (a rented box, Linux 7.0.0-42, /home/ubuntu/dev/harnesses/sandbox-landlock) the hosted cases that failed with `EPERM` pass with a stand-in program and with Bun 1.4.4, every other case and every refusal the harness probes is as before, two hosted calls at once each get their own host's answers and hold no descriptor but stdio and 3, and Pyramid's hand-free workspace steps, which started a Hand before, run in the sandbox.
- A cell's nested calls move into its reply metadata instead of being copied twice (2026-11-11). `claude_tools::code_reply` built the `_nanocode_code` metadata with `json!`: every nested call's input, structured result and identifiers were rebuilt as a new `Value` tree through the serializer, and the finished array was serialized into a tree a second time when `json!` placed it in the outer object, after which the originals were dropped: 0.40 to 0.44% of a 20,000-agent swarm's CPU samples, paid by every cell of every Claude session. The reply owns the execution, so each call's `input` and `structured_result` are taken out of it and the objects are assembled as `serde_json::Map` values; the progress observer, which only borrows a call, clones the two values directly instead of going through the serializer. The JSON is the same (the map is ordered by key either way): output/durability-ledger `turns memory x 40 3 4000` writes the same 4,077,560 logical bytes (1,697,350 head, 2,380,210 records) as the build from master. Measured (sampled.sh, inclf.py): `claude_tools::code_reply` 0.44% -> 0.11%, `Progress::update` 0.22% -> 0.15%. Three interleaved 20,000-agent runs do not resolve it in user CPU (38.6, 39.3, 38.9 s before; 39.0, 38.6, 40.2 s after, with the load rising from 230 to 250 during the set). Left as it is: `ClaudeToolReply::metadata` and `ClaudeNestedToolUpdate::Completed` are still `Value` trees that the turn serializes again; a typed payload there belongs to the turn path. Landed on master by cherry-pick over `e853b6bda`; rechecked there (output/durability-ledger: `cells`, `preludecheck`, `cellreplay`, `sinkreplay`, the 3,000-agent matrix on memory, JSONL, SQLite and rows, kill and resume, kill twice, trees with and without hibernation, cancel, close, reopen; workspace `cargo check`, clippy and the wasm32 check of the touched crates): three interleaved 20,000-agent runs at load 220 to 240, the five lifecycle commits together, user CPU 40.1, 39.8, 40.4 s before and 39.1, 38.1, 38.4 s after.
- Owned agents are a keyed map, not a vector copied on every adopt and release (2026-11-11). `Ownership` kept the agents a runtime owns (those built through the runtime or spawned through an SDK handle; subagent children are tracked elsewhere) as an `ArcSwap<Vec<(usize, WeakAgent)>>` that `adopt` and `forget` rebuilt in full, cloning every `WeakAgent` (eight reference counts each): with 100 live children each spawn and each shutdown copied 100 entries, 25 KB and 24 KB of allocation per child and 4.5% of lifebench's CPU samples, growing linearly with the number alive, so N SDK-spawned agents cost N squared. `owned` is now an `Atom<nanocode_sync::Map<usize, (usize, WeakAgent)>>` keyed by the owner key with the adoption order beside the agent; `adopt` and `forget` touch one path of the trie, and dead entries are pruned when the size reaches a power of two, as `RunnerAgents` does. `shutdown` still stops the most recently adopted agent first (it scans for the highest order, which is what the old loop cost per step anyway) and `Ownership::agent` still answers the earliest adopted live agent of a session. Measured with output/durability-ledger `lifebench memory x 4000 100`: the two `Vec<(usize, WeakAgent)>` sites (24,879 B and 24,443 B per child) are gone from the allocation trace; with the three commits before it shutdown is 39 -> 22 allocations and 32 KB -> 5.7 KB per child. The swarm does not exercise this path (its children go through `Router::tracked_one`), so the 20,000-agent numbers do not move with it.
- A tool set's derived catalog is built once and shared, and a session enters the executors lazily (2026-11-11). Building a child's tools was 1.93% of a 20,000-agent swarm (the tools factory under `ClaudeBuilder::build`, 2.31%) and 63 us of a 380 us child in lifebench, most of it recomputing what every child of one recipe computes identically. (1) `ToolRegistry::catalog` interns, by the registry's definitions, exposures and exclusions (compared by pointer first: descriptions and schemas are shared `Arc`s), the registered Code Mode definitions, their sorted order, their names and normalised names, and the nested metadata; live catalogs are found through a static list of weak references, as the nested-metadata cache already was. `model_specs` no longer clones, normalises and sorts every definition twice per agent, and a cell start no longer rebuilds the definition list to validate cached metadata when no provider offers definitions; children of one recipe get the same `Arc<[Value]>` metadata, so the cell-tools and journal-catalog caches downstream hit by pointer. Every mutator of the registry resets the cached catalog. (2) `ToolsBuilder::build` collects the definitions once and checks names by reference; a name that is already a JavaScript identifier is not copied. (3) `SpawnAgent::definition` is cached by the registry's policy pointer instead of formatting the policy's `Debug` text on each of three calls per agent, and the fixed subagent tools are memoized by their static names instead of an allocated key. (4) The Claude `exec` description is cached by the source description's pointer: 44 KB was formatted per agent only to find the shared copy. (5) `RoutingCatalog::wrap` hands the router the definition the registry already holds, and a runtime's process-route id (a v4 UUID, one `getentropy` call per agent) is generated by `ProcessRoutes::runtime_id` when a process session first needs it; the stored format is unchanged. (6) `Tools::for_session` and `for_backend` keep the session and backend on the tool set and the runtime's `CodeModeExecutors` handle is bound to them (`for_session`, previous entry), so the process-wide executors map is no longer written twice per session at build. Measured with output/durability-ledger, 20,000 agents on JSONL, three interleaved runs at load 230 to 310, this and the two commits before it: user CPU 40.6, 41.2, 39.7 s -> 39.2, 39.1, 38.1 s; max RSS 1594, 1661, 1586 MB -> 1564, 1550, 1495 MB; by sample share `ClaudeBuilder::build` 2.31% -> 1.10%, the tools factory 1.93% -> 0.86%, `NativeToolRuntime::with_tools` 0.39% -> 0.13%, `route_workspaces` 0.25% -> 0.05%, `model_specs` 0.27% -> 0.05%, `add_shared_tools` 0.24% -> 0.13%, `shared_nested_tool_metadata` 0.31% -> 0.10%, `Tools::for_session` + `for_backend` 0.33% -> 0.06%. lifebench (`LIFE_SINGLE=1 lifebench memory x 4000 100`, three interleaved runs): 278, 244, 226 us -> 219, 200, 208 us of CPU per child created. `turns memory x 40 3 4000` writes the same 4,077,560 logical bytes as master.
- An agent gets a runner notice worker when there is a notice (2026-11-11). `RunnerAgents::register` gave every agent an unbounded channel (a 2,090 B block) and a spawned task that waits for runner status notices, and `unregister` rewrote three process-wide maps (`agents`, `folded`, `code_mode_hosts`) whether or not the session was in them; with no runner connected, which is every subagent of a swarm, none of it is used. The entry in `agents` is now a `Listener { agent, notices: Option<sender> }`; the channel and the worker are created by the first notice (a runner event, or the initial summary when a runner is connected) and installed with one `try_update`, so two notifiers cannot start two workers and the worker is bound to the agent that is in the map. `unregister`, `register` and `code_mode_host` read before they write. A session whose tools are not a Code Mode host is recorded as `false` only when the map is not empty: the lookup falls back to the parent and then to `false`, so the explicit `false` matters only when some session is a host. Measured with output/durability-ledger: `RunnerAgents` 0.68% -> 0.33% of a 20,000-agent swarm's samples (what is left is the one insert and one remove per agent in `agents`); `lifebench memory x 4000 100` (a root, then children spawned through the SDK handle and shut down in batches of 100), with the commits around it: 905 -> 684 allocations and 211 KB -> 124 KB per child created, 39 -> 22 allocations and 32 KB -> 5.7 KB per child shut down. A runner event now creates the channel and task for each live agent that has none (one map update each), which is the work registration used to do up front.
- A session's hand placement is one record, written only when it changes (2026-11-11). `CodeModeExecutors` kept `selections`, `roots`, `backends` and `sessions` as four process-wide copy-on-write maps in one `Atom`, and every session's start (`link`, `bind_session`), every cell (`record`), every turn end (`settle_cells`) and every session's end (`forget`, four removes) rewrote it: 1.42% of a 20,000-agent swarm's CPU samples under `executors::State`, of which `settle_cells` 0.46% cleared nothing and `record` 0.15% recorded nothing. A session's root, backend, touched hands and running cells are now one `Session` entry in one map (`selections` stays apart: it is written by the user, not per session). `record`, `settle_cells` and `forget` read first and write only when something would change; `wait_route` and `touched` read through the guard instead of cloning the state `Arc` (a contended reference count). `CodeModeExecutors::for_session(session, root, backend)` returns a handle bound to one session: its `placement`, `ready_placement`, `wait_route`, `selection` and `call_on` record the session's root and backend inside the same read loop the first time the state is not idle (a hand attached, a selection, a default, a fallback or an awaited replacement), so a runtime with no hands writes nothing per session and a hand attached later still finds the root and backend of sessions that are running. The trait's `link_session` and `bind_session` stay eager. Measured with output/durability-ledger, `AGENTS=20000 MAX_CONCURRENCY=2000 QUEUED=1 ./sampled.sh <name> 4 45 <swarm> run jsonl <dir> "SWARM flat 20000"` then `inclf.py`, master against this and the next two commits: `executors::State` 1.42% -> 0.10%, `settle_cells` 0.46% -> 0.01%, `CodeModeExecutors::forget` 0.39% -> 0.02%, `record` 0.15% -> 0.00%, `NativeToolRuntimeControl::cancel` 0.78% -> 0.31%, `cancel_turn_with_updates` 0.65% -> 0.26%.
- A sqlx host hears how long each batch took (2026-11-11). `PgConnections::ran(operation, took, committed)`, a no-op by default, is called by `SqlxSql` after every batch with the store's name for it (`peek`, `acquire`, `put_records`, `row_state`, `compact`, …), the time from asking for the connection to the answer, and whether it committed. Why: tempoxyz/pyramid-core gives every statement a name and a latency histogram, and since its durable sessions run on `RowStore` through `SqlxSql` (e853b6bda) those statements are nanocode's batches, which the host could not see: `SqlxSql` dropped the operation name. Checked on 2026-11-11 on dev-georgios: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-store-sql`; output/rowcheck `pg` 49 of 49 with a host that counts `ran` calls and prints them per operation.
- RowStore serves a database that several processes share and that holds more states than fit in memory (2026-11-11, for tempoxyz/pyramid-core, whose durable sessions move from a store of its own onto this one; Georgios: "reusing 100% of upstream for durability"). Eight changes, each because that host needs it. (1) The index is per state: a record is stored once in every state that names it, as JSONL stores it once per session file, where one map covered the database and a record any state had written was never written again. A host with 100,000 threads cannot hold every key, a state's dead records cannot be deleted while other states read them out of its pages, and what a root's sessions share already goes through the pool (f2e065514). An unbounded store, the default, still reads the whole index with two statements at its first read; `bounded(keys)` reads a state when something names it and drops the least recently used states past `keys`. A state another process wrote is noticed by its tail's length and page count at `acquire`, by the page count at `put_records`, and by a reload when a read misses or a page is gone; a reload takes effect only if its revision and page count are not behind the index's. (2) `put_records` is implemented: records staged ahead of a commit become a page of their own, written only while the state's page count is the one the index holds, and retried once after a reload. (3) `lent(host)` is the store over a connection a host lends inside its own transaction: it keeps no shared index, since the transaction may roll back, writes a page for a commit that carries records and only moves the head for one that does not, and the shared index learns of the commit as it would of another process's. `nanocode_store_sql::SqlxTransaction` is public for it. (4) `in_schema(name)` places both tables; the statement texts are rendered once per schema and kept. (5) `examine` and `compact` delete what a head no longer reaches, when the dead records weigh at least what stays or a page is not yet packed; `unswept` lists the states whose revision moved since, by `state_rows.swept` (rows format 2); `collect` takes the dead keys from the caller as SqlStore's does. A compaction moves the fence and the page count, so an owner or a staged page from before it is refused and never left naming a deleted record. (6) `packed(codec)`: pages go through a `PageCodec` the host gives (`nanocode_store_sql::Zstd`), and on Postgres `state_pages.body` is `BYTEA` (rows format 3), a packed page being a newline and the codec's bytes; SQLite keeps the page as text, the bytes in base64. A sealed page is now built by the store rather than as `tail || ?` in SQL, guarded by the tail's length. (7) A commit that adds no record leaves the tail column alone, where `tail || ''` rewrote it. (8) The conversion from SqlStore's tables gives every state its own copy of a record several hold. Checked on 2026-11-11 on dev-georgios (output/rowcheck and output/rowbench, their own workspaces; Postgres 18 in Docker and SQLite through a rusqlite `Sql` host in the harness; load 8 to 22). `rowcheck`: 3,000 random steps a seed against a model, two store instances standing for two processes plus reopens, over six states (acquire, commit with fresh records, repeated ones and other states' records, put_records, collect, examine and compact, lent commits that commit or roll back, reads of held and absent keys, list_records, owner and peek after every step, a fresh instance reading every state whole at the end): 24 of 24 seeds on SQLite and 48 of 48 on Postgres (half in a named schema, half bounded to 40 keys, a third packed with zstd), and the conversion of five SqlStore states that share 12 records, each read whole and one continued. `rowbench`, the build before against this one, interleaved, 200 states of 30 commits of 3 fresh records of 600 B plus one record every commit of every state repeats: Postgres WAL 42.6 to 43.0 KB a state before and 41.9 to 42.5 KB after, the tables 6.5 MB before and 6.9 MB after three runs (the repeated record once per state instead of once); SQLite 44.7 MB before and 47.0 MB after, writes 0.55 to 0.57 s both; a new store's first commit on a database of 600 states 0.027 s before and 0.002 s after. 100,000 states of 20 records (`seed-scale.sql`): before, a new store's first commit takes 1.3 s and the process holds 462 to 635 MB; unbounded now, the first read loads the index and it holds 535 MB; `bounded(250000)` commits in 0.01 s and holds 13 MB after 2,000 states were read. The conversion of 2,000 SqlStore states holding 668,002 records of 1.18 GB (`seed-big.sql`): 32 to 41 s, 78,000 pages, 1.44 GB of WAL. pyramid-core on this store (its runtime harness against mocks of the Responses and Messages APIs): the model requests of a six-turn session with cells, a handoff mid model call, a subagent handoff and a crash at each of 50 commit points equal those on its own store but for one crash request whose text depends on a race (it differs between two runs of either build); sessions converted from SqlStore's tables, then swept and repacked, continue with the same requests; its measurements are in its NOTES.md. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability-core -p nanocode-durability -p nanocode-store-sql` natively and the first two for wasm32-unknown-unknown.
- 2026-11-11: **`TypedHandler::invalid`: a typed tool can answer arguments that don't decode with the call in hand.** `failed` is synchronous and sees only the error, which is enough for a fixed text. Some of tempoxyz/pyramid's tools do more before they answer such a call: record the failed call on its row, check the turn may still act, or read the raw arguments to say which operation moved. `invalid(input, error, context)` is that hook: it gets the `ToolInput` as sent, the decode error and the `ToolContext`, may await, and returns the `Failure`; its default is `failed(error)`, so existing handlers are unchanged and `failed` still answers every error of a call that ran. Checked on dev-georgios: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-tool-host` natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, no warnings; `output/typed-tools` 10 of 10 (the two new checks: an overriding handler answers from the raw arguments and the call ID after an await, and a handler without one still answers through `failed`).

The typed handler now decodes `Args` from the raw arguments (`ToolInput::decode_json`): `failed` gets that `serde_json::Error` as it is (``missing field `operation` at line 1 column 16``), and freeform input still arrives as a custom error with `ToolInputError`'s text. `FunctionTool::new` and `FunctionHandler` are unchanged: a handler of `Value` still gets a `Value` and `invalid_input`. `FunctionTool::output_schema(schema)` puts a result's schema on the definition, as `#[tool]` does from a function's return type, so Code Mode declares a typed result for a host's stateful tool too; `content_results` keeps its own. For tempoxyz/pyramid-core's tool registry, which builds every Pyramid tool as a `FunctionTool::typed_with_parameters` with the parameters it derives. Checked on dev-georgios: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-tool-host` natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, no warnings; `output/typed-tools` (a typed tool run with arguments that decode, four that don't, each answered with exactly `serde_json::from_str::<Args>`'s error, freeform input, and the definition with and without an output schema): 8 of 8. Its decode of a 3,463-byte argument object, five interleaved rounds of 20,000 at load 12: 1.5 to 2.3 µs through a `Value`, 1.1 to 1.8 µs direct.

- 2026-11-11: **`nanocode_sync::Lanes::bounded`: per-key batches with every bound named and nothing dropped unseen.** nanocode-sync had a `Lanes` whose bounded mode dropped items silently and lost it (9238bf177), then lost the unbounded one for want of a user; tempoxyz/pyramid-core kept its own for the Hand broker's admissions and receipts, and that one moves here with its numbers as arguments. `Lanes::bounded(Bounds { queued, batch, idle, lanes }, refused)` routes each `send(key, item, commit)` to its key's lane: a lane commits what arrived together, at most `batch` at a time and in order, one commit at a time per key, ends after `idle` without an item and is replaced when the key's next item comes (the new lane waits for the old one's last commit); finished lanes are swept once more than `lanes` are known. Both ways an item is turned away are visible: `send` gives the item back when `queued` items already wait for the router, and an item that reaches a lane already holding `batch` goes to `refused`, so the host answers whoever waits on it. `together(batch, commit)` is the commit helper that goes with it: one commit for the batch, and when that fails, one per item, so one bad item fails alone; an item whose own commit returned nothing is `Ok(None)`. Native only, like the other task-owning blocks here (it spawns and uses timers). Checked: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sync` natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`; output/lanes-check on dev-georgios (bounds 64 queued, batches of 8, 200 ms idle): 30 items over 5 keys all commit in key order in batches of at most 8; 200 items sent at once for one key are 8 committed in order, 56 refused by the full lane and 136 handed back by the full queue, none unaccounted; after the idle time the key's next item commits on a new lane; `together` on a failing batch of three answers `Ok(Some)`, the item's own error and `Ok(None)`. pyramid-core's broker runs on it with its bounds unchanged (16,384 queued, 4,096 a batch, 5 s idle, 1,024 lanes).
- 2026-11-11: **`nanocode-observability` maps nanocode's spans to the GenAI conventions, holds a request's spans until its root says whether to keep them, and gives a host its events as lines and its counters by name.** Three pieces a server host needs beside `ObservabilityBuilder`, each from tempoxyz/pyramid-core's `telemetry.rs` with its names turned into arguments; none changes what `ObservabilityBuilder::install` does. `GenAi<E>` wraps a span exporter: `model.call` becomes `chat <model>` with `gen_ai.request.model`, the response id, token counts and the provider (taken from the span, else from the backend crate that emitted it), `tool.call` and `tool.execute` become `execute_tool <name>`, the host's own agent span (`Agent { span, name }`) becomes `invoke_agent <name>`, and the content events nanocode emits when message content is captured (`prompt`, `model.input`, `model.output_item`, `reasoning`, `tool.arguments`, `tool.output`, `tool.panic`) are folded into `gen_ai.input.messages`, `gen_ai.output.messages` and the tool call attributes; every other span and event passes through. `Held<P>` wraps a span processor: spans whose target is one of `Holding::targets` wait until their trace's server root ends, and the trace is exported whole if the root took `slow` or longer, failed, or its trace id is a multiple of `one_in`; otherwise the root's subtree is dropped and whatever else the trace held is exported. A trace whose root does not arrive within `slow` is released, at most `most` spans wait, and without a `Holding` everything passes. `Lines` is a layer that formats an event as `LEVEL target: message field=value` for a host's log function, `Counters` turns the `monotonic_counter.*` fields of `nc_metrics` events into `nanocode_<name>_total` for a host's own metrics, and `Exports` is the filter for what a host exports (spans of the listed targets, content events only when `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT` is true, request spans only when asked). What they count goes to the host through plain functions (`Exported`, `Ended`), because the crate links no metrics library and the names are the host's. The Prometheus listener stays in pyramid-core: it needs `metrics-exporter-prometheus` and axum, which `nc` would then link for nothing, and Cargo features are not allowed here. The crate gains `nanocode-sync` and `imbl` (the held spans are an `Atom` of a `Map` and vectors). Checked on dev-georgios: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-observability` natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` (the crate is empty there); /home/ubuntu/dev/harnesses/telemetry-capture builds pyramid-core's `telemetry::init` and `serve_metrics` before (42fbdbf, its own exporter and processor) and after (on these), emits a turn with model calls of four providers, tool calls, every content kind, slow, failed, fast and rootless request traces, log lines and counter events in three settings (slow request traces with content, all request traces, neither), captures the OTLP trace requests on a local server and scrapes `/metrics`: 61 spans decoded attribute by attribute, the log lines and 445 metric lines, 715 lines in all, identical.

- 2026-11-11: **`nanocode-sandbox` runs a confined program for a host: `run::Runner`.** The crate had the parts (`Bubblewrap`, `confine::Policy`, the allowlisting `Egress`, `Budget`) and tempoxyz/pyramid-core had the code that put them together for its organization tools; that assembly is now here, without the names. A `Runner` is a `Confinement` (`Bubblewrap { bwrap, root, work }`, where what the program reads is mounted under `root` and its scratch directory at `work`, or `Landlock { launcher }`, where it reads the host's paths in place), a scratch directory, a socket directory it creates and removes, the proxy's `Reach`, the `Caps` on what comes back and the `Budget`. `Runner::run(Call, compose)` makes the call's own scratch directory and proxy (a unix socket bound into the mount namespace, or a loopback port the Landlock policy allows), builds the confined command from the call's program and `reads`, and hands `compose` the `Seen` (`Mounted` or `InPlace`: where each read, the scratch directory, the proxy and the host socket appear to the program) so the host adds its arguments and environment; nothing about the program's command line or variable names is decided here. It writes `input` to stdin, keeps stdout up to `Caps::output` and the last `Caps::errors` bytes of stderr, and answers with one `Ran`: `Exited` with both and the hosts the proxy refused or could not reach, `TimedOut` after `within`, `Overflowed`, or `Stopped` by the budget's watch of the admission the caller passed. A call with a `Host` gets a socket on which the program sends length-prefixed header and body frames and reads a header and the reply's parts; parts are charged to the budget, and a refusal is the header `Host::busy` gives. A channel failure is handed to `Host::failed` when it happens rather than logged here, and the scratch directory, the host socket and, under Landlock, the process group are removed however the call ends. Admission stays with the caller because what counts as a computing call is its policy. Unix only, as the crate is. Checked on dev-georgios (Linux 6.8, so Landlock ABI 6 is absent and only the bubblewrap arm ran; the Landlock arm is built and reviewed, not run): `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sandbox` natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`; /home/ubuntu/dev/harnesses/sandbox-run builds pyramid-core's `Sandbox` before (eec0437, its own runner) and after (on this `Runner`) and drives 16 cases through a program standing where bubblewrap does, which reports its argument vector and environment, the scratch directory and proxy socket, its stdin and a host channel session (an echo, a host failure, parts within and beyond the budget, a header that is not JSON): a plugin directory and a single file, credentials that override `PATH`, declared hosts, describe, garbage with a 70 KB stderr, 5 MiB of output, a refusal, exit 3, stdin closed early, a 30 s timeout and an input too large to admit. The 700 lines each side prints (results, log lines, metrics, what is left in the scratch and socket directories) are identical.

Every host function is synchronous and answered in call order, so tool call ids, events and journal entries are in the order QuickJS produced and an existing cell journal replays. A denied call returns `Tool blocked by host: <reason>; tool was not executed` and a failed hook `PreToolUse hook failed: <error>; tool was not executed`, as Claude's `hooked_handler` words them, as the call's failed result, journaled like any other, with nothing run. Tool search, whose output carries no text, is never asked. Like `before_compaction`, the hook is the root's: a branch's spawner sets none. Only `Deny` is offered, not Claude's `UpdateInput`, because no host needs it yet. Why: tempoxyz/pyramid's turn machine refuses a top-level call while a message the agent read mid-turn has no reply, so a member's steer is answered before the agent goes on; on Claude it does this with `ClaudeToolHooks`, and Codex had no way to. Checked on 2026-11-10: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-codex` natively and `cargo check` for wasm32-unknown-unknown; an out-of-repo harness (output/tool-gate) against a local mock of each provider, whose first response makes two `exec` calls and the hook denies only the first, then one more call: on Codex (HTTPS Responses) through this hook and on Claude (Messages) through `ClaudeToolHooks`, the hook was asked once per call, the denied call's result was the text above and its cell never ran, the call after it ran, and the turn completed, 6 of 6 checks on each. Not checked against the live APIs.

A 100,000-agent run's peak (7.1 to 8.7 GB over four runs of both builds) is set by the agents alive at once and did not move.
- `JsonlStore::flush` saves the index, so a runtime that shut down cleanly opens without replaying its journal (2026-11-10). `Nanocode::shutdown` ends with `StateStore::flush`, which for JSONL was an empty job: the index sidecar was saved only when a journal doubled and when its `Journal` was dropped on the store's worker thread, after the last handle went, which a process that exits right after `shutdown` does not wait for. The 100,000-agent harness left a half-written `.index-*` copy beside an index from 3.9 GB into a 4.8 GB journal, and the next open replayed the rest (`durability.jsonl.recover` 1.4 to 4.4 s under load); a 10,000-agent store 0.31 s. `flush` now runs `Sessions::flush`, which saves the index of every open journal whose index is behind (`Journal::flush_index`, what the drop does), and is awaited by its caller. After it the 10,000-agent store opens in 0.05 s with no replay and no leftover copy, and a finished 100,000-agent tree reopens (store, root session and subagent registry, `reopen.sh`, load 35 to 60) in about 1.3 s where the build before the registry changes took 2.5 to 2.6 s: the index header 0.5 s (170,710 states as 78 MB of JSON, not changed), the root session and the rest of the open 0.3 s, the registry 0.47 s instead of 1.6 to 1.7 s. Loading a state's record block also took a second pass over its keys to note which state first held each one; `decode_records` now hashes each key as it reads it (`durability.jsonl.index.records` for the root's 290,000-record journal state 0.12 to 0.13 s, 0.14 to 0.17 s before). Decoding the message log on every worker was tried and gave nothing (0.44 to 0.77 s against 0.46 to 0.58 s) and is not in. Checked: `jsonlcheck` as in the entry below, 2,000 agents, kill and resume and kill twice of 3,000, a 30x100 tree and three rounds of clean reopens on JSONL.
- The JSONL index keeps a record's key as its 32 bytes (2026-11-10). A state's record map was `HashMap<String, Record>`, and nearly every key is `b3:` or `c:` followed by 64 hex digits: a 24-byte `String` and an 80-byte allocation beside each 56-byte record. `records::RecordMap` keys the map by `RecordKey` (`Blake([u8; 32])`, `Chunk([u8; 32])`, `Text` for anything else, which round-trips unchanged) and takes and gives keys as text, so the index file, the journal and every caller are as they were. Measured with output/durability-ledger `heapdone.sh` (10,000 finished agents, JSONL): the store's live heap 5.42 KB to 4.38 KB an agent and 32.5 to 13.4 allocations an agent, the process's footprint 800 MB to 721 MB; what is left is the table slots themselves (96 bytes a record, tables sized to a power of two). Checked: `jsonlcheck` reads every record of every session of a 10,000-agent store and prints the same count, bytes and key checksum with the saved index, with the index rebuilt from the journal, after `compact` (which relocates every record through the map) and after reopening, and the count matches the journal read by `jsonlcheck.py`; 2,000 agents, kill and resume and kill twice of 3,000, 30x100 trees with and without hibernation, and three rounds of clean reopens, all on JSONL.
- Finished subagents leave memory and are read back when something names them (2026-11-10, Georgios: "Cut the rest too"). The registry keeps a `ChildSession` only for agents that are doing something; a leaf of the journal's agent tree whose 16 agents are all settled is cold: `AgentScope::cold` holds its record key and stub key, the task tree keeps each agent's parent and session id, `Sessions::by_spawn` its spawning call, and nothing else of it is in memory. Cooling (`AgentScope::cool`) runs in the journal writer's own registry call, so it sees the writer's cache: a leaf goes cold when it has a stub, every agent in it is settled in memory too (`ChildSession::settled`: no harness, task, hibernation, watcher, held residency lock or in-memory checkpoint), every record is the one the leaf holds (`JournalCache::written`), nothing is pending for it (messages, status jobs, captures, unsaved or unrecorded checkpoints), no operation pins it, and all its agents' children are cold or in the same leaf, so a warm agent always has warm ancestors. The writer offers a leaf when a fold writes its stub and when a snapshot finds an agent of a stubbed leaf touched but unchanged, and runs once more after either. Warming (`Registry::warm`) pins the leaves of the ids it is given and of every cold ancestor, reads cold ones back under one sequencer per root (`thaw`: leaf, profiles, `restored_session`, the same registrations a restart makes) and returns a guard that unpins on drop; cooling and warming an agent is a restart of that agent and nothing more. `wait`, `rewait`, `interrupt`, `close` (their subtree), message delivery and every other rehydration, `child_session_id`, `host_context`, `set_budget`, `respawned`, a reservation by a cold parent, and lookups by session id warm what they name; `list_agents` warms the page it returns (`directory_page`), `directory` with completed agents and `resent` warm everything, `resent_to` only the recipient; `running`, `stop_all` and `activity` read the agents in memory, which are all that can be active; `close_all`, shutdown and `cancel_all` act on the agents in memory, and a full journal write (`close_all`'s final one, a fresh writer) carries the cold leaves over (`JournalSnapshot::cold`). A restart reads a stub instead of a leaf and its 16 profiles unless a delta touches the leaf or a warm agent descends from it (`durable::load_leaves`). Two things this made visible are fixed with it. A root's completion notice now leaves its mark in the child's journaled `waited` when the root reads it, so a restart or a cooled child does not hand the root the same result again as new from `wait_agent`. And a clean shutdown could journal children as closed: `release_scope` marks them closed in memory, and a deferred journal slot open at that moment was filled with that state; this build opens such slots more often (unpinning wakes the writer) and hit it in 2 of 4 rounds, the build before in 0 of 12. `release_scope` now saves the journal first, a released scope answers every later save as frozen, and a slot open when the writer finishes is filled with the last payload saved (`refill`). Measured with output/durability-ledger, Claude mock, JSONL, load 45 to 100, against the build before (`swarm-a1`): memory of a finished child held by the registry 4.1 KB to 1.15 KB (`heapdone.sh` 10,000: the whole heap 21.6 KB to 18.6 KB an agent; what remains is the JSONL index 5.4 KB, the root cell's journal 2.4 KB and the session and spawn maps); reopening a finished 100,000-agent tree (`reopen.sh`, 6,250 of 6,251 leaves cold) restores the registry in 0.46 to 0.54 s instead of 2.5 to 3.0 s, of which 0.30 to 0.33 s is the 100,000-message log, which is still read whole, 0.07 to 0.09 s the stubs and 0.08 to 0.10 s placing them, and the process holds 0.92 to 0.96 GB instead of 2.05 to 2.09 GB; at 10,000 agents 40 to 55 ms instead of 130 to 150 ms and 170 MB instead of 236 MB. What it does not change: opening that store's 4.8 GB journal and the root session takes 2.1 to 7.6 s under this load, far more than the registry (`durability.jsonl.recover` 4.4 s of one 6.2 s open: the harness exits before the final index save finishes); a tree killed while its root still holds unread completions has no settled leaf and restores as before (a 100,000-agent run killed at 25,000 finished: 0 stubs); listing every agent warms every agent (0.33 s at 10,000, the same as before). CPU of a 20,000-agent run 72.6 s to 74.7 s, mean of four interleaved, including the final listing that thaws all of it. Checked: 2,000 agents on memory, JSONL, SQLite and rows; kill and resume and kill twice of 3,000 on JSONL, SQLite and rows; 30x100 trees on JSONL and SQLite, hibernating on JSONL; cancel and close with and without hibernation; a 100,000-agent run (6,245 leaves cold at the end, all listed completed after a thaw); `coldcheck` on JSONL and SQLite (session id, interrupt, a message, close and a budget on cold agents, then the same tree after reopening); `relcheck.sh`, 18 rounds of three clean reopens on JSONL, SQLite and rows with no agent closed.
- The subagent journal says which leaves hold only finished agents, and folds when the tree goes quiet (2026-11-10, journal version 9; first step of loading finished children on demand, Georgios: "Cut the rest too"). A level-0 page of the agent tree now lists, beside each leaf's record, a stub record for every leaf that is full (all 16 ids, 15 in leaf 0) and whose agents are all settled: completed, failed or closed, no turn in flight, no completion pending, no accepted output, not unstarted (`AgentRecord::settled`). The stub (`LeafStub`: the leaf's size and, per agent, its id, parent, session id and the call that spawned it) is what a restart needs to place such an agent in the task tree without reading its record or its profile; nothing reads it yet. Stubs are written when a leaf is folded (`JournalSnapshot::encode`, `AgentTree::set_stub`), cost 160 B an agent, and a writer set to version 8 or lower writes none. A journal also folds its deltas when no agent is active, owed a completion notice or being resumed (`Sessions::quiescent`, kept by `refresh`; `JournalCache::folds`), where before it folded only when the deltas outgrew the leaves, so an idle tree's journal is its leaves alone: after a 2,000-agent run 125 of 126 leaves have stubs and there are no delta pages (`output/durability-ledger/stubs.py`). A version 8 journal opened by this build is folded whole on its first save so every leaf gains its stub: on the 100,000-agent store killed at 50,000 that once costs 170 to 179 MB written instead of 82 to 99 MB and a first resumed request at 3.1 to 3.2 s instead of 2.4 to 2.8 s (`restart.sh`, interleaved, load 45 to 52); builds before this one refuse a version 9 journal. `Sessions::by_context` is a set per context, where it was a list searched on insert. Checked with output/durability-ledger: 2,000 agents on memory, JSONL, SQLite and rows; kill and resume of 3,000 on JSONL, SQLite and rows, killed twice on JSONL, SQLite and rows; 30x100 trees on JSONL and SQLite and hibernating on JSONL; cancel and close of 300 running agents with and without hibernation; all complete.
- 2026-11-10: **A session with no executable to name keeps no request template.** `4236c177f` wrote the template reference into every paged snapshot, but a rebuilt session only uses it when the snapshot and the process name the same executable, and on wasm32 there is none, so the record was written and never read. The snapshot now references the template only where `environment::build()` has an identity. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude` native and wasm32; `output/cache-loss` `retool` unchanged (reads 17,507, writes 3,911 after reopening).
- 2026-11-10: **Where the restart of a 100,000-agent tree spends its two seconds, and what a tenfold cut needs.** Measured, nothing changed. `output/durability-ledger` `restart.sh` on the JSONL store killed with 100,000 agents added and 50,000 finished (1.65 GB journal, 130 MB index), stage timers added for the run and removed: the store opens in 0.55 to 0.72 s (`durability.jsonl.recover` 0.39 s reading the part of the journal written after the last index save, `index.load` 0.10 s); `subagent.restore` takes 1.29 to 1.36 s, of which the delta pages 0.18 s (36,254 changed agents), the 6,251 agent leaves 0.14 s to read (45.6 MB) and 0.19 s to decode and fold, the agents' profiles 0.36 s to read (100,000 records, one per agent, each distinct) and 0.40 s to decode, and building the sessions in the registry's owning task 0.28 s; the first resumed request leaves 2.0 to 2.3 s after start, with 2.2 to 2.5 GB resident. No stage is more than a fifth of the total, so no single change is a tenfold one: reading the profiles in pages like the leaves, keeping an appended index so a killed store has no long tail to scan, and overlapping the delta and leaf reads would together take it to about one second. Ten times needs a restart that does not read per-agent data at all: a head that lists the agents that are running, interrupted or owed a completion notice, the rest (finished and not yet started) left on disk and loaded when a message, a wait or a listing names them. That changes the journal format and every path of the registry that looks an agent up, and it is the same change that would stop a finished child from costing memory (22 KB live, 42 KB resident, of which the JSONL index 6.3 KB and the registry 5.7 KB; a completed child also holds its result twice, in its status and in `last_output`). Not started. Also today: a 100,000-agent run on JSONL settles in 75 s, one second after the last agent starts, with 12,000 to 14,000 completion notices pending throughout and no backoff tail (the tail recorded on 2026-11-10 was not reproduced on this store); peak 6.7 GB resident, 67 KB an agent. The ledger's mock answered compactions by matching the old prompt text; it now answers the `compaction` parameter with a block and the stock prompt with text, without which a 100,000-agent root fails its first compaction.
- 2026-11-10: **A Claude session rebuilt in the same build sends the system prompt and tools it sent before, and appends what changed.** A session's `system` and `tools` were fixed for as long as its state lived, but a reopened, reloaded or rehydrated session rendered them again, and a different tool list (a tool added, removed or described differently) re-keyed the whole conversation. The snapshot now references the request template the session last sent (the content-addressed record the turn cursor already pools) together with the identity of the executable, and a session rebuilt by the same executable for the same model keeps that `system` and `tools` byte for byte. What the current tool list has that the kept one lacks or defines differently goes out as `tool_addition` blocks carrying the definition, and what it no longer has as `tool_removal` blocks, in a `role: "system"` message after the prompt, with the `inline-tools-2026-09-15` beta (Anthropic's mid-conversation tool changes; Claude Code 2.1.304 carries the same header). What has been announced is read back from the history, so a compaction that summarizes the message away makes the next request announce it again, and tool calls are checked against the current handlers. A static system block the kept prompt does not hold is listed in the "A section of your instructions was updated" reminder next to AGENTS.md. A system message a later user message would follow is moved after it on the wire, since the API accepts one only between a user turn and an assistant turn or at the end. A request refused for its tool changes drops the kept template for that state, sends the current tools and retries once. A new executable, another model, a switch between Code Mode and plain tools, or a store that does not page records renders fresh as before, and tool changes left in the history are removed then. Forks take their parent's template. `output/cache-loss` `retool` (JSONL store, a session reopened with one tool described differently and one added; the mock refuses a misplaced system message and a tool block without the beta): before, the first request after reopening read 0 tokens and wrote 17,563; after, `tools` is byte-identical, it reads 17,507 and writes the 3,911-token redefinition of `exec`, later turns append nothing, a cell calls the new tool, the turn after a compaction announces again, and a second reopening with a tool removed appends one more change; `REFUSE_TOOLS=1` falls back to the fresh tools and completes. Live on the subscription wire with Haiku 5.5 (`LOG=1 live retool`): the reopened session sent the same `tools` (16,771 bytes, same digest) and one `tool_addition(exec)`, got 200, read 8,704 cached tokens and wrote 5,855, and the model called the new tool through `exec` and answered with its word and the code word from before the reopening; `live tools` shows the API accepting an addition by value, a removal, a redefinition and text beside them, and refusing them without the beta. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude-client -p nanocode-backend-claude` native and wasm32; `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- 2026-11-10: **A hibernating child that wakes during a cancel reads the interrupt when it resumes, not when the wake was planned.** The run that still stalled after `07226bbc6` had three children in the same state when the 30 s ran out: resident, turn marked interrupted, their harness already told to stop (`harness true hibernated false interrupted true told stopped true`). The wake had read "not interrupted" before the cancel marked the turn; the cancel then told the new harness to stop while it had no turn yet, and the queued resume re-attached the parked call as an ordinary turn. `Harness::resume` now asks the registry whether the turn is interrupted when it runs. `output/durability-ledger` `swarm` with hibernation, 500 agents, cancel at 350 to 500 ms: 160 of 160 runs end with every agent interrupted in under a second (before, about one run in thirty left children running for the 30 s). `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-subagents` native and wasm32.
- 2026-11-10: **The cache refresh, seen end to end on the live API.** `LOG=1 output/cache-loss live idle 3700`: a nanocode root session on the subscription wire (Haiku 5.5, one-hour cache) takes one turn, waits 3,700 s and takes another. The session sent one request of its own in between, 3,595 s after the first: unstreamed, `max_tokens: 0`, answered 200 with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`, 8,526 tokens read from cache, 0 written, 0 output. The turn 3,701 s after the first, past the hour, read the same 8,526 tokens from cache and wrote 86; its reported usage holds both reads (17,052 cached input tokens). Docs only.
- 2026-11-10: **Cancelling a tree stops the children that had not started, and no longer waits 30 s on the ones it missed.** `cancel_all` and `interrupt` marked the turns that existed and waited for them to end. A child still queued for a turn slot had no turn, so it started afterwards and ran to completion; a child attached but not yet in its first turn got its interrupt before the turn began and then ran un-interrupted; and both kinds then blocked on the message pause the cancel was holding, so the cancel sat until `AGENT_STOP_TIMEOUT` and the children failed or completed afterwards. Three changes. A queued child that has not started becomes `Interrupted` and keeps its unstarted runtime; its queued start finds it no longer pending and stops, a later message starts it with its task and then delivers the message, and a restart restores it interrupted. The interrupt loops instead of waiting: on every change it marks whatever turn is active, tells each harness once and wakes each sleeping child once, so a turn that begins after the first pass is stopped on the next. And a message's delivery is settled by a task of its own once it is committed, so a sender whose turn is cancelled between the commit and the release no longer leaves a message pending for ever (which kept a hibernating tree from ever settling after a cancel). `output/durability-ledger` `swarm`, 500 agents, 300 ms model latency, cancel issued between 60 and 700 ms: before, any cancel that found queued children took 30.0 s and left them running (`before {"pending": 379, "running": 121} after {"interrupted": 288, "running": 212}`, then 212 completed and 9 failed); after, 27 of 27 runs without hibernation and 25 of 27 with it end in 0.02 to 0.4 s with every agent interrupted, one is the harness's own peer messages restarting children after an early cancel, and one hibernating run still left 14 running for the 30 s (hibernation is opt-in and nothing but this harness turns it on; open). The suite after the change: `matrix` 2,000 agents on memory, JSONL, SQLite and rows, and hibernating on JSONL and rows; `killresume` and `killtwice` 3,000; `treecheck` 20x50 both ways; `stopcheck`; `cellresume`: all complete. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-subagents` native and wasm32.
- 2026-11-10: **A compaction drops the request the cache refresh was keeping.** The refresh resends the last request a session opened; after a compaction that request is the conversation that was just summarized, so an idle root would have paid a cache read of the whole old conversation every hour for a prefix no later request reads. The kept request is now cleared when a compaction lands, and the next real request is kept as usual. `output/cache-loss` `keepalive compacted 320` (a root on the five-minute cache compacts, then waits): 0 refreshes, and the next turn writes its 5,483-token prompt (system, tools and the summary); before, it refreshed the 17,459-token conversation at 299.6 s. Also checked today against a mock that refuses a compaction request ending in an unanswered tool call or a block that is not first (`autocompact`): a compaction at the start of a turn, one in the middle of a turn (the summary covers the request already made, the tool round since then follows the block) and a second compaction over a block all complete on the server path; and asked on the subscription wire with Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 (`MODEL=… live warm`, `live compact2`): the unstreamed `max_tokens: 0` refresh reads the whole prompt and writes nothing on both, compaction behaves as on Haiku 5.5 in every case, and a block written by one model is accepted by the others (Opus to Fable, Fable to Opus, Haiku to Opus). `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude` native and wasm32.
- 2026-11-10: **Cache refreshes are counted in the session's usage, and the traces say where refreshing pays.** A refresh's tokens and estimated cost are added to the usage of the next model call the session completes, so a turn's usage, a subagent's budget and the session total include them (`keepalive idle 320`: the turn after one refresh reports 34,916 cached input tokens, the refresh's 17,458 and its own 17,458, with the cost of both). The stop rule stays "as many refreshes as one cache write costs", the ski-rental bound: keeping the cache never costs more than rebuilding it once. Measured on the traces of 2026-11-04..09 (`/tmp/cache/idle.py`, `idle_root.py`, in input-token equivalents): for roots, forks and side conversations on the one-hour cache, 728 idle periods, of which 536 resumed within the hour, 35 in 1 to 2 h, 18 in 2 to 4 h, 10 later and 129 not in the trace; refreshing for up to 4 h would have spent 7.8M to save 62.3M, up to 12 h 16.8M for 70.5M, and the price bound (20 to 80 refreshes) 24M to 39M for 70.5M, so the bound is past the best point but well inside the gain. For subagents between turns on the five-minute cache, 875 idle periods: 421 resumed within five minutes, 108 later, 346 never; two refreshes would have spent 22.9M to save 28.9M and five 53.9M to save 45.7M, so a subagent that has ended its turn is still not refreshed. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude` native and wasm32.
- 2026-11-10: **Claude compacts on the server, as Codex does; Claude Code's prompt is the fallback.** Anthropic's compaction guide says to use on-demand compaction wherever it is available ("Claude writes the summary on the server, so you need no summarization code of your own"); `8f066cbea` had adopted Claude Code 2.1.304's client-side prompt, and that binary carries no `compact-2026-09-04` header. A compaction is now the conversation as it stands, same system and tools, with `compaction: {"type":"summarize"}`, without `context_management` (the API refuses the two together) and with the `compact-2026-09-04` beta; the reply ends with `stop_reason: "compaction"` and one signed `compaction` block, whose tokens arrive in `usage.iterations` and are counted from there. The block is kept exactly as returned and becomes the first block of the first user message, followed for an automatic compaction by Claude Code's "Continue the conversation from where it left off…" line and, when messages are kept after it, by its note that the summary did not see them; every request whose first message holds a block sends the beta. A request the API refuses as invalid, or one that ends without a block, falls back in the same compaction to the prompt of `prompts/compact.md`; when the refusal names compaction the session stops asking. When a later request is refused for the block it carries (another route or model), the block's summary is resent as text under Claude Code's continuation line and the request retried once; both refusals close their step as `cf44244d2` does. Context-overflow recovery keeps the prompt path. Asked on the subscription wire with Haiku 5.5 (`output/cache-loss` `live compact2` and `LOG=1 live session`, about 25 small requests): the compaction request returns 200 streamed and unstreamed and reads the conversation from cache (27,906 of 27,972 tokens; through nanocode 8,606 read, 6 written); the block is accepted alone in a user message, followed by text in the same message, and followed by a user message; `context_management` on the compaction request is a 400 and on a request carrying the block is accepted; `tool_choice: none` is accepted; a session of two turns, a compaction, a question, a second compaction and a question answered "heliotrope, 4172" and "heliotrope", each post-compaction request reading the 7,830-token system and tools prefix from cache. Against the mock (`compact`): the server path, `REFUSE_COMPACTION=1` (falls back to the stock prompt, later compactions go straight to it) and `REFUSE_BLOCK=1` (summary resent as text, turn completes). Not verified: models other than Haiku 5.5, Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry routes, message threads. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude-client -p nanocode-backend-claude` native and wasm32; `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- 2026-11-10: **A model step the provider refuses is closed before the request is sent again with different history.** When Claude refuses the thinking signatures in a session's history (they belong to another API key's organization), the turn drops the thinking blocks and retries under a new step id. The refused step stayed `EffectPending`, and a durable operation may not complete with an unfinished step, so the turn that had just recovered failed with `invalid durability state: operation … completed with an unfinished step` and the session stopped accepting prompts. This is the located cause of the "invalid durability state" turn failure left open on 2026-11-09. The refused step is now completed with `{"refused": <error>}` where the provider error is returned, and a replayed step holding that value fails the same way, so a recovered process takes the same retry. `output/cache-loss` `unsigned` (JSONL store; the mock answers with a thinking block, then refuses histories that hold one): before, the second turn fails with that error and the third with "the agent stopped before accepting the command"; after, both complete, the retry carrying the history without thinking. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude` native and wasm32.
- 2026-11-10: **The cache refresh is sent unstreamed, because the API refuses a streamed one.** The refresh of `6f49aa8cf` went out as a streamed request and had only met a mock that accepted it.
