Checked on 2026-11-09 with output/durability-ledger (`swarm`, mock model, `SWARM flat 3000` killed with `KILL_AT_FINISHED=1500`, then `swarm resume`): on 59b663bad, 7278ea6bf and f97a41704 the resume stopped after `continuing the root's turn` with 764 agents and an idle process (on f97a41704, 3 of 3 runs on SqlStore and one each on JSONL and RowStore); with this change the JSONL and RowStore stores f97a41704 left resume to 3,000 agents, as do SqlStore runs killed the same way, and `cellresume` still runs its slow call once on each. `SWARM flat 30000` on JSONL with the grouped saves and maps alone: 50.8 s and 128 s of CPU instead of 121.1 s and 271 s, 347,636 commits instead of 447,656, 2,543 MB written to disk instead of 4,721 MB. A 30,000 agent run killed at 15,000 and resumed spent 30 s on one core in `flush` without adding an agent before the queue; after it the 10,671 agents left were added and run in under 10 s.
- Fixes from driving `tempo/` and `tempo/boundless/` models hard (2026-11-09, Georgios: "go and brutalize this stuff again until theres more bugs"; `output/gateways/brutal.sh` and `brutal-tui*.sh`, Georgios's wallet, about $0.21 spent, $0.18 of it two Claude Opus 5.5 calls on Boundless). `exec --resume <id> --model <other>` ran the session's own model and dropped `--model` without a word (a `tempo/vercel/zai/glm-5.3-flash` resume of a Boundless session was paid to Boundless); it now refuses, naming the model the session runs, as the interface refuses a model change once a thread has started, and a `--model` naming the session's own model still resumes. The thinking picker and dial, the harness mismatch error and `nanocode sessions` named a Tempo or Boundless model without its route (`Thinking · z-ai/glm-5.3-flash`, `model z-ai/glm-5.3-flash does not belong to the claude harness`, `boundless/z-ai/glm-5.3-flash`, which `-m` does not take); they now use `Route::label` (`tempo/boundless/z-ai/glm-5.3-flash`), and native models keep their display names. `nanocode-tui`'s effort dial widens to its title, which a 45-character route label had cut at the border. Checked the same day: the empty `tempo/boundless/`, `--harness claude` with a Boundless model and an unknown Boundless model (400, no retry, nothing charged) fail with their reasons; a shell call, thinking none/max on DeepSeek V4 Flash and low to max on GLM-5.3 Flash, resumes with tool history across processes, `list_models({query: "boundless/deepseek"})` (4) and a `spawn_agent` child on `boundless/deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731` from a Boundless root, six processes at once on one named session, an interrupted turn followed by another, and `tempo/boundless/anthropic/claude-opus-5.5` with a tool call all worked. Not fixed here: GLM-5.3 Flash on Boundless answers thinking none with "the model rejected the request" (`upstream_rejected`, nothing charged) while nanocode offers every level for a model it knows nothing about; Claude models on Boundless read no prompt cache over Responses (two Opus calls in one turn each cost $0.088, where GLM read 12.2k of 14.0k tokens cached); and processes sharing a named session each count the others' spend as theirs (six identical calls showed $0.000591 to $0.002680 each).
- Claude's `Read` resizes an image about ten times sooner, to the same bytes, and the agent no longer decodes it a second time (2026-11-09). In the four days of this machine's telemetry up to 2026-11-04, 3,028 of 8,464 local `Read` calls took over 120 ms, nearly all of them screenshots, where a text file takes under 5 ms. `image_block` (the native `Read` of an image, a PDF page or a notebook image) fits an image within 1568 pixels a side and 1,150,000 pixels with `image`'s `resize_exact(…, Lanczos3)`, which computes each output sample on its own through `get_pixel`: 151 ms of CPU for a 1440x900 screenshot and 419 ms for 2880x1800, nearly all of the call. `nanocode_image::lanczos3(&image, width, height)` (core/image, `resample.rs`) adds the same f32 products in the same order, so its bytes are `image`'s, but a line at a time: for each output line it adds every source line of its window times that line's weight into one line of sums, a loop over neighbouring samples that the compiler vectorizes, and it runs the horizontal pass as that same loop over the transposed lines, each transpose written in order (0.5 to 1.3 ns a pixel; filling a zeroed buffer in tiles of 8 to 256 pixels took 2.1 to 3.0). The last pass rounds half away from zero with a saturating cast and a compare, 0.16 ns a sample where `value.clamp(0.0, 255.0).round() as u8` took 0.95, because `f32::clamp` keeps the loop from vectorizing. It takes 8-bit gray, gray with alpha, RGB and RGBA; other depths, an empty image and an unchanged size go to `image`. The agent then prepared the tool's image again (`prepare_tool_images`, `load_for_prompt_bytes`) and decoded every pixel a second time only to learn its size: `nanocode_image::remember(bytes, width, height)` notes that bytes decoded to that size, by SHA-1 and for the newest 32 (`MAX_IMAGE_CACHE_ENTRIES`), `image_block` calls it for the image it returns, `load_for_prompt_bytes` for each PNG, JPEG or WebP it decodes, and one whose remembered size fits the limits asked for is returned as it is, which is what decoding it would return. Nothing is remembered in the brain for a `Read` that ran on another machine's hand, an MCP tool's image or a WASM host's `Read`, so those are decoded once as before; and an image already within the tool's limits is still decoded once by the tool, which is how it refuses a damaged file, so that call takes what it did. Measured with output/image-bench's `read` (`ClaudeWorkspaceFiles::execute_output("Read", …)`, then the agent's `prepare_base64` for a model of 2576 pixels; each round a first read, the file differing by a text chunk and forty one-pixel images clearing the caches in between; 5 runs of 9 rounds interleaved with a build of bfe6249dd, median CPU on an M1 Max at load average 20 to 30), tool then agent: 1440x900 PNG 156.6 and 6.3 ms before, 14.4 and 0.7 after; 1280x2400 PNG 296.4 and 6.4, 23.8 and 1.4; 390x3200 PNG 110.5 and 2.6, 9.7 and 0.9; 2880x1800 JPEG 449.1 and 6.7, 44.5 and 0.7; 2880x1800 PNG 450.1 and 6.5, 48.0 and 0.7 (25 ms of it decoding the PNG); 1280x800 PNG, kept as it is, 3.9 and 4.2, 4.0 and 0.5; 414x900 PNG 2.7 and 2.9, 2.7 and 0.4; the nine samples together 1,672 ms and 170. The resize alone (`resize`) went from 150.7 to 8.3 ms (1440x900), 288.7 to 14.2 (1280x2400), 102.2 to 4.5 (390x3200) and 419.1 to 19.2 (2880x1800); built for x86_64 and run under Rosetta from 279.5 to 12.5 and 756.9 to 26.7; as WASM in Node 22 (wasm32-unknown-unknown, no SIMD) from 235.7 to 33.8 and 613.8 to 77.0, what `thumbnail_exact` takes there (31.6 and 77.0). Checked: `equiv` resizes 3,000 random images of the four kinds (noise, noise of 0 and 255, checks, gradients, alternating columns, flat; sides of 1 to 3,000 pixels to sides of 1 to 400) both ways and none of 188,198,466 samples differ, `ratio` the same for reductions of up to 1,000 times, and the bytes the tool returns and the bytes the agent keeps are the same before and after for all nine samples (`DUMP`). Tried and left: 14-bit fixed-point sums took a quarter less (6.4 ms for 1440x900) but were one level off `image` on 0.05 to 0.2% of a screenshot's samples and two levels off past a 200-fold reduction; `fast_image_resize` 5.5.0 took 19.5 ms for the same resize and clamps between its passes (up to 29 levels off).
- A `/btw` side conversation answers from the main thread's prompt cache (2026-11-09, Georgios: "/btw threads feel very slow on long running threads, when they shoudl be using the prev conversaw … prev message id thing"). Two things kept it off the cache. (1) Since 5fede2a34 a fork took its parent's system context (the environment section and project instructions) only while the parent's environment still named today's date, so a fork of a thread started on an earlier day rendered a new date, its system prompt differed and its first request rewrote the whole inherited prefix. In the last five days of `~/.nanocode/log/otel` traces, every side conversation forked on a later day than its parent read only the tools from cache (12,552 to 13,768 tokens) and wrote 248K to 857K tokens (01a1b83a…, forked on 2026-11-07 from a thread of 2026-11-06: 870,750 input, 13,768 cached, 856,978 written, 23.8 s), while same-day forks read their parent's prefix (01a1b82c…: 916,953 of 917,782 cached). Forks and side conversations (lineage origin `Fork` or `SideConversation`) again take the parent's context whenever they run in its workspace, as abe100e33 had them; spawned and restored subagents still compute their own on a new day. (2) A side conversation forked at or over the auto-compaction threshold compacted the inherited context before answering. 01a1c365… was forked from 01a1c23d… at 967,506 tokens (threshold 967,000) while the main thread was compacting, from the boundary before that compaction, and each of its three questions started a 3.18 MB compaction that was cancelled after 41.6, 18.7 and 41.9 s (the main thread's own took 70 s). A side conversation's snapshot now starts with `auto_compaction_suppressed`, so its first request goes out over the inherited context, the prefix the parent's last request cached. The flag clears at its first response, so later steps compact as usual, and a request that does exhaust the window still takes the context-recovery compaction. Checked with `output/btw-speed` (a mock Messages transport; `btw compaction` reports 990,000 input tokens for the main turn, `btw date` starts under `TZ=Etc/GMT+12` and forks under `Etc/GMT-14`) in two interleaved runs each of b3b2f1b56 and this change: the side's requests went from a compaction plus the answer to the answer alone, and its system prompt went from dated 2026-11-10 against the main's 2026-11-09 to the main's own. The code landed in 9cbc3d97f, whose commit picked up these hunks from the shared index.
- A Boundless session pays its gas in the stablecoin the wallet holds most of (2026-11-09). Boundless sponsors no gas and names USDC.e as its fee token, so a wallet without USDC.e failed the channel open ("gas estimation failed … out of gas") unless `--tempo-fee-token` named another. Without that flag, the Boundless wallet now reads the signed-in account (`TempoAccountsWallet::active_account`, `tempo-alloy` 1.11.0, the version `mpp` already uses) and its USDC.e, USDT0 and pathUSD balances (`eth_call` `balanceOf` on `DEFAULT_RPC_URL`), the tokens nanocode names that pay gas, and pays in the largest (`Gas::Held`); none held is an error that names `--tempo-fee-token`. The Tempo gateway sponsors its sessions' gas, so its wallet keeps the challenge's fee token (`Gas::Challenge`). Checked on 2026-11-09 with Georgios's wallet (84.97 MACH, 9.67 USDT0, 0.000041 USDC.e) and no flag: `tempo/boundless/z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` opened a 1 MACH Boundless channel and answered, and `tempo/vercel/zai/glm-5.3-flash` still answered through the gateway; both sessions were closed.
- `tempo/boundless/<model>` runs on Boundless directly, paid from the Tempo wallet over MPP, without the Tempo gateway or a Tempo Key (2026-11-09, Georgios: "boundless/.. models MUST work without a tempo key, just with a tempo wallet … assuming our own Tempo gateway doesnt even exist"). The gateway's `boundless/…` IDs answer an MPP caller "send Authorization: Bearer sk-tempo-…", so nanocode goes to `https://api.inference.boundless.network/mpp/v1` itself: Responses only (its `/messages` answers 404), so a Boundless model is a custom model on the Codex harness, sent by Boundless's own ID (`z-ai/glm-5.3-flash`; `boundless/z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` is a 400 there), and `/harness claude` from one goes to the Claude default natively. The route is its own provider, `boundless` (`Route::Boundless`, persisted in `SessionRecord::provider`, a `SpawnProvider` beside `tempo`, so `spawn_agent` takes `boundless/<model>`), with its own client and MPP session (Boundless's suggested 1 MACH deposit, in `--tempo-currency`, MACH by default), its group in `/model` and `nanocode models` from Boundless's `/mpp/v1/models` (26 models with prices on 2026-11-09), and the gateway's `boundless/…` IDs still left out. Boundless sponsors no gas and names USDC.e as its fee token, so a wallet without USDC.e needs `--tempo-fee-token` (`NANOCODE_TEMPO_FEE_TOKEN`) naming a token it holds: Georgios's wallet (84.97 MACH, 9.67 USDT0, 0.000041 USDC.e) failed the open with "gas estimation failed … out of gas" without it, and with `usdc.e` as the currency with "no balance in 0x20C0…8b50". Checked on 2026-11-09 with that wallet (`dogfood.sh`, `--tempo-fee-token usdt0`): `tempo/boundless/z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` opened a 1 MACH channel with Boundless and answered ($0.001687), `tempo/boundless/openai/gpt-6-luna` answered on the same channel ($0.001326), and `--tempo-close-session` closed it with 0.996987 MACH left.
- Correction to the entry below (2026-11-09): the `vercel/…`, `openrouter/…` and `@cf/…` IDs the gateway listed with provider `boundless` never ran on Boundless for nanocode. The gateway's preference (`Models.prefer`) moved them to Boundless only for callers with a Tempo Key, and an MPP caller took the ID's own provider (`/api/speed`: `vercel/zai/glm-5.3-flash` served by `vercel:baseten`, `vercel/openai/gpt-6-luna` by `vercel`). Georgios: "When somebody chooses a provider, that is for a provider", so tempoxyz/gateway#601 (d3b58e1, deployed the same day) removed the preference and routes no call to auctions; `/api/auction/models` then named the ID's own provider for all 837 IDs, and with the `boundless/…` IDs still left out (they need a key over MPP) `nanocode models` (45dce1b94, no change needed) listed workers-ai 31, openrouter 456 and vercel 324, `tempo/claude-fable-5-2` and `tempo/gpt-6-luna` under vercel.
- Each Tempo model is listed once, under the provider that serves it, and the `boundless/…` IDs are left out because the gateway refuses to be paid for them over MPP (2026-11-09, Georgios with a screenshot of `/model` filtered on fable, showing a "Tempo through the Tempo gateway" group beside Fable under boundless, and one of `tempo/boundless/z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` failing). The separate group of built-in models is gone: a built-in Codex or Claude model appears under its own name (`tempo/claude-fable-5-2`, with its capabilities) in the group of the provider that serves its gateway route (the `vercel/…` ID, else the `openrouter/…` one) at that route's price, and every other row is one (provider, upstream) as before. A `boundless/…` ID answers on both `/v1/responses` and `/v1/messages` "runs on Boundless, which the caller's API key pays directly: send Authorization: Bearer sk-tempo-…", while the `vercel/…`, `openrouter/…` and `@cf/…` IDs it serves through Boundless are paid over MPP, and on 2026-11-09 each of the 26 Boundless upstreams had one of those (Fable 5.2 only as `vercel/anthropic/claude-fable-5.2` and `openrouter/anthropic/claude-fable-5.2`), so the groups are boundless 25 (Fable 5.2's two upstream names are one built-in model), workers-ai 24, openrouter 431 and vercel 300; `tempo/boundless/…` typed by hand still reaches the gateway and its error. Checked on 2026-11-09 with paid requests from Georgios's Tempo wallet (`exec --tempo-session dogfood -m <model> 'Reply with exactly: ok'`, `output/gateways/dogfood.sh`, about $0.05 in holds over two 1 MACH channels, both closed): answered `tempo/claude-haiku-5-5` and `tempo/vercel/anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5` (Messages), `tempo/gpt-6-luna`, `tempo/vercel/openai/gpt-6-luna`, `tempo/vercel/zai/glm-5.3-flash` (also on `--harness claude`) and `tempo/@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash` (all served by Boundless), `tempo/openrouter/liquid/lfm-3-1.7b:free`, `tempo/vercel/reflection/beam-free` and `tempo/@cf/meta/llama-3.2-1b-instruct`; failed `tempo/boundless/z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` (above), `tempo/@cf/cloudflare/clef-flash` (Workers AI: "required properties at '/' are 'model,state,questions'"), and the batch IDs the gateway lists, `vercel/openai/gpt-6-luna-batch` (Vercel 404 `model_not_found`) and `openrouter/openai/gpt-6-luna:batch` (OpenRouter 404: "cannot be used with the chat/completions endpoint"), each retried five times as a `server_error` or `api_error` and each attempt charged $0.000001 after its hold came back. The spend a run shows counts each model call's hold, which the gateway credits back once usage is known (a Codex call held $0.003 to $0.011 and a channel's remaining rose again by the next run). In tmux (`picker-tempo3.sh`) the filter boundless listed the Boundless models with `tempo/claude-fable-5-2` at $8/$40 once, and fable the Claude group, Fable 5.2 and 5.1 under boundless, and the openrouter and vercel routes.
- The Tempo groups are the providers that serve each model, and the picker aligns each group by itself (2026-11-09, Georgios with a screenshot of `/model` filtered on boundless: "Still seems buggy to me"). The filter showed `tempo/openrouter/…` and `tempo/vercel/…` models labelled boundless, and their details were cut at the right edge. The gateway sells 56 IDs under another provider's prefix (25 `openrouter/…`, 24 `vercel/…` and 7 `@cf/…` on 2026-11-09) that it serves through Boundless at the price of the matching `boundless/…` ID, so each (provider, upstream model) is now listed once, under the ID named for its provider, and the groups follow the provider the gateway names (boundless 26, workers-ai 24, openrouter 431, vercel 300) instead of the ID's first segment; an ID left out still runs as `tempo/<id>`. A model's detail is its price, with "\$ per 1M input/output tokens" in the group header, and the thinking levels only for models whose levels are known (a custom model lists all six). `nanocode-tui`'s picker pads labels and badges to the widest in their group instead of in the whole list, and sizes itself the way it draws rows, since 50-character `tempo/` IDs pushed every native model's detail off the popup. Checked on 2026-11-09 in tmux at 135 columns (`picker-tempo3.sh`, run from a worktree of 7278ea6bf with this change, as the main checkout held another session's work in progress that did not compile): the filter boundless listed the 26 Boundless models and nothing else, and fable listed the Claude, Tempo, boundless, openrouter and vercel groups with every row whole.
- Restoring a subagent reads its running turn once (2026-11-09). Three places each read the whole of it. `RoutedFactory::restore` asked `SessionStore::recovery_checkpoint` for the child's stored checkpoint, which loaded the whole stored session, every turn's input, its transcript and the running turn's continuation included, to return the checkpoint alone; it now reads the head and that checkpoint (`session_checkpoint` over a record and a checkpoint). `persistent_recipe` loaded the stored session again for its record, its pending turns and whether it has a checkpoint; `SessionStore::resumable(id)` answers those three (`Resumable`) from one peek and the pending turns' inputs. And a Claude turn that resumes asked its policy for the continuation twice, once in `freeze_admitted` for the model and frozen prompt and once in `cursor`, each hydrating its messages, code calls and 22 KB request template from the store; `ClaudeExecution` keeps the continuation it hydrated until it is asked again (`hydrated`, taken by the second reader, dropped when the operation has none). Checked on 2026-11-09 with output/durability-ledger on JSONL, the store of 3,000 children killed once each had sent its first request (497 finished) and reopened by `swarm resume`: a child stopped in its first turn read 12 times instead of 24 (36 KB instead of 85 KB; `TRACE_STATE=<child>`), the 3,000 children 37,854 times and 108 MB instead of 51,209 and 176 MB, and all 3,000 completed. What repeats still: three peeks, the checkpoint twice and the turn's input twice.
- A host whose older builds share its store can hold back the formats this build added (2026-11-09). `SessionStore::with_state_format(8)` (`state_format()`; the method 0330349cb removed, now for formats 8 and 9 only: 8 keeps a running operation's steers in its head as before, 9, the default, seals them) and `SubagentControl::set_journal_version(6)` (6 writes the tree alone, every save a fold, and no `keeps_result`; 7, the default, writes deltas) make this build write what the build before format 9 and journal 7 reads; both refuse a number this build does not write. Why: a build starts writing a new format in the release that first reads it, so a host that deploys by rolling, or rolls back, has an older build meet heads it refuses (`unknown field \`steered\``, `unsupported subagent journal version 7`); tempoxyz/pyramid held format 6 this way from 2026-11-05 to 2026-11-09 and lost the means when the cap went. The rule for such a host: deploy the build that reads a format with the cap set, and lift the cap once no older build can open the store. Not capped: `JsonlStore` filing a subagent in its root's file and agent-host's cell journal format 2, which only the CLI writes. Checked on 2026-11-09 with output/durability-ledger (`STATE_FORMAT`, `JOURNAL_VERSION`): a swarm of 600 killed at 300 finished on `SqlStore` with `STATE_FORMAT=8 JOURNAL_VERSION=6` wrote a format 8 head with 23.8 KB of inline steers and a version 6 journal without deltas, and the build from before these changes (59b663bad) opened it and restored its 600 agents; the same swarm uncapped wrote format 9 (a 5.9 KB head) and version 7, which that build refused.
- A subagent that had a result keeps it across a restart (2026-11-09). Two cases lost it. (1) A child whose `submit_result` was accepted and journaled but whose turn had not ended when the process stopped is restored as completed with that result, and its own session still holds the turn as pending; the next message to it runs that turn to its end, which ended without a submit in the new process and so failed the child with "subagent turn ended without a valid submit_result call" over the result it had. A turn that starts for a child that is completed (and was not delegated a new task) now keeps the child's last result whether or not the turn is a recovered one (`harness_turn_started`; it kept it only for a turn that was not recovered). (2) A completed child interrupted in a follow-up turn, which a peer's message starts and which keeps the earlier result when it ends without a submit, forgot that it kept one: the journal's agent record now says so (`keeps_result`, written only when set; a journal with it is refused by builds before this) and restore gives the interrupted turn the result back. Root children's completions that steer into a running root turn are watched by one task per root (`NoticeOutcome::of_steers`, `Registry::watch_steer`): it subscribes to the root's events once, learns each steer's carrier turn from `run.steered` and settles every watched steer at the run's end, where each steer had its own subscription and decoded every `run.steered`, so s steers waiting on one root turn cost s² decodes and s copies of every root event. Checked on 2026-11-09 with output/durability-ledger on JSONL: `LATENCY_MS=1000 KILL_AT_FINISHED=500 swarm run jsonl <dir> 'SWARM flat 1000'` and then `swarm resume`, which now also resumes the root's pending turn as a host does (`pending_turns`, `durable_prompt`). A store killed with 507 children in follow-up turns, 431 accepted but unfinished and 61 in their first turn ended with 568 completed and 432 failed before, under the build that wrote it and under this one alike, and with 1,000 completed after; a second store, killed and resumed under this build (402 accepted, 85 in their first turn, 511 finished), ended with 1,000 completed. `SWARM flat 10000` used 54 and 63 s of user CPU instead of 80 and 86 s (two interleaved runs each at load average 27 to 80, so their wall times, 27 to 58 s, say nothing).
- `/harness` chooses the Codex or Claude harness (2026-11-09, Georgios: "i am not sure how do i select harness here? it should be obvious … just /harness should let me select which of the two"). `/harness` opens a picker whose two entries say what each would run, and `/harness codex|claude` switches directly, before the first prompt or after `/new` like a model change. A `tempo/` model keeps its ID on the other harness, since the Tempo gateway serves every model over both Responses and Messages; a native model, which a login ties to its harness, gives way to that harness's default (`claude-opus-5-5`, `gpt-6.1-sol`, or a host's first listed Codex model, `ModelClients::default_model`). A `tempo/` model that is not a built-in Codex or Claude model (`host::follows_harness`) runs on the current harness when `/model` picks it, where it always ran on Codex, and `--harness` chooses it for `-m tempo/…` (Codex unless set). `/model`'s title names the current harness and its footer points to `/harness`. Two SDK additions make a model of the other family possible on a harness: `SpawnBuilder::harness_model` and `RuntimeBuilder::harness_model` take any `ModelSelection`, which the CLI now uses for every start instead of the typed `backend::<Codex>().model(…)`, and `ClaudeBuilder::knows_max_tokens` reports whether the builder has an output budget; for a model the Claude backend has none for, the CLI's `configure` hook sets 32,768 (`Tempo::OUTPUT_TOKENS`), the output the Tempo gateway documents for a request that sets none ("Without max_output_tokens a request may write 32,768 tokens"). Checked on 2026-11-09 in `output/gateways` with a throwaway `HOME`: `exec -m tempo/boundless/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash --harness claude` stopped at the gateway's payment step over Messages ("Unknown Claude model: configure max_tokens explicitly" before the hook), without `--harness` over Responses, and `-m claude-opus-5-5 --harness codex` was refused; in tmux (`harness.sh`) `/harness` on the native `claude-opus-5-5` offered Codex running `gpt-6.1-sol`, `/model tempo/boundless/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash` stayed on Claude, `/harness` then offered that model on both, and `/harness codex` switched to Codex with it. WASM checks of `nanocode-backend-claude` and `nanocode-agent` and clippy on them and `nanocode-cli` are clean.
- The Tempo group lists every model the Tempo gateway sells (2026-11-09, Georgios after trying 8ae770531: "This doesn't seem to include the OpenRouter models? Or the boundless ones?"). The catalog is `/api/auction/models` alone, 837 IDs on 2026-11-09: 456 `openrouter/…`, 324 `vercel/…`, 31 `@cf/…` and 26 `boundless/…`, with every ID of the curated `/v1/models` (17) among them, so that second fetch is gone. `/model` and `nanocode models` show the built-in Codex and Claude models the gateway serves under their own names first, then one group per ID prefix (`tempo/boundless/`, `tempo/openrouter/`, `tempo/vercel/`, `tempo/@cf/`), each model with the provider the gateway says serves it and its price per million input and output tokens; a model sold through several routes appears under each, so a filter such as `deepseek-v4` shows every route and price, and `boundless` every model Boundless serves (which includes `@cf/…`, `openrouter/…` and `vercel/…` IDs). `list_models` takes an optional `query` that keeps the models whose full name contains it, since the catalog is 849 models, and `spawn_agent`'s definition is memoized on the policy without the providers' models and notes, so a catalog does not grow its key. Checked on 2026-11-09 in `output/gateways`: `nanocode models` printed the five Tempo groups and 849 `tempo/` models, `tempo/boundless/claude-fable-5.2` at "boundless · $8/$40 per 1M"; in tmux (`picker-tempo2.sh`) the filter `deepseek-v4` showed the `@cf/`, `boundless/` and `openrouter/` routes with their prices; a cell's `list_models({query: "boundless/deepseek"})` returned the four Boundless DeepSeek models, and `spawn-tempo.sh` routed as before.
- Models Tempo proxies are named `tempo/<model>`, and the gateway notion is gone (2026-11-09, asked for by Georgios: "do it all through the Tempo Gateway integration, remove the notion of the gateway, and let's just do tempo/... as the prefix if it's a proxied provider from us"). This replaces the two entries below about gateways. A bare model ID runs natively, as before 640b9ca50: on the ChatGPT and Claude Code logins, on a host's own clients, or, for Codex, through `--gateway openrouter|vercel|cloudflare|cloudflare-gateway`'s Responses route, which stays as it was. `tempo/<model>` runs on the Tempo gateway (`https://gateway.tempo-dev.workers.dev`), paid over MPP from the Tempo wallet: a Claude model's dashed ID on the Claude harness through `/v1/messages` and a Codex model's on the Codex harness through `/v1/responses`, each keeping its model's capabilities and prompts, and any other ID on the Codex harness as a custom model, since the gateway routes every ID it lists for sale and resolves Claude Code and upstream names to its providers (Vercel before OpenRouter). The picker's Tempo group and `nanocode models` list the built-in models whose upstream name `/api/auction/models` lists (837 callable IDs on 2026-11-09, without Claude Fable 5.5 or either Mythos) and the IDs of `/v1/models`' curated list that name no built-in model (9 of its 17), loaded in the background through the payment layer's one HTTP client, built when first used. One MPP wallet pays the gateway's models and tools, and the spend ledger tells models from tools by URL. Removed: `--gateway tempo` (Tempo's `openai.mpp.tempo.xyz` and `anthropic.mpp.tempo.xyz` proxies, their warm-up, and shell commands paying any mpp.dev service, which came with it), `--gateway-base-url`'s MPP endpoints and `--tempo-network`, the Boundless endpoint (its models are `boundless/…` IDs on the gateway), the gateway registry with its preferences, `/model <model> <gateway>` and `spawn_agent`'s `gateway`. `--tempo-currency` (MACH by default), `--tempo-fee-token`, `--tempo-deposit` (2 MACH unless set) and `--tempo-close-session` apply to the gateway. The SDK carries the route as a provider: `SpawnOptions::provider`, `SpawnBuilder::provider` and `SessionRecord::provider`, persisted, copied when a record is derived and kept when one is merged, so a resumed, switched or forked session keeps its provider, and `RoutedFactory` spawns and restores a same-harness child with a provider through its recipe instead of cloning the parent's client; `SpawnPolicy::providers` (`SpawnProvider`: name, about, models, note) lets `spawn_agent` take `<provider>/<model>`, infer the harness from the provider's models, and `list_models` list each provider model by its full name. A bare model in `spawn_agent` runs on the spawning agent's client for its harness and natively for another. Checked on 2026-11-09 in `output/gateways` with a throwaway `HOME` (no wallet, no logins, no proxy variables): `exec -m tempo/claude-haiku-5-5` failed at "Messages transport: payment failed … to pay gateway.tempo-dev.workers.dev", `tempo/gpt-6-luna` and `tempo/vercel/google/gemini-4-argon` at the same payment step over Responses, bare `gpt-6.1-sol` at the ChatGPT login, `claude-fable-5.2` as an unknown model whose error names `tempo/`, and `tempo/` alone was refused (`tempo-routes.sh`); a `tempo/gpt-6-luna` session resumed in a second run reached the gateway again, its record holding provider tempo. With a root on a mock through `--gateway openrouter --gateway-base-url` (`spawn-tempo.sh`, `cell-tempo.js`), `list_models` listed 21 tempo models, and `spawn_agent` with `tempo/claude-haiku-5-5`, `tempo/gpt-6-astra` and `tempo/vercel/google/gemini-4-argon` each reached the gateway's payment step while bare `gpt-6-astra` reached the mock and bare `claude-haiku-5-5` the Claude login. In tmux (`picker-tempo.sh`) `/model` filtered on fable showed the Claude and Tempo groups, and `/model tempo/claude-haiku-5-5` switched to a Claude session labelled `tempo/claude-haiku-5-5`. A debug `exec` failing at the missing login (`bench.py`, interleaved, 40 runs each, load average 7 to 20) took 39.9 ms before 640b9ca50 and 44.5 ms now with `--no-tempo-tools`, 44.9 and 47.6 ms with the tools; the gateway's background listing, sharing `exec`'s single Tokio worker, accounted for about 3.4 ms of it (47.9 ms against 51.3 ms without it, before the listings shared one client) and building the Tempo clients for about 1 ms. Not checked with a paid request or with a real model choosing to fan out. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-agent-core -p nanocode-subagents -p nanocode-agent -p nanocode-durability --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --tests` of those crates and clippy on them and `nanocode-cli` are clean.
- Restored subagents resume together (2026-11-09): `Registry::resume_interrupted` sends every interrupted child its resume message at once (`join_all`) instead of one child after another, each of which waited for that child's session to be reopened from the store, its harness rebuilt and its turn admitted, a dozen or more store round trips, before the next began. `JsonlStore` offers `pipeline_handle()` (another sender to its one worker, so its order is the worker's), which lets `SharedStore` send reads as they arrive and form the next group while one is written, where every read was a barrier that ran alone between groups, and `acquire_many` writes a group's acquisitions as one batch, one write and one fsync per session file. Checked on 2026-11-09 with output/durability-ledger on JSONL: 3,000 children killed once each had sent its first request (`LATENCY_MS=2000 KILL_AT_STARTED=3000 swarm run jsonl <dir> 'SWARM flat 3000'`, 762 finished, 2,238 running) and reopened with `swarm resume`: every agent was restored and resumed in 15.4 s before, 10.6 to 11.2 s with the pipeline handle and 7.4 s with the children resumed together; the same on `SqlStore` over SQLite took 5.1 s. `swarm run jsonl <dir> 'SWARM flat 3000'` settled in 7.4 to 7.6 s instead of 9.0 to 9.6 s. What a resumed child still costs is its reads, 9 to 22 store round trips of which most repeat: `persistent_recipe` loads the whole stored session, transcript and running turn included, to learn its record and pending turns, and the running turn's continuation (its messages and the 22 KB request template) is then read twice more.
- `JsonlStore` keeps a root's subagents in the root's session file (2026-11-09). `StateStore::colocation()` (default none; `SharedStore` and `CachedStore` forward it) answers a `Colocation` whose `colocate(state_id, beside)` asks a store to keep one state where another is; a session driver calls it for a session it is about to create with `Origin::Subagent`, naming its lineage's root, before its first acquisition. `JsonlStore` takes the hint on a channel its worker drains before each job and, unless the session already has a file of its own, files every state of that session (`<child>`, `<child>:cells`) in the root's journal and appends `["<child>","<root>"]` to `sessions/.homes`, which it reads when it opens, so a child is found by its ID in a later process without its root; a root's journal also names its members when it opens, so a line lost in a crash costs nothing once the root is open. `list_states` and `list_summaries` still list each child (after its root, newest first), with a remembered summary kept while the child's revision is the one it was remembered at, since the file's length now changes with every sibling. A journal with members keeps the index sidecar the shared `sessions.jsonl` had (`<root>.jsonl.index`), written when the journal has doubled since the index was last written and when it closes, so reopening reads the index and at most the newer half of the journal. `Journal::share`, which writes a record another state of the file already holds as a stand-in, finds the holder in an index of record-key hashes (`Index::holders`) and walks only the states whose records it has not loaded (`Index::unshared`), where it tried every state of the file for every commit. Why: with a file per child, 3,000 children were 3,001 files of which the store keeps 32 open, so nearly every commit reopened a file and replayed it, every child's file held its own 22 KB of request template and 14 KB of tool catalog, and a group of commits was a write and an fsync per file. Checked on 2026-11-09 with output/durability-ledger, `swarm run jsonl <dir> 'SWARM flat 3000'`: settled in 9.0 to 9.6 s instead of 24.4 s, one 183 to 193 MB file (61 to 64 KB a child) and a 9.5 MB index instead of 3,001 files of 315 MB (105 KB a child), 483 to 497 MB written to disk instead of 669 MB; `swarm resume` reopened the 3,000 in 0.19 s (0.35 s without the sidecar); `listing jsonl <dir> <child>` read a child's record in a new process in 166 ms through `.homes` and listed 3,001 sessions (1 root, 3,000 subagents), the second listing from remembered summaries in 4.5 ms. A swarm of 600 killed at 300 finished resumed and settled from its one file, a store the build before this wrote (601 files) resumed under this one with its children left in their own files, and `cellresume` passes on JSONL. With every state in one file, `share` as it was made the same run take 37 s. A store that an earlier build opens finds no file for a colocated child; that build refuses the root's format 7 journal first.
- Agents can run subagents on any gateway (2026-11-09, asked for by Georgios after session 01a1c2a0, where Claude Opus on the Claude login, asked "which one of the boundless gateway models is the abliterated deep seek?", searched the repository for "boundless" because nothing told it gateways exist: "i would've expected that it thinks 'i should launch a bunch of subagents w/ various models from diff gateways and find out' … some gateways would require MPP to work"). `SpawnPolicy::gateways` (`SpawnGateway`: name, about, the models it serves, an optional note) is a host's catalog; while it is set, `spawn_agent` takes a required, nullable `gateway` (an enum of the names, each described by its about text, and the description says a subagent can run on any of them), infers a model's harness from the gateways that list it before the parent's (a Claude parent asking for `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash` gets the Codex harness, where it used to get its own and send the ID to Anthropic), refuses a gateway that is not offered or does not list the model on that harness, and `list_models` lists every gateway with its note and its models and their harnesses. A named gateway, or with none the only gateway that lists the model, travels as `SpawnOptions::gateway` to the `HarnessRequest`, and `RoutedFactory::spawn` builds such a child through its harness's recipe instead of the parent's native spawn, which cloned the parent's client, so the host's `client_for` picks the gateway and its payment: before this a same-harness subagent always ran on its parent's client (the earlier entry's "a subagent runs on its parent's gateway" held for that reason only), and a Claude-login agent could not run a Claude subagent on Tempo. With no gateway and several listing the model, a same-harness child still runs on its parent's client. The CLI publishes its gateways when the runtime is built and again once the background listings have answered (`Routes::offer`), and a requested gateway is the first hint `client_for` resolves with. A child restored after a restart is rebuilt from its checkpoint without its spawn options, so a same-harness child restores on its parent's client and one of another harness by the CLI's resolution. Checked on 2026-11-09 against `output/gateways/mock.py` with `spawn-gateways.sh`: a root on the mock endpoint ran a cell (`cell-gateways.js`) whose `list_models` listed chatgpt (4), claude (11), tempo (15), tempo-gateway (17), boundless (26) and 127.0.0.1 (2) once the listings had answered, and "listing models…" for the two endpoints in a cell run at once; `spawn_agent` with gateway 127.0.0.1 and mock-sub reached the mock, boundless with mock-sub was refused, tempo with gpt-6-luna reached Tempo's proxy and stopped at "to pay openai.mpp.tempo.xyz" (no wallet in the throwaway `HOME`), no gateway with deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash went to Boundless and stopped at "to pay api.inference.boundless.network", no gateway with mock-sub reached the mock, and no gateway with gpt-6-luna (chatgpt and tempo list it) ran on the parent's mock client. Before `RoutedFactory` took the recipe path, tempo with gpt-6-luna reached the mock. Not checked with a real model deciding to fan out, nor from a Claude-harness root, which the mock cannot serve. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-agent-core -p nanocode-subagents -p nanocode-agent --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --tests` of the first two and clippy on them, `nanocode-agent` and `nanocode-cli` are clean.
- The subagent journal `<root>:subagents` is format 7 (2026-11-09): a save writes the agents that changed and the messages that arrived as one delta record, `{"agents":[[id,record],…],"messages":[…]}`, and the payload names the deltas since the tree was last written (`deltas`, the unsealed keys of each level, 16 to a page, as sealed receipts and steers). The tree of format 6 (leaves of 16 agents under 64-entry pages, message leaves of 64) is now the base the deltas apply to: a save folds them into it, rewriting the leaves of every agent changed since the last fold and the message leaves, when the deltas written since then are as many bytes as the tree's leaves (`JournalCache::folds`), when it is the writer's first save, or when the message log was rewritten rather than appended to. So a restore reads at most twice the tree (`load_deltas` reads the delta pages level by level and `load_leaves` lets the newest record of an agent win), and folding costs at most what the deltas did. An agent whose record is byte for byte the one last written is left out of a delta (`CachedAgent::record`): every `Sessions::get_mut` gives an agent a new journal generation, and 6,093 of the 15,610 agent records 1,000 children wrote were copies of the one before. Why: an agent's record is about 700 bytes and changes 9 to 15 times in its life (started, each nested call's evidence, its accepted result, its settle, its completion's delivery), and each change rewrote its leaf of 16 (9.5 to 11 KB) and the 64-entry page above; each new message rewrote the unfilled leaf of up to 64. Versions 1 to 6 still load, a journal restored from them is written as 7 at its first save, and binaries before this refuse 7. Checked on 2026-11-09 with output/durability-ledger, `swarm run sqlite <db> 'SWARM flat 1000'`: the journal wrote 12.0 to 12.7 MB of records in 4,423 to 4,430 records and 2.0 MB of payloads, instead of 35.9 MB in 8,619 and 0.6 MB (7.1 MB of it deltas, 2.0 MB folded leaves, 1.5 MB the children's first checkpoints, 0.3 MB profiles). `swarm resume` after a run of 1,000 and of 3,000 children (whose runtime was shut down, which writes no final journal, so the 3,000's payload still named deltas) restored every agent as completed; a swarm of 600 killed at 300 finished (`KILL_AT_FINISHED`, `LATENCY_MS=1000`) resumed its 305 running children and settled, and so did one killed under the build before this, whose journal was format 6.
- A running operation's steers are sealed records, not part of its head (state format 9, 2026-11-09). Each steer an operation accepts is written once as a record of its own (`{message_id, input, input_key, accepted_after_model_call_index}`), and the operation keeps a `steered` log in the head: how many it sealed, the unsealed page keys of each level (16 to a page, as sealed receipts, `seal_page`), the slots that were withdrawn in the order they were, and, only on the wire, which model call each run of steers is bound to (`bound`, runs of `[through steer index, model call]`). In memory an operation's `steers` and `steer_receipts` are what they were, so the state machine, its checks and every reader are unchanged: `OperationState::wire` leaves them out of the head while the log holds them, and `DurableState::hydrate` and `hydrate_read` read the log back level by level (`JournalState::steer_pages`, `steer_page_children`, `absorb_steers`) wherever they read sealed receipts. A change to an operation whose log was not read is refused (`was changed before its sealed steers were loaded`), and a head that was not hydrated writes itself back unchanged. An operation that settles drops its log and carries its receipts in its receipt page, as before, so settled operations read as they did; an operation whose first steer an earlier build accepted keeps its steers inline until it settles, and binaries before this refuse format 9. Why: steers and their receipts lived in the head (about 510 bytes a steer: the message ID twice, the input key twice) and every commit rewrote the head, so the n steers of one operation cost n²/2 x 510 bytes. A root's subagents report through steers while its turn runs: 300 children steered 155 to 177 times into one root turn, whose head reached 85 KB and was rewritten by each. Checked on 2026-11-09 with output/durability-ledger. `swarm run sqlite <db> 'SWARM flat 300'`: the root session wrote 2.78 MB of heads instead of 50.2 MB (and 1.93 MB instead of 21.6 MB with `LATENCY_MS=1500`, where the children report into the root's notice turns); `SWARM flat 1000` wrote 116 MB to `SqlStore` instead of 686 MB, of which the root's heads were 11.2 MB instead of 581 MB, and 108 KB a subagent to JSONL instead of 549 KB. `statecheck 300 600` drives `JournalState` through 134,092 random valid transitions (74,602 steers, 14,736 withdrawn, binds, retirements, completions) and after each one reloads the head it wrote from the records it staged: steers, receipts and statuses equal the live state's every time, the reloaded state writes the same head, and the largest head was 2,940 bytes. A root killed with 85 sealed steers in its pending turn (`KILL_AT_FINISHED=300`, 600 children) reopened and settled, and so did one killed under the build before this, with 41 steers inline. What a commit of a steered turn still rewrites is the operation's inline continuation, 4.3 to 4.7 KB for a Claude root.
- A native session's Code Mode cell journal (agent-host's `DurableCellJournals`, state `<session>:cells`, format 2, 2026-11-09) stores each update as a content-addressed record that names the update before it, and the state's payload names each live cell's newest update (`{"version":2,"cells":{"<cell>":"b3:…"}}`); a header's tool catalog is a record of its own (`catalog`, chunked like any payload past 16 KiB), written once per session and process and named by every header after it. Until then an update was the record `<cell>/<seq>` with the catalog inline in every header. Two things were wrong with that. Bytes: the catalog was 14.8 KB of a 15.2 KB header with no host tools at all, so a cell that printed 2 KB wrote 16.7 KB of journal. And `SqlStore` and `RowStore` keep one record per key for the whole database (`ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING`), so every session's `1/0` was the first session's: after 1,000 subagents each ran one cell on `SqlStore`, the database held 1,004 such records for 892 `:cells` states, all the root's. A payload written by the earlier format (a bare map of cell to seqs) still loads, its cells are read by their numbered keys, and it is kept beside the new cells (`numbered`) until each is replaced or forgotten; binaries before this refuse format 2. Forgetting a cell still blanks its records, which only JSONL's compaction reclaims. Checked on 2026-11-09 with output/durability-ledger (its own workspace; a `StateStore` wrapper that counts every commit's payload, record and event bytes by state, over `JsonlStore` and over `SqlStore` and `RowStore` on a SQLite `Sql` host kept in the harness, with an in-process Messages mock). `turns memory '' 6 3 2000` (6 turns of 3 cells that each print 2,000 bytes): the `:cells` state wrote 68,615 bytes for 18 cells instead of 300,639, and a turn 72 KB instead of 110 KB. `cellresume` (output/native-resume's check that kills the process 1 s into a resumable MCP call and reopens the session) resumed the call on JSONL, `SqlStore` and `RowStore`, and with `EARLIER=1`, which first runs another session's cell to its end in the same store, on all three, where `SqlStore` before this answered "Tool execution interrupted by a host crash; outcome unknown" because the journal it read was the earlier session's; a journal written by the build before this (`CHILD_EXE`) resumed under this one on JSONL and `SqlStore`. A subagent that runs one cell still writes its own copy of the catalog on JSONL, whose files share nothing.
- Every gateway is offered at once, and `/model` groups the models by gateway (2026-11-09, asked for by Georgios: "allow easy merging of gateways … all the models grouped by gateway and easy way of switching across all the gateways incl models and filtering when i search for a model i wanna see all the gateways that offer it"). The CLI keeps a list of gateways (`gateways.rs`): `chatgpt` and `claude` (the logins, or the clients a host supplies), `tempo` (Tempo's MPP proxies), `tempo-gateway` (`https://gateway.tempo-dev.workers.dev`, whose `/v1/models` lists Workers AI, Vercel, OpenRouter and Boundless models) and `boundless` (`https://api.inference.boundless.network/mpp`), the last two paid from the Tempo wallet and listed in the background at start, then `openrouter`, `vercel`, `cloudflare` and `cloudflare-gateway` when their keys are in the environment, and `--gateway tempo --gateway-base-url`'s endpoint, named by its host (the URL of a built-in endpoint is that endpoint). `--gateway` (new values `tempo-gateway`, `boundless`) now names the gateway to prefer, not the only one. `-m` takes any gateway's model, a listed ID waiting for the listings when no catalog names it, so `nanocode -m claude-fable-5.2 -t high` runs on Boundless without `--gateway`; it resolves to the preferred gateway when that serves the model, else the first that does, and refuses a model the preferred gateway's harness offers but it does not list, as before. `/model` shows one group per gateway headed `<name> · <about>`, and its filter keeps every gateway's matching models under that gateway's header and all of a gateway's models when the header matches, so typing `fable` shows each gateway that serves a Fable model (`nanocode-tui`'s picker); the footer names a listing that is loading or failed. `/model <model> [gateway]` picks one by name. Picking a model on a gateway chooses that gateway for the model (`Routes::choose`), and a model on another gateway than the current agent's builds a new agent instead of switching in place. The status line says `via <gateway>` for any gateway but the logins, `/status` describes it, compaction is refused per gateway, and `/reload` keeps the main session's gateway. Each agent runs on one gateway: `CodexHarness::client_for` and `ClaudeHarness::client_for` (additive) let a host pick the client from the `HarnessRequest`, and the CLI records the gateway of each session it builds, so a session keeps its gateway, a subagent runs on its parent's when that serves the subagent's model, and otherwise on the one chosen for the model, the preferred one or the first that serves it. Resuming a session from another run takes the same order, since the store keeps no gateway. Tempo's gateways share one `Payments` (one spend panel, one paying proxy, one reqwest client), and an endpoint's wallet opens on its first payment with the endpoint's chain, currency, fee token and deposit (`Terms`), where `--gateway-base-url` opened it at start and refused to start without a wallet; `--tempo-currency`, `--tempo-fee-token` and `--tempo-close-session` apply to every MPP endpoint. `--no-tempo-tools` now leaves out the tools and paying proxy also with `--gateway tempo`. Checked on 2026-11-09 with `output/gateways` (a throwaway `HOME`, no proxy variables): `nanocode models` printed the seven gateways, Boundless's 26 models and the Tempo gateway's 17; against a mock endpoint (`mock.py`) `exec --gateway tempo --gateway-base-url http://127.0.0.1:18731 --tempo-network mainnet` answered from the mock with `-m mock-model` and with its first listed model by default, refused `-m gpt-6.1-sol` naming the endpoint's models, and a root that called `spawn_agent` for `mock-sub` had the subagent's request reach the mock (`subagent.sh`); `exec -m claude-fable-5.2 -t high` with no gateway flags reached Boundless and stopped at "sign in to a Tempo wallet with /login tempo to pay api.inference.boundless.network". In tmux (`picker.sh`, `picker2.sh`) `/model` grouped the models, `fable` showed the claude, tempo, tempo-gateway and boundless groups, `boundless` showed all of Boundless's, `/model claude-fable-5-2 tempo` and then `… claude` each started a new session (`via tempo`, then none), and `/model gpt-6.1-sol 127.0.0.1` was refused. Startup to the first request (debug builds, `bench.py`, interleaved, 20 runs each, `exec -m gpt-6.1-sol` failing at the missing ChatGPT login): 40.2 ms before and 46.4 ms after with `--no-tempo-tools`, 346.7 and 354.2 ms with the tools (network-bound); `nc.gateways.build` (building every gateway's client) took 2.3 to 3.9 ms, where `nc.host.build` had built one OpenAI client in about 2.2 ms, and sharing one reqwest client among the MPP layers left the difference within noise. In a shell behind nanocode's own paying proxy the Tempo gateway's listing fails, since the proxy answers its paid origin with a certificate reqwest does not trust. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-codex -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-tui --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and clippy on those crates and `nanocode-cli` are clean.
- `--gateway tempo --gateway-base-url` keeps its session open on exit, Ctrl-C included, so the next run reuses the channel instead of opening another; `--tempo-close-session` (`NANOCODE_TEMPO_CLOSE_SESSION`) closes it cooperatively on exit, returning the unspent deposit at once, as every exit did before. Each process still pays from the lowest of the 64 slots no other process holds (`session_slot`), so concurrent processes keep a channel each and later runs reuse them, as Tempo's proxies already did. Boundless suggests a 10 USDC deposit for Claude Fable 5.2, so every run locked 10 MACH, paid the open's gas and got the rest back on exit. `--tempo-keep-session`, now the default, is still accepted, hidden and conflicting with `--tempo-close-session`. Checked 2026-11-09 with `--tempo-currency mach --tempo-fee-token usdt0 --tempo-session reuse-check exec -m deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash`: the first run opened a 1 MACH channel and left it open, the second paid $0.000165 on that channel without opening one, and a third with `--tempo-close-session` paid on it and closed it cooperatively.
- `--tempo-fee-token TOKEN` (`NANOCODE_TEMPO_FEE_TOKEN`) pays the gas of `--gateway tempo --gateway-base-url`'s session opens and top-ups in the token the caller names (usdc.e or usdt0 on mainnet, pathusd or a token address; MACH and OUSD are refused, as neither can pay gas), through mpp's `with_session_fee_token`, instead of the `feeToken` the endpoint's challenge names. Boundless (`https://api.inference.boundless.network/mpp`) names USDC.e and sponsors no fees, so a wallet paying in MACH needed USDC.e for gas: on 2026-11-09 a wallet holding 0.000041 USDC.e, 9.67 USDT0 and 86.1 MACH failed every Claude Fable 5.2 request with "gas estimation failed: … out of gas: gas exhausted during precompiled contract execution: 68333", the gas that balance buys at Tempo's 600,000,000 gas price (41 × 10^12 / 6 × 10^8). USDT0 can pay fees (`FeeAMM.getPool` held 39.3 USDC.e and 42.8 pathUSD against it) but the DEX had no liquidity to swap it into USDC.e (`tempo wallet swap 1 USDT0 USDC.e --dry-run`: InsufficientLiquidity), and MACH cannot be swapped, so the gas had to be paid in USDT0 itself. With `--tempo-currency mach --tempo-fee-token usdt0`, `nanocode exec -m claude-fable-5.2 -t high "Reply with exactly: ok"` opened a 10 MACH session, answered "ok" for $0.174296 and closed the session cooperatively; the open's gas cost 0.000061 USDT0.
- Subagent budgets (2026-11-05, asked for by Georgios for tempoxyz Swarms: "each subagent can also have a budget … so that we can fund sub-populations of a given swarm or redirect our funding from a given sub-agent swarm"). `SpawnPolicy::budgets`, off by default, offers `spawn_agent` a required, nullable `budget_usd`: the most, in USD, the child and its descendants may spend together. The SDK keeps it on `AgentDescriptor::budget_usd`, in the subagent journal (a journal without it reads as none), and refuses a budget of 0, any budget while the policy is off, and one above the smallest budget in the spawning agent's lineage (`budget_usd $0.05 exceeds the $0.02 that agent 1 and its subagents may spend together`). The assignment tells the child its budget and that requests past it are refused, ending its turn. `SubagentControl::budgets(session_id)` answers the budgets along a session's lineage, the agent's own first, for a host's request context; `SubagentControl::set_budget(root, id, budget)` sets or clears one, persists it and announces the descriptor again (an unknown id is `unknown agent_id`); `AgentSummary`, `AgentDirectoryEntry` and `spawn_agent`'s report carry `budget_usd`. The SDK only records budgets: the host meters what each request costs and refuses requests once a lineage's budget is spent, because only it sees prices, refunds and paid tools (tempoxyz/gateway does, from the lineage gakonst/nanocode-ts sends with each request). Checked on 2026-11-05: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-subagents -p nanocode`, clippy on `nanocode-subagents` natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, `cargo check -p nanocode-cli`, and gakonst/nanocode-ts's WASM build against this commit. End to end through a local pack of nanocode-ts and tempoxyz/gateway under `vp dev` (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on Codex, paid from a throwaway wallet's key): a child spawned with `budget_usd` 0.01 ran a loop of paid tool calls until the gateway refused it at $0.0105 and its turn failed; after `set_budget` to 0.03 a message started it again and it completed at $0.0156; a child given 0.02 had its own `spawn_agent` with 0.05 refused with the message above, and a grandchild given 0.005 stopped at $0.0054 while its parent's subtree counted it.
- A Code Mode cell sends a call to a nested tool missing from its catalog to the host instead of rejecting it in the cell (`code-tools.mjs`), and the host asks its providers to find it before answering. `DynamicToolProvider::resolve(name)` (by default `false`) lets a provider register a tool it learned after the cell started, such as one read from an MCP server in the background, and return `true`; the registry then runs the call through that provider's `execute` like any other. `ToolRegistry::execute_nested` asks each provider in turn and stops at the first `true`, before the call's span and nested admission, so a slow resolve holds no admission slot and a name nobody resolves (any string a script wrote) opens no span; a name whose input names another attached `hand` goes to that hand without resolving. A name no provider resolves fails with the same `TOOL_NOT_AVAILABLE` message the cell raised before, with `code` and `tool` on the cell's error (`embedded::tool_not_available`), and so does a missing name in `LocalCells`. Object's own names and `toJSON`, which `String(tools)` and `JSON.stringify(tools)` call, still reject in the cell. A cell fixes its tool names when it starts, so before this a tool a provider registered after that failed its first call with nothing sent while the next cell's call worked (tempoxyz/pyramid's first-call gap for an app whose tools it reads in the background), and the host could not count calls to names it did not have. `exec`'s description and the cell's catalog are unchanged, so prompts stay cached; the description's line that a missing nested tool "rejects locally" now holds for every name the host can't resolve. A cell journaled before this that called a missing name diverges if it is replayed after it, since the call now reaches the host, and stops with the usual could-not-be-resumed note.
- Codex requests can ask for a Cyber access program, as Codex's `--cyber-access-program` (openai/codex `codex-rs/core/src/cyber_access_program.rs`): `OpenAiBuilder::cyber_access_program(Some(CyberAccessProgram::DaybreakRed))` (`ModelConfig::cyber_access_program`; `Standard`, `DaybreakBlue`, `DaybreakRed`) sends `"access_programs": {"cyber": "daybreak_red"}` on every Responses request, and `OpenAiBuilder::model_cyber_access_program(model, program)` (`ModelConfig::model_cyber_access_programs`, resolved per request by `cyber_access_program_for(model)`) asks for a program on one model's requests only, over the client's, because a host such as tempoxyz/pyramid runs several models on one client (subagents, a retry on Daybreak Blue); with neither (the default) no field is sent, leaving it to the server, which decides entitlement and which models accept it. `nanocode` and `nanocode exec` take `--cyber-access-program <standard|daybreak_blue|daybreak_red>` for the process, and refuse it with `--gateway`, since only OpenAI reads it. Checked on 2026-11-05 with `nanocode exec` against a mock Responses server (`NANOCODE_OPENAI_BASE_URL`): with `--cyber-access-program daybreak_red` the request carried `{"cyber":"daybreak_red"}`, without it no `access_programs`; with `--gateway openrouter` it is refused before any request. A unit test checks the per-model lookup. Not checked against the live API.
- nanocode-computer: a driver can start without named environment variables (`Install::without_env`, `Driver::without_env`), and an app is leased by its bundle where the backend has bundles. tempoxyz/pyramid-core's Hand marks every process it starts (`PYRAMID_HAND_PID`) and terminates the marked processes that escaped its process group when it pauses or stops (`shell::terminate_marked`); an external cua-driver inherited the mark, left the group and was killed on every pause, so core starts it `without_env("PYRAMID_HAND_PID")`, as it already starts Pyramid.app's provider (tempoxyz/pyramid main #2160 kept a list of helper executables instead). `Computer::execute` used to lease the app by the name it was asked for, so "Notes" and "com.apple.Notes" were two leases and two threads could drive one app; now the provider resolves the name first (`Desktop::lease_key`: on macOS, `Backend::keys_by_bundle`, the running app that `engine::find` names, else the installed one, without launching it) and leases its bundle identifier, falling back to the name when nothing resolves; other backends and providers keep the name, and the refusal names the app as asked. Checked on 2026-11-05 on dev-georgios: `cargo test -p nanocode-computer` 43 passed (new: an engine with bundles resolves a running app by name, path or bundle and an installed one without launching it, and an unresolved name or a backend without bundles gives none; a Computer leases "Notes", "com.apple.Notes" and "/Applications/Notes.app" as one app for another session while a desktop without bundles keeps names apart); an out-of-repo harness starts a script as the driver and sees `PYRAMID_HAND_PID` removed and other variables kept, through `Install` and `Driver`. The macOS backend's one-line `keys_by_bundle` isn't compiled here (no Apple SDK on Linux).
- `SessionStore::cancel_pending(id, to)` settles the operations a session left pending (a turn its process stopped mid-attempt, or a handed-off turn its claimer couldn't resume): it acquires the session as an agent, readmits and attempts each pending operation, and cancels it to a checkpoint chosen by `CancelTo`: `Latest` (the session's newest), `Checkpoint(payload)` (a base the host kept; if it doesn't load, the newest, with the reason in `CancelledPending::unresolved`), or `Fresh` (none). It answers `None` when there is no checkpoint to settle to, leaving the operations pending, and otherwise how many it cancelled and the checkpoint used. Ported from pyramid-core's runtime (`durable::settle_pending`), which now calls it. Checked on 2026-11-05 with an out-of-repo harness on dev-georgios that builds the same crashed session twice in a `MemoryStore` (a checkpoint, a completed operation with a second checkpoint, then an attempted operation left pending) and settles one copy with pyramid-core's own function and the other with this. Six cases (latest, a kept base, a base that doesn't load, fresh, no checkpoint at all, nothing pending) gave the same answers and the same turn statuses each time. pyramid-core's runtime-harness smoke, laterpass, subhandoff and crash (58 points, 0 failed) gave the same results with and without the change.
- `Recent::get` and `get_if` run a read in a task of its own (`tokio::spawn`), started when the shared read is first awaited, so a read whose callers all went away (a cancelled turn, a dropped request, a timeout) still runs to its end and lets go of what it holds; a read that panics, or is cancelled as the runtime stops, panics in its callers as before, and the API is unchanged. Before, the read was a `Shared` future kept in the map and polled only by its callers: once all of them dropped it, a pool acquire inside it kept its semaphore permit until the entry was evicted, which an entry keyed per turn never is. In tempoxyz/pyramid-core with Postgres stopped for 90 s under 8 turns, the hot pool stayed at 0 free permits for 90+ s after the database came back, with 12 waits woken and never polled again (fix-db's repro, 2026-11-05); pyramid-core spawned the read in a wrapper of its own until this. Checked on 2026-11-05 with an out-of-repo harness on dev-georgios: a read whose only caller is aborted after 10 ms runs to its end, releases its semaphore permit and is kept for the next caller (at master the read never finished and kept the permit); 8 concurrent callers share one read; a panicking read panics its caller; an error is returned as before. With the harness's other 10 cases, 12 of 12 in each of 5 runs.
- Claude Bash gives a call from a Code Mode cell (its call ID holds `/code-`) 128 KiB of stdout and of stderr (`NESTED_STREAM_BYTES`), where the model's own call keeps Claude Code's 30,000 bytes (`MAX_STREAM_BYTES`), because a nested call's output goes to the cell's script and the model sees only what the cell prints. Why: gakonst/opentempi's Temini runs every shell command inside cells, and of 1,457 nested Bash results in 25 of its recorded research turns on 2026-11-05, 65 were cut at 30,000 bytes, 57 of them under 120 KiB (the 99th percentile of all 1,457 was 105 KB), and scripts that parsed or split the cut output failed with `JSON.parse` errors or used the cut text as file paths. Checked on 2026-11-05 in opentempi's local Worker with gakonst/nanocode-ts built against this tree: a cell's `tools.Bash` of `rg -l` over 6,632 archive files returned 131,072 bytes of paths with `truncated: true`, and the session log kept 10,947 characters of each nested result.
- `ServedTools::redacting(redactions)` scrubs what a served shell call returns (its text, content, metadata and structured result) of each value the host's `Redactions` lists, replaced by its placeholder, without exporting anything to the command. `served::proxy_redactions(secrets)` lists the credentials of the proxy URLs in the process environment and the secrets file (`HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY` and their lowercase names) in every form a command can print: as written, percent-decoded, and as the Basic auth `curl -v` shows, for passwords of at least 8 bytes, longest first, each as `[secret <NAME>]`. `file_secrets` also passes `http_proxy`, `https_proxy`, `no_proxy` and `all_proxy`, which curl and Python read; other lowercase names stay out. Why: a tempoxyz/pyramid hosted Hand's egress login reaches its commands through the environment (tempoxyz/pyramid #1876, pyramid-core #237), and pyramid-core's kernel-hand kept its own served tools, read_file and proxy redactor (about 330 lines) for this. Checked on 2026-11-05 with an out-of-repo harness on dev-georgios that builds the tools as kernel-hand does and ports tempoxyz/pyramid main's `hands/src/machine.rs` tests (secrets reach commands and are redacted; lowercase proxies reach commands and every form of their credentials is redacted; the Hand's own percent-encoded egress login from its environment; short or missing passwords redact nothing; workdirs outside the served directories are refused; read_file reads, refuses `..` and reports links and missing files): 6 of 6.
- nanocode-sync has `Lines`, `Coalesce` and `Refreshed`, from tempoxyz/pyramid (its backend's `core/src/sync.rs`, `api/src/coalesce.rs` and `api/src/refresh.rs`), so Pyramid and pyramid-core take them from here. `Lines` is a `Sequencer` per key, held weakly: work on a key waits for that key's earlier work and never for another key's, and a key's line goes once no `Turn` holds or awaits it (`enter`, `try_enter`). `Coalesce<V, E, C>` shares a read among requests that arrive together: while one read for a key runs, later requests for it wait for the next read, which starts when that one ends and answers them all, so none sees older state than it would alone and a burst costs at most two reads. Each read runs in a task of its own, so a request that goes away strands nobody, with the context `C` of the first request it answers (Pyramid passes its span, route and GitHub caller, so the read's work shows in that request's trace and metrics); a read that panics or is cancelled answers its requests and those queued behind it with `E::from(Stopped)` and frees the key. `Refreshed<T>` answers with a key's newest value at once and refreshes it in the background when it is older than `fresh`, or when `now_unless`'s `outdated` says it no longer describes what it was read from; one refresh runs per key at a time, and a read that fails, panics or passes `max_read` keeps the old value until the next refresh. `Coalesce` and `Refreshed` are native only, like `Recent`. Checked on 2026-11-05 with an out-of-repo harness on dev-georgios (tempoxyz/pyramid main 83c59243b's coalesce and refresh tests ported to these types, plus a hung refresh, keys that don't wait for each other, a lead request that goes away, and `Lines`' arrival order, independence and weak holding): 10 of 10 in each of 5 runs.
- A model call whose response stream is cut part way is retried, and the retried attempt's text replaces what the cut attempt showed instead of appearing twice. Every reqwest error classifier (`nanocode_http::retryable`, which Codex's HTTPS and Chat Completions transports, the Claude client's transport and `reqwest_error` now share) counts an error while reading the response body as retryable: reqwest 0.13's `bytes_stream` reports a connection reset, a close in the middle of a chunk or a read timeout as `Kind::Decode` (it maps body errors through `error::decode`), never `is_body`, so a reset or FIN after the stream's first event failed the call on its first attempt. Claude retries a transient failure after it streamed text, which it refused before; it shows every attempt of a call under the first attempt's message ID (a retry's `message_start` keeps it) and records the completed response under that ID, so a replay after a handoff rewrites the same message, and its `model.attempt.retrying` payload numbers the call as its deltas do (`model_call_index` from 1, it was the 0-based index) and carries `error_class` (`retry_class`: `http_rate_limit`, `http_overloaded`, `http_server`, `transport`, `transport_timeout`, `stream_overloaded`, `incomplete_stream`, ...), as Codex's does. `AssistantText` follows `model.attempt.retrying`: the messages the cut attempt showed restart empty, their first update after the retry has `delta: None` (a host that appends deltas takes that text whole), and the next attempt's messages take their keys in order, so a host writes the retried text over the cut attempt's message; it forgets a call's attempts at its `model.call.completed` or `model.call.failed`. A host must read a pass's late events with the same `AssistantText` it streamed with, or the keys a retry took over are lost. A tool call whose input was cut is never dispatched: calls still run only from a completed response. Why: in tempoxyz/pyramid a turn whose model stream was cut (a dying sidecar at a deploy, a reset, a proxy's error page) failed with "Turn failed before it could reply", Claude never retried once text was shown, and where Codex did retry (a clean close before `response.completed`, a stall, an `error` event) the partial text stayed beside the full reply as a second message. Checked on 2026-11-05 on dev-georgios with tempoxyz/pyramid#2061's backend (bdf3c4357, this repository by path) against a raw HTTP/1.1 mock of the Responses and Messages APIs that cuts streams on purpose (out of repo: /home/ubuntu/perf/a50/harness, `cuts`), 17 cases for each of Codex and Claude: a TCP reset, a FIN mid-chunk, a clean end before completion, a proxy's error page, a 20 s stall past a 6 s read timeout, the provider's overloaded and rate-limit events mid-stream, 502 after a reset, 503, 529 and 429 with `retry-after` before the stream, a cut in a tool call's input, after its input completed and after its command ran, a cut after a whole message, and resets on every attempt. Before: the reset, FIN and reset-then-502 cases and every tool-call cut failed the turn on both; Claude failed 13 of the 17 cases, every one whose stream had begun, and Codex failed 8 and left the partial text as a second message in the other 5 it retried. After: every case but the last succeeded with one message holding the whole reply, each tool command ran once (Pyramid's Hand ledger: 1 command, none duplicated), and resets on every attempt failed the call after 5 attempts (Codex 15.9 s, Claude 9.6 s) with the partial text kept. The WASM targets were not built (no wasm32 target on the machine); clippy of nanocode-types-core, nanocode-http, nanocode-backend-codex-client and nanocode-backend-claude is clean.
- Computer use is one crate, nanocode-computer (crates/integrations/computer), replacing nanocode-cua and nanocode-cua-tools and taking in tempoxyz/pyramid-core's own macOS engine (kernel-computer's native.rs, from tempoxyz/pyramid's hands/src/desktop, after Vercel Labs' agent-desktop). Old paths keep working: `nanocode::cua` re-exports it, the Sky-compatible cua_repl surface (`ComputerConfig`, `ComputerTools`, `browser`, `browser_socket`, `embedded_driver`, the catalogs and `cua_driver.mjs`, now under `src/repl/`) is at its root, `driver` (the cua-driver client, with `Leases` and `app_key`) and `embedded` (macOS) keep their items, and `nanocode-cua-driver` is the same executable. New is the `computer` tool, `Computer`: one schema on every platform (`definition(Capabilities)`; the description names no platform but in its examples of app identifiers and keys and states only what the default provider can do, the pointer, screenshots, change diffs and whether a policy refuses apps, worded so that a model reading the diffs text and given whole states reads them right; with all four it is the same on every platform and byte for byte tempoxyz/pyramid's pinned definition, `tool/pinned.json`, which Linux Hands also present. Until 2026-11-05 it opened with the owner's Mac on macOS, with AT-SPI on Linux and with its refusal on Windows, which the Windows engine's `ready` still gives) over `Provider`s: `Native` (this platform's engine), `Driver` (cua-driver, built in or external), `Mcp` (an MCP server that serves the actions as tools, such as Pyramid.app's `--computer mcp`; `rename` maps argument names and `_scope` carries the turn for its diffs) or `Missing(reason)`; `Computer::or(name, provider)` adds one that a call's `_provider` picks. The tool enforces for every provider the action list, arguments of at most 32 KiB, one session per app until its turn ends (`end_turn`) or after 180 s idle (`Computer::refusal` words the refusal), a 45 s step and 10 s start deadline (`Limits`), state clipped at 192 KiB on a character boundary, a screenshot of at most 480 KiB of base64 or `screenshot_omitted`, and a step line that never holds typed text. Platform engines implement `Backend` (state: `read`; act: `press`, `set_value`, `select`, `scroll`, `perform`; keys: `type_text`, `press_key`; `screenshot`; apps: `apps`, `installed`, `launch`; an optional `pointer`), which is synchronous and runs in `spawn_blocking`, and the generic `Engine` holds the safety model so no backend can skip it: the host's `Policy` (`Fn(AppIdentity) -> Result<(), String>`, given the app's name and each of its identities in turn, `App::id`, the most specific, then `App::aliases`, so an app is refused when any of them is) before an app is read, acted on or launched, with `SENSITIVE`/`sensitive` as a starting list (terminals, password managers and authentication agents on macOS, Linux and Windows, and on Linux also shells, system settings, keyring and polkit prompts and privileged tools such as package managers and `pkexec`, by .desktop id and executable name); elements only by index from the app's latest state, checked alive first; the app's whole new state after every action, so an index is valid only within the state that showed it; secure fields (`Node::secure`) rendered as `••••`; typing and keys refused unless the focused element is still the one the latest state showed; the pointer (coordinates, drags, middle and multiple clicks) only when the backend has one and the host allows it (`Native::pointer(true)`); selections as UTF-16 ranges for AX (`Selection::utf16`) and character offsets for AT-SPI (`Selection::chars`). Backends: macOS (`macos`: AX, CoreGraphics and ImageIO, keys posted to the app's pid, no pointer; `macos/ax.rs` is the crate's only `unsafe` code, so the crate sets its own lints with `unsafe_code = "deny"` and that module allows it, where the workspace forbids it), Linux (`linux`: AT-SPI over D-Bus through zbus and atspi-proxies, read breadth-first with up to 64 calls in flight, 1 s per call and 5 s per tree, 3,000 nodes; actions through Action, EditableText, Text, Value, Selection and Component, a primary click on a text field focusing it rather than running its `activate`; with `DISPLAY` set, keys and the pointer through XTEST, only into the X window that has keyboard focus and belongs to the app, and screenshots through GetImage of the app's window; under Wayland without XWayland those refuse and the accessibility actions still work; passwords are never read; an app's id is its .desktop id, from `GIO_LAUNCHED_DESKTOP_FILE` (when `GIO_LAUNCHED_DESKTOP_FILE_PID` is absent or its own PID) or `BAMF_DESKTOP_FILE_HINT` in /proc/<pid>/environ, else `_GTK_APPLICATION_ID` or `WM_CLASS` of its X windows matched to an entry's `StartupWMClass` or file stem, else the entry whose Exec runs its executable, or the script its interpreter runs, with the process's arguments beginning with the entry's (the longest such entry), else its script's name (the first argument that isn't an option, for python, perl, ruby, node, java, the shells and other interpreters), else its executable's name, and the names after it are its aliases, so a Python app is no longer `python3.12` and a terminal behind a harmless desktop id is still refused; an app found for launch through an entry has the entry's id and the same aliases, and starts as GIO starts one, with `GIO_LAUNCHED_DESKTOP_FILE` and its own PID (exported by `/bin/sh` before it execs the program), so its children, which inherit them, do not claim the entry;
